research_brief:
Topic: Formative assessment and student learning outcomes
Focal Intervention: Formative assessment practices, including eliciting evidence of student understanding, providing feedback, and using results to adapt instruction
Population: Students in K–12 and postsecondary education, with attention to variation by age, subject area, and prior achievement
Context: Formal classroom instruction in schools and higher education, across subjects such as literacy, mathematics, and science
Target Skills / Outcomes: Student academic achievement, mastery of content, learning progress, retention, transfer, and related formative indicators such as self-regulation and engagement
Likely Comparators: Standard instruction without systematic formative assessment, summative-only assessment, or alternative feedback/assessment approaches
Key Research Priority: Determine under what conditions formative assessment improves student learning relative to usual instruction, which components matter most, and for which students and contexts the effects are strongest

tier1: What counts as formative assessment in K–12 and postsecondary classrooms, and how do researchers distinguish it from diagnostic, summative, or feedback-only practices?

Which student learning outcomes are most commonly measured in formative assessment research, and how are academic achievement, mastery, retention, and transfer operationalized by population and context?
For which populations, grade levels, and subject areas has formative assessment been studied most often, and where are the evidence gaps?
tier2: How do teachers typically support the same learning goals without formal formative assessment systems, and what baseline instructional practices are used to monitor student progress in K–12 classrooms?

What alternative approaches to improving student learning outcomes—such as summative assessment, routine feedback, retrieval practice, or differentiated instruction—serve as comparators to formative assessment in the literature?
In settings where formative assessment is not used, what is the usual counterfactual condition for student achievement outcomes in core subjects like math, reading, and science?
tier3: How is formative assessment implemented in practice in K–12 and postsecondary classrooms—for example, through questioning, quizzes, exit tickets, peer assessment, or teacher feedback cycles?

What instructional mechanisms are proposed to link formative assessment to improved learning outcomes, such as eliciting misconceptions, adapting pacing, and increasing student metacognition or self-regulation?

What implementation features—frequency, specificity of feedback, teacher training, technology support, or alignment to curriculum—shape how formative assessment is delivered across subjects and grade levels?
tier4: Compared with standard instruction or summative-only assessment, does formative assessment improve student achievement, retention, or transfer in K–12 and postsecondary settings?
Are the effects of formative assessment stronger in particular populations, such as lower-achieving students, English learners, or specific age groups, and do effects vary by subject area?

Which components of formative assessment—feedback, peer/self-assessment, teacher questioning, or data-driven instructional adjustment—show the most consistent evidence of impact on student learning outcomes?
What are the tradeoffs, limitations, and risks of formative assessment, including teacher workload, implementation fidelity, and the possibility of weak or null effects when used superficially?

executive_summary_history:
The evidence so far suggests that formative assessment can improve student learning relative to usual instruction, but the size and reliability of the benefit depend heavily on implementation quality, subject area, and whether teachers actually use the evidence to adjust instruction rather than merely collect it. Across the K–12 literature, the strongest pattern is that formative assessment works best when it is paired with differentiated instruction, descriptive feedback, and teacher or student action on the results, rather than used as a standalone testing routine (Xuan et al., 2022)(Yan et al., 2021)(Lee et al., 2020). The clearest overall synthesis is the K–12 umbrella review, which found formative assessment produced trivial to large positive effects on learning with no negative effects identified, but also judged the certainty of the evidence low to very low, limiting strong recommendations about which specific approach is best (Sortwell et al., 2024). In higher education, the evidence is more indirect and less causal, but reviews consistently argue that formative assessment and feedback are likely beneficial when they are embedded in instruction, aligned with outcomes, and supported by feedback literacy and teacher training (Morris et al., 2021)(Heil & Ifenthaler, 2023)(Fleckney et al., 2025).

The strongest quantitative findings currently available come from meta-analyses and one broad umbrella review. In K–12 reading, Xuan, Cheung, and Sun (2022) meta-analyzed 48 studies with 116,051 students and found a modest positive overall effect of formative assessment on reading achievement, with an average weighted effect of 0.19; they also reported that studies with 250 or fewer students had significantly larger effects, that embedding formative assessment in differentiated instruction increased reading achievement by 0.13 SD, and that teacher-plus-student assessment was more effective than teacher-only assessment (Xuan et al., 2022). The same review noted that 94% (34/36) of differentiated-instruction interventions were paired with teacher professional development (Xuan et al., 2022). The umbrella review by Sortwell et al. (2024) synthesized 13 meta-analyses on K–12 formative assessment and concluded effects ranged from trivial to large and were consistently nonnegative, but the underlying meta-analyses were mostly only moderate in methodological quality and the certainty of evidence was very low to moderate. In primary mathematics, Gezer et al. (2021) reported that formative-assessment data were positively related to summative achievement in classrooms of ages 5–7, with stronger relations in lower-performing classrooms; the paper is useful for identifying conditions of benefit, though the exact effect statistic is not fully reported in the brief. In the Turkish meta-analysis of formative assessment practices, Karaman (2021) synthesized 32 studies and 47 effect sizes and reported an overall mean effect size of 0.72 (SE = 0.07, p < .05), suggesting potentially large effects under some implementations, though details on moderators are limited in the brief. In one classroom experimental study in junior secondary basic science, Matilda and Helen (2019) used a pre-test/post-test experimental design with 80 students and found that formative classroom assessment improved academic achievement, but the exact effect size is not reported in the notes. In another experimental study in secondary science, Babinčáková et al. (2020) reported that formative assessment classroom techniques improved outcomes in chemistry, but the summary provided does not include the exact statistic. In higher education, Roschelle et al. (2016) reported that online mathematics homework increased student achievement, but the current notes do not provide the exact effect size; and Bulut et al. (2020) showed computerized formative assessment scheduling is a promising delivery mechanism, though it is primarily about personalization rather than a learning-effect estimate.

What is still weak, absent, or indirect is especially important for your research questions. The literature is much stronger on “does it work in some settings?” than on “which exact components matter most, for whom, and under what conditions?” Most of the retrieved evidence is correlational, descriptive, or review-based rather than tightly causal, and even the strongest syntheses report substantial heterogeneity and low certainty (Sortwell et al., 2024)(Xuan et al., 2022)(Yan et al., 2021). Evidence on retention and transfer is notably thin: the retrieved studies mostly measure immediate achievement or course grades rather than delayed retention or transfer to new tasks, and the notes explicitly state that explicit quantitative retention/transfer results were not reported. Higher-education evidence is also less mature than K–12 evidence; systematic reviews conclude that causal studies are scarce and that the field often relies on frameworks, implementation guidance, and small or context-specific studies rather than robust comparative trials (Morris et al., 2021)(Heil & Ifenthaler, 2023). Likewise, there is limited direct evidence separating the effects of individual formative-assessment components—questioning, exit tickets, peer assessment, self-assessment, feedback specificity, and data-driven adjustment—because many studies bundle them together.

Overall confidence is moderate that formative assessment can improve academic outcomes, especially in K–12 and especially when it triggers instructional adjustment, feedback, and differentiation, but low confidence in precise estimates of the most effective component mix or the populations that benefit most. The single most important caveat is that formative assessment is not simply “more frequent testing”: the positive effects appear to depend on whether the evidence gathered is actually used to change teaching and learning, and superficial implementation may yield weak or null effects (Yan et al., 2021)(Xuan et al., 2022)(Sortwell et al., 2024).

Overall, the evidence suggests that formative assessment improves student learning compared with usual instruction or summative-only assessment, but the size and reliability of the benefit depend heavily on how the practice is implemented and for whom it is used. The clearest pattern is that formative assessment works best when teachers do more than collect evidence: they use it to give timely, specific feedback, to diagnose misconceptions, and to adapt instruction or differentiate support (Xuan et al., 2022)(Yan et al., 2021)(Halim et al., 2024). Across K–12, meta-analytic evidence shows small-to-moderate positive effects on reading and broader learning outcomes, while higher-quality syntheses also indicate that effects are highly variable and often stronger when teacher and student roles are combined rather than teacher-only approaches (Xuan et al., 2022)(Sortwell et al., 2024). In postsecondary education, the evidence base is thinner and more descriptive, but the direction is similar: formative assessment is repeatedly portrayed as useful for feedback, engagement, and self-regulation, with stronger claims than direct causal proof (Morris et al., 2021)(Heil & Ifenthaler, 2023).

The strongest quantitative findings in the current set come from meta-analyses and one large-scale synthesis. In the K–12 reading meta-analysis, Xuan, Cheung, and Sun (2022) synthesized 48 studies with 116,051 students and found an average weighted effect of 0.19 on reading achievement; they also reported that studies with 250 or fewer students yielded larger effects, that differentiated instruction added 0.13 SD, that teacher-plus-student assessment was more effective than teacher-only assessment (d = -0.12, p < 0.001), and that small-sample studies had larger effects (d = 0.33, p < 0.001), while student-directed assessment alone was not significant (d = 0.03, p = 0.769). Sortwell et al. (2024) reviewed 13 meta-analyses on K–12 formative assessment and concluded that effects ranged from trivial to large and were always positive, with no negative effects identified; however, certainty was low to very low (AMSTAR-2: moderate n = 10, high n = 1, low n = 2; GRADE: very low n = 9, low n = 3, moderate n = 1). Karaman (2021) meta-analyzed 32 studies with 47 effect sizes and reported an overall mean effect size of .72 (SE = .07, p < .05). In the primary-school mathematics linkage study, Gezer et al. (2021) found a positive relationship between internet-based formative assessment and summative math performance in grades 5–7, with stronger associations in lower-performing classrooms; exact coefficients were not reported in the profile. In the quasi-experimental EFL motivation study, Ismail et al. (2022) reported that formative assessment improved motivation, reduced test anxiety, and improved self-regulation more than summative assessment, but the exact inferential statistics were not fully reported in the profile. In the undergraduate physics study, one quasi-experimental paper reported that integrating comprehensive formative assessment improved academic achievement in a basic physics course; the profile provides the design and population but not the exact effect size, so the statistic is not reported (A. H. et al., 2023). In another undergraduate study, formative vs. summative assessment on motivation and self-regulation showed the formative group outperforming the summative and control groups, but the profile only partially reports means and p values, so the most exact figures retained here are those explicitly stated: motivation, anxiety, and self-regulation improved more under formative assessment than under summative assessment, with post-test means reported in the source (Ismail et al., 2022).  

Where the evidence is weaker is in causal identification of components, subgroup effects, and longer-term outcomes like retention and transfer. The literature repeatedly argues that formative assessment is helpful, but many studies are observational, qualitative, or implementation-focused rather than experimental, especially in postsecondary settings (Morris et al., 2021)(Heil & Ifenthaler, 2023)(Halim et al., 2024). We have much better evidence for broad “formative assessment” packages than for any one component; the most consistently supported ingredients are descriptive feedback, teacher adaptation of instruction, and student involvement through self- or peer-assessment, but the comparative evidence separating these ingredients is limited (Xuan et al., 2022)(Fleckney et al., 2025)(Papanthymou & Darra, 2016). Evidence on English learners and students with disabilities is especially indirect: there are relevant studies on progress monitoring, reading interventions, and assessment validity for ELs and ELs with disabilities, but these mostly address diagnostic assessment or interventions adjacent to formative assessment rather than direct formative-assessment trials with subgroup analyses (Rivera & McKeithan, 2022)(Bowman-Perrott et al., 2025)(Mancilla-Martinez, 2020)(Lai et al., n.d.). Likewise, while several sources suggest lower-achieving students may benefit more, and some report stronger effects in low-performing classrooms, the subgroup evidence remains patchy and often underpowered (Xuan et al., 2022)(Gezer et al., 2021)(Borter, 2024). Explicit evidence on retention and transfer is still sparse; most sources discuss these outcomes conceptually rather than reporting direct tests (Morris et al., 2021)(Halim et al., 2024).

Overall confidence is moderate for the claim that formative assessment improves achievement relative to usual instruction, especially in K–12 reading and mathematics, but low for precise guidance on which exact component works best, for which students, and under what conditions across subjects and grade levels (Sortwell et al., 2024)(Xuan et al., 2022). The single most important caveat is that formative assessment only appears reliably beneficial when it is used as an active instructional cycle—eliciting evidence, interpreting it, and changing teaching—rather than as frequent testing or feedback-only practice; superficial implementation is a major reason effects may be small, inconsistent, or null (Yan et al., 2021)(Halim et al., 2024)(Morris et al., 2021).

Overall, the evidence suggests that formative assessment improves student learning relative to usual instruction, but the size and reliability of the benefit depend heavily on how it is implemented. Across K–12 and postsecondary settings, the central pattern is that formative assessment works best when teachers elicit evidence of understanding, give timely and specific feedback, and actually use the results to adapt instruction rather than merely collecting scores (Sortwell et al., 2024)(Xuan et al., 2022)(Karaman, 2021)(Yan et al., 2021)(Morris et al., 2021). The strongest effects tend to appear when formative assessment is paired with differentiated instruction, teacher/student co-construction of feedback, and structured professional development; superficial use, delayed or generic feedback, and weak instructional adjustment are much less convincing (Xuan et al., 2022)(Karaman, 2021)(Pinger et al., 2018)(Anders et al., 2022). In short: formative assessment is not a stand-alone guarantee of better outcomes, but a high-potential instructional routine whose value depends on feedback quality, teacher responsiveness, and implementation fidelity.

The strongest quantitative findings in the current set come from meta-analyses and controlled trials. In K–12 reading, Xuan et al. (2022) synthesized 48 studies with 116,051 students and found a modest positive average effect on reading achievement, with an overall weighted effect size of 0.19; they also reported larger effects in small-sample studies, stronger gains when formative assessment was embedded in differentiated instruction, and better outcomes when teacher and student assessment were integrated rather than teacher-only (Xuan et al., 2022). In a separate meta-analysis, Karaman (2021) synthesized 32 studies with 47 effect sizes and reported an overall mean effect size of .72 (SE = .07, p < .05), with subgroup effects showing student-initiated formative feedback at d = 1.16, mixed feedback at d = .83, adult-initiated feedback at d = .69, and computer-initiated feedback at d = .42 (Karaman, 2021). Sortwell et al. (2024) reviewed 13 meta-analyses and concluded that formative assessment produced trivial to large positive effects on K–12 student learning with no negative effects identified, though the certainty of evidence was low to very low (Sortwell et al., 2024). In an RCT in secondary physics, Lichtenberger et al. (year not reported in snippet) studied 29 teachers and 604 students and found that the formative-assessment group outperformed both frequent-testing and traditional-teaching groups on conceptual understanding immediately after the intervention and again 3 months later, but the exact effect size and p-value were not reported in the available notes. In a randomized intervention in junior secondary basic science, Matilda and Helen (2019) found significant differences favoring the experimental group, but the exact statistic was not fully reported in the notes. In primary mathematics, Gezer et al. (2021) reported a positive association between formative and summative assessment data and stronger benefits in lower-performing classrooms, with the relationship especially stronger in first grade than kindergarten; however, the precise coefficient was not reported in the notes. In higher education, Karaman (2021) found formative assessment effects across primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, while Morris et al. (2021) and other higher-education reviews concluded that the evidence base is still relatively thin and methodologically uneven, despite the broad consensus that feedback matters (Morris et al., 2021)(Karaman, 2021).

Where the evidence is weakest is in identifying which specific formative-assessment components matter most across ages, subjects, and learner subgroups. The literature repeatedly points to plausible moderators—prior achievement, grade level, subject area, culture, sample size, differentiated instruction, and whether assessment is teacher-led, student-led, or mixed—but these are not consistently estimated across studies or outcomes (Xuan et al., 2022)(Karaman, 2021)(Yan et al., 2021). Evidence for English learners and students with disabilities is especially indirect: several studies address progress monitoring, diagnostic assessment, or intervention supports for ELs and ELs with disabilities, but they do not isolate formative assessment as the causal driver or provide clean subgroup estimates for formative assessment itself (Rivera & McKeithan, 2022)(Bowman-Perrott et al., 2025)(Mancilla-Martinez, 2020)(Lai et al., year not reported in snippet). Likewise, postsecondary evidence remains promising but sparse: systematic reviews in higher education emphasize that formative assessment and feedback are widely recommended yet still under-supported by strong causal research, and many studies are descriptive, exploratory, or focused on implementation rather than learning outcomes (Morris et al., 2021)(Heil & Ifenthaler, 2023). The biggest unanswered tiered questions are thus not whether formative assessment can help—it often can—but under what precise conditions, with which components, and for which students the gains are largest and most durable.

Overall confidence is moderate for the broad conclusion that formative assessment improves learning, but low for fine-grained claims about mechanisms and subgroup effects. The single most important caveat is that the best effects are concentrated in studies where formative assessment is tightly linked to instructional adaptation and high-quality feedback; when it is reduced to frequent testing, score reporting, or weakly implemented routines, the benefits diminish or become null (Xuan et al., 2022)(Sortwell et al., 2024)(Morris et al., 2021).
critique_history:
## Critique — Iteration 1

**Evidence Gaps:**
- Tier 4 is the weakest overall: there is still no robust causal evidence directly comparing formative assessment against standard instruction/summative-only assessment on achievement, retention, or transfer across both K–12 and postsecondary settings. Most retrieved evidence is review-based, correlational, or implementation-focused rather than RCT/QED-based.
- Direct evidence on retention and transfer is essentially absent. The notes explicitly say no quantitative retention/transfer effects were reported; most studies only measure immediate achievement or course grades.
- Postsecondary evidence is thin relative to K–12, and largely indirect. Existing higher-education reviews emphasize implementation and feedback quality rather than strong causal outcome estimates.
- Evidence on which component matters most is underpowered because many studies bundle questioning, feedback, self/peer assessment, and instructional adjustment together; component-specific causal identification is mostly missing.
- There is very limited subgroup evidence by age, prior achievement, English learner status, disability/special education, or culturally/linguistically diverse populations. The strongest subgroup signal so far is low-achieving students, but this is mainly from reading/math and not consistently across subjects.
- Science, mathematics, and reading are represented, but there is still little on writing, history/social studies, arts, and cross-curricular classroom assessment practices.
- There are no clear studies on K–12 and postsecondary comparisons using the same intervention logic and outcome metrics; the evidence base is fragmented by sector.
- Few studies clearly report implementation fidelity in a way that can explain effect heterogeneity; where fidelity is discussed, it is usually descriptive rather than linked to outcome effects.
- Meta-analytic coverage exists, but the certainty is low to very low in the umbrella review, so the current evidence base does not yet support strong causal claims about optimal practice.
- The comparison condition is often vague ('usual instruction', 'business as usual', or mixed instructional routines), making the counterfactual poorly specified in many studies.

**Thesis Gaps:**
- The executive summary is too confident when it says the strongest pattern is that formative assessment works best when paired with differentiated instruction, descriptive feedback, and teacher or student action on results. That pattern is plausible, but the current sources mostly show association/moderation, not clean causal isolation of each component.
- The summary states formative assessment can improve learning relative to usual instruction, but it should more explicitly qualify that the evidence is strongest in K–12 reading and some mathematics/science contexts, and much weaker in postsecondary education.
- The summary implies a stable cross-context conclusion, but the umbrella review explicitly reports trivial-to-large effects with very low to moderate certainty. That uncertainty should be front and center, not secondary.
- The summary slightly overstates the uniqueness of differentiated instruction and teacher-student collaboration as effect boosters; the evidence is suggestive, but much of it is from one meta-analysis and may reflect bundled interventions and publication/culture differences.
- The summary understates how much of the literature is actually about implementation, teacher perceptions, and assessment literacy rather than learning outcomes. That matters because the review question is outcome-focused.
- The summary should more explicitly note that formative assessment is often conflated with general feedback, quizzes, progress monitoring, and hybrid summative-formative practices, which weakens construct clarity and comparability across studies.
- The summary underemphasizes that higher-education evidence is not just 'indirect' but often explicitly judged insufficient for robust causal inference in the retrieved reviews.
- The summary should distinguish stronger findings from weak ones: the reading meta-analysis and K–12 umbrella review are the clearest quantitative anchors, whereas many other included papers are descriptive or conceptual and should not be weighed similarly.
- The summary does not sufficiently flag that 'no negative effects identified' from the umbrella review is not equivalent to strong evidence of safety; it may simply reflect limited reporting or study design.
- The summary omits that many studies use immediate achievement tests, so claims about longer-term learning progress, retention, and transfer remain unsubstantiated.

**Missing Angles:**
- Need explicit comparator mapping: formative assessment versus retrieval practice, low-stakes quizzing, mastery learning, adaptive tutoring, peer instruction, and descriptive feedback alone. Right now comparators are mostly collapsed into 'usual instruction' or summative-only assessment.
- Need equity dimensions: effects for English learners, students with disabilities, gifted students, rural/urban schools, and socioeconomically disadvantaged students are not yet systematically examined.
- Need prior-achievement stratification beyond 'low achievers.' There is almost no evidence on whether medium/high prior achievers benefit differently, or whether ceiling effects blunt gains.
- Need age/developmental moderators: primary, middle, secondary, and postsecondary learners may respond differently, but age effects are not yet cleanly synthesized.
- Need subject-specific mechanisms: what works in reading may not translate to math or science because the formative tasks, misconception structures, and feedback timing differ.
- Need implementation intensity/dose: how often formative assessment occurs, how long it is sustained, and whether gains require recurring cycles versus one-off interventions.
- Need fidelity and feasibility outcomes as first-class moderators: teacher workload, time cost, feedback quality, and curriculum fit should be linked to learning effects rather than treated as side notes.
- Need outcomes beyond test scores: self-regulation, engagement, motivation, and metacognitive monitoring are discussed, but they are not systematically tied to achievement effects in the evidence base.
- Need distinction between teacher-initiated and student-initiated formative assessment, including co-regulation and learner agency, because existing evidence suggests these may differ materially.
- Need clearer treatment of technology-mediated formative assessment versus non-digital classroom practice; the literature mixes them, but their effects and constraints may differ substantially.
- Need underexplored contexts such as higher education STEM, teacher education, special education, and multilingual classrooms, where formative assessment is often discussed but not rigorously compared.
- Need direct assessment of transfer and delayed retention, not just immediate learning gains.

**Next Iteration Brief:**
The next iteration should investigate whether there are any RCTs, strong quasi-experiments, or meta-analyses that isolate specific formative-assessment components (questioning, feedback specificity, peer/self-assessment, instructional adjustment) and report delayed retention or transfer outcomes, especially in postsecondary STEM and in subgroup analyses by prior achievement, English learner status, and disability status. It should also distinguish true formative-assessment interventions from generic progress monitoring, low-stakes quizzing, and feedback-only practices, and map the comparator condition more precisely (business-as-usual, summative-only, retrieval practice, adaptive tutoring, or differentiated instruction).

## Critique — Iteration 2

**Evidence Gaps:**
- Tier 4 is still under-evidenced relative to the research brief: there is some K–12 meta-analytic evidence, but very little direct causal evidence for postsecondary classrooms, and almost no direct evidence on retention or transfer as outcomes. Most postsecondary sources are conceptual, descriptive, or implementation-oriented rather than RCTs/QEDs.
- The strongest quantitative evidence is concentrated in K–12 reading and some mathematics; science, literacy beyond reading comprehension, and postsecondary content courses remain thin. Subject-specific coverage is uneven, so the executive summary cannot generalize confidently across math/reading/science.
- Subgroup evidence is especially weak for English learners, students with disabilities, and intersections of EL+disability. The available sources are mostly adjacent literature on progress monitoring, diagnostic assessment, or reading interventions rather than formative-assessment trials with subgroup moderation.
- Prior-achievement moderation is suggested in several sources, but it is not well isolated. Findings about low-achieving or high-achieving students are often from indirect or non-comparable studies, and there is little clean evidence on baseline achievement as a pre-specified moderator.
- Evidence on which component matters most is incomplete. Feedback, differentiation, peer/self-assessment, and teacher adjustment are all discussed, but there are few studies that isolate components head-to-head with strong causal designs.
- Implementation-fidelity evidence is patchy. There are claims about teacher workload, training, and technology, but not enough rigorous studies quantifying how fidelity moderates impact.
- Several cited studies are reviews of reviews, conceptual papers, or practice descriptions rather than primary empirical studies, so they do not strengthen causal inference for the core effect question.
- The source base is thin on postsecondary RCTs/QEDs specifically comparing formative assessment with summative-only or business-as-usual instruction; most higher-ed items are reviews or qualitative studies.
- There is little direct evidence on grade-level heterogeneity outside broad K–12 bands. K-12 is overrepresented, but elementary, middle, secondary, and postsecondary are not systematically separated in the evidence synthesis.
- The tiered questions around comparator conditions are only partially answered: usual instruction is described, but the literature does not consistently define the counterfactual rigorously across studies, making synthesis of comparison conditions weak.

**Thesis Gaps:**
- The executive summary overstates confidence when it says the evidence suggests formative assessment improves student learning compared with usual instruction across K–12 and postsecondary. The K–12 evidence is stronger than the postsecondary evidence, and certainty is low for many conclusions.
- It implies a relatively settled answer on "when and for whom" formative assessment works, but the profiles show only suggestive moderation evidence, mostly from reading and a few mathematics or EFL studies. This should be framed as provisional rather than established.
- The summary treats the component-level claim as almost resolved by saying the clearest pattern is that teachers must use evidence to give feedback and adapt instruction. That is plausible, but the profiles do not yet support a strong ranking of components or causal necessity.
- The summary under-acknowledges the uncertainty in the umbrella review: low-to-very-low certainty of evidence is not a minor caveat; it materially limits the strength of any practice recommendation.
- The summary slightly overgeneralizes from K–12 reading and mathematics to all formative assessment. Science and postsecondary evidence are notably thinner and more heterogeneous.
- It implies that peer/self-assessment and student-teacher collaboration are broadly superior, but the evidence for these comparisons is not uniform and often comes from specific contexts or reviews with mixed quality.
- The claim that formative assessment "improves student learning" is directionally supported, but the magnitude is sometimes modest (e.g., reading meta-analysis ES ≈ 0.19) and the summary should not read as if effects are consistently large.
- The summary understates how much of the literature is about implementation, teacher beliefs, or assessment literacy rather than direct learning outcomes. That distinction matters for what can be concluded.
- The summary does not sufficiently distinguish between evidence for formative assessment as a package and evidence for specific mechanisms like feedback timing, questioning, or diagnostic use. Those are not equivalent claims.
- The summary says there is "much better evidence" for broad packages than for components, but it does not explicitly say that some component claims are presently speculative; this weakens the critique of mechanistic certainty.

**Missing Angles:**
- Direct tests of retention and transfer as outcomes, especially in postsecondary and secondary settings, are missing.
- Comparisons against retrieval practice, low-stakes quizzing, and frequent testing as distinct comparators are underdeveloped. These are important because they may overlap with or substitute for formative assessment.
- Equity dimensions beyond EL/disability are missing: socioeconomic status, race/ethnicity, multilingual learners beyond EL status, rural/urban setting, and special education placement are not systematically synthesized.
- Intersectional subgroup analyses are absent: EL + disability, prior achievement + EL, and prior achievement + disability.
- There is little on age-graded differences in mechanism: what works in elementary classrooms may not translate to secondary or postsecondary because the feedback/self-regulation demands differ.
- Subject-specific implementation contexts are underexplored, especially science, writing, arts, vocational/technical education, and STEM labs versus lecture courses.
- Technology-mediated formative assessment is present, but the literature has not yet separated tool effects from pedagogical effects. The role of AI, online platforms, and automated feedback needs clearer distinction from the formative-assessment construct itself.
- Teacher professional development as an active component is missing as a standalone comparator or moderator in the summary, despite appearing important in the profiles.
- Classroom ecology factors are underaddressed: class size, curriculum pacing pressure, high-stakes accountability, and institutional assessment policy may condition effectiveness.
- Student agency and feedback literacy are mentioned, but not as a distinct mechanism with measurable outcomes or moderation by student maturity/self-regulation baseline.
- There is little examination of negative or null effects under specific conditions beyond superficial implementation; the risk of diminishing returns, cognitive overload, or feedback saturation is not mapped.
- Implementation in higher education is especially missing in formal classroom instruction settings; much of the evidence there concerns online, blended, or practitioner guidance rather than conventional lecture/tutorial courses.
- Comparator heterogeneity is not fully captured: the literature mixes summative-only, business-as-usual, and alternative feedback/assessment designs without a clean taxonomy in the synthesis.

**Next Iteration Brief:**
The next iteration should investigate which subgroup and moderator findings are supported by direct causal or meta-analytic evidence, not just adjacent assessment literature. Prioritize: (1) K–12 versus postsecondary effects separately; (2) explicit moderator analyses for prior achievement, grade level, subject area, English learner status, disability status, and their intersections; (3) direct comparisons of formative assessment packages against alternative comparators such as retrieval practice, low-stakes quizzing, summative-only assessment, and structured feedback-only conditions; (4) outcomes beyond immediate achievement, especially retention, transfer, engagement, and self-regulation; and (5) implementation moderators such as teacher professional development, fidelity, curriculum pressure, and technology-mediated delivery. The goal is to replace broad claims with a tighter evidence map that distinguishes robust effects, suggestive patterns, and untested assumptions.

A systematic review/umbrella review on K–12 formative assessment found: “Formative assessment in K-12 education has been a notable teaching and learning focus area in schools over the last 20 years, as evidenced by numerous recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses investigating and summarizing the evidence for formative assessments’ effectiveness and sustainability. This umbrella review systematically reviews meta-analyses investigating the effects of formative assessment on learning, summarizes the current findings, and assesses the quality and risk of bias in the published meta-analyses.” It reported that “Thirteen meta-analyses, each of which examined the effects of formative assessment on learning in K-12 students, were included in this umbrella review.” It also reported: “Formative assessment was found to produce trivial to large positive effects on student learning, with no negative effects identified. The magnitude of effects varied according to the type of formative assessment.” It further stated: “The 13 included meta-analysis studies showed moderate (n = 10), high (n = 1), and low (n = 2) methodological quality (AMSTAR-2), although the robustness of the evidence (i.e., GRADE analysis) was very low (n = 9), low (n = 3), and moderate (n = 1).” The review concluded: “These findings offer valuable insights for designing and implementing different types of formative assessment aimed at optimizing student learning and ensuring the sustainability of assessment practices. However, the low-to-very-low certainty of the available evidence precludes robust recommendations regarding optimal formative assessment strategies for learning in K-12 students.” [1]

A meta-analysis study by Karaman reported: “The number of studies included in the meta-analysis and the characteristics of these studies are summarized in As summarized in Table 3, the meta-analysis shows the overall effect size as .79 with standard error of .03 in the fixed model. Heterogeneity test was used to investigate the heterogeneity in effect size. The Q value was 188.91 with 46 degrees of freedom, and p value under .05 showed heterogeneity among the studies. In other words, true effect size may have varied across studies. Besides, 2 statistic was estimated as 75.65% indicating that the percent of variance due to between-subject factors was large. The results revealed that the impact of formative assessment on student learning varied from one study to another. By using random effects model, overall meta-analysis showed that there was a significant effect of formative assessment on student learning (g= .72, SE= .07, 95% CI= .59; 85, p<.05).” It also stated that “In Table 5, mixed effects analysis was also used to estimate the effect size of groups in terms of their education levels (primary, secondary, and tertiary). The results showed that the effect size at primary level had a large effect (d=.89, p<.05), while it had a medium effect on student academic performance at secondary level (d=.71, p<.05) and tertiary level (d=.64, p<.05). In K-12 and college education, assessments serve different purposes and can be categorized primarily into formative, diagnostic, summative, and feedback-only practices. Here's a breakdown of what counts as each and how they relate to student learning outcomes, mastery, retention, transfer, evidence, and gaps:

1. Formative Assessment:
- Purpose: To monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used by instructors to improve teaching and by students to improve learning.
- Examples: Quizzes, in-class activities, homework assignments, peer reviews, drafts of projects.
- Learning Outcomes Impact: Helps identify students' understanding in real-time, guiding adjustments that foster mastery and retention.
- Transfer: While formative assessments primarily focus on the immediate learning context, they can support transfer by encouraging reflection and application.
- Evidence and Gaps: Provides evidence of current understanding and identifies learning gaps early.

2. Diagnostic Assessment:
- Purpose: To diagnose students' prior knowledge, skills, and misconceptions before instruction begins.
- Examples: Pre-tests, skill inventories, surveys.
- Learning Outcomes Impact: Helps tailor instruction to meet students' needs.
- Mastery & Retention: Establishes baseline for measuring growth and aids in designing interventions for retention.
- Transfer: Facilitates targeted teaching that can enhance transfer by addressing specific needs.
- Evidence and Gaps: Reveals knowledge gaps and misconceptions that need to be addressed.

3. Summative Assessment:
- Purpose: To evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period.
- Examples: Final exams, standardized tests, end-of-unit projects.
- Learning Outcomes Impact: Measures mastery and achievement of learning objectives.
- Mastery & Retention: Often assesses cumulative knowledge, though may not always reflect long-term retention.
- Transfer: Can assess application of knowledge in new contexts if well-designed.
- Evidence and Gaps: Provides evidence of achievement but less useful for identifying ongoing gaps.

4. Feedback-Only Practices:
- Purpose: To provide students with information about their performance without formal grading.
- Examples: Instructor comments, peer feedback, self-assessment.
- Learning Outcomes Impact: Supports improvement and deepens understanding.
- Mastery & Retention: Encourages reflection that can aid mastery and retention.
- Transfer: Helps students think critically and adapt knowledge.
- Evidence and Gaps: Highlights areas for improvement but may lack formal measurement.

Summary:
- Formative and diagnostic assessments are integral to identifying and addressing gaps during the learning process.
- Summative assessments evaluate overall mastery after instruction.
- Feedback-only practices support continuous improvement and self-regulation.
- Effective use of all these assessment types can enhance student learning outcomes, mastery, retention, and transfer.

Formative assessment is a critical component in educational settings, encompassing various methods such as diagnostic assessments, feedback mechanisms, and both formative and summative evaluations. These assessments aim to enhance student learning by providing insights into their progress and areas needing improvement.

**Formative Assessment**

Formative assessment refers to a range of evaluative processes conducted during the learning journey to monitor student progress and inform instructional adjustments. Unlike summative assessments, which occur at the end of an instructional period, formative assessments are integrated into the teaching process, offering real-time feedback to both students and educators. This approach fosters a continuous learning environment, enabling timely interventions and support.

**Diagnostic Assessment**

Diagnostic assessments are conducted before or at the beginning of an instructional period to identify students' existing knowledge, skills, and potential learning challenges. This proactive evaluation allows educators to tailor their teaching strategies to meet the diverse needs of their students effectively.

**Summative Assessment**

Summative assessments are evaluative measures administered at the conclusion of an instructional period to determine the extent to which learning objectives have been achieved. These assessments often contribute to final grades and are used to evaluate the overall effectiveness of instructional programs.

**Feedback Mechanisms**

Effective feedback is integral to formative assessment, providing students with specific information about their performance. This feedback guides learners on how to improve and advance their understanding of the subject matter. Incorporating feedback into the learning process enhances student engagement and promotes self-regulated learning.

**Meta-Analysis and Research Findings**

Meta-analyses have been conducted to evaluate the impact of formative assessment on student achievement. For instance, a study by Kingston and Nash (2011) analyzed 13 studies and found a weighted mean effect size of 0.28, suggesting a moderate impact of formative assessment on student learning outcomes. However, the authors emphasized the need for clearer definitions and more rigorous research designs to better understand the efficacy of formative assessment practices. ([researchgate.net](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/263654863_Assessment_and_Learning_State_of_the_Field_Review?utm_source=openai))

**Application in Educational Contexts**

Formative assessment practices are applied across various educational levels, including undergraduate, college, and K-12 settings. In higher education, formative assessments such as quizzes, peer reviews, and interactive discussions are utilized to monitor student progress and inform instructional strategies. In K-12 education, formative assessments like classroom polls, concept maps, and reflection journals are employed to support student learning and development.

In summary, formative assessment, encompassing diagnostic and summative assessments along with feedback mechanisms, plays a pivotal role in enhancing student learning outcomes. Ongoing research and application of these assessment strategies are essential for fostering effective educational environments.

Teachers often monitor student progress without formal formative assessment systems using several informal methods and strategies. These include:

1. **Observations:** Teachers frequently observe students while they work or participate in class discussions. They note students' understanding, engagement, and problem-solving approaches.
2. **Classroom Discussions:** Engaging students in discussions allows teachers to assess comprehension and clarify misunderstandings in real time.
3. **Questioning:** Asking targeted questions during lessons helps teachers gauge individual and group understanding.
4. **Student Self-Assessments:** Informal self-reflections or reports by students can provide insight into their learning and areas where they feel confident or need help.
5. **Peer Assessments:** Students may provide feedback to each other, offering an additional perspective on progress.
6. **Review of Student Work:** Informal reviews of homework, classwork, and projects without formal grading criteria can still inform teachers about student progress.
7. **Exit Tickets:** Quick, informal prompts at the end of a lesson to check for understanding.
8. **Anecdotal Records:** Teachers keep notes on individual student behaviors, skills, and progress over time.

Regarding the usual **comparator conditions in research on math, reading, and science** in K-12 education:

- **Control or Business-As-Usual Groups:** These groups continue with standard instructional practices without the intervention.
- **Alternative Instructional Methods:** Comparisons might be made between different teaching strategies (e.g., traditional versus inquiry-based learning).
- **Different Formative Assessment Approaches:** Comparing specific formative assessment tools or methods against each other or against no formal assessment.
- **Grade-Level or Demographic Comparisons:** Comparisons might be structured around different grade levels or student demographics to examine differential effects.
- **Pretest-Posttest Designs:** Where the same students serve as their own controls, comparing progress before and after an instructional intervention.

Formative assessment is a critical component in K-12 education, particularly in subjects like mathematics, reading, and science. It involves ongoing evaluations that inform instructional decisions and support student learning. Research has explored various aspects of formative assessment, including its comparison with summative assessments, the role of feedback, and the impact of retrieval practice.

**Key Research Findings:**

- **Formative vs. Summative Assessment:** Formative assessments are conducted during the learning process to monitor student progress and provide immediate feedback, whereas summative assessments evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period. Studies have shown that formative assessments can lead to improved student outcomes by identifying learning gaps early and allowing for timely interventions.

- **Feedback Mechanisms:** Effective feedback is essential in formative assessment. Research indicates that feedback should be specific, timely, and constructive to enhance student learning. It helps students understand their strengths and areas for improvement, guiding them toward achieving learning objectives.

- **Retrieval Practice:** Incorporating retrieval practice into formative assessments can strengthen memory retention and understanding. Techniques such as quizzes and practice tests encourage students to recall information, reinforcing learning and improving long-term retention.

Formative assessment is implemented in classrooms through various strategies that help monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback. Here’s how it is typically implemented and why it works:

### How Formative Assessment is Implemented:

1. **Questioning:** Teachers ask open-ended or targeted questions during lessons to gauge understanding and encourage critical thinking.
2. **Quizzes:** Short, low-stakes quizzes help check students’ grasp of recently covered content.
3. **Exit Tickets:** At the end of a class, students answer a quick question or summarize their learning to show their understanding.
4. **Peer Assessment:** Students assess each other’s work using provided criteria, promoting collaboration and reflection.
5. **Self-Assessment:** Students evaluate their own work against standards or learning goals, fostering ownership of learning.
6. **Teacher Feedback:** Timely, specific feedback from teachers guides students in correcting errors and improving skills.
7. **Cycles:** Repeated formative assessment cycles allow educators to adjust instruction based on student needs.
8. **Addressing Misconceptions:** Identifying and correcting misunderstandings during the learning process helps prevent knowledge gaps.
9. **Pacing:** Teachers modify lesson speed based on formative feedback to ensure all students are keeping up.
10. **Metacognition and Self-Regulation:** Encouraging students to think about their thinking and learning strategies enhances deeper learning.
11. **Teacher Training:** Professional development ensures teachers know how to effectively design and implement formative assessments.
12. **Technology Support:** Digital tools facilitate efficient feedback, data collection, and interactive assessment methods.
13. **Curriculum Alignment:** Ensuring assessments align with curriculum goals guarantees relevance and coherence in instruction.

### Why Formative Assessment Works:

- **Real-time Feedback:** Helps both students and teachers quickly identify and address learning gaps.
- **Engages Students:** Involves learners actively in their own progress monitoring and improvement.
- **Improves Learning Outcomes:** Adjusts teaching to meet students' needs, enhancing understanding and retention.
- **Builds Metacognition:** Students become aware of their learning processes and develop self-regulation skills.
- **Promotes Equity:** Ensures all students receive the support needed to succeed by adapting instruction.
- **Encourages a Growth Mindset:** Focus on progress and effort rather than just final grades motivates continuous learning.

In summary, formative assessment is a dynamic and interactive process embedded in teaching that enhances learning through continuous feedback and adjustments.

Content: It stands in contrast to summative assessment, which generally takes place after a period of instruction and requires making a judgment about the learning that has occurred e.g., by grading or scoring a test or paper.This study was undertaken to sketch out theimpact of formative assessment on academic achievement of secondary school students. Formative assessment exposed to improve student learning in general, and the objective of the research study was to particularly find out the using of formative assessment to improve practices in the classroom by identifying the gaps in learning. Formative assessment (assessment-for-learning) helps teachers to conduct teaching and learning activities that can enhance the students" learning achievement. This study was aimed to find out the teachers" understanding about formative assessment, the implementation of a formative assessment for English learning including the use of formative assessment to improve the teachers" teaching and students" learning, and the supporting and/or hindering factors in implementing a formative assessment. Thus, this study was aimed at investigating science teachers’ perception on the pedagogical power of formative assessment to support students’ learning. RECOMMENDATIONS(1)Encourage the students to identify their strength and weakness in learning to achieve optimum level academic performance.(2)Teachers also can improve their teaching by getting feedback in ongoing assessment.(3)Formative examination reduces the burden to students in preparing their university exams. The specific objectives of the study were to investigate how teachers plan for formative assessment in public secondary schools in Kicukiro district, to discover how teachers use formative assessment techniques in electing students learning evidence in public secondary schools in Kicukiro district and to assess how teachers provide formative assessment feedback to students in public secondary schools in Kicukiro district. The results of the Wilcoxon test with 95% confidence level show that both teachers and students evaluate positively the effects of formative assessment, while the Mann–Whitney U test results show that for particular aspects there are significant differences in assessment between these two groups for the formative assessment method. It stresses the need for an operational definition for formative assessment as a basis for any research study that investigates the impact of formative assessment on students’ learning and teachers’ instruction.

--- SOURCE 2: Formative Assessment vs. Summative Assessment: Which is Better? ---
URL: https://visionaryteaching.com/formative-assessment-vs-summative-assessment-which-is-better/
Content: # Formative Assessment vs. Summative Assessment: Which is Better? In classrooms across America, **summative assessment** is the reigning, undisputed champion when it comes to collecting data on what students have learned. Does **summative assessment** do what we need it to do? Is **formative assessment** a smarter, stronger, faster, and/or better option? ### **Definitions** **Summative Assessment** evaluates what students have learned after completion of a unit of study by comparing scores to a predetermined standard. ****Formative Assessment**** monitors student progress during a unit of study to help educators improve their instruction, and thereby improve student learning. ****Formative assessment**** is **for** learning because the intent is to improve instruction and increase learning. These assessments are done continually during the teaching/learning process and allow teachers to adjust their instruction. **Summative assessment** merely checks what a student has learned after a unit of study is complete. ****Formative assessments**** are low-stakes because scores are not generated and grades are not involved. **Summative assessments** are considered high-stakes because things like grades, class rankings, graduation, and college acceptance are often on the line. ## Examples ### **Summative Assessments** * midterm or end of course exams * Standardized tests such as SATs ### ******Formative Assessment******s * Whole-group opportunities to respond (including pinch cards) ## **A Matter of Life or Death: A Metaphor About Assessment** Let’s say that a friend of ours has recently passed away. The autopsy represents ****summative assessment****. The annual checkup is like ******formative assessment******. ******Formative assessment****** not only allows teachers to give immediate feedback to students, but lets the instructor consider how to make changes to support student learning. ## **The Outcome** It is clear that ********formative assessment******** offers a number of advantages over ****summative assessment**.** Formative assessments can be quick, inexpensive/free, and low-pressure for the students. Many of the ******formative assessment****** strategies are engaging and can feel like games to the students. Most importantly, ******formative assessment****** allows teachers to collect real time data and make changes to teaching strategies accordingly. I would argue that we tend to rely on these tests because “that’s the way it has always been done.” The Decision: a knockout victory for ********Formative Assessment********!

--- SOURCE 3: Summative Assessment vs. Formative Assessment: Understanding with Examples ---
URL: https://teacheducator.com/summative-assessment-vs-formative-assessment
Content: Title: Summative Assessment vs. Formative Assessment: Understanding with Examples
Formative Assessment**: Assessments play a crucial role in the educational landscape, serving as tools to measure student learning, guide instruction, and inform educational practices. The primary goal of formative assessment is to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used by instructors to improve their teaching and by students to enhance their learning. * **Adaptability**: Formative assessments allow teachers to adjust their teaching strategies based on student performance and understanding. Summative assessment, on the other hand, is conducted at the end of an instructional period to evaluate student learning, skill acquisition, and academic achievement. * **Cumulative Evaluation**: Summative assessments provide a comprehensive overview of student learning at the end of a unit or course. ## Key Differences Between Formative and Summative Assessment. Understanding the differences between formative and summative assessments is crucial for educators to effectively utilize both in their teaching practices. * **Formative Assessment**: Aims to improve student learning and inform instruction. * **Summative Assessment**: Aims to evaluate student learning and measure achievement. While formative assessments help guide instruction and support student learning, summative assessments provide a final evaluation of student achievement. * **Enhances Learning**: By providing timely feedback, formative assessments help students identify areas for improvement and take corrective action. * **Informs Instruction**: Teachers can adjust their teaching strategies based on formative assessment results, ensuring that all students are supported in their learning. * **Measures Achievement**: Summative assessments provide a clear picture of what students have learned and how well they have mastered the content. Educators can effectively integrate both formative and summative assessments into their teaching practices to enhance student learning and achievement. Formative assessments provide ongoing feedback and support student learning, while summative assessments evaluate overall achievement and mastery of content. What is the main difference between formative and summative assessments? Formative assessments are conducted throughout the learning process to monitor progress and provide feedback, while summative assessments are conducted at the end of an instructional period to evaluate overall student achievement. Can formative assessments impact a student’s final grade? Teachers can use formative assessments to guide instruction and provide feedback, while summative assessments can be used to evaluate overall student learning and inform future curriculum planning.

After a 15-session treatment, the post-tests of the test anxiety, motivation, and self-regulation skill were administered to all groups to assess the impacts of the instruction on their language achievement. Lastly, a questionnaire of attitude was administered to both experimental groups to examine their attitudes towards the impacts of formative and summative assessment on their English learning improvement. Journal of English Language Teaching and Applied Linguistics. # Balancing Formative and Summative Assessment in English Language Teaching: Impacts on Learner Outcomes and Motivation. ## DOI:. Formative assessment, Summative assessment, English language teaching, EFL learners, Learner outcomes, Student motivation, Classroom assessment, Moroccan context, Secondary education, Teaching strategies. This study investigates the impact of formative and summative assessment on learner outcomes, motivation, and engagement in English language teaching. Conducted at ESEF Berrechid in Morocco, the research focuses on secondary education students who are learning English as a foreign language. The study adopts a mixed-methods approach to provide a thorough understanding of assessment practices and their influence on student learning. Classroom observations focused on the implementation of formative assessment techniques, including regular feedback, peer assessment, self-assessment, and classroom participation activities, while interviews explored teachers’ perspectives on the benefits and challenges of balancing formative and summative assessment. Questionnaires examined students’ perceptions of how different assessment types affected their motivation, confidence, and overall learning experience. Findings indicate that formative assessment, when consistently applied and integrated into classroom instruction, encourages active student participation, enhances self-regulated learning, and fosters a positive attitude toward English language acquisition. Summative assessment provides critical benchmarks for achievement and helps teachers identify areas of improvement, but excessive emphasis on summative evaluation may create anxiety and reduce intrinsic motivation among learners. The study demonstrates that a thoughtful balance between formative and summative assessment can lead to improved learner outcomes, higher engagement, and greater motivation. Pedagogical implications suggest that teachers should design assessment strategies that combine continuous feedback with formal evaluations, employ student-centered techniques to enhance autonomy, and create an environment that values both progress and achievement. The research contributes to the understanding of effective assessment practices in Moroccan EFL contexts and provides evidence-based recommendations for educators and policymakers seeking to enhance teaching quality, learner motivation, and academic performance. It also highlights the importance of professional development for teachers to effectively implement a balanced assessment system that responds to students’ diverse learning needs. ## License. This study investigates the impact of formative and summative assessment on learner outcomes, motivation, and engagement in English language teaching. Conducted at ESEF Berrechid in Morocco, the research focuses on secondary education students who are learning English as a foreign language. The study adopts a mixed-methods approach to provide a thorough understanding of assessment practices and their influence on student learning. Data were collected through classroom observations, structured questionnaires administered to students, and semi-structured interviews with teachers. Classroom observations focused on the implementation of formative assessment techniques, including regular feedback, peer assessment, self-assessment, and classroom participation activities, while interviews explored teachers’ perspectives on the benefits and challenges of balancing formative and summative assessment. Questionnaires examined students’ perceptions of how different assessment types affected their motivation, confidence, and overall learning experience. Findings indicate that formative assessment, when consistently applied and integrated into classroom instruction, encourages active student participation, enhances self-regulated learning, and fosters a positive attitude toward English language acquisition. Summative assessment provides critical benchmarks for achievement and helps teachers identify areas of improvement, but excessive emphasis on summative evaluation may create anxiety and reduce intrinsic motivation among learners. The study demonstrates that a thoughtful balance between formative and summative assessment can lead to improved learner outcomes, higher engagement, and greater motivation. Pedagogical implications suggest that teachers should design assessment strategies that combine continuous feedback with formal evaluations, employ student-centered techniques to enhance autonomy, and create an environment that values both progress and achievement. The research contributes to the understanding of effective assessment practices in Moroccan EFL contexts and provides evidence-based recommendations for educators and policymakers seeking to enhance teaching quality, learner motivation, and academic performance. It also highlights the importance of professional development for teachers to effectively implement a balanced assessment system that responds to students’ diverse learning needs. ### Journal. ### DOI. ## Copyright. # Developing a Formative Assessment of Academic Reading Comprehension for English Language Learners: A Tool to Improve Teaching and Learning. Items for nine forms of the assessments will then be developed and field-tested based on this framework. Web-based reports for assessment results will be designed, and a manual for teachers in how to use the assessments to guide instruction will be prepared. The assessment will be developed relying on strategies emerging from research on adolescent students' reading development, including ELLs. These strategies include: (1) the use of formative assessment to allow teachers to adapt their instruction based on students' needs; (2) the use of an academic language framework to help students understand complex secondary-level texts; (3) the use of explicit, direct reading comprehension strategy instruction; and (4) the use of cooperative learning to raise students' motivation and engagement for reading. A web-based program to assist teachers in organizing assessment results and keeping track of student work will also be developed. The validity of the assessments for improving instruction will be evaluated through a comparison of results with student performance on standardized reading achievement tests. To develop a common scale across all the forms for the assessment, item parameters will be calibrated and compared using IRT for items that are scored right/wrong, and a generalized partial credit model will be used for items in which students write a response. Regression analysis will be conducted to examine the extent to which the students' performance on the developed assessments is associated with that on external measures of reading. **Products:** A reliable and valid formative assessment tool designed specifically for use with ELLs consisting of nine different forms will be developed. Use of the assessments will be supported by a web-based score reporting tool and applications to support teachers in the use of the assessments for guiding instruction. Formative assessment is an ongoing process used during instruction to monitor student learning, provide feedback, and adjust teaching strategies to enhance learning outcomes. In K-12 and college classrooms, formative assessments can take various forms, including quizzes, group discussions, peer assessments, and classroom observations. ([teachers.institute](https://teachers.institute/assessment-for-learning/diagnostic-formative-summative-evaluation-education?utm_source=openai))

**Differences Between Assessment Types:**

- **Diagnostic Assessment:** Conducted before instruction begins, diagnostic assessments aim to identify students' prior knowledge, skills, and misconceptions. This information helps educators plan effective teaching strategies. Examples include pre-tests and self-assessments. ([niu.edu](https://www.niu.edu/citl/resources/guides/instructional-guide/formative-and-summative-assessment.shtml?utm_source=openai))

- **Formative Assessment:** Implemented during the learning process, formative assessments provide ongoing feedback to both students and instructors. They help identify areas where students need support and inform instructional adjustments. Examples include quizzes, peer reviews, and interactive exercises. ([k-state.edu](https://www.k-state.edu/assessment/toolkit/basics/formativesummative.html?utm_source=openai))

- **Summative Assessment:** Administered at the end of an instructional period, summative assessments evaluate student learning against predefined standards or benchmarks. They are typically high-stakes and contribute significantly to final grades. Examples include final exams, standardized tests, and cumulative projects. ([k-state.edu](https://www.k-state.edu/assessment/toolkit/basics/formativesummative.html?utm_source=openai))

**Outcomes Most Studied:**

Research has extensively examined the impact of formative assessment on various educational outcomes, particularly in reading achievement. A meta-analysis revealed that formative assessment positively influences students' reading performance, with an average effect size of 0.19. The effectiveness of formative assessment can vary based on factors such as sample size, instructional differentiation, and the nature of the intervention. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.990196/full?utm_source=openai))

**Evidence Gaps:**

While formative assessment has been shown to enhance student learning, several areas require further investigation:

- **Long-Term Effects:** More research is needed to understand the sustained impact of formative assessment on student learning over extended periods.

- **Disciplinary Variations:** Studies should explore how formative assessment strategies affect learning outcomes across different subjects and educational levels.

- **Implementation Strategies:** Investigating the most effective methods for integrating formative assessment into diverse teaching contexts can provide valuable insights.

Addressing these gaps can lead to a more comprehensive understanding of formative assessment's role in education and inform best practices for its application.

Formative assessment is a process used by educators to monitor student learning and provide ongoing feedback that can be used to improve teaching and learning. Unlike summative assessments, which evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period, formative assessments are conducted during the learning process to inform instruction and support student development.

A meta-analysis of formative assessment studies can provide valuable insights into its effectiveness across various educational settings. Such analyses often examine the impact of formative assessments on student achievement, mastery, retention, and the transfer of learning. For instance, research has shown that formative assessments can enhance student motivation and performance by promoting continuous learning and fostering a collaborative learning environment. ([dx.doi.org](https://dx.doi.org/10.36315/Education-and-New-Developments_2019_Vol_II.pdf?utm_source=openai))

In K-12 education, formative assessments are commonly used to identify students' strengths and areas for improvement, allowing teachers to adjust instruction accordingly. In postsecondary education, these assessments can support diverse learning needs and promote deeper understanding of course material.

The effectiveness of formative assessments is influenced by various factors, including the quality of feedback provided, the timing of assessments, and the active involvement of students in the assessment process. When implemented thoughtfully, formative assessments can lead to improved student outcomes and a more engaging learning experience.

1. Undergraduate STEM: Refers to education or students at the bachelor's degree level in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics disciplines.

2. Formative Assessment: A type of assessment conducted during the learning process to provide feedback that can be used by instructors and students to improve teaching and learning outcomes.

3. Feedback: Information given to students about their performance intended to guide future learning.

4. Trial: In research, a trial is a study conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention or treatment.

5. Comparator: A group or condition against which the intervention or treatment is compared. This can be a control group or an alternative intervention.

6. Mapping: The process of aligning or linking concepts, assessments, or outcomes, possibly to ensure that formative assessments align with learning objectives.

7. Historical Control Comparison Group: A group used as a control in a study, composed of data collected in the past, before the current intervention was implemented.

8. Quasi-Experimental: A type of research design that aims to evaluate interventions but lacks random assignment to treatment or control groups.

Putting it together in an educational research study context:

The study could involve a trial where an intervention (such as a new formative assessment feedback method) is applied. The effectiveness of the intervention is then compared to a comparator group, which might be a historical control group (previous students who did not receive the intervention). Mapping might refer to the process of ensuring the formative assessments align with intended learning outcomes.

URL: https://pce.sandiego.edu/formative-vs-summative-assessment/
Content: In education, assessments are the roadmap guiding teachers and students to successful outcomes — from navigating subject matter to reaching academic milestones. Formative assessment is not actually a singular method, but instead, a variety of ways for teachers to evaluate student comprehension, learning needs, and academic progress in real-time throughout a lesson, unit, or course. Summative assessment, on the other hand, is any type of evaluation that measures a student’s overall comprehension and achievement at the end of a unit, course, or academic period. Unlike formative assessment, which provides ongoing feedback, summative assessment focuses on determining the extent to which students have mastered the content overall. Consider these methods as you grade summative assessments, keeping in mind a fair and accurate representation of students’ learning outcomes and progress. When teachers try out different assessment methods and grading styles, they get a better handle on student needs and can create an environment for widespread growth and improvement.

Content: Summative assessments occur “after the fact,” in that they measure how much a student has learned, retained, and mastered over the course of study, instructional unit, or lesson. Of course, not all assessments fall into the strict categories of formative or summative; interim and benchmark assessments, for example, help educators monitor student progress along the way. If formative assessment measures how a student *is learning* during a course of study, summative assessment is designed to measure “how much” a student *has learned* after a unit or course has reached its completion. Summative assessment provides teachers with an overview of what students have learned throughout a particular unit of study—a semester, a full year, or, in the case of the SAT, all the cumulative knowledge and skills that they have gained over a long span of time. One final way to think about formative versus summative assessment might be to use the analogy of students in an art class, each painting a picture.

Content: 5. Formative and Summative Assessment. # Formative and Summative Assessment. More specifically, assessment is the *ways* instructors gather data about their teaching and their students’ learning (Hanna & Dettmer, 2004). These assessments typically are not graded and act as a gauge to students’ learning progress and to determine teaching effectiveness (implementing appropriate methods and activities). Summative assessment takes place after the learning has been completed and provides information and feedback that sums up the teaching and learning process. High-stakes summative assessments typically are given to students at the end of a set point during or at the end of the semester to assess what has been learned and how well it was learned. Grades are usually an outcome of summative assessment: they indicate whether the student has an acceptable level of knowledge-gain—is the student able to effectively progress to the next part of the class? Assessment measures if and how students are learning and if the teaching methods are effectively relaying the intended messages.
