    Authors: Dargusch J. (2010)
    Source: Scopus / 2-s2.0-79951547087
    URL: https://api.elsevier.com/content/abstract/scopus_id/79951547087
  [ABSTRACT ONLY — no PDF available]

Formative assessment, summative assessment, and diagnostic assessment are key components in educational evaluation, each serving distinct purposes:

- **Formative Assessment**: Conducted during the learning process, formative assessments aim to monitor student progress and provide ongoing feedback to enhance learning outcomes.

- **Summative Assessment**: Administered at the conclusion of an instructional period, summative assessments evaluate the cumulative knowledge and skills acquired by students, often contributing to final grades.

- **Diagnostic Assessment**: Implemented before or at the beginning of an instructional period, diagnostic assessments identify students' existing knowledge, skills, and learning needs, informing instructional planning.

A comprehensive framework for these assessments is detailed in the article "Formative assessment and science education" by B. Bell and B. Cowie, published in 2001. This work explores the characteristics and applications of formative assessment within science education, providing valuable insights into assessment strategies. ([scholar.google.com](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Lm9AMAMAAAAJ&utm_source=openai))

Additionally, the study "Effects of a computer-assisted formative assessment intervention based on multiple-tier diagnostic items and different feedback types" by U. Maier, N. Wolf, and C. Randler, published in 2016, examines the impact of formative assessments incorporating diagnostic elements and varied feedback mechanisms. This research contributes to understanding how formative assessments can be structured to effectively support learning. ([scholar.google.com](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=kBmiHXUAAAAJ&utm_source=openai))

These resources offer a foundational understanding of assessment frameworks and their roles in facilitating learning.

Formative assessment, which involves ongoing evaluations to inform teaching and enhance student learning, has been extensively studied in K-12 education. However, research specifically comparing its effectiveness between K-12 and college classrooms is limited.

**K-12 Education:**

A meta-analysis by Xuan et al. (2022) examined 48 studies involving 116,051 K-12 students and found that formative assessment had a modest positive effect on reading achievement (effect size = +0.19). The study also identified that smaller sample sizes and the integration of differentiated instruction were associated with larger effect sizes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

Another comprehensive review by Sortwell et al. (2024) analyzed multiple meta-analyses and concluded that formative assessment consistently positively impacts K-12 students' learning outcomes, with effect sizes ranging from trivial to large. The strongest effects were observed in literacy, particularly writing, followed by vocabulary and reading. STEM subjects showed smaller effects overall. ([monash.edu](https://www.monash.edu/msdi/connect/news/articles/2026/how-formative-assessment-influences-learning-in-k-12-education?utm_source=openai))

**College Education:**

While specific meta-analyses focusing on college-level formative assessment are scarce, existing studies suggest that formative assessment can be beneficial in higher education. For instance, student-directed interventions, such as self-assessment and peer feedback, have been found to be particularly effective for secondary and tertiary students, who possess more learning experience and metacognitive readiness. ([monash.edu](https://www.monash.edu/msdi/connect/news/articles/2026/how-formative-assessment-influences-learning-in-k-12-education?utm_source=openai))

**Comparative Insights:**

The available evidence indicates that formative assessment positively influences student learning in both K-12 and college settings. However, the magnitude and specific characteristics of its effectiveness may vary across educational levels. In K-12 education, formative assessment appears to have a more pronounced impact on literacy skills, especially writing, while in higher education, student-directed approaches may be more effective due to students' advanced metacognitive abilities.

In summary, while formative assessment is beneficial in both K-12 and college classrooms, its impact may differ based on educational context, subject area, and the nature of the assessment strategies employed.

Formative assessment, which involves ongoing evaluations to inform teaching and learning, has been shown to positively impact student achievement across various groups. However, its effectiveness can vary based on student characteristics such as achievement levels, language proficiency, and disabilities.

**General Effectiveness of Formative Assessment:**

A meta-analysis by Xuan et al. (2022) encompassing 48 studies with 116,051 K-12 students found that formative assessment had a modest positive effect on reading achievement, with an effect size of +0.19. Similarly, Yao et al. (2024) analyzed 118 studies and reported an overall effect size of 0.25, indicating a positive impact on student learning outcomes. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

**Impact on Low-Achieving Students:**

Formative assessment has been particularly beneficial for low-achieving students. Black and Wiliam (1998) found that frequent formative assessment practices significantly improved the performance of students from disadvantaged backgrounds. Their study indicated that these practices were especially advantageous for low-achieving students, leading to substantial gains in academic achievement. ([scholarworks.waldenu.edu](https://scholarworks.waldenu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=7622&context=dissertations&utm_source=openai))

**Impact on English Language Learners (ELLs):**

While specific meta-analyses focusing solely on ELLs are limited, formative assessment can be tailored to support language development. By providing timely feedback and opportunities for self-assessment, formative assessment practices can help ELLs identify language gaps and receive targeted support, thereby enhancing their language acquisition and academic performance.

**Impact on Students with Disabilities:**

Formative assessment has also been effective for students with disabilities. Fuchs and Fuchs (1986) conducted a meta-analysis of 21 controlled studies involving students with learning disabilities and found a mean effect size of 0.70, indicating a significant positive impact. This suggests that formative assessment practices can be particularly beneficial for students with disabilities, aiding in their learning and achievement. ([winginstitute.org](https://winginstitute.org/student-formative-assessment-all-research?utm_source=openai))

**Conclusion:**

Formative assessment has been shown to positively influence student learning outcomes across various groups, including low-achieving students and those with disabilities. While specific studies focusing on English language learners are limited, the adaptable nature of formative assessment suggests it can be effectively implemented to support their unique learning needs.

[20] Title: Online feedback assessments in physiology: Effects on students' learning experiences and outcomes
    Authors: Marden N.Y. (2013)
    Source: Scopus / DOI:10.1152/advan.00092.2012
    URL: https://doi.org/10.1152/advan.00092.2012
  [ABSTRACT ONLY — no PDF available]

Comparative studies examining the effectiveness of formative assessment, retrieval practice, summative testing, and feedback-only conditions have provided valuable insights into their impact on student learning outcomes.

**Formative Assessment vs. Summative Assessment:**

Formative assessments, conducted during the learning process, aim to provide ongoing feedback to both instructors and students, facilitating adjustments to teaching and learning strategies. Summative assessments, on the other hand, evaluate student learning at the end of an instructional period. Research indicates that formative assessments can enhance student engagement and critical thinking, leading to improved learning outcomes. For instance, a study in undergraduate medical education found that formative assessments, which offer immediate feedback, support instructors in refining teaching strategies and promote reflective teaching practices. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11590208/?utm_source=openai))

**Retrieval Practice:**

Retrieval practice involves actively recalling information from memory, which has been shown to strengthen memory and learning. A study comparing the effectiveness of very short answer questions (VSAQs) and multiple-choice questions (MCQs) in retrieval practice found that VSAQs, requiring active recall, were more effective in enhancing knowledge retention among health science students. ([bmcmededuc.biomedcentral.com](https://bmcmededuc.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12909-024-06538-0?utm_source=openai))

**Feedback Timing:**

The timing of feedback in conjunction with retrieval practice also plays a crucial role. A laboratory study with English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students revealed that immediate feedback following retrieval practice led to better long-term retention compared to delayed feedback. ([nature.com](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-024-03983-6?utm_source=openai))

**Comparative Effectiveness:**

While both formative assessments and retrieval practice are effective in enhancing learning outcomes, their comparative effectiveness can depend on various factors, including the learning context, subject matter, and individual student differences. Integrating both strategies—using formative assessments to provide ongoing feedback and incorporating retrieval practice to reinforce learning—may offer a more comprehensive approach to improving student achievement.

In summary, evidence suggests that formative assessments and retrieval practice, especially when combined with timely feedback, can be more effective than summative-only testing or feedback-only conditions in enhancing student learning outcomes.

Unfortunately, I couldn't find any articles that match all these criteria. However, I can provide an overview of these concepts and suggest alternative search strategies to help you find relevant research.

**Formative Assessment**: This refers to assessments conducted during the learning process to monitor student progress and inform instructional decisions.

**Retrieval Practice**: A learning strategy where students actively recall information, enhancing long-term retention.

**Low-Stakes Quizzing**: Frequent, low-pressure quizzes that encourage regular review and reinforce learning.

**Comparative Experiment**: A research design comparing different instructional methods to assess their effectiveness.

**Classroom Setting**: The environment where teaching and learning occur.

**Alternative Search Strategies**:

- **Broaden Search Terms**: Use synonyms or related terms, such as "formative evaluation" instead of "formative assessment," or "active recall" instead of "retrieval practice."

- **Use Boolean Operators**: Combine terms with AND, OR, and NOT to refine your search. For example, "formative assessment" AND "retrieval practice" AND "classroom."

- **Search Multiple Databases**: Explore other academic databases like JSTOR, ScienceDirect, or ERIC.

- **Consult Recent Reviews**: Look for literature reviews or meta-analyses summarizing research on these topics.

Formative assessment, which involves ongoing evaluations to inform teaching and learning, has been shown to positively impact various aspects of student learning beyond traditional test scores, including retention, transfer, student engagement, and self-regulation. Several studies employing randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental designs, meta-analyses, and systematic reviews have explored these effects in K-12 and college classrooms.

**Impact on Student Learning:**

- **Meta-Analysis on Reading Achievement:** A meta-analysis encompassing 48 studies with over 116,000 K-12 students found that formative assessment had a modest positive effect (effect size = +0.19) on reading achievement. The study also highlighted that integrating differentiated instruction with formative assessment led to a significant increase in reading scores. ([pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36072038/?utm_source=openai))

- **Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses:** A comprehensive review of multiple meta-analyses indicated that formative assessment practices generally enhance K-12 students' learning outcomes. The review emphasized that student-initiated formative assessments, such as self-assessment and peer assessment, were particularly effective in promoting self-regulated learning and deeper understanding. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/16/17/7826?utm_source=openai))

**Impact on Student Engagement and Self-Regulation:**

- **Quasi-Experimental Study on EFL Students:** A study involving 89 middle school English as a Foreign Language (EFL) students in China found that formative assessment enhanced students' motivation and English achievement. The study, grounded in Self-Determination Theory, suggested that formative assessment practices satisfied students' psychological needs, leading to improved engagement and self-regulation. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2025.1664871?utm_source=openai))

- **College-Level Learning to Learn Course Evaluation:** An evaluation of a college "learning to learn" course, which incorporated formative assessment strategies, reported improvements in students' self-regulated learning and academic engagement. The course was associated with increased use of self-regulation strategies and reduced procrastination among students. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1041608023000274?utm_source=openai))

These findings collectively suggest that formative assessment practices can enhance student learning outcomes, engagement, and self-regulation across various educational settings. The effectiveness of these practices is influenced by factors such as the type of assessment (e.g., student-initiated vs. teacher-directed), the integration of differentiated instruction, and the specific educational context.

Formative assessment (FA) is a continuous evaluation process aimed at monitoring and enhancing student learning. The effectiveness of FA implementation is influenced by various factors, including teacher professional development, curriculum pressures, and the use of technology-mediated delivery. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have identified several moderators that impact the outcomes of FA practices:

**Teacher Professional Development (PD):**
High-quality PD is essential for teachers to effectively implement FA strategies. A meta-analysis examining the impact of teacher PD on student mathematics achievement found a positive average effect size of 0.34, indicating that PD can enhance student outcomes. However, the study also noted that specific features of PD, such as duration, format, and focus, did not significantly moderate its effectiveness. ([mdpi.com](https://www.mdpi.com/2227-7102/15/9/1177?utm_source=openai))

**Curriculum Pressures:**
The integration of FA into existing curricula can be challenging due to time constraints and standardized testing requirements. Teachers often face pressure to cover extensive content, which may limit their ability to implement FA practices effectively. A systematic review highlighted that data-based decision-making (DBDM) is crucial for improving student learning outcomes. However, the review also noted that teachers' use of data to inform instruction is often hindered by external pressures, such as curriculum demands and accountability measures. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0883035520300082?utm_source=openai))

**Technology-Mediated Delivery:**
The use of technology in delivering FA can enhance engagement and provide immediate feedback. A systematic review on the impact of teacher professional development on digital instructional integration found that effective PD programs can promote teachers' adoption of digital tools, leading to improved teaching practices. The review emphasized the importance of PD programs that focus on teachers' beliefs and attitudes toward digital integration to facilitate the adoption of technology-mediated FA practices. ([frontiersin.org](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/education/articles/10.3389/feduc.2025.1541031/full?utm_source=openai))

In summary, while teacher professional development is a critical factor in the successful implementation of formative assessment, other elements such as curriculum pressures and the integration of technology also play significant roles. Addressing these factors through targeted PD programs and supportive policies can enhance the effectiveness of FA practices in educational settings.

The use of formative assessment has become common in classrooms as educators seek ways to use assessment data to differentiate instruction (Johnson, Sondergeld, & Walton, 2019). In their seminal work, Black and Wiliam (1998) describe formative assessment as teaching and learning activities that are adapted to meet student needs based on feedback received from students. Formative assessment supports the recursive feedback loop of instruction, assessment, analysis, and goal setting (Conderman & Hedin, 2012). The goal of formative assessment is to allow teachers to obtain systematic evidence about student thinking during instruction and to use those data to adjust and adapt instruction to meet individual students' needs. (Confrey, Toutkoushian, & Shah, 2019;Johnson, Sondergeld, & Walton, 2019;Wilson, 2018). 

Formative assessments are typically informal and are embedded within an instructional activity. Examples include observations of students, student interviews or informal question-answer activities, admit slips or exit slips, journals, classroom discussions, and short written assignments (Bahr & Garcia, 2010). Technology tools, such as interactive white boards, mobile device apps, and educational software can support the use of formative assessment while providing students with immediate feedback (Pilli & Aksu, 2013). 

By contrast, summative assessments are typically administered after instruction has occurred, with the goal of evaluating how well students have mastered the content or achieved the learning objectives (Bahr & Garcia, 2010). Summative assessments may take the form of a final exam, report card grades, or a large cumulative project. They may be used to evaluate school-wide goals or program effectiveness (Conderman & Hedin, 2012). Because they are administered at the end of a term or unit of study, summative assessments do not provide data that teachers can use during the learning process to adjust instruction (Garrison & Ehringhaus, 2007). Summative assessments are sometimes referred to as assessments of learning, while formative assessments are assessments for learning (Johnson, Sondergeld, & Walton, 2019). [2]

Classroom assessments allow K-12 teachers to evaluate student learning (i.e., monitor students' progress) and make a variety of important decisions about learning outcomes (e.g., producing feedback, assigning grades). Teachers use two types of assessments to evaluate student learning in the classroom: summative and formative (Black and Wiliam, 2009). Summative assessments are typically used at the end of an instructional period, such as a unit or a semester, to evaluate student learning relative to content standards or benchmarks. Quizzes, midterm exams, or a final project are common examples of teacher-made summative assessments. There are also statewide accountability assessments for measuring student performance on specific learning standards (e.g., Common Core State Standards). Unlike summative assessments, formative assessments are used during instruction to monitor student learning, provide students with feedback, and help them identify target skills that need improvement. When Scriven (1967) first proposed the idea of formative assessment in education, he specifically emphasized that it should be used to inform "on-going improvement of the curriculum" (p. 41). Over the past few decades, formative assessments have evolved to be much broader, and now include uses such as monitoring student's response to instruction, identifying at-risk students, and informing the instruction to address individual student needs. Today, the primary goal of formative assessments is to provide students with timely and descriptive feedback based on the learning goals or criteria for success (Hattie and Timperley, 2007;McManus, 2008). 

During the past decade, the introduction of various educational technologies, such as computerized assessments including computer-based and computerized-adaptive tests, has drastically changed the implementation of formative assessments in the classroom. Computerized formative assessments provide an integration of computer technologies and measurement theory to effectively manage and deliver classroom assessments (Russell, 2010;Webb et al., 2013). [3]

Formative assessment is a "gap minder" (Roskos and Neuman, 2012) enabling teachers and students to identify the gap between where students are and where they need to go in their reading development (Wiliam and Thompson, 2007). Consequently, teachers can stay alert to these gaps and differentiate their instruction to various students. Differentiated instruction is taken as an optional component in the formative assessment practice. In our review, there were several teacher's practices that were coded as "without interventions." For instance, teachers who kept track of students' learning gaps without changing their teaching plan, or who just monitored the interim/benchmark assessment results without further action on differentiating or individualizing their teaching to different students aligned with the data from assessment. [4]

This study used hierarchical linear modeling to examine the relationship between data from an internet-based mathematics formative assessment and data from a mathematics summative assessment for primary grade learners (ages 5-7). Results showed a positive relationship between formative assessment data related to the concepts of counting and decomposing numbers and summative data. This relationship was stronger in classrooms where students demonstrated lower average performance on the formative assessment data. The results suggest that formative assessment can be more beneficial to encourage low-achieving students in primary-grade mathematics classrooms. Therefore, we recommend teachers use formative assessment practices more frequently in low-achieved primary grade classrooms. The formative assessment process includes the cycle of data collection, data analysis, planning future instruction, and examining the impact of that instruction through cycling back to data collection. This study contributes to the field by providing more empirical data about the relationship between formative and summative assessment with primary grades’ learners. [6]

There is widespread agreement about the importance of accounting for the extent to which educational systems advance student learning. Yet, the forms and formats of accountable assessments often ill serve students and teachers; the summative judgements of student performance that are typically employed to indicate proficiencies on benchmarks of student learning commonly fail to capture student performance in ways that are specific and actionable for teachers. Timing is another key barrier to the utility of summative assessment. In the US, summative evaluations occur at the end of the school year and may serve future students, but do not help teachers better support the students who were tested. In contrast, formative assessments provide actionable grounds to improve the quality of instruction on the basis of both the granularity and specificity of their content and their timing. Unfortunately, the psychometric qualities of formative assessments are often unknown. I describe an innovative approach to assessment that aims to blend the productive characteristics of both summative and formative assessment. The resulting assessment system is accountable to students and teachers by providing actionable information for improving classroom instruction, and at the same time, it addresses the demands of psychometric quality for purposes of system accountability as it is currently practiced (in the US). The innovative assessment system relies on partnership with teachers to generate (1) a shared conceptual frame for describing instructional goals and valued forms of teaching and learning; (2) a set of electronic tools to help teachers detect, share, analyse, and interpret student learning data; and (3) classroom and school-level community professional development structures to support and sustain a widespread practice of assessing to guide instruction. These features are coupled with new psychometric models, developed by the Berkeley Evaluation and Research Center, that provide more robust estimates of student learning by linking information from multiple sources, including student classroom work, student responses to formative assessments, and summative evaluations. (Mark Wilson will address the psychometric modeling during this conference.) Here I describe challenges and prospects for this innovation with a case study of its implementation in a K–5 elementary school that is seeking to improve the quality of instruction and students’ understandings of measure and rational number arithmetic. [7]

The term "formative evaluation" was first used by Scriven (1967) to account for the continuous development of the curriculum. Over the next two decades the term "formative" was not frequently used in the literature; however, some studies examined the integration of assessment within classroom instruction, which resulted in the emergence of what is knows as Cognitively Guided Instruction (CGI) (Wiliam, 2011). CGI was examined in a research project by Carpenter, Fennema, Peterson, Chiang, and Loef (1989) in which they concluded that students who were taught by CGI teachers, achieved remarkably better results compared to other students. This was followed by a growing interest in the literature to investigate the effectiveness of formative assessment on students' achievement. In a review of about 600 studies that are potentially relevant to classroom formative assessment, Black and Wiliam (1998) concluded that the use of assessment to inform classroom instruction could dramatically increase the speed of students' learning. 

Despite the agreement in the literature about its effectiveness, formative assessment's definition remains controversial. In the literature, formative assessment is usually compared with summative assessment, which refers to the evaluation of learners' achievement out of a given course or program (Harlen & James, 1997). However, the distinction between the formative and summative evaluation is not that simple. Wiliam (2011) notes that even summative evaluation procedures can be used formatively, and he provides an example of a teacher who did not score one of the tests that she gave to her students. Instead, she divided them into groups and asked them to work together in order to arrive at the best possible answers. In trying to clear the ambiguity of the distinction between formative and summative evaluation, Wiliam and Black (1996) claim that it is meaningful to view the distinction in terms of the way that assessment data is used, and not the way in which the assessment is conducted. 

The majority of attempts to generate a holistic definition for formative assessment assign a central role for feedback. Feedback can either be positive or negative. Positive feedback confirms a learner's response and provides motivational support for the learner that can aid further learning (Ellis, 2009). [8]

Assessment involves the systematic collection and analysis of evidence to inform educational decisions. 

Two key types of assessment commonly used in education are formative assessment and summative assessment. Formative assessment focuses on providing ongoing feedback and monitoring student progress, while summative assessment evaluates overall learning outcomes and assigns grades. Together, pág. 593 these assessment types contribute to a comprehensive understanding of student learning and inform instructional practices. 

Formative and summative assessments have separate functions and characteristics. Formative assessments are constant and frequent, with the primary purpose of guiding instruction and providing feedback for progress (Black & Wiliam, 2009). They aim to be useful, helping students and teachers to identify areas of strength and weakness and transform teaching and learning strategies accordingly. 

Summative assessments, on the other hand, are often given at the end of a learning period and are primarily concerned with measuring success against established standards (Gronlund, 2013). They provide an overview of students' overall performance and are frequently used for grading, program evaluation, and accountability. 

For decades, traditional assessments in education have been most frequently carried out by means of paper tests, quizzes and assignments. These methods were at the center of assessing students' knowledge and understanding. However, they have limitations that have prompted the exploration of innovative assessment approaches. [9]

During the school year, teachers have opportunities to assess student learning and to use this evidence to adjust instruction. It is important to align the different assessments teachers use to guide instruction. Formative assessments provide feedback teachers and students use during the course of instruction (Hattie, Fisher, & Frey, 2016). This type of assessment differs from summative assessments that occur after an instructional unit and require a decision that learning occurred (Clark, 2012). The seminal work of Black and Wiliam (1998) broadly defined assessment to include all activities that gather diagnostic information to change teaching and learning. Modern researchers such as Adesope, Trevisan, and Sundararajan (2017) and Metcalfe (2017) still use the same definition. Under this definition, formative assessment includes many aspects of classroom activities. Some of the activities include observation, discussions, and analysis of homework and tests. Assessments are considered formative when the data collected is then used to adjust instruction and learning. These adjustments are intended to meet student needs more completely (Dixson & Worrell, 2016). [10]

In teaching and learning, assessment is defined as a procedure applied by instructors and students during instruction through which teachers provide necessary feedbacks to modify ongoing learning and teaching to develop learners' attainment of planned instructional aims (Robinowitz, 2010). According to Popham (2008), assessment is an intended procedure in which evidence of learners' status is utilized by educators to adjust their ongoing instructional processes or applied by learners to change their present instructional strategies. Assessment intends to improve learning and it is used to reduce the gap between students' present instructional situation and their target learning objectives (Heritage, 2012). 

Two types of assessment are formative and summative. According to Glazer (2014), summative assessment is generally applied to give learners a numerical score with limited feedback. Therefore, summative assessment is commonly used to measure learning and is rarely used for learning. Educators can make the summative assessment more formative by giving learners the opportunity to learn from exams. This would mean supplying pupils with feedback on exams and making use of the teaching potentiality of exams. Wininger (2005) proposed an amalgamation of assessment techniques between summative assessment and formative assessment. This marriage between summative assessment and formative assessment is referred to as summative-formative assessment. Based on Wininger, summative-formative assessment is used to review the exam with examinees so they can get feedback on comprehension. Formative-summative assessment occurs in two primary forms: using a mock exam before the final or using the final exam before the retake. 

Formative assessment allows for feedback which improves learning while summative assessment measures learning. Formative assessment refers to frequent, interactive assessments of students' development and understanding to recognize their needs and adjust teaching appropriately (Alahmadi et al., 2019). According to Glazer (2014), formative assessment is generally defined as tasks that allow pupils to receive feedback on their performance during the course. In the classroom, teachers use assessments as a diagnostic tool at the termination of lessons or the termination of units. In addition, teachers can use assessments for teaching, by identifying student misconceptions and bridging gaps in learning through meaningful feedback (Dixson & Worrell, 2016). [11]

The current study extends the research on progress monitoring for young students by using an automated assessment tool that allows frequent tests in regular-education settings and provides educators with detailed information about students' skills. The primary goal of the study was to determine the adequacy of the newly-developed progress monitoring tool. First-grade students work independently on the short online tests, so that diagnostic information about students' performance and progress is obtained with minimal instructional time. The tool uses a combination of robust indicator and curriculum sampling approaches to comprehensively assess nine short measures of mathematic performance forming three competences. Static scores and longitudinal psychometric properties were investigated alongside feasibility and usefulness for instructional changes. 

First, with regard to reliability, the overall scores of the progress monitoring tests showed good internal consistencies within a narrow range. Consistencies of individual competence scoresparticularly Basic Precursors and Computationwere considerably lower. Low coefficients for Basic Precursors may be due to ceiling effects; Computation consistencies were larger for later tests, which may indicate that the three measures within the competence set are distinct skills at first. The distribution of difficulties (see Figure 2) contributes to this interpretation. Correlations between adjacent tests as a measure of delayed alternate-form reliability were strong, which indicates reliable assessment of students' performance despite the young age of the students. Increasing adjacent-test correlations after test 3 (see Table 6) argue that frequent tests are advantageous. 

Second, progress monitoring tests 1 to 4 were closely related to the paper pencil results and teacher ratings at the end of first and second grade (pp2 and pp3). Noteworthy is the stability of the predictions over time, which indicates that the progress monitoring tests in the first half of the school year assess skills particularly important for long-term mathematics success. Somewhat lower correlations between tests 5 to 8 and the standardised tests pp2 and pp3 may be becauseas indicated in Figure 2 some children showed ceiling effects at the end of the school year. Some ceiling effects are a desired result because test items are designed to represent end-of-year competence goals, which several students typically already reach earlier in the school year. Yet, reduced variance of progress monitoring tests is likely to result in a slight reduction of correlations with standardised measures of mathematical competence. [12]

One of the key findings in our review was the positive effects of differentiated instruction during or after formative assessment on reading achievement for K-12 students. This significant result is in accord with the findings from an influential U.S. data-driven reform model on state assessment program. Slavin et al. (2013) found that, for fifth-grade reading, those schools and teachers adjusting reading instruction produced educationally important gains in achievement, while others did not if they merely understood students' data without further action on instructional adjustment. Formative assessment was analogous to taking a patient's temperature, while differentiated instruction was analogous to providing a treatment (Slavin et al., 2013). 

In a study included in our review with a comparatively promising large effect size (d = + 0.63) on an early literacy program designed for students at-risk, the researchers concluded that "if one practices formative assessment seriously, one will necessarily end up differentiating instruction" (Brookhart et al., 2010, p. 50). In a recent review on formative assessment (Lee et al., 2020), the research team coded a similar moderator "instructional adjustment" and revealed no significant contrast between their four moderator variables: no adjustment, planned adjustment, unplanned adjustment and mixed. We assumed that the effects might be ameliorated if too many variables were coded which led to the insufficient numbers in each category. Additionally, in our own model, primarily we added professional development as a moderator. However, this moderator was highly correlated with "differentiated instruction." Meta-regression could not be computed due to the collinearity. It is worth mentioned, in our qualified studies, 94% (34/36) of the interventions embedded with differentiated instruction were coupled with professional development for teachers. The evidence in turn implied that professional development is vital in fostering high fidelity of implementing formative assessment on reading programs. [13]

Teachers who engage in formative classroom assessment using practices that accurately measure student learning should be better positioned to diagnose the instructional needs of their students and to act on that information. Although teachers spend 20% to 30% of their time engaged in some form of assessment (Barton & Coley, 1994), researchers have found that teachers lack expertise in sound assessment practices (Marso & Pigge, 1993;Haydel, Oescher, & Banbury, 1995;Plake & Impara, 1997). Aschbacher (1999) found that among sampled middle school teachers, only one quarter to one third had coherent assessments. Aschbacher defined coherence as the extent to which teachers aligned the learning task for students to their stated learning goals and the criteria used to evaluate students' work. Incoherent assessment practices likely signify an issue larger than a lack of understanding of best practices for measuring student learning. [14]

In conclusion, this systematic literature review highlights the practice and role of formative assessment resulting from the implementation of teaching and assessment conducted by teachers, students, and peers in the classroom. Formative assessment is defined as a systematic process to continuously gather evidence and provide feedback about learning while instruction is under way (CERI, 2008). Formative assessment can therefore be considered as a diagnostic method of assessing teaching and learning as it provides a platform for teachers and students to give and receive feedback before and during lessons. Formative assessment also allows teachers to monitor and guide students' performance over time in multiple problem-solving situations. Summative assessment, on the other hand, takes place after a period of instruction and requires making a judgment about the learning that occurred for example scoring a topical test or grading a monthly test paper. 

Scholars generally agree that formative assessment is the process of using information about students' learning on the course of instruction to make decisions to improve learning (see for example, Atkin et al., 2001;Black, 1993;Black et al., 2003;Black & Wiliam, 2004;Bell & Cowie, 2001;Harlen et al., 1992;Harlen & James, 1996;Shepard, 2000). How the process of formative assessment is conceptualised and implemented by teachers is varied accordingly, but all of the recently mentioned scholars agree that regular testing and simply informing students of their scores do not constitute formative assessment. Instead, according to Black et al. (2004), the evidence of student understanding (and learning) as a result of one round of the formative assessment process should be used to adapt the teaching work to meet learning needs. 

Reviews of research by Crooks (1988) have demonstrated that substantial learning gains are possible when teachers introduce formative assessment into their classroom practices. When teachers know how students are progressing and where they are having trouble, such information can be used to make necessary instructional adjustments, such as reteach, trying alternative instructional approaches, or offering more opportunities for practice. An essential feature of formative assessment is feedback. Black (1993) considers an assessment as formative when it provides feedback to students and teachers about the learning that is occurring, during the teaching and learning, not after the learning ends. Other researchers such as Clarke (2005) also agreed that feedback is seen to be the fundamental aspect of formative assessment interaction for the purpose to support learning. [16]

The use of formative assessment in classrooms is often described as a recursive feedback loop of instruction, assessment, analysis, and goal setting. Formative assessment practices are commonly informal and embedded in instruction, including observations, classroom discussions, short written assignments, exit slips, journals, interviews, question-answer activities, homework, quizzes, and tests, with data used to adjust instruction. Summative assessments are typically end-of-unit or end-of-term tests, report-card grades, or cumulative projects used for evaluation, accountability, and grading rather than during-learning adjustment. The usual counterfactual condition in core subjects like mathematics, reading, and science was most often a control or business-as-usual comparison: "standard/traditional methods (aka business-as-usual groups)" [34], "control group(s) using standard/traditional methods (aka business-as-usual groups)" [34], or a comparator described as "the typical district PD opportunities and no VMC" [35]. In mathematics, studies repeatedly compared formative assessment against summative assessment, state summative assessment scores, state-wide academic readiness assessment, or classrooms where teachers merely understood students' data without further instructional adjustment [5,6,13,20,21,36]. In reading, the counterfactual often was "intervention without differentiated instruction" or standard/traditional methods [13,34], and the meta-analysis noted that teachers' differentiated instruction was linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction [13]. In science, the comparator commonly was usual classroom instruction or usual PD, and one RCT explicitly reported "control teachers who only received in the typical district PD opportunities and no VMC" [35]. Another science paper noted that "the relationship between the two key aspects may influence science classroom practice" and that teachers have a generally positive perception about formative assessment but "teachers felt that formative assessment increases the amount of administrative work as the feedback has to be provided to each learner at regular intervals" [19]. Primary science papers also emphasized that formative decision-making is hard to enact because of "limited lesson time" and because primary science is often perceived to be of lower status than English and mathematics, meaning less time for both teaching and teacher professional learning [18].

Additional literature described the counterfactual or baseline classroom condition as routine instruction characterized by:

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

Formative assessment is defined repeatedly across sources as a classroom practice where evidence of student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers to inform teaching and improve learning [2, 3, 15, 20, 24, 29, 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39]. One source states: “Practice in a classroom is formative to the extent that evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers, to make decisions about the next steps in instruction that are likely to be better, or better founded, than the decisions they would have taken in the absence of the evidence that was elicited” [3, 15, 20, 24, 29, 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39]. Another source states formative assessment is “a systematic process to continuously gather evidence and provide feedback about learning while instruction is under way” and “can therefore be considered as a diagnostic method of assessing teaching and learning as it provides a platform for teachers and students to give and receive feedback before and during lessons” [15]. Another source states it is “a classroom practice that has been suggested as a possible way to support student motivation” and that “implementing high-quality formative assessment is associated with challenges and barriers to overcome” [2].

A recurring framework is Black and Wiliam / Wiliam and Thompson / Black and Wiliam (2009), with repeated practical strategies including clarifying learning intentions / sharing learning objectives / criteria for success, gathering evidence through questioning, discussions, short written tests, quizzes, and assignments, providing feedback that moves learners forward, activating students as instructional resources for one another, and activating students as owners of their own learning [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 10, 11, 15, 17, 19, 20, 21, 24, 30, 32, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39]. One source lists the five key strategies as: “1. Clarifying and sharing learning intentions and criteria for success, 2. Engineering effective classroom discussions and other learning tasks that elicit evidence of student understanding, 3. Providing feedback that moves learners forward, 4. Activating students as instructional resources for one another, and 5. Activating students as the owners of their own learning” [4, 10, 21, 24, 29, 33, 38]. Another source states formative assessment “can also be considered as a set of elements (questioning, self-assessment, peer-assessment, quality formative feedback, and reflection) that helps in eliciting students’ responses, interpreting their responses and based on the evidence adjusting classroom instruction and improve students learning” [4]. Another source states: “The assessment for learning takes place ‘with feedback rotations to ensure that students receive tips to review their learning and move on’” [17].

**Classroom strategies observed across sources**

1. **Questioning / classroom dialogue / Socratic questioning / strategic questioning**
   - Teachers may use “classroom questioning (100%)” [2].
   - Teachers may use “teacher questioning practices” [1].
   - Teachers may use “teacher questioning in the classroom, conferences, or any other mechanism that gives him/her useful information for planning and teaching” [17].
   - Teachers may use “classroom dialogue or short written tests” [3, 15].
   - Teachers may use “the Socratic questioning or other evidence-eliciting techniques” [15].
   - Teachers may use “dialogical and strategic questioning” as an “effective formative assessment practice” [8].
   - Teachers may use questioning “to collect data about student learning but also as a vehicle for coregulation where they further prompted students to extend and explain their thinking” [8].
   - Teachers may use questioning techniques to “assess student comprehension” and “identify misunderstandings” [5].
   - In science education, “questioning strategies that elicit evidence of student learning” and “feedback loops during questioning” were among the ten dimensions examined [15].
   - One study notes that “teachers may use portfolios, journals, rubrics, checklists, graphic organisers, written reports, the Socratic questioning or other evidence-eliciting techniques” [15].

2. **Quizzes / short quizzes / mini-assessments / periodic testing / informal quizzes**
   - “periodic testing (84%)” was among the most commonly used tools [2].
   - “informal quizzes or mini-assessments” are named as effective strategies in interactive lectures [5].
   - These may include “short quizzes, concept checks, or quick polls” [5].
   - “short written tests” are repeatedly mentioned as a teacher-gathered evidence source [3, 10, 17, 24].
   - Formative assessment may be “in the form of questioning, discussion, quizzes, assignment, homework, or observation of students’ present work” [10].
   - “Formative assessments are used throughout the learning process to gauge student understanding and identify areas for improvement. They can take the form of quizzes, class discussions, or project checkpoints” [7].
   - “Formative assessments at the basic education includes a range of strategies such as classroom discussions and quizzes designed to generate feedback on student performance” [16].
   - One source states regular formative assessments “may be questions, tasks, quizzes or more formal assessments” [16].
   - One study compared a “matching quiz and half-minute paper” as formative assessment tools and explicitly states it is “quasi-experimental research” [11].

3. **Exit tickets**
   - “Exit ticket statements of teachers in step 2” were used as feedback in a participatory study [7].
   - “exit-tickets” were a key strategy in online / day-to-day assessment practice [18].
   - “exit tickets” are described as a formative assessment tool that allows teachers to “gauge the effectiveness of their instruction and identify areas that may need reteaching” [12].
   - “exit tickets” were among the most useful “short cycle assessments embedded within instruction to inform subsequent teaching steps” [18].
   - One paper notes that “The implementation of formative assessment as a completion of the formative assessment cycle following gathering and assessing learning evidence and providing the feedback” [19].
   - The general web summary also lists exit tickets as a classroom strategy used to check understanding at the end of class [25].

4. **Peer assessment / peer feedback / peer-assisted learning / peer review**
   - “peer-assessment” and “peer-assessment feedback” are explicitly recurring terms [1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 24, 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39].
   - A review found the “three subthemes” of assessment diversity were “i) teacher assessment; ii) peer-assessment; and iii) self-assessment” [1].
   - “Peer-assessment Feedback: − Correct and accurate feedback ... formative feedback ... positive feedback ... and verbal feedback” [1].
   - “Feedback methods consist of tailoring feedback as well as providing feedback” [1].
   - “Teachers conduct assessments by providing feedback to low-achieving students” [1].
   - “Group work activities” include peers helping each other complete assignments and understand the task [1].
   - “High-achieving students help each other with their low-performing peers with activities planned with the teacher” [1].
   - “Students may support each other’s learning through peer-assessment and subsequent peer-feedback” [3].
   - Peer feedback may involve “providing explanations and suggestions to peers on how they can act to reach their learning goals” [3].
   - Peer assessment can be used to “activate students as instructional resources for one another” [24].
   - In one survey, peer assessment was used by only “24%” of teachers [2].
   - Peer feedback was used in online / digital contexts and “the number of grade-giving and -receiving activities” was studied [13].
   - One source states “peer assessment and success criteria have a significant positive impact on the development of metacognitive skills in the teachers” [10].
   - Another source notes “peer assessment (28%) and peer assessment (24%) are utilized less frequently” in some settings [2].
   - The review on peer feedback states it can contribute to “the development of learners capable of self and shared regulation of metacognition” [14].
   - Another source states “peer-and self-assessment were least evident in classroom practice, compared to the other AfL strategies studied” [23].

5. **Self-assessment / self-evaluation / self-reflection / self-feedback**
   - “self-assessment” is repeatedly named as a core strategy [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 11, 15, 16, 17, 18, 20, 21, 24, 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39].
   - One source states “A test question instrument, where the students can self-assess each concept, they learned” [1].
   - Self-assessment was “one of the most commonly used activities in the classroom” [9].
   - It is defined as “the act of observing, analyzing, and evaluating a student’s own performance based on criteria and determining how to improve it” [9].
   - One source says self-assessment helps students “to regulate their own learning and get motivated by identifying their own strengths and weaknesses” [4].
   - Another says self-assessment “encourages self-reflection and metacognition, allowing students to monitor their own progress, identify their strengths and weaknesses, and set improvement goals” [5].
   - One survey found self-assessment was used by only “28%” of teachers [2].
   - A structured tool was used to “stimulate SRL skills and to assist students’ learning, particularly in the context of tutorial PBL” [26].
   - The same source says integrating self-assessment tools can “cultivate self-regulated learners ... by stimulating self-reflection, providing structure for self-monitoring of learning, enhancing tutorial performance, and highlighting the importance of external feedback” [26].
   - It also says self-assessment with tutor feedback can “mitigate common self-assessment biases” and “align their self-perceptions with their actual performance” [26].
   - Another source states self-assessment can be quite diverse but the “fundamental idea is to reflect about one’s own work” [20].

**Proposed instructional mechanisms linking formative assessment to improved learning**

Across sources, the proposed mechanisms include eliciting evidence of learning, diagnosing misconceptions and knowledge gaps, adapting instruction/pacing, providing actionable feedback, supporting self-regulation and metacognition, scaffolding student agency, and enabling co-regulation [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 24, 26, 29, 30, 31, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39].

- **Eliciting misconceptions / prior knowledge / learning gaps**
  - Formative assessment “provides information teachers, and students can use to plan and enhance upcoming educational activities” [4].
  - “Formative assessment could provide more information about students’ understanding and misconceptions” [10].
  - Diagnostic tests “are essential for informing instructional planning and tailoring teaching strategies to meet the needs of all students” [12].
  - Diagnostic assessments “enable teachers to address misconceptions and support personalised learning” [12].
  - Teachers “find out students’ prior knowledge and learning gaps” [16].
  - One source states that assessment “gives teachers feedback to help them enhance the teaching and learning process” [4].
  - Another source says classroom activities provide “the granular information needed to guide instruction” [18].

- **Adapting pacing / instruction / next steps**
  - Teachers use evidence “to make decisions about the next steps in instruction” [3, 15, 24, 29, 30, 33, 36, 37, 38, 39].
  - The approach is used to “adjust current instruction to improve students’ achievement of expected instructional results” [11].
  - Teachers can “reteach, trying alternative instructional approaches, or offering more opportunities for practice” [15].
  - Teachers can “modify teaching and learning activities” [2, 19].
  - Teachers “adjust their methods” [5].
  - Teachers can “regulate feedback and interventions to attain the learning objectives” [10].
  - Teachers can “provide ongoing feedback” and “complete the formative assessment cycle” [19].
  - Formative assessment is “a continuous cycle of activities or events” [10].
  - “The assessment for learning takes place ‘with feedback rotations to ensure that students receive tips to review their learning and move on’” [17].
  - One source explicitly states formative assessment is used to “adapt feedback or subsequent learning activities to the students’ knowledge, skills and learning needs identified in these assessments” [2, 3].
  - Another states “teachers could select from the formative assessment strategies prescribed by the university and have the flexibility to adjust the proportions of each assessment strategy in the whole formative assessment” [2].

- **Supporting metacognition, self-regulation, autonomous learning**
  - Formative assessment is “closely” aligned with self-regulated learning (SRL) [2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 20, 26, 29].
  - It encourages students to “set learning goals, monitor their progress, and act on feedback from teachers and peers” [2].
  - Students “select different learning strategies, implement the strategies, and then reflect on the extent to which their strategies allowed them to attain their learning goals” [9].
  - “Metacognition and self-regulation are related concepts; students need to be able to think about their learning and understand their cognitive processes (metacognition) in order to regulate their behaviors” [9, 20].
  - Formative assessment “serves as both a tool and a catalyst for developing lifelong learning skills” [2].
  - Students can “take ownership of their learning” [4, 17, 24, 33, 38].
  - Students “can better understand the learning conditions including the expectations while also providing them with a sense of agency” [9].
  - Students “can better understand the learning conditions” and “provide them with a sense of agency” [9].
  - Self-assessment with tutor feedback “boosts internal factors such as student motivation and metacognitive awareness” [26].
  - A student-centered framework supports “goal setting, metacognitive awareness, and habitual reflection” [26].
  - A source states formative assessment “can support student motivation” [2] and that “self-regulation strategy repertoire” can be developed through formative assessment [6].
  - Another source states formative assessment “helps students learn by making them actively involved in the assessment process” [21].
  - One source says peer feedback contributes to “self and shared regulation of metacognition” [14].

- **Co-regulation / purposeful interaction**
  - “The process of formative assessment can be facilitated by the teacher or by the students” [9].
  - Teachers need to “explicitly design a co-regulatory process that guides students in this regulatory process” [7].
  - “Actively involving teachers in explicating expected students and teacher co-regulatory behavior” was “helpful in elevating teachers’ practical knowledge on coregulatory formative assessment in the classroom” [7].
  - Formative assessment and co-regulation have “shared purposes including the need for students to be active agents in the learning process” [8].
  - Shared purpose also includes “the aim to extend and scaffold student thinking” [8].
  - Teachers and ECEs “observed and listened to students frequently” and “remained ready to step in and co-regulate when students struggled” [8].
  - “Questioning, prompting, and dialogic assessment” were used to develop students’ self-regulation [8].
  - Another source states formative assessment may facilitate co-regulation, “however, much of the literature ... has focused on how formative assessment can be used to promote the development of self-regulation” [8].

- **Feedback literacy / evaluation literacy**
  - Formative feedback helps students “enhance their work and learning strategies by making sense of information from their teacher and their peers” [4].
  - “Students need to be trained on how to receive feedback from their teachers and peers and give quality formative feedback to their peers” [4].
  - The use of formative assessment can help “students’ assessment and feedback literacy” [23].
  - Self-assessment practices now emphasize “self-feedback,” “internal feedback,” and “feedback literacy” [20].

**Implementation features across subjects and grade levels**

- **Frequency**
  - Formative assessment may occur “throughout the teaching and learning process” [1, 15].
  - It may take place “at any point within a course or module” [30].
  - “Formative assessments are conducted periodically throughout different terms, such as instructional unit, course, semester, or year” [11].
  - “Formative assessment takes place on a day-to-day basis during teaching and learning” [16].
  - “Formative assessments were not documented or consistently used by teachers in this study” [18].
  - “Most teachers used short cycle assessments embedded within instruction” [18].
  - “Feedback rotations” and repeated feedback during lessons are noted [17].

- **Specificity of feedback**
  - Effective feedback is described as “specific, concrete, and promote a change in learning for students” [18].
  - Feedback may be “correct and accurate,” “formative,” “positive,” or “verbal” [1].
  - Feedback may be “descriptive” and “forward-focused” [2, 3, 20, 24, 29].
  - Teachers may provide “only general feedback” or feedback like “good job” and check marks [9, 18].
  - One source notes “feedback can be quick and immediate” using communication technology [22].
  - Another source notes “timely and specific feedback” supports learning and active participation [5].
  - Another source notes feedback is effective when it is “directly after the assessment” [30].
  - “The provision of effective feedback to pupils” is a central factor [17, 24].
  - “Feedback loops during questioning” and “individualised descriptive feedback” are explicit dimensions of formative assessment practice [15].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

### 1) Overall K–12 evidence: umbrella review of meta-analyses
The umbrella review titled **“A Systematic Review of Meta-Analyses on the Impact of Formative Assessment on K-12 Students’ Learning: Toward Sustainable Quality Education”** found that formative assessment in K-12 education has been a notable teaching and learning focus area in schools over the last 20 years, as evidenced by numerous recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses investigating and summarizing the evidence for formative assessments’ effectiveness and sustainability. The umbrella review systematically reviews meta-analyses investigating the effects of formative assessment on learning, summarizes the current findings, and assesses the quality and risk of bias in the published meta-analyses. Meta-analyses were identified using systematic literature searches in Scopus, ERIC, Academic Research Complete, ProQuest, APA PsycArticles, SPORTDiscus, Web of Science, and Humanities International Complete. Thirteen meta-analyses, each of which examined the effects of formative assessment on learning in K-12 students, were included in this umbrella review. The review considered evidence for the potential effectiveness of using formative assessment in class with primary and secondary school students. Formative assessment was found to produce trivial to large positive effects on student learning, with no negative effects identified. The magnitude of effects varied according to the type of formative assessment. The 13 included meta-analysis studies showed moderate (n = 10), high (n = 1), and low (n = 2) methodological quality (AMSTAR-2), although the robustness of the evidence (i.e., GRADE analysis) was very low (n = 9), low (n = 3), and moderate (n = 1). These findings offer valuable insights for designing and implementing different types of formative assessment aimed at optimizing student learning and ensuring the sustainability of assessment practices. However, the low-to-very-low certainty of the available evidence precludes robust recommendations regarding optimal formative assessment strategies for learning in K-12 students. [1]

The web search snippet for the same article repeated that: **“Thirteen meta-analyses, each of which examined the effects of formative assessment on learning in K-12 students, were included in this umbrella review.”** It also stated that the review’s overarching objective was to systematically review and assess available meta-analyses investigating formative assessment-based strategies or interventions on student achievement and learning within primary and secondary school settings; address methodological approaches used and robustness and credibility of the meta-analytical evidence; and identify current limitations and suggest areas for further research. The same snippet also repeated that formative assessment was found to produce trivial to large positive effects on student learning, with no negative effects identified. [1]

### 2) K–12 reading achievement meta-analysis
The meta-analysis **“The effectiveness of formative assessment for enhancing reading achievement in K-12 classrooms: A meta-analysis”** reported that, without publication bias, formative assessment is making a positive and modest difference in enhancing students’ reading achievement in diverse settings. The average weighted effect over all included studies was **0.19**. The exact size a researcher finds may deviate considerably depending on the sample size, teachers’ differentiated instruction and type of intervention. Studies involving a large sample size with over **250 students** led to low and attenuated estimate of formative assessment. The implementation of teachers’ differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction. Also, the results suggested that collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers. Findings suggest that teachers are strongly encouraged to adjust their reading instruction in terms of content, process and product catering to student diversity, with effective components that facilitate differentiated instruction and professional development. [2]

The abstract for the same meta-analysis stated that this quantitative synthesis included **48 qualified studies** with a total sample of **116,051 K-12 students**. It also stated that formative assessment generally had a positive though modest effect (**ES = + 0.19**) on students’ reading achievement. Meta-regression results revealed that: (a) studies with **250 or less students** yielded significantly larger effect size than large sample studies, (b) formative assessment embedded with differentiated instruction equated to an increase of **0.13 SD** in the reading achievement score, and (c) integration of teacher and student directed assessment was more effective than assessments initiated by teachers. The subgroup analysis indicated that effect sizes were significantly different between Confucian-heritage culture and Anglophone culture and had divergent effective features. The result cautions against the generalization of formative assessment across different cultures without adaptation. [2]

The same review also stated limitations: it merely focused on the quantitative measurement of reading achievement; there is much to learn from non-experimental studies that can interpret the effects of formative assessment on students’ reading; the review centered on a standardized test of reading achievement; other outcomes may be of great value to policymakers and practitioners; and student-directed assessment is often referred to peer-or selfassessment, but the qualified studies in this meta-analysis only include self-assessment. [2]

A related snippet from the same paper stated: the types of intervention result indicated that an integration of teacher-directed and student-directed would be more effective than formative assessment in reading program directed by teacher or student alone in K-12 settings. In a previous meta-analysis, other-directed formative assessment that encompassed educators or computer software programs was more effective than student-directed formative assessment. They included nine studies in their review, six of which were designed for students with special education needs. These participants might be less capable of making self-or peer-directed formative assessment. In the present review, a more holistic picture was depicted for general population was obtained advocating an integrated usage of teacher-directed and student-directed assessment. [2]

The same snippet further stated: integrating teacher and student in formative assessment might be more effective than teacher-or student-directed assessment to enhance students’ reading achievement. It offered a caveat that this was not a “one size fits all” suggestion from screening studies in Anglophone and Confucian heritage cultures. It also stated that reading is a comprehension-based subject that requires explicit instruction necessitated by teachers’ guidance and that feedback messages require students’ active construction on deciphering with the help of teachers. [2]

Another snippet from the same article stated that a previous review of 13 of over 300 studies in grades K-12 found moderator analyses showing that formative assessment effect sizes in English language arts (**ES = + 0.32**) were larger than in mathematics (**ES = + 0.17**) and science (**ES = + 0.09**). The snippet also noted that one of the marked flaws threatening that conclusion was study retrieval and selection approach, explaining the paucity of the research base. [2]

The same paper’s introduction stated that Black and Wiliam (1998) reported that effect sizes of formative assessment of student achievements were between **0.4 and 0.7** ranging over age groups from **5-year-olds to university undergraduates**. It also stated that the impact of teachers’ formative evaluation on student achievement was ranked third with an effect size of **0.9** in **138 learning activities** influencing student achievement (Hattie, 2009). [2]

The same paper’s rationale for the present review stated that existing subject-based reviews had covered mathematics, writing, and science, but not reading. It framed the review questions as: (1) What is the effect size of formative assessment on K-12 reading programs? and (2) What study and research features moderate the effects of formative assessment interventions on student reading achievement? [2]

### 3) Teacher-directed, student-directed, and combined interventions; differentiation and professional development
The same K-12 reading meta-analysis explicitly identified several implementation moderators and tradeoffs. It found that studies with **250 or less students** yielded significantly larger effect size than large sample studies; the effects of formative assessment embedded with differentiated instruction equated to an increase of **0.13 SD** in the reading achievement score; and integration of teacher and student directed assessment was more effective than assessments initiated by teachers. [2]

It also stated that **94% (34/36)** of the interventions embedded with differentiated instruction were coupled with professional development for teachers. The evidence in turn implied that professional development is vital in fostering high fidelity of implementing formative assessment on reading programs. [2]

The same article stated that the exact size may deviate depending on sample size, teachers’ differentiated instruction, and type of intervention. It also stated that the implementation of teachers’ differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction and that collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers. [2]

### 4) General K–12 review article on formative assessment practice
The review **“A Systematic Review on factors influencing teachers’ intentions and implementations regarding formative assessment”** stated that formative assessment enables teachers to monitor students’ progress and activates students to self-regulate their learning. It stated that formative assessment has been recognised as a beneficial strategy to promote students’ learning and achievement in different circumstances. It also cited Gikandi et al.’s review study suggesting that formative assessment can enhance the active cognitive engagement of students and facilitate their understanding of learning contents. It cited Li (2016) as finding that formative assessment had a positive relation with students’ PISA reading achievement, mediated by teacher-student relationship and attitude towards reading. Furthermore, formative assessment can also help to reduce the achievement gaps among students. As Black and Wiliam (1998) mentioned, **“improved formative assessment helps low achievers more than other students and so reduces the range of achievement while raising achievement overall”** (p. 141). The benefits of formative assessment manifested in research studies have made it an important agenda in educational reform all round the world although the effects vary widely among different implementations and student populations. [3]

### 5) Secondary school systematic review: themes, assessment diversity, and low-achieving students
The systematic review **“A systematic review on the formative assessment practice in teaching and learning in secondary school”** reported that the first theme is the diversity of assessments. The three subthemes under this first theme were: i) teacher assessment; ii) peer-assessment; and iii) self-assessment. The diversity of assessment in the classroom suggests that AfL has three agent roles: teacher, student, and peer. In general, teachers play a role as educators and assessors in teaching to encourage the development of student learning with the support of student and peer involvement in the classroom. The review further stated specific practices: teacher records the objectives and lists the activities that support the achievement of those objectives; teachers explain the criteria of learning in the context from the beginning to the teaching part; peer-assessment feedback includes correct and accurate feedback, formative feedback, positive feedback, and verbal feedback; feedback methods consist of tailoring feedback as well as providing feedback; teachers conduct assessments by providing feedback to low-achieving students; teachers questioning practices were also practiced as a measure to assess their students; follow-up action on teacher feedback was also implemented by teachers; group work activities included peers helping each other with tasks and understanding; and self-assessment used a test question instrument, where the students can self-assess each concept they learned. [4]
