**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

The search process produced a broad set of findings related to formative assessment, subgroup effects, English learner status, disability status, prior achievement, progress monitoring, feedback, and related instructional/assessment contexts. Several outputs are directly relevant; many are adjacent but still informative for the research thread.

### Formative assessment overall effects and subgroup/moderator findings

A meta-analysis found that formative assessment generally has a positive but modest effect on reading achievement in K-12 contexts. The review reported: “without publication bias, formative assessment is making a positive and modest difference in enhancing students' reading achievement in diverse settings. The average weighted effect over all included studies was 0.19.” It also stated that “the exact size a researcher finds may deviate considerably depending on the sample size, teachers' differentiated instruction and type of intervention.” Studies involving “a large sample size with over 250 students led to low and attenuated estimate of formative assessment,” while “the implementation of teachers' differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction.” The review further reported that “collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers” [1]. The same review’s abstract stated that it included “48 qualified studies with a total sample of 116,051 K-12 students,” and that the “effect sizes of formative assessment intervention on reading were significantly different between Confucian-heritage culture and Anglophone culture and had divergent effective features” [1]. In the body of the same paper, subgroup analysis was described as yielding “significant differences in effect sizes that were from seven moderators: grade level, type of intervention, program duration, differentiated instruction, sample size, publication type and cultural setting,” while “the effect sizes comparisons of subcategories in rest three moderators, student characteristics, digital technology and research design were non-significant” [1]. In meta-regression, only three pairs were significant: “small sample size studies yielded a significantly larger effect size (d = 0.33, p < 0.001) than large sample studies”; “formative assessment only engaged by teachers had a significantly smaller effect size than integrating teacher and students' assessment in the intervention for reading (d = -0.12, p < 0.001), whereas, student-directed assessment (selfassessment) showed no significant difference (d = 0.03, p = 0.769)”; and “If a teacher adopted differentiated or individualized instruction during or after formative assessment, students' reading achievement would be significantly higher than those of their peers taught by a teacher only applied formative assessment (d = 0.13, p < 0.001). When formative assessment was directed by the student, the effect size on reading achievement was larger than formative assessment with teachers' differentiated instruction, albeit not significantly (d = 0.17, p = 0.124)” [1].

A different meta-analysis of formative assessment practices on student learning in Turkey reported “32 studies with 47 effect sizes” and an “overall mean effect size of .72” [2]. It said subgroup analysis examined whether the mean effect size was influenced by “features of formative assessment interventions, education level, and publication type” [2]. A separate summary of the same study indicated that “the feedback from the students had the largest effect but the feedback from the computers had the smallest effect on student learning” and that “Moderator analysis showed that the effect sizes made a significant difference as to different types of formative feedback” [2]. Another snippet from that study stated that the main purpose was “to provide a synthesis of the experimental and quasi-experimental studies about the effectiveness of formative assessment practices on student learning in Turkey,” and that “in addition to the effectiveness of formative assessment in each education level from primary to tertiary, features of formative assessment interventions and publication types were also examined as moderator variables” [2]. Another extracted passage from the same paper stated: “The overall mean effect size of the study was obtained as .72 ( SE = .07, p < .05 )” and that “the effect size was not statistically related to grade level, types of formative feedback, or study quality” in prior studies cited by the authors [2].

A systematic review / meta-analysis on formative assessment in K-12 reading reported: “This review has revealed that, without publication bias, formative assessment is making a positive and modest difference in enhancing students' reading achievement in diverse settings. The average weighted effect over all included studies was 0.19” [1]. It also stated that “Studies involving a large sample size with over 250 students led to low and attenuated estimate of formative assessment” [1]. Another search snippet for the same review stated: “The implementation of teachers' differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction” and “our results suggested that collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers” [1].

A review on formative assessment in elementary school student academic achievement from IES indicated that the team identified “23 studies that it determined had been conducted rigorously enough to have confidence that the formative assessment interventions caused the observed effects on student outcomes,” and that “Overall, formative assessment had a positive effect on student academic achievement” [3]. Another source from IES relayed a table of effect sizes and subgroup information, including student-directed formative assessment interventions and specific study designs, but the extracted table content is not directly tied to the subgroup question beyond showing that effects vary by domain and intervention type [4].

A separate paper on formative assessment and growth mindset found that formative assessment practices were modeled as “sharing learning progressions, providing feedback, and instructional adjustments,” and that in the English-speaking sample “growth mindset on reading achievement” had “ß = .20, SE = 1.39, p < .001” while “sharing learning progressions had direct negative and significant relation with reading achievement (ß = -.11, SE = 2.79, p < .001), while instructional adjustments had direct positive and significant relation with reading achievement (ß = .14, SE = 2.99, p < .05)” [5]. In the Confucian sample, “Two formative assessment strategies showed significant and positive relation with growth mindset: sharing learning progressions (ß = .07, SE = .05, p < .001), and providing feedback (ß = .06, SE = .05, p < .001),” while “instructional adjustments had direct positive and significant relation with reading achievement (ß = .14, SE = 1.78, p < .05), while providing feedback had direct negative and significant relation with reading achievement (ß = -.09, SE = 1.43, p < .001)” [5]. This study is relevant because it explicitly compares contexts and includes formative assessment strategy variation, though it does not address EL or disability subgroup moderation directly [5].

A study on intrinsic motivation in primary school mathematics instruction notes that differential effects are of particular interest and that “differential effects at the edges of the achievement spectrum seem conceivable” [6]. It states that research on student achievement has shown “differential effects in favor of high-achieving children,” “in favor of low-achieving children,” and that some reviews “did not find evidence for differential effects regarding different classroom types” [6]. It also says, “The limited research base nevertheless does not allow us to formulate directed hypotheses about the differential effectiveness of FA” [6].

A state-wide mathematics support program study said formative assessment “has a positive impact on the whole group of students,” while also reporting that “Phelan et al. (2011) report findings that students with higher pretest scores benefited especially from the formative assessment” and “Other studies show that formative assessment is an effective means for low-achieving students” [7]. It further reports Kingston and Nash meta-analysis effects by subject: “higher effect on English language arts, d = .32, than on mathematics, d = .17, or science, d = .09” [7].

A paper on teachers’ perceptions and use of formative assessment in mathematics stated that formative assessment “correlates positively with student achievement,” and cited that an analysis of 23 studies showed students who participated in formative assessment “performed better on measures of academic achievement than those who did not” [8]. It also said formative assessment in mathematics had larger effects than in reading and writing, and that both student-directed and teacher-directed formative assessment were effective in mathematics [8]. The paper also noted “Early recognition of and response to learner needs through formative assessment analysis has been found to be important in preventing struggling elementary students from falling further behind their peers” [8].

A paper on automatic formative assessment for adaptive teaching defines formative assessment and describes it as part of adaptive teaching; it says “Some of the strategies for adaptive teaching are formative assessment, feedback and self-regulated learning” [9]. It also includes Black and Wiliam’s definition: “Practice in a classroom is formative to the extent that evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used by teachers, learners, or their peers, to make decisions about the next steps in instruction that are likely to be better, or better founded, than the decisions they would have taken in the absence of the evidence that was elicited” [9].

A conceptual paper on formative assessment and feedback in a multicultural classroom reviewed databases and set inclusion criteria around “formative feedback” and “ethnic or culture,” and explicitly excluded or filtered out studies only tangentially related to formative feedback and culture [10]. It is relevant to the broader theme of subgroup/cultural moderation, but no quantitative subgroup results were extracted.

A systematic review on formative assessment in inclusive mathematics education in secondary schools concluded that “Formative assessment is a way to individualize learning and tailor instruction to learners’ specific needs” and that there is “little known about how the benefits of formative assessment can be achieved in inclusive secondary mathematics education, with its heterogeneous learning groups” [11]. It found that “diagnostics must be highly individualized while considering contextual factors to be accurate; second, teachers should be advised on how to proceed with the diagnosed issues; and, finally, teachers should provide their students with frequent, easily accessible feedback” [11].

A paper on formative feedback in special school classrooms with e-books stated that “e-books can facilitate the process of formative assessment and support the needs of students at special schools through eliciting responses from various students, providing immediate feedback to students, facilitate classroom interaction, offer chance(s) for peer assessment, and allow teachers to reward positive behaviours of students with special education needs” [12]. It also said e-books could help students by providing materials “appropriate at their own levels” and supporting assessment with “audio and video aids” [12].

A short conceptual piece on formative assessment in mathematics concluded that formative assessment is “highly effective,” with continuous feedback helping students understand learning objectives, address weaknesses, and enhance motivation, selfregulation, and conceptual understanding [13]. It recommended alignment between learning objectives, activities, and formative assessment designs, and stated that formative assessments should “accommodate the individual needs of students, including those with varying learning styles or paces” [13].

A paper on formative assessment strategies in higher education states that formative assessment “has the potential to reduce performance gaps between different groups of students by offering personalized and adaptive support that meets individual needs” [14]. It also says self-assessment promotes self-reflection and self-management of learning [14].

A paper on continuous assessment in Ethiopian universities argued that “Feedback systems should be structured to guide teachers on which students require further review and support, and which ones are prepared to advance to more challenging tasks” and that “the feedback culture should go to the level of identifying individual students' progress so that students learn based on their pace and performance” [15].

### English learner status, disability status, and combined EL/disability issues

Several sources directly address English learners, special education, and disability identification or intervention, which are highly relevant to subgroup effects by English learner status and disability status.

A paper on progress monitoring of language acquisition and academic content for English learners states that effective assessment and systematic progress monitoring is particularly important when planning instruction for English learners “to ensure equitable, culturally responsive, and linguistically accessible instruction” [16]. It says ELs “face the challenge of simultaneously learning a second language and academic content,” that they often require linguistic accommodations during instruction and assessment, and that “systematic progress monitoring (PM) of academic and linguistic skill acquisition is critical when making instructional decisions for this group of students” [16]. The article further notes that “This article offers educators considerations regarding the use of PM to inform instruction of ELs, especially those who experience learning difficulties” [16].

A systematic review / report on “Reading Interventions to Support English Learners with Disabilities in High School” found that “all studies reported largely positive effects on improving students’ reading outcomes” but that it is “difficult to draw a firm conclusion about effective reading interventions for high school ELs with disabilities because of the limited number of studies, small sample sizes of ELs with disabilities, few disability categories represented, and lack of stand-alone reading interventions” [17]. The review’s method used ERIC, PsycINFO, Education Source Ultimate, and Academic Search Ultimate for the period from 1975 to July 2024 [17].

A paper on “Understanding and Supporting Literacy Development Among English Learners” states that the intersection of EL and special education status remains underresearched despite the documented misidentification of ELs in special education, and gives a statistic: “50% of ELs with disabilities have a specific learning disability compared with 38% of non-ELs (U.S. Department of Education, 2014Education, -2015))” [18]. It also says “Specific learning disability subsumes language-based and other learning disabilities that do not fit into other special education categories, including reading comprehension difficulties” [18].

A paper on “Progress Monitoring of Language Acquisition and Academic Content for English Learners” likewise emphasizes that ELs are a diverse population, that they “often require the use of linguistic accommodations during instruction and assessment,” and that they “consistently lag behind their native-speaking peers” in reading and math [16].

A paper on “Evidence-based reading interventions for English language learners: A multilevel meta-analysis” reported that “the overall mean effect size of reading interventions of ELLs yielded an effect size of 0.653” [19]. It also said “there were no differences between ELLs and their peers who spoke English as a first language in reading intervention outcomes or growth intervention” in a cited study, and that “For students’ socioeconomic status (SES), there was no significant difference between the low-middle group and the nonresponse group” [19]. The same paper stated that “interventions that focused on improving reading comprehension and listening comprehension obtained better effects than other reading outcomes,” and that “strategy instruction was statistically significant for improving the reading skills of ELLs” [19].

A paper on “Reading Achievement of English Learners Who Participated in the Response to Intervention Model” said RTI is designed to “assist all students, identify learning disabilities early, and prevent the failure of struggling learners,” and that there are “relatively few studies that show a relationship between RTI and English Language Learners (ELs)” [20]. It explained that ELs are often grouped with English Only students in reading intervention groups and have not been studied separately [20]. It also states that “Review of the CST scores for EL students over two years indicated a significant relationship between EL student participation in RTI and reading achievement” [20].

A paper on “Examining Bridges in Mathematics and Differential Effects among English Language Learners” was surfaced in ERIC search results [21]. The search snippet says the study used “a quasi-experimental design (difference-in-differences) to examine the impact of a standards-based elementary mathematics curriculum,” and that “Examining effectiveness heterogeneity is also crucial to better understanding mathematics achievement among English language learners (ELLs)” [21]. No further extracted quantitative subgroup results were available in the raw output.

A paper on “Differential Returns to Academic Preparation for English Learners: Evidence from New York City” was surfaced in ERIC search results [22]. Its abstract snippet says it uses longitudinal data from New York City “(n = 178,155)” and tests interactions between middle school preparation “in the form of math achievement and advanced math and science coursework” and subgroups of ELs [22]. No full result details were extracted in the raw output.

A paper on “Formative Information Using Student Growth Percentiles for the Quantification of English Language Learners' Progress in Language Acquisition” surfaced in ERIC search results [23]. Its abstract snippet indicates the article focuses on creating systems that more effectively measure ELL progress across years and on “student growth percentiles” for progress in language acquisition [23]. No effect sizes were provided in the raw output.

A paper on “The Effect of Embedding Formative Assessment on Pupil Attainment” surfaced in ERIC search results [24]. Its abstract snippet says it is “a randomized trial conducted in 140 English secondary schools” and explores how formative assessment can operate when embedded as standard practice [24]. No subgroup results were extracted.

A paper on “Implementation of Formative Assessment--Effects of Quality of Programme Delivery on Students' Mathematics Achievement and Interest” also surfaced in ERIC search results [25]. Its abstract snippet says “Teachers (n = 17) implemented formative assessment in their ninth-grade mathematics classes and provided their students (n = 426) with written process-oriented f...” [25]. No subgroup results were extracted.

A paper on “The Effect of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Learning: A Meta-Analysis Study” was listed in ERIC search results and also surfaced from Semantic Scholar enrichment [2,26]. The ERIC abstract said 32 studies with 47 effect sizes and noted that “using true experimental or quasi-experimental design” was a criterion [26]. The Semantic Scholar abstract said the same study had “32 studies with 47 effect sizes” and overall mean effect size .72 [2]. No subgroup findings by EL or disability status were extracted from the raw output.

A paper on “A Randomized Experiment of a Cognitive Strategies Approach to Text-Based Analytical Writing for Mainstreamed Latino English Language Learners in Grades 6 to 12” reported “A total of 961 ELs participated across seven studies” with “a range of 75 to 351 participants per study (Mean = 137.3, SD = 96.4)” [27]. It also reports a positive effect size of “.35” on an on-demand assessment of analytical writing and references a prior quasi-experimental study with effect size “.34” [27]. It includes a follow-up analysis with treatment-by-grade interactions, but the extracted snippet ends before the result of whether those interactions were significant. The study is highly relevant as it explicitly concerns English learners and differential effects [27].

A paper on “Understanding the role of working memory and phonological memory in mathematics and response to intervention for emergent bilingual kindergartners” reports that there were “approximately 5.1 million students classified as English Learners (ELs) in public schools in 2019, which accounts for 10.4% of the population of students attending public schools in the United States” [28]. It also states that “only 14% of students classified as English Learners in 4th grade and 4% of students classified as English Learners in 8th grade have scored at or above proficient levels in mathematics” [28]. It further says students at risk for math learning difficulties require additional instructional supports and discusses the subgroup of students at risk for math difficulties in kindergarten [28].

A paper on “Developing Literacy in Second Language Learners” was surfaced indirectly via other snippets, and a related article on “Addressing Literacy Needs of Struggling Spanish-Speaking First Graders” notes that “instructional programs that invest in the development of students' first language are more effective than those that are English medium or English only” [29]. It also states that the 2006 report has been criticized for privileging monolingualism, and that “language-minority students are, by default, defined as 'behind' from the outset” [29].

A paper on “Literacy development of English language learners: the outcomes of an intervention programme in grade R” reported that “ELLs in group 2 (the ELL control group) performed significantly better than their ELL peers in groups 3 and 4 (the two experimental groups) on two subtests” and that “the pre-intervention results of this study highlight the considerable variation in performance of L2 learners” [30]. It also said “some L2 learners exhibit similar emergent literacy skills than their L1 peers, at times even outperforming them, without intervention and before entering grade 1” [30]. Post-intervention ANOVA showed significant differences between the four groups on all eight subtests [30].

A paper on “Reading Interventions to Support English Learners with Disabilities in High School” is a systematic review and directly addresses the combined subgroup of ELs with disabilities [17]. It is one of the most directly relevant sources for the research thread, although it is about interventions rather than formative assessment per se.

A paper on “Identifying Emergent Bilinguals at Risk for Reading Difficulties: A Systematic Review of Criterion-Validity of Existing Assessments” states that EBs are “overrepresented in special education services” at upper-grade levels and that there is a need for “unbiased, accurate assessments that help teachers understand the literacy progress of EB students” [31]. It focuses on “the current validity evidence on the use of cognitive, language, and literacy assessments among EBs” [31]. This is highly relevant to assessment validity and subgroup identification, though not formative assessment specifically.

A paper on “Effects of a Technology-Assisted Reading Comprehension Intervention for English Learners with Learning Disabilities” surfaced in a search result list, but only the title was available in the raw paper relevance results and no snippet was provided [32]. It is potentially relevant but no further detail was extracted.

A paper on “Achievement gaps for English learners with disabilities” surfaced in search results but no further metadata or snippet content was extracted [33].

A paper on “Special Education Representation Trends Vary by Language Status: Evidence of Underrepresentation in Tennessee” provided a detailed snippet. It reported that for Current ELs, “being a student of Hispanic background ... was associated with a higher likelihood of SLD identification,” while “being an elementary-level (Grades 3-5) student, being female, not being chronically absent, and having higher English reading achievement was associated with a lower likelihood of SLD identification” [34]. For SLI, “being an elementary-grade student (Grades 3-5) compared with a middle-grade student (Grades 6-8) was most strongly associated with a higher likelihood of SLI identification” [34]. The study says these adjusted analyses underscore that factors other than language status are significant for understanding special education placement for Current ELs [34].

A paper on “Pre-Service ESL Teachers’ Self-Reported Knowledge of English Language Learners’ (ELLs) Reading Assessments” emphasizes that ELLs are often “erroneously evaluated and misplaced in educational programs where they do not belong” and that there is a “pronounced overrepresentation of ELLs among those that qualify for special services” [35]. It notes that professionals may confuse language acquisition issues with learning disability and that fear of litigation has contributed to under- and over-referral to special education [35].

A paper on “Linguistic Influences on Cognitive Test Performance: Examinee Characteristics Are More Important than Test Characteristics” states that “the diagnostic process can be challenging when a standardized, norm-referenced test is used to assess students from diverse backgrounds” and notes “the disproportionate number of students from diverse backgrounds qualifying for special education services under a variety of disability categories” [36]. It argues that English learner status is more appropriate than bilingual as a descriptor because ELs can fall at various points along the English proficiency continuum [36].

A paper on “IQ-Achievement Discrepancy for Identification of Disabilities in Spanish-speaking English Learners” reported that “Findings indicated significant overidentification when the language of assessment was not matched to the language of the instruction,” with effects varying “predictably over time and by language of instruction” [37]. It also reported that “low achieving and discrepant children differ from typically developing children, and from one another in predictable ways based on differences in IQ” [37].

A paper on “Supporting Children Who Are English Language Learners Succeed in Their Early Literacy Development” states that “The bilingual children who were identified as having dyslexia performed better on tasks such as phonological, morphological, word reading, and spelling skills than their monolingual peers with dyslexia” [38]. It also notes that systematic monitoring of ELLs’ response to Tier 1 and Tier 2 literacy instruction can help identify those requiring Tier 3 support [38].

A paper on “Early Childhood Educational Settings and School Absenteeism for Children With Disabilities” noted that little attention has been paid to children with disabilities in the literature on heterogeneity of program effects [39]. It said this omission is significant because children with disabilities comprise approximately 12% of the student population in the United States [39]. This is not formative-assessment-specific but is relevant to disability subgroup heterogeneity.

A paper on “Self-Regulation, Engagement, and Developmental Functioning in Preschool-Aged Children” stated that traditional norm-referenced developmental assessments were found to be inadequate or insufficient for children whose development was not following the normative path, and that norm-referenced assessments “tend not to be sensitive to children’s disability characteristics” [40]. It also described the use of a norm-referenced developmental assessment and selection of children with disabilities, at-risk children, and typically developing children [40].

A paper on “Dimensions of Classroom-Based Assessments in Inclusive Education” described an instrument called “Progress Monitoring,” which “refers only to formative assessments,” and said it is “primarily aimed at special education teachers, but is also suitable for regular education teachers” [41]. It also notes that formative assessment results can be transferred to the classroom and used for data-based decision-making [41].

A paper on “The Analysis of the Problems in Business English Teaching Assessment System and Suggestions for Improvements” provides a general conceptual review of formative assessment, stating that formative assessment can “develop differentiated assessment criteria based on student differences” and “promote students' development in all aspects” [42]. It is not specific to K-12 subgroup effects, but it reinforces the conceptual rationale for differentiation [42].

A paper on “An Argument-Based Framework for Validating Formative Assessment in the Classroom” conceptualizes formative assessment as a process of eliciting, interpreting, and using evidence about student achievement to make decisions [43]. It also says “the essence of formative assessment involves establishing 1) where the learners are going; 2) where the learners currently are in their learning; and 3) what needs to be done to get them there” [43]. This is relevant to how formative assessment may interact with learner subgroup characteristics, though no subgroup results are presented.

A paper on “Measuring course learning outcomes” states that formative assessment is used to aid learning and that formative assessments are diagnostic, and contrasts formative and summative assessment [44]. It is not subgroup-specific.

A paper on “Differential Effects of Additional Formative Assessments on Student Learning Behaviors and Outcomes” states that “the efficacy of additional formative assessments likely depends on individual differences in students' characteristics” [45]. It says “Prior knowledge and experience are also important factors, as students with more prior knowledge tend to benefit more from the testing effect than those with less prior knowledge,” but also notes that students who already possess effective learning strategies may not benefit as much from formative assessments [45]. It concludes that various types of students may exist and some may not experience the same benefits from additional formative assessments [45]. It is directly relevant to subgroup effects by prior achievement / prior knowledge, although not specifically EL or disability status.

A paper on “What can we learn from the KZN ANA results ?” was returned by relevance search, but no title-specific snippet or details were extracted beyond the paper ID and title [46].

### Prior achievement / baseline achievement / achievement-level moderation

The clearest direct references to prior achievement as a moderator or subgroup factor were from the formative assessment literature and adjacent intervention literature:

- In the meta-analysis on formative assessment for reading, “small sample size studies yielded a significantly larger effect size (d = 0.33, p < 0.001) than large sample studies,” and the discussion explicitly frames differences as depending on sample size and differentiated instruction rather than prior achievement [1].
- The paper on intrinsic motivation states that “differential effects at the edges of the achievement spectrum seem conceivable” and cites prior work showing effects in favor of high achievers, low achievers, or no difference, but also says the limited research base does not allow directed hypotheses [6].
- The evaluation of a state-wide mathematics support program says “students with higher pretest scores benefited especially from the formative assessment” in prior work and that other studies found formative assessment effective for low-achieving students [7].
- The paper on additional formative assessments states that “students with more prior knowledge tend to benefit more from the testing effect than those with less prior knowledge” and that students with limited prior knowledge may not benefit as much [45].
- The Bookworms curriculum study explicitly added baseline achievement interactions “to explore differentiation in impacts across student subgroups that might respond differently to instruction,” and defined baseline achievement as a z-score based on the first observed MAP score; however, the extracted snippet only notes that the moderation analyses are “preliminary in nature” and “do not guarantee” that differences are attributable to differential effects, without reporting the actual moderation coefficients [47].

A few adjacent studies also speak to prior achievement or initial ability:
- In the cognitive guided phonetic instruction study, the ANCOVA controlled for initial ability level using pre-assessment scores, and no significant differences were found between RTI groups: “F(2, 36) = .13, p = .877” for the overall assessment and “F(2, 36) = .078, p = .925” for part one [48]. This was a response-to-intervention / achievement-level comparison rather than a formative assessment subgroup study, but it is relevant to the general research thread.
- In the kindergarten vocabulary and language status study, the results “did not find a significant individual influence of language status,” but “Project EVI Tier 2 vocabulary intervention was beneficial to first grade reading comprehension for students with lower levels of initial vocabulary knowledge” [49]. The snippet also says educators should consider DLL status as a possible indicator of risk but that risk is dependent on vocabulary knowledge when students enter school [49].
- The same study’s limitations note that “Vocabulary demonstrated a significant relationship with reading comprehension in this study” and that future studies should consider socioeconomic status as mediating or moderating effects on comprehension [49].

### Studies on progress monitoring / diagnostic / assessment validity in English learners and disability contexts

A range of sources emphasized that assessment and progress monitoring should be individualized and linguistically responsive for English learners, especially those with learning difficulties or disabilities:

- “Progress monitoring of academic and linguistic skill acquisition is critical” for ELs [16].
- “Using evidenced-based practices to meet the needs of multilingual students is essential” and there is “a subgroup of students, those at risk for math learning difficulties, that require additional instructional supports” [28].
- In “Supporting Children Who Are English Language Learners Succeed in Their Early Literacy Development,” the authors state that “One opportunity to identify ELL who require more specialized support is systematically monitoring how these learners respond to evidence-based literacy instruction in their early months at school” [38].
- “Reading Interventions to Support English Learners with Disabilities in High School” underscores the importance of interventions but says the limited evidence base prevents firm conclusions [17].
- “Identifying Emergent Bilinguals at Risk for Reading Difficulties” states there is a need for “unbiased, accurate assessments” and that assessments in EBs’ developing L2 may not fully capture foundational skills [31].
- “Linguistic Influences on Cognitive Test Performance” emphasizes that standardized norm-referenced tests can be problematic for students from diverse backgrounds [36].
- “IQ-Achievement Discrepancy for Identification of Disabilities in Spanish-speaking English Learners” says language of assessment not matched to instruction leads to significant overidentification [37].
- “Special Education Representation Trends Vary by Language Status” provides evidence that placement varies by grade, sex, chronic absenteeism, and English reading achievement, beyond language status alone [34].

### Studies on formative assessment implementation, teacher behavior, and context

Several studies relate to how formative assessment is implemented and how context or teacher characteristics mediate effectiveness:

- “Effects of formative assessment on intrinsic motivation in primary school mathematics instruction” notes that the core elements of formative assessment, feedback and adaptive teaching behavior, might help promote competence, and that instructional impact depends on students’ perception of teacher behavior [6].
- “Examining Elementary School Teachers Perceptions of and Use of Formative Assessment in Mathematics” notes that teachers “find formative assessment” useful and that “Specific formative assessment strategies have been found to support student learning” including peer-assisted learning, self-assessment using rubrics, and self-regulated learning [8].
- “From Standardized Assessment to Automatic Formative Assessment for Adaptive Teaching” discusses adaptive teaching and formative assessment as a means to tailor instruction to different groups of students, including those with learning disabilities [9].
- “Formative feedback in a multicultural classroom: a review” describes a literature search and selection criteria around feedback and culture, with the explicit concern that broad categories like “diverse students” may mask the effect of culture relative to other factors [10].
- “Formative Assessment Practices in Special School Classrooms With the Support of E-Books: A Case Study” found e-books can facilitate formative assessment and support students at special schools through responses, immediate feedback, interaction, peer assessment, and positive behavior reinforcement [12].
- “Dimensions of Classroom-Based Assessments in Inclusive Education” indicates that “Progress Monitoring” is a formative assessment tool aimed at special education teachers and regular education teachers [41].

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

### K–12 evidence on formative assessment

A systematic review/umbrella review on K–12 formative assessment found: “Formative assessment in K-12 education has been a notable teaching and learning focus area in schools over the last 20 years, as evidenced by numerous recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses investigating and summarizing the evidence for formative assessments’ effectiveness and sustainability. This umbrella review systematically reviews meta-analyses investigating the effects of formative assessment on learning, summarizes the current findings, and assesses the quality and risk of bias in the published meta-analyses.” It reported that “Thirteen meta-analyses, each of which examined the effects of formative assessment on learning in K-12 students, were included in this umbrella review.” It also reported: “Formative assessment was found to produce trivial to large positive effects on student learning, with no negative effects identified. The magnitude of effects varied according to the type of formative assessment.” It further stated: “The 13 included meta-analysis studies showed moderate (n = 10), high (n = 1), and low (n = 2) methodological quality (AMSTAR-2), although the robustness of the evidence (i.e., GRADE analysis) was very low (n = 9), low (n = 3), and moderate (n = 1).” The review concluded: “These findings offer valuable insights for designing and implementing different types of formative assessment aimed at optimizing student learning and ensuring the sustainability of assessment practices. However, the low-to-very-low certainty of the available evidence precludes robust recommendations regarding optimal formative assessment strategies for learning in K-12 students.” [1]

A meta-analysis study by Karaman reported: “The number of studies included in the meta-analysis and the characteristics of these studies are summarized in As summarized in Table 3, the meta-analysis shows the overall effect size as .79 with standard error of .03 in the fixed model. Heterogeneity test was used to investigate the heterogeneity in effect size. The Q value was 188.91 with 46 degrees of freedom, and p value under .05 showed heterogeneity among the studies. In other words, true effect size may have varied across studies. Besides, 2 statistic was estimated as 75.65% indicating that the percent of variance due to between-subject factors was large. The results revealed that the impact of formative assessment on student learning varied from one study to another. By using random effects model, overall meta-analysis showed that there was a significant effect of formative assessment on student learning (g= .72, SE= .07, 95% CI= .59; 85, p<.05).” It also stated that “In Table 5, mixed effects analysis was also used to estimate the effect size of groups in terms of their education levels (primary, secondary, and tertiary). The mean effect sizes that were estimated at different education levels ranged between .89 and .64 and were statistically significant. The results showed that the effect size at primary level had a large effect (d=.89, p<.05), while it had a medium effect on student academic performance at secondary level (d=.71, p<.05) and tertiary level (d=.64, p<.05). The results of the heterogeneity test yielded that comparison of subgroups at different education levels did not make a significant contribution to the variance (Q=.66, df=2, p= .71).” [2]

The same meta-analysis also stated in its abstract: “32 studies with 47 effect sizes that met the specified criteria such as using true experimental or quasi-experimental design and measuring learning outcomes were included as the final analysis in the meta-analytical review method. The overall mean effect size of the study was obtained as .72 ( SE = .07, p < .05). Further investigation through subgroup analysis showed that the effect sizes made a significant difference on different types of formative feedback. The effect of features of formative assessment interventions on student learning indicated that student initiated formative feedback ( d =1.16) and mixed feedback ( d =.83) had a large effect, which was followed by a medium effect of adult initiated formative formative feedback ( d =.69) and a small effect of computer initiated formative feedback ( d =.42). On the other hand, education level and publication type had no effect on student academic performance in the study.” [3]

A second K–12 meta-analysis on reading achievement reported: “The findings of this review indicate that formative assessment produce a positive effect (ES = + 0.18) on reading achievement. The magnitude could be interpreted as a small effect aligned with the oft-cited indication of small (d = 0.2), medium (d = 0.5), and large (d = 0.8) effect size (Cohen, 1988). However, Kraft (2020), taking study features, program costs and scalability into account, proposed a new benchmark frame for effect size from causal studies of pre K-12 education intervention, namely small (d < 0.05), medium (0.05 to <0.20), and large (≥0.20). Accordingly, the overall aggregated effect size in this review could be taken as a medium effect size. Compared with effect sizes (from +0.22 to +0.70) from previous metaanalyses, the weighted average effect size reported in this review was the smallest one.” It further noted: “In this review, two large scale studies (Konstantopoulos et al., 2016;Allen, 2019) involving over 35,000 student reported negative effects of formative assessment on reading achievement.” [4]

The same reading meta-analysis also reported moderator results: “Given that research design might influence the effect size, we categorized all studies into randomized controlled studies (RCT) and quasi-experiments (QED). Results from the regression model indicated that effect sizes generated from RCT were smaller than QED design, but not significant (d = -0.04, p = 0.465).” “Digital technology involvement was examined. Surprisingly, students' reading achievement was not influenced significantly by formative assessment with digital technology (d = 0.001, p = 0.978).” “Formative assessment in reading classrooms seemed to exert a similar impact on students of different grade levels. The effect sizes in elementary level were slightly larger than those for kindergarten studies (d = 0.02, p = 0.790). Effect sizes for middle/high school studies were also slightly smaller than those for kindergarten studies (d = -0.03, p = 0.696).” “Student characteristics were coded into mainstream students and at-risk students. The estimated effect size of formative assessment on mainstream students was slightly higher than that on at-risk students, albeit not significant (d = 0.001, p = 0.982).” “With respect to program duration, studies that lasted less than 1 year were coded as short programs, others were coded as long ones. Programs in one-year or longer showed smaller effect size than short-term ones, but the difference was non-significant (d = -0.02, p = 0.576).” “Different from the result of the subgroup analysis result regarding cultural setting, the effect size of formative assessment in CHC appeared to be smaller than those in Anglophone culture, though not significant (d = -0.10, p = 0.297).” “Results of publication type revealed that no significant differences were found between published and unpublished articles (p = 0.701), indicating that no publication bias existed in this review.” “The pseudo R 2 value in this meta-regression model estimated the moderators accounted for 95% of heterogeneity.” [5]

The same reading meta-analysis also stated: “Variation yielded significant differences in effect sizes that were from seven moderators: grade level, type of intervention, program duration, differentiated instruction, sample size, publication type and cultural setting. The effect sizes comparisons of subcategories in rest three moderators, student characteristics, digital technology and research design were non-significant.” [6]

The same reading meta-analysis stated: “The impact of different types of formative assessment interventions on student learning varied. The feedback from the students had the largest effect but the feedback from the computers had the smallest effect on student learning. Moderator analysis showed that the effect sizes made a significant difference as to different types of formative feedback.” It also stated: “Variation in effect sizes may be related to the features of formative assessment interventions in the present study.” [7]

Another statement from the same reading meta-analysis reported: “While the highest mean effect size was found at primary school level, the lowest mean effect size was found at tertiary level. Mixed effects analysis was used to examine whether group differences were significant or not. The results showed that education level did not make a significant contribution to the variance. Likewise, King and Nash (2011) found that grade level did not make a difference on the effect of formative assessment on student learning. It can be interpreted that formative assessment is effective for all levels of education (Black & William, 1998;King & Nash, 2011).” [8]

OpenAI web search also returned a summary stating: “A meta-analysis by Xuan et al. (2022) examined 48 studies involving 116,051 K-12 students and found that formative assessment had a modest positive effect on reading achievement (effect size = +0.19). The study also identified that smaller sample sizes and the integration of differentiated instruction were associated with larger effect sizes.” [9] This was echoed in another OpenAI web search summary stating: “This review has revealed that, without publication bias, formative assessment is making a positive and modest difference in enhancing students' reading achievement in diverse settings. The average weighted effect over all included studies was 0.19. The exact size a researcher finds may deviate considerably depending on the sample size, teachers' differentiated instruction and type of intervention. Studies involving a large sample size with over 250 students led to low and attenuated estimate of formative assessment. The implementation of teachers' differentiated instruction is linked to much stronger effects than intervention without differentiated instruction. Also, our results suggested that collaboration of teachers and students in formative assessment would be more effective than formative assessment merely initiated by teachers.” [10]

A randomized controlled intervention study in secondary school physics reported: “In a cluster-randomized controlled intervention study with 29 teachers and 604 students (mean age 15.6 years) at secondary school level, we examined the yield of formative assessment with regard to students’ conceptual understanding and quantitative problem-solving skills in physics. Ten teachers applied formative assessment (FA group) in a 14-lesson curriculum on kinematics after having undergone a training that focused on the implementation of multiple-choice concept questions together with monitoring tools, clicker sessions, and reflective lessons. In the frequent testing group (FT group), ten teachers had no training on formative assessment but implemented the same concept questions as those used in the FA group. Nine teachers taught kinematics in their traditional way (TT group). The results revealed that students in the FA group outperformed students in the other two groups in a test on conceptual understanding immediately after the intervention as well as 3 months later, whereas students from the FT group and the TT group did not differ. Importantly, a better conceptual understanding in the FA group was not at the expense of performance in quantitative problem solving, as students of this group better integrated both kinds of knowledge. Our study has shown that a short but well-structured formative assessment teacher training could unfold its potential in terms of students’ learning of challenging content.” [11]

A randomized study of formative assessment in junior secondary Basic Science reported that “the result of the study showed a significant differences in the formative classroom assessment between the experimental and the control group in favour of the experimental group. The result of the analysis showed that the students in the experimental group scored higher on the assessments which had strong effect on the academic performance of the junior secondary school two Basic Science students. This implies that students in the experimental group demonstrated a much deeper conceptual understanding of the topics in the unit and were better able to articulate their thinking in a concise manner compared to the control group. This indicate that formative classroom assessment strategy is effective in enhancing the students' academic performance.” It also reported: “The result of the study also revealed that formative assessment strategy is effective in improving the academic performance of the junior secondary school two Basic Science students as it was observed that a significant difference existed in the experimental group between the pre-test and the post -test scores and the difference is in favour of the post-test scores. This is an indication that the formative feedback promoted the junior secondary school two Basic Science students performance.” [12]

Another K–12 experimental paper reported: “The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group used as a comparison (Madadizadeh, 2022;Rusmana & Suprihatin, 2019). Two groups of elementary school students will be randomly selected from different schools. One group will be the experimental group receiving technology-based formative assessments, while the other group will be the control group receiving traditional formative assessments. The research sample will include fourth to sixth-grade elementary school students from two different schools. Each group will have a minimum of 30 students to ensure statistical validity.” It also stated: “The t-test will produce a t-statistical and significance values (p-value). Suppose the p-value is less than a predetermined significance level (usually 0.05). In that case, we can conclude that the two groups significantly differ in mathematics achievement.” [13]

Another study in primary grade mathematics reported: “Primary grade students' mathematics formative and summative assessment data came from a school district that included schools with urban, suburban, and rural characteristics located in the southeastern United States. In this school district, 77 teachers participated in an 80-hours, one-year-long professional development experience, funded by the <state blinded> Mathematics Science Partnership grant program, to learn about formative assessment and students' number sense. Two groups of teachers with their students participated in this study. Group 1 consisted of 27 teachers and 258 students from Grade 1 (38%) and Grade 2 (62%). Group 2 consisted of 50 teachers and 477 students from Kindergarten (63%) and Grade 1 (37%). Group 1 and Group 2 took different parts of the online formative assessment tool (AMC Anywhere), which were hiding and counting, respectively.” [14]

A U.S. school reform rapid assessment study reported: “The first experiment involving 1,665 Memphis students (a district where 71 percent of all students are eligible for free/reduced price lunch) found an average effect size of 0.270 SD per grade in grades K through 6 on the STAR Reading test, over a 9-month school year (Ross et al., 2004). Using HLM, the second experiment involving 978 students (89.9% African American and 83% eligible for free/reduced price lunch) found an average effect size of 0.175 SD per grade in grades 3 through 6 on the STAR Reading test and the STAR Early Literacy test over a 9-month school year (Nunnery et al., 2006).” It also stated: “The only randomized study of Math Assessment, which involved 1,880 students in grades 2 through 8 in 80 classrooms and 7 states, found an effect size of 0.324 SD over a 7-month period on the STAR Math test, after controlling for treatment integrity (Ysseldyke & Bolt, 2007). The only national, refereed quasi-experimental evaluation of Math Assessment, involving 2,202 students in grades 3 through 10 in 125 classrooms and 24 states, found that students in the treatment group gained an average of 0.392 SD per grade over one semester (18 weeks) on the STAR Math test, compared to students not receiving Math Assessment (at pretest the scores of treatment and comparison students were not significantly different) (Ysseldyke & Tardrew, 2007).” [15]

A study on teacher use of practice tests for formative purposes reported: “This paper describes an intensive professional development program focused on supporting teachers at high-need urban high schools in use of practice tests for formative assessment purposes. Teachers engaged in professional development while offering intensive summer school to students with histories of failure on state tests in science and mathematics. Specific skills that teachers developed included item analysis of practice tests, planning around assessment results, and providing feedback to students. The study used a quasi-experimental pretest/posttest design with an intervention and a comparison group, analysis of classroom artifacts, follow-up surveys, and long-term follow-up with teachers. Students in the summer programs experienced large gains in performance, and teachers reported more frequent and varied use of tests for formative purposes, even one-and-one-half years after the end of training.” [16]

A study about formative assessment and student achievement in Turkey reported: “The main purpose of this meta-analysis study is to investigate how formative assessment practices promote student learning in Turkey. 32 studies with 47 effect sizes that met the specified criteria such as using true experimental or quasi-experimental design and measuring learning outcomes were included as the final analysis in the meta-analytical review method. The overall mean effect size of the study was obtained as .72 ( SE = .07, p < .05).” It also stated: “The impact of features of formative assessment interventions on student learning indicated that student initiated formative feedback ( d =1.16) and mixed feedback ( d =.83) had a large effect, which was followed by a medium effect of adult initiated formative feedback ( d =.69) and a small effect of computer initiated formative feedback ( d =.42). While the highest mean effect size was found at primary school level, the lowest mean effect size was found at tertiary level. Mixed effects analysis was used to examine whether group differences were significant or not. The results showed that education level did not make a significant contribution to the variance.” [19]

A study on high school teachers’ readiness for formative assessment reported: “Figure 1 illustrates the proposed formative assessment model with its four-phase cycle: initial instruction, assessment for learning, response to formative assessment, and reassessment. At the beginning of a class, a teacher prepares the lesson and selects a teaching strategy (i.e., initial instruction). To achieve the maximum benefits of formative assessment practices, the teacher adopts a student-centered initial instruction. The next phase is assessment for learning, where the teacher provides students with an opportunity to demonstrate their understanding during the learning process. The teacher uses one or more assessment methods to verify how well the students have achieved the lesson's learning objectives. The following phase is the response to formative assessment, where the teacher analyzes the student data to determine if further instructional activities are needed. If the formative assessment indicates that the students have not adequately learned the lesson objectives, then the teacher plans for "reteaching" using different teaching strategies. The final phase is reassessment, where the teacher provides an additional planned assessment to determine student growth in understanding.” [27]

## Executive Summary

The overall evidence indicates that formative assessment can improve student learning, but the size and reliability of benefits depend strongly on implementation quality, subject area, and whether assessment evidence is actually used to adapt teaching. The best-supported definition across the literature is not “more testing,” but a recursive instructional process in which teachers or learners elicit evidence of understanding, interpret it, and use it to decide next steps in instruction (Black & Wiliam, 2009)[238][245]. Across K–12, the evidence is more convincing than in postsecondary education: K–12 meta-analyses show small-to-moderate average effects with substantial heterogeneity, whereas higher-education sources are dominated by reviews, conceptual papers, and implementation studies rather than robust causal tests [214][185][243][245][246].

The strongest experimental findings come from K–12 and secondary-school studies. The umbrella review of 13 meta-analyses found that formative assessment produced “trivial to large positive effects” on K–12 learning, with no negative effects identified, but certainty was low to very low [214]. In K–12 reading, the meta-analysis of 48 studies and 116,051 students found an average weighted effect of 0.19 on reading achievement, with larger effects in small studies, stronger effects when formative assessment was embedded in differentiated instruction, and better outcomes when teacher and student assessment were integrated rather than teacher-only [185]. In the Turkish meta-analysis of 32 studies and 47 effect sizes, the overall mean effect size was .72 (SE = .07, p < .05), and student-initiated formative feedback had the largest effect (d = 1.16), followed by mixed feedback (d = .83), adult-initiated feedback (d = .69), and computer-initiated feedback (d = .42) [243]. In a cluster-randomized controlled intervention in secondary physics with 29 teachers and 604 students, formative assessment training plus multiple-choice concept questions, clicker sessions, and reflective lessons improved conceptual understanding immediately and 3 months later; the frequent-testing and traditional-teaching groups did not differ, and the report gives no effect size in the extracted text (Lichtenberger et al., year not reported in snippet). In a randomized study in junior secondary basic science with 80 students, formative classroom assessment significantly improved achievement relative to control, again with no exact effect size reported in the extracted text (Matilda & Helen, year not reported in snippet).

The strongest quasi-experimental and observational findings generally corroborate the experimental pattern, while also clarifying moderators. A quasi-experimental study in primary-grade mathematics found that formative and summative assessment scores were positively related, with stronger relations in lower-performing classrooms and in first grade than kindergarten, suggesting stronger utility when teachers use evidence to adjust instruction for weaker classrooms [186]. A study of formative and summative assessment in primary mathematics found that low-performing classrooms benefited more, and that the relationship between formative and summative assessment was stronger among first graders than kindergarteners [186]. In a state-wide mathematics support program, formative assessment had positive impacts overall, but prior work suggested that higher pretest students may benefit especially in some settings, indicating that prior achievement moderates effects rather than yielding a uniform pattern (van den Ham & Heinze, 2022). Observational and review evidence also suggests that teacher-directed assessment alone is weaker than teacher-plus-student assessment, and that differentiated instruction and professional development are often bundled with stronger effects, especially in reading [185][238]. In higher education, the evidence is much less causal, but several studies suggest that formative assessment, self-assessment, and peer assessment are associated with improved motivation, self-regulation, engagement, and sometimes achievement, while direct learning evidence remains thinner [184][221][250][245].

The tiered questions are answered unevenly. Tier 1 is partially answered: the intervention is well defined in principle, and the most studied outcomes are achievement, reading and mathematics performance, self-regulation, motivation, and engagement, but retention and transfer are rarely measured directly (Black & Wiliam, 2009)[214]. Tier 2 is partially answered: baseline conditions are typically usual instruction, summative-only assessment, or loosely defined business-as-usual practice, but comparator definitions vary and are often vague [185][186][245]. Tier 3 is partly answered: common implementations include questioning, quizzes, exit tickets, self- and peer-assessment, and feedback cycles, but many studies bundle components, making causal attribution to any single ingredient difficult [193][238][244]. Tier 4 is partially answered for K–12 and still largely unresolved for postsecondary education: effects vary by sample size, subject, culture, prior achievement, and whether formative assessment is paired with differentiation or student participation, but evidence on retention, transfer, English learners, disability status, and direct K–12 versus postsecondary comparisons remains limited [185][214][321][245].

Overall confidence is moderate for the claim that formative assessment improves learning in K–12 classrooms, especially when it triggers feedback and instructional adaptation, but low for precise claims about optimal components, long-term retention/transfer, and higher-education causal effects. The single most important caveat is that the strongest benefits are associated with formative assessment as an active instructional cycle, not as routine testing or score reporting; superficial implementation, weak feedback, and failure to use results for instruction likely explain many null or inconsistent findings [238][245][214].
