It instead examined how course social and cultural features predicted students’ engagement in active learning, reporting that relevance, trust, mastery, and lower competition were associated with higher engagement indirectly through control, value, and emotions.
finding.measure: Cognitive engagement in introductory STEM active learning courses

paper_profiles.title: Technology-Enhanced Writing Pedagogy for EFL Learners: A Multi-Study Dissertation on Practice, Effectiveness, and Teacher Perceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines how digital tools support English as a Foreign Language (EFL) writing in higher education, with a focus on academic writing performance, collaborative writing, and teacher perceptions. It addresses a broader problem in EFL writing instruction: despite rapid growth in technology-enhanced learning tools, evidence about what works, for whom, and under what conditions remains fragmented, especially in non-Western university contexts.

The dissertation contains three studies. Study 1 is a classroom experiment with 111 Chinese undergraduates comparing infographic-based prewriting to traditional reverse outlining for a source-based summary and an opinion paragraph. Study 2 is a meta-analysis of 17 experimental/quasi-experimental studies (N=1,085) comparing web-based collaborative writing with non-technological collaborative writing among EFL college learners. Study 3 is a qualitative interview study with seven Chinese university EFL writing instructors about technology integration during and after the pandemic, including their views on hybrid instruction and generative AI.

Across the studies, the dissertation concludes that technology is most effective when it is aligned with the task and supported by instruction. Infographic-based planning improved summary writing quality, source use, and writing self-efficacy, but not opinion writing. Web-based collaborative writing showed a moderate positive effect on writing quality (Hedges’ g=0.51), with training emerging as an important moderator. Teacher interviews suggested that actual classroom use of digital tools depends on teacher knowledge, institutional support, and policy conditions, and that adoption of GenAI remains cautious because of integrity and guidance concerns.

finding.finding_summary: In the experiment with 111 Chinese undergraduates, infographic-based prewriting improved source-based summary writing quality relative to reverse outlining. The infographic group scored higher on total summary quality and on content selection, integration/cohesion, and elaboration, with the regression models showing a significant treatment effect even after controlling for baseline writing and preparation time (β=1.21 to 1.61, SE=0.46-0.48).
finding.measure: Rubric-based summary writing quality; source use in summary writing
finding.std_deviation: Treatment summary quality SD=2.22; Control summary quality SD=2.64

finding.finding_summary: The infographic condition increased students' writing self-efficacy for summary writing compared with reverse outlining. The dissertation reports that pre/post survey results showed gains in confidence related to capturing main ideas, presenting essential details, organizing information, and using proper language, although no specific effect size or test statistic is reported in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Writing self-efficacy survey

finding.finding_summary: For opinion writing, infographic-based planning did not significantly outperform reverse outlining. After controlling for baseline writing performance, the multivariate test was non-significant and none of the follow-up ANCOVAs reached significance, indicating no reliable difference in opinion-writing quality between groups.
finding.measure: Rubric-based opinion writing quality

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis found that web-based collaborative writing (WBCW) improved EFL college learners' writing quality relative to non-technological collaborative writing. Across 17 studies and 38 effect sizes (N=1,085), the pooled effect was moderate and statistically significant (Hedges' g=0.51), and moderator analyses indicated that training was an important factor associated with stronger outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing quality in collaborative writing tasks

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis also examined conditions that shaped WBCW effects, including training, genre, intervention duration, group size, and time/place settings. The clearest moderator finding reported is that training significantly enhanced outcomes, suggesting that collaborative writing benefits are stronger when students receive explicit preparation for using the web-based tools and collaborative process.
finding.measure: Moderator analyses of WBCW studies (training, genre, duration, group size, time/place settings)

finding.finding_summary: Teacher interviews showed that technology integration in EFL writing is strongly shaped by institutional support, access, and policy guidance. Instructors reported that digital tools were embedded in instruction but used cautiously, especially for GenAI, because of concerns about academic integrity and a lack of clear institutional direction.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher interview themes on technology integration, institutional support, and policy constraints

paper_profiles.title: Improving Retention Factors and Student Success Online Utilizing the Community of Inquiry Framework’s Instructor Presence Model
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether professional development focused on the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework’s instructor presence model can improve online teaching practices and, in turn, improve student retention-related outcomes. The authors argue that effective instructor presence—comprising teaching, social, and cognitive presence—may help reduce dropout and improve pass rates in online higher education, but that the concrete strategies needed to do so are often insufficiently specified.

To test this, the researchers created seven self-paced training modules for instructors at a fully online for-profit university in health and behavioral sciences. They compared instructor presence rubric scores and course outcomes before and after training, using a quasi-experimental causal-comparative design with pre/post course evaluations and multiple extraneous variables. The sample included 47 instructors who completed the modules and 188 courses rated for instructor presence (94 pre-training and 94 post-training).

The findings show statistically significant improvements in all three instructor presence dimensions after training, along with improved course pass rates and reduced course drop rates. However, the pattern suggests effects may depend partly on implementation context: instructors with higher institutional performance ratings showed stronger gains, while several other covariates were not significant. The study concludes that structured professional development on CoI-based engagement strategies can improve online retention and success, but it also implies that the effects are tied to how faithfully and effectively the strategies are enacted.

finding.finding_summary: Instructor training in the Community of Inquiry instructor presence model improved institutional retention-related outcomes in online courses. After the seven-module professional development series, course pass rates improved significantly (paired t-test, p = .05) and course drop rates decreased significantly (paired t-test, p < .001) across 47 instructors and 188 evaluated courses (94 pre-training, 94 post-training).
finding.measure: Course pass rates and course drop rates in online university courses
finding.std_deviation: SD=11.39 for pass-rate change; SD=9.34 for drop-rate change

paper_profiles.title: ESL Teachers’ Experiences on XReading as a Formative Assessment Tool in Extensive Reading: A Study of a Federal Institution in the UAE
paper_profiles.venue: Future Trends in Education Post COVID-19
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter examines how ESL teachers in a UAE federal college perceive XReading as a digital formative assessment tool for extensive reading. The paper addresses a practical question in language education: whether a technology-mediated reading platform can support monitoring, accountability, feedback, and student engagement in a program where reading is part of the curriculum and contributes to course grades.

XReading is described as an electronic library and LMS that lets teachers track student progress through post-reading quizzes, short responses, and reading-speed monitoring. The study uses a qualitative phenomenological design, relying on semi-structured interviews and observations with teachers in the English Bridge Program at a federal college in the UAE. The context is undergraduate ESL instruction, where XReading had become a mandatory component of the curriculum.

The main conclusion is that teachers viewed XReading positively as a formative assessment approach because it encouraged engagement, collaboration, learner autonomy, and cooperative learning while helping teachers monitor student progress. The chapter emphasizes perceived benefits more than measured achievement outcomes, and it does not provide causal evidence that XReading improves reading scores relative to a comparison condition. Reported challenges and implementation concerns are discussed at a high level, but the evidence is primarily teacher-perception based rather than quantitative.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived XReading as supporting extensive reading and improving students’ reading-related performance through post-reading quizzes, short responses, and tracking of reading speed. The chapter reports that XReading fostered engagement and accountability in reading, but it does not provide quantitative effect sizes or controlled outcome data.
finding.measure: Teachers’ perceptions of students’ extensive reading performance and reading-skill development

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports that XReading fostered student engagement, collaboration, motivation, and learner autonomy, which teachers viewed as important benefits of the formative assessment tool. These are qualitative perceptions rather than measured survey or behavioral outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student engagement, collaboration, motivation, and learner autonomy

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described XReading as supporting cooperative learning and learner autonomy, both of which align with durable skills. The chapter frames these as important 21st-century learning skills, but provides no quantitative estimate of magnitude.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported collaboration/cooperative learning and learner autonomy

paper_profiles.title: Student Evaluations of Teaching Fail to Predict Learning: Meta-Analysis of Bias, Grade Inflation, and Incentive Distortion in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: Open Journal of Transformative Education & LifeLong Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether end-of-course student evaluations of teaching (SETs) are valid indicators of instructional quality and whether tying institutional decisions to SETs changes instructor behavior in ways that harm learning. The authors synthesize multiple strands of secondary evidence: a PRISMA-registered meta-analysis, reanalysis of quasi-experimental datasets with random instructor assignment, psychometric audits of evaluation instruments, text analysis of open-ended comments, and program-level links to alumni and employer outcomes.

The paper focuses on higher education, especially undergraduate settings, and evaluates outcomes beyond immediate course satisfaction: subsequent course performance, cumulative GPA, licensure or standardized exam performance, alumni career readiness, and employer satisfaction. It argues that SETs correlate weakly or not at all with durable learning outcomes, and in some rigorous designs the association is slightly negative.

The paper also examines the incentive effects of using SETs in high-stakes personnel decisions. It reports evidence of grade inflation, leniency bias, and teaching-to-the-evaluation behaviors when SETs are tied to renewal or promotion, alongside measurement bias against female and racially minoritized faculty. The main conclusion is that SETs are better treated as formative feedback than as summative measures of teaching quality, and that universities should use multi-measure systems anchored in actual learning and stakeholder outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Across 89 studies (≈5.4 million students), the pooled random-effects correlation between SET scores and subsequent performance was r = 0.04 (95% CI -0.03, 0.10), which is effectively null; after grade controls it became slightly negative. Quasi-experimental reanalyses similarly found that higher-rated instructors were not associated with better later-course performance, and in some cases higher ratings coincided with worse long-term outcomes.
finding.measure: SET scores correlated with subsequent course grades, standardized/licensure exam performance, cumulative GPA, and follow-on course value-added performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that courses with higher SETs tended to be easier, more entertaining, and less demanding, which increased immediate student satisfaction but did not improve durable learning. This is framed as an illusion-of-learning pattern: students felt they learned more from fluent or charismatic teaching, but objective test performance was unchanged.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction / perceived learning / evaluation ratings in relation to teaching fluency, humor, warmth, and workload

finding.finding_summary: The strongest direct evidence in the paper concerns durable learning and transfer: follow-on course performance, cumulative GPA, and later exam outcomes were not improved by higher SET scores, and in rigorous quasi-experimental studies the relationship was sometimes negative. The authors also note that challenging, effortful instruction may lower short-term ratings while improving long-term mastery, which is consistent with a satisfaction-versus-retention tradeoff.
finding.measure: Follow-on course grades, cumulative GPA, standardized/licensure exams, and value-added learning scores
finding.study_size: n=89 studies overall; reanalysis of randomized-assignment datasets not separately quantified in the excerpt
finding.effect_size: r=0.04; simulated GPA increase of 0.27-0.31 points under SET-linked incentives

finding.finding_summary: When departments tied renewal or promotion to SET thresholds, the paper reports a 0.27 GPA-point rise relative to matched controls, indicating grade inflation rather than improved teaching efficiency. The authors also describe instructor self-reports of reducing workload, softening feedback, and simplifying courses to protect evaluations, which reflects incentive-driven distortion of teaching practice.
finding.measure: Course GPA, grade distributions, faculty self-reports of instructional changes

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that SET-driven personnel systems produce institutional harms: grade inflation, erosion of rigor, and differential item functioning against female and racially minoritized faculty. It also reports that high SET programs showed no advantage in alumni career readiness or employer satisfaction, suggesting poor criterion validity for institutional decision-making.
finding.measure: Departmental policy effects, measurement invariance/DIF in SET instruments, alumni career readiness, employer satisfaction
finding.study_size: 14 institutional SET instruments; 23 common items; 2.1 million open-ended comments; program-level linkage not separately quantified
finding.effect_size: 0.27 GPA-point rise; r = 0.04 for SET-learning correlation

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Peer Grading: A Systematic Literature Review of Reviewer Assignment Strategies and Quantity of Reviewers
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12, Postsecondary, MOOC/undergraduate and classroom contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how reviewer-assignment strategies and the number of reviewers affect the quality of peer grading. It is motivated by concerns that peer assessment can improve learning and reduce instructor workload, but only if reviewer allocation is fair, accurate, and pedagogically useful. The authors focus on two design levers: how reviewers are assigned to submissions, and how many reviews each submission receives.

Using a PRISMA-style systematic literature review, the authors screened 626 records and included 87 studies published from 2010 to 2024. The review covers peer grading in traditional classrooms and MOOCs, and it identifies four major assignment strategies: random, competency-based, social-network-based, and bidding-based assignment. Random assignment is the most common approach, but the review argues it can produce noisy and unfair outcomes when low-quality reviewers are unevenly distributed. Competency-based assignment is presented as a more robust alternative because it can reduce grading skew and improve fairness, though direct comparative evidence remains limited.

A second major conclusion is that reviewer count matters: accuracy generally improves as the number of reviews per submission increases, but gains diminish after about 3–5 reviews. The review suggests that three to five reviews per submission often balances reliability, learning value, and student workload, while more than five may increase disengagement or superficial grading. Overall, the paper emphasizes tradeoffs between accuracy, fairness, engagement, and scalability, and calls for more rigorous empirical comparisons of assignment strategies, especially social-network and bidding approaches.

finding.finding_summary: This review focuses on peer grading quality rather than a specific subject-matter achievement domain. Across 87 studies (2010–2024), it reports that peer assessment design choices—especially reviewer assignment strategy and reviewer count—shape the accuracy and fairness of grading, which indirectly supports academic tasks such as assignment evaluation in both classrooms and MOOCs. However, subject-specific academic achievement outcomes are not the central focus and are only indirectly addressed.
finding.measure: Peer grading accuracy, fairness, and validity

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that peer assessment can support engagement and learning, but also that too many required reviews may reduce engagement or lead to rushed, low-effort grading. The authors summarize prior studies suggesting that three to five reviews per student or submission often balances engagement and workload, while more than five can create burnout or disengagement.
finding.measure: Student engagement, perceived workload, participation in peer review

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer grading can help students understand requirements, see alternative approaches, and receive complementary feedback from different reviewers, which supports learning-related durable skills such as metacognition and critical evaluation. It reports that competency-based reviewer assignment can provide feedback from diverse perspectives and that increasing reviewer counts generally improves grading accuracy and educational value, though benefits plateau after about 3–5 reviewers.
finding.measure: Learning value of peer review, feedback diversity, grading accuracy as a proxy for evaluative skill development

finding.finding_summary: Operational efficiency is a central focus of the review. The authors conclude that random assignment is scalable and simple, but competency-based, dynamic, and reliability-weighted assignment can improve accuracy and fairness; they also note that three to five reviews per submission typically balances grading reliability with reviewer workload. The review repeatedly emphasizes that too many reviews can increase burden and reduce timeliness, while too few degrade validity.
finding.measure: Reviewer workload, grading accuracy, timeliness, workload balance

finding.finding_summary: At the institutional level, the review discusses scalability, fairness, and design tradeoffs in peer-grading systems used in classrooms and MOOCs. It highlights that assignment design can influence trust, objectivity, and implementation feasibility, and it notes that social-network and bidding-based methods are promising but insufficiently tested. The paper also identifies limitations to generalizability because many reviewed studies are context-specific and because comparative evidence across strategies remains limited.
finding.measure: Scalability, fairness, trust, and feasibility of peer-grading systems

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pre-existing social relationships among students affect the accuracy, fairness, and perceived value of peer assessment in an e-learning course. The authors focus on a practical concern in online and blended learning: whether peer grading remains trustworthy when students know one another, and whether relationship bias can distort grades or feedback.

The study was conducted in a Master’s course in Information Systems and Computer Engineering at the University of Lisbon, using a Moodle plugin called PeerForum to support peer assessment of skill-tree assignments. Students first nominated peers they liked most and least, then completed peer reviews under a single-anonymized setup with rubric-based training; each post was reviewed by five students, and analysis centered on posts with at least three peer assessments. The authors found that peer assessment was generally reliable and accurate relative to professor grades, with three or more reviewers usually sufficient for stable agreement. Social relationships did matter in the expected direction—liked peers tended to receive slightly higher grades and disliked peers slightly lower ones—but the magnitude was small and usually did not materially affect the final aggregate peer grade. Students also reported that peer assessment was useful and fair, and most did not perceive their relationships as strongly influencing grading or feedback.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment reduced instructor grading burden in a scalable online setting and was presented as a viable replacement for traditional evaluation. The paper reports that peer assessment was reliable and accurate with at least three peer assessments per post, suggesting a workable workflow for courses with many submissions (e.g., 625 posts with at least three peer assessments; 2681 total peer assessments analyzed).
finding.measure: Peer assessment reliability/accuracy and instructor workload implications
finding.study_size: n=64 students; 588 posts for accuracy analysis; 625 posts with at least three peer assessments

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that peer assessment became more useful and fair over the semester, and many felt it helped them engage with the course and complete the skills. In the final questionnaire (n=53 respondents who peer-graded), 54.7% agreed peer assessment was helpful after the course, 52.8% agreed it was fair, and several open-ended responses described increased engagement and motivation.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of usefulness, fairness, difficulty, engagement, and learning value (Likert questionnaire and open responses)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues and reports that peer assessment supported learning-related durable skills such as reflection, judgment, and evaluating peer work. Students stated that peer grading helped them learn the skills, improve their work, and think about what teachers expected; however, the study did not directly measure metacognition or critical thinking with a validated instrument.
finding.measure: Student-reported learning from grading peers and using rubrics; feedback usefulness

finding.finding_summary: The authors conclude that peer assessment can replace traditional evaluation in this e-learning context, provided it is not high-stakes and is supported by training and reviewer curation. They also argue that anonymity is not necessary if reviewer selection is balanced by relationship status and that at least three peer assessments should be required for dependable final grades.
finding.measure: Feasibility of replacing traditional evaluation; implementation recommendations for peer assessment design

paper_profiles.title: Exposía: Academic Writing Assessment of Exposés and Peer Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Exposía, a new public dataset for higher-education research on academic writing and peer feedback. The dataset captures a full drafting-and-revision workflow for undergraduate Computer Science students writing research project exposés, along with peer and instructor feedback, inline comments, and fine-grained instructor scores on both drafts and feedback.

The main contribution is not an instructional intervention study, but a data resource and benchmark for automated assessment. The authors define detailed rubrics for exposé quality and review quality, then use the dataset to analyze revision patterns and to test open-weight large language models (LLMs) on criterion-based scoring tasks. They report that final exposés improve over drafts, especially on content-heavy dimensions such as Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology, suggesting feedback is associated with substantive revisions.

The study population is 55 consented exposés and 306 reviews from a Bachelor-level Computer Science course (“Introduction to Scientific Work”) taken by undergraduate students. The paper also compares human raters and LLM scorers, finding that combined multi-criterion prompting works best and that model performance is stronger on low-expertise criteria than on content-dependent criteria. The authors caution that the resource supports decision-support and assessment research, not fully automated grading, and note limitations related to consent-based missing data, modest corpus size, and potential scoring bias.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies academic writing quality in research proposal/exposé writing. Across 55 drafts and final versions, final exposés improved relative to drafts, with the largest gains on content-oriented writing dimensions such as Approach, Motivation, Language/Quality, and Methodology; the authors describe the revisions as focused on conceptual and argumentative elements.
finding.measure: Instructor criterion-based scores on exposé writing rubrics (36 criteria across 9 rubrics), comparing draft vs. final exposés

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can reduce grading workload by automating criterion-based scoring of exposés and peer reviews. Combined prompting was more effective and more computationally efficient than single-criterion prompting, and the authors frame the system as a decision-support tool to reduce instructional effort rather than replace human grading.
finding.measure: Quadratic weighted agreement (QWA) of LLM-generated criterion scores against human ratings; comparison of single-criterion vs. combined prompting
finding.study_size: 55 exposés and 110 student reviews for scoring experiments

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s feedback rubric explicitly targets learning-supportive review skills such as clarity, specificity, usefulness, and future guidance, making peer reviewing a central durable-skill outcome. Human-rated review scores show relatively high agreement overall, and the dataset is positioned as a testbed for studying how feedback supports learning, reflection, and revision, but the paper does not report a causal effect estimate for skill gains.
finding.measure: Instructor criterion-based scores on peer review rubrics (24 criteria across 8 rubrics) and descriptive analyses of review quality

finding.finding_summary: The exposé task itself requires students to formulate research questions, specify methodology, and justify an academic proposal, so the paper directly studies scientific-reasoning-related writing performance. In the revision analysis, the strongest improvements were on Approach and Methodology rubrics, indicating better articulation of research design and proposal logic after feedback.
finding.measure: Criterion-based scores for exposé rubrics related to Motivation, Approach, Methodology, Schedule, and Bibliography

paper_profiles.title: Systematic Review of Approaches to Improve Peer Assessment at Scale & Possible Research Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a survey-style review of peer assessment at scale, with emphasis on MOOCs and other large-scale learning environments. It asks how peer assessment can be improved through better tools for automatic grading, methods to identify and mitigate rogue reviews, and natural-language-processing approaches that help reviewers write more useful feedback.

Across the review, the author synthesizes prior work on automated grading systems, peer feedback platforms, reviewer grouping methods, and NLP-based feedback analysis. The paper does not present a new empirical study of one intervention; instead, it compares prior systems such as PeerStudio, Critique-Kit, and SWoRD-related tools, highlighting where they improve grading accuracy, feedback quality, or reviewer experience and where they fall short. A recurring conclusion is that peer assessment can scale, but many solutions are domain-specific, work best for structured or programming tasks, and become burdensome when rubrics are complex or when reviewers are asked to address many criteria.

The review also argues that aggregation methods and reviewer-grouping strategies can improve score reliability and feedback quality, but these gains are limited by sparse data, reviewer bias, and implementation constraints. It notes that rapid or iterative feedback can improve performance, yet superficial or overly detailed review workflows may reduce student interest and increase workload. Overall, the paper positions peer assessment as promising but still technically and pedagogically challenging, especially for open-ended assignments and high-volume MOOC contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that peer-assessment tools and automated grading approaches can improve scalability, grading speed, and feedback delivery in large courses, but they also introduce workload and implementation burdens. For example, rapid/iterative feedback systems such as PeerStudio are described as helping performance, while the paper also notes that complex rubric-by-rubric reviewing is time-consuming and can reduce student interest.
finding.measure: Scalability, grading speed, reviewer workload, and implementation burden as described across reviewed peer-assessment systems

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed systems aim to improve the quality of peer feedback, reviewer judgment, and collaboration-related processes. The paper reports that adaptive guidance, rubric scaffolding, and NLP-based comment support can make feedback more specific and helpful, but that some static suggestions were rarely used and complex peer-review workflows can still be difficult for students to sustain.
finding.measure: Peer feedback quality, reviewer performance, and collaborative review processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes evidence that peer assessment and related support tools can improve performance on open-ended or programming assignments, especially when feedback is rapid or better structured. It also emphasizes that many approaches are domain-specific and work best for constrained tasks, with weaker applicability to complex assignments requiring multiple rubric dimensions.
finding.measure: Assignment grades, grading accuracy, and performance on programming/open-response tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies suggesting that grouping strategies and feedback tools can affect students’ experience, motivation, and perceptions of peer review. However, it also notes negative tradeoffs such as reduced interest when review tasks become cumbersome and the fact that some systems may not be used enough to support revision behavior.
finding.measure: Student perceptions, interest, and reported helpfulness of feedback/review systems

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide that examines how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame formative assessment around three core questions: where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that LLMs can potentially assist with each stage by generating student-friendly learning objectives, facilitating co-construction of success criteria, creating exemplars, producing questions for short-cycle checks, and drafting different levels of feedback.

Rather than testing a single intervention in a classroom experiment, the paper synthesizes examples, prompting strategies, and design considerations drawn from prior research and author demonstrations. It emphasizes that LLMs can reduce teacher workload and scale formative assessment, but only when used with pedagogical judgment and careful prompt design. The review repeatedly warns that generic benchmark metrics do not capture formative quality, that outputs vary and can be inaccurate or misaligned, and that educators must check and adapt AI-generated materials.

The paper’s main conclusion is that LLMs should be viewed as tools to augment, not replace, expert pedagogy in formative assessment. It highlights promise for accessibility and efficiency, but also tradeoffs involving fidelity, overreliance, privacy, transparency, and the risk that superficial use of AI will fail to produce meaningful formative effects. The discussion is conceptual and practice-oriented, with no original outcome study or effect estimate reported.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can save teacher time by automating or supporting tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating formative questions, drafting feedback, and producing sample work. These claims are illustrated with examples and prior studies, but the paper does not report original empirical effects from the authors' own sample or any controlled comparison.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, time required to create formative assessment materials, and ease of generating prompts/outputs

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that LLM-supported formative assessment may help develop transferable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, and the ability to evaluate exemplars. At the same time, it warns that students may over-rely on LLM-generated responses, which could weaken these durable skills if tools are used superficially or without reflective tasks.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, self-regulation, and evaluation of exemplars/prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs can improve the clarity and usability of learning objectives and exemplars across subjects, including biology and fMRI/neuroimaging examples. It cites prior work showing GPT-3.5 can outperform some simplification methods and that LLMs can generate sensible learning objectives, but these are cited examples rather than original empirical results in this paper.
finding.measure: Quality and clarity of learning objectives, exemplars, and subject-specific formative materials

paper_profiles.title: Measurement Integrity in Peer Prediction: A Peer Assessment Case Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how well peer prediction mechanisms work in peer assessment, especially when the goal is not only incentive compatibility but also fairness in the ex post sense that students should receive rewards that reflect the quality of their grading. The authors introduce a new concept, measurement integrity, defined as whether the rewards assigned by a mechanism meaningfully measure report quality, and argue that this is crucial for peer-grading applications such as MOOCs and course meta-grading.

To study this, the paper runs computational experiments on two settings: an agent-based model of semester-long peer assessment and a real peer-grading dataset from an undergraduate algorithms course at Northwestern University. The authors compare several mechanisms, including simple baselines (MSE, output agreement), standard peer prediction mechanisms (PTS, Φ-divergence variants), and parametric versions that incorporate a statistical model of grading behavior. They evaluate whether mechanism payments track report quality using ordinal and correlation-based metrics.

The main finding is that generic peer prediction mechanisms usually perform poorly on measurement integrity relative to simple baselines, and that theoretical incentive properties are only noisy predictors of empirical performance. Some parametric mechanisms improve results and can better balance measurement integrity with robustness to strategic reporting, but there is an apparent tradeoff: the mechanisms that best measure report quality can be more vulnerable to strategic behavior. The paper does not evaluate student learning outcomes directly; it is about the properties of grading mechanisms and their implications for peer assessment practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer grading can reduce course-staff workload because students grade one another’s work, which is especially valuable in MOOCs and large classes. This is a conceptual/practical claim rather than a causal estimate, and no effect size is reported, but the paper consistently frames peer assessment as an efficiency mechanism for instructors and administrators.
finding.measure: course staff workload / grading workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies whether peer prediction mechanisms are suitable for institutional deployment in peer assessment systems by examining measurement integrity and incentive properties. It finds that off-the-shelf mechanisms often fail to provide fair ex post rewards, while parametric augmentations can improve performance, implying important implementation tradeoffs for adoption in educational institutions.
finding.measure: mechanism suitability for peer assessment deployment; empirical measurement integrity and robustness against strategic reporting

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines the value of formative assessment and proposes an e-learning implementation using Blackboard (BB) at a university campus in Malaysia. The authors frame formative assessment as a diagnostic process that provides ongoing feedback during instruction, contrasting it with summative assessment, and argue that it can support better learning and improved performance on end-of-semester exams.

The practical component describes a Blackboard-based online testing approach: a series of weekly or fortnightly low-stakes tests with immediate, detailed feedback. The paper reports survey data from university students about their perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and the Blackboard test option. Students generally favored frequent short assessments and immediate feedback, especially because it broke content into manageable units and helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, though some expressed concerns about stress and overemphasis on grades.

Overall, the paper is primarily descriptive and perception-based rather than an outcome study of achievement. It concludes that formative assessment, especially when paired with timely individualized feedback and structured frequent testing, is likely to support learning and may improve summative results, but it also notes implementation challenges such as pressure, workload, and the need for careful design. The paper also suggests that effects may be particularly helpful for lower achievers, aligning with prior literature cited by the authors, but this claim is not directly tested in their own data.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments and immediate feedback were helpful for monitoring progress, building confidence, and keeping in touch with the subject throughout the semester. However, some students also reported stress and pressure from too many tests, and concerns that learning was overemphasized relative to grades.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognition and self-monitoring by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses and understand how to improve. Students also said that breaking coursework into small topic assessments made learning more manageable and helped them stay engaged with the subject over time.
finding.measure: Student perception survey and qualitative open-ended responses about learning process and feedback

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported weekly or fortnightly Blackboard quizzes as a way to improve learning in subject content, with the authors concluding that formative assessment may help prepare students for semester-end summative tests. The paper does not report direct achievement gains, but it presents perceptions that frequent assessment and immediate feedback are useful for subject learning.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard online tests; implied course learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Efficient Face Image Quality Assessment via Self-training and Knowledge Distillation
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (computer vision / face image quality assessment benchmark data; no human learner population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of making face image quality assessment (FIQA) models computationally efficient enough for practical deployment. The authors note that many state-of-the-art FIQA systems are accurate but too heavy for real-time or resource-constrained use, such as mobile or large-scale platform settings.

To solve this, they propose a two-stage framework combining self-training and knowledge distillation. First, a high-capacity teacher model is trained on labeled face images and then improved iteratively using pseudo-labels generated for large pools of unlabeled face images. Second, a compact student model is trained using the original labeled data plus pseudo-labeled data from both the initial and enhanced teacher models.

The experiments are conducted on the ICCV 2025 VQualA FIQA Challenge dataset, using labeled images from CelebA and Flickr along with about 400,000 unlabeled Internet-sourced face images. Results show that the enhanced teacher slightly outperforms the original teacher, and the student model achieves performance comparable to the teacher while drastically reducing parameters and GFLOPs. The paper concludes that iterative pseudo-labeling and distillation can preserve predictive accuracy while making FIQA models much more deployable in practice.

finding.finding_summary: The main contribution is improved computational efficiency for FIQA deployment. The distilled student model achieves near-teacher performance (SRCC=0.9855, PLCC=0.9914) with only 1.18M parameters and 0.4949 GFLOPs, compared with the teacher’s 86.88M parameters and 50.13 GFLOPs. The authors report about a 99% parameter reduction and nearly 100x lower FLOPs.
finding.measure: SRCC, PLCC, parameter count, GFLOPs

paper_profiles.title: National peer-review research assessment exercises for the hard sciences can be a complete waste of money: the Italian case
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether Italy’s first national research assessment exercise (VTR, covering 2001–2003) was worth its cost for evaluating hard-science university performance. The authors compare the VTR’s peer-review-based rankings against a bibliometric benchmark built from Web of Science publication and citation data, and against several zero-cost proxy rankings derived from geography, regional economics, and freely available online university rankings.

The central approach is comparative rank analysis across 61 Italian universities and eight hard-science UDAs, using Spearman correlations and quartile-shift analyses. The paper finds that peer-review rankings were not clearly better than some zero-cost indicators, and were consistently weaker than a normalized citation-impact ranking from SCImago. In several disciplines, latitude-based or other proxy rankings correlated with the bibliometric benchmark as well as or better than the VTR rankings.

The population/context is the Italian public university system in the hard sciences, with analysis aggregated at university, UDA, and macro-UDA levels. The main conclusion is that the VTR’s direct and indirect costs could potentially have been avoided, because the peer-review exercise produced rankings that were not more accurate than inexpensive alternatives and were less accurate than bibliometric measures based on full publication output.

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that the Italian VTR peer-review exercise produced rankings that were no better than several zero-cost proxy rankings and worse than bibliometric rankings. Across universities, the VTR correlated with the bibliometric benchmark at ρ=+0.6162, while SCImago normalized impact correlated more strongly at ρ=+0.7225; quartile shifts also showed more instability for VTR than for NI.
finding.measure: Rank correlations and quartile-shift distributions comparing VTR peer-review rankings, bibliometric benchmark rankings, and zero-cost alternative rankings
finding.study_size: n=61 universities (ranking comparisons), with discipline-level analyses across 8 UDAs
finding.effect_size: ρ=+0.6162 (VTR vs bibliometric P); ρ=+0.7225 (NI vs P)

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that the peer-review-based VTR was highly costly and time-consuming relative to alternatives. The authors report the exercise covered 102 research institutions, about 18,000 outputs, 183 panelists, and 6,661 reviewers, took almost two years, and cost 3.5 million euro in direct costs; they argue these costs could have been avoided by using bibliometric or zero-cost rankings.
finding.measure: Administrative burden, direct costs, time to execute the evaluation, and number of outputs/reviewers involved

paper_profiles.title: Large Language Model-Driven Dynamic Assessment of Grammatical Accuracy in English Language Learner Writing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) can be used to scale up computerized dynamic assessment (DA) for grammatical accuracy in second-language writing. The authors argue that traditional teacher-led DA is pedagogically valuable but difficult to deliver at scale, especially in large language classes, because it requires individualized, graduated hints. To address this, they developed DynaWrite, a modular web application that gives learners increasingly explicit feedback on grammatical errors in their own writing.

The system was tested primarily with Japanese university students writing English, using corpus-derived sentences and learner writing to evaluate error detection and feedback quality. The authors first screened 21 LLMs, then conducted deeper testing with GPT-4o and neural chat on 200 sentences. They evaluated detection accuracy with classification metrics and also judged whether feedback was pedagogically usable based on consistency, gradation, and resolution. GPT-4o and neural chat performed similarly in error detection (F1 about 0.74), but GPT-4o produced far more usable graduated feedback than neural chat.

The paper also assessed technical deployment characteristics such as response time, stability, and scalability. The authors conclude that LLMs can support dynamic assessment in learners’ free writing and that a platform like DynaWrite can deliver real-time, scalable feedback. At the same time, the paper highlights important limitations: false positives remain a concern, usable feedback quality varies substantially by model, and the current system requires stronger infrastructure, broader model coverage, and more robust user-experience evaluation before wide deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies grammatical error detection and dynamic feedback in English writing, an academic literacy task. On a 200-sentence test set, GPT-4o achieved TP=87, TN=53, FP=46, FN=14 with precision=0.654, recall=0.861, and F1=0.743; neural chat achieved TP=82, TN=59, FP=41, FN=18 with precision=0.667, recall=0.820, and F1=0.735. GPT-4o also produced usable graduated feedback for 59 of 87 true positives and 38 of 46 false positives, while neural chat produced usable feedback for only about 7 of 59 true positives and 9 of 41 false positives.
finding.measure: Grammatical error identification and quality of dynamic feedback for learner writing
finding.study_size: n=200 sentences for the main comparison; initial screening on n=8 sentences across 21 models

finding.finding_summary: A major goal of the system is scalability and real-time deployment of dynamic assessment. The paper reports that the selected models had acceptable response times and stability for real-time interaction, and that the platform could support multiple concurrent users without significant degradation. The system architecture was explicitly designed to reduce the labor and time burden of teacher-delivered dynamic assessment through automated, scalable hint delivery.
finding.measure: Average response time, response time stability (standard deviation), and scalability under concurrent requests
finding.std_deviation: Reported qualitatively; specific values not reported in the extracted text

finding.finding_summary: The paper positions LLM-driven dynamic assessment as a way to make individualized formative writing assessment feasible at larger institutional scales than traditional teacher-student DA. It argues that the microservices-based architecture, authentication, reporting, and model-switching design could support deployment in classroom, institutional, or even nationwide contexts. However, the evidence remains technical and prototype-oriented rather than showing institutional outcomes in practice.
finding.measure: Platform design for scalable deployment, reporting, and multi-user support

paper_profiles.title: The Study of Peer Assessment Impact on Group Learning Activities
paper_profiles.venue: FECS'21 (The 17th Int'l Conf on Frontiers in Education: Computer Science and Computer Engineering)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how peer assessment affects group learning activities and student perceptions of fairness, contribution, and feedback in undergraduate computer science modules. The authors frame peer assessment as a formative process intended to improve group learning and make assessment more transparent, while also acknowledging common concerns such as reliability, conflict, and freeloading.

The study combines a preliminary survey of 582 students (276 responses), a focus group with 12 participants (10 undergraduates and 2 Ph.D. students), and a case study of an HCI coursework group project using Facebook for collaboration and evidence of contribution (27 returned questionnaires). The context is a Malaysian university school of computer science, where peer assessment had already been used in several modules. Findings are largely descriptive: many students valued transparency and feedback, but substantial minorities preferred individual work, reported conflict, or were uncomfortable giving negative feedback.

In the case study, most respondents reported enjoying group work with Facebook, believing peer assessment was fair, and appreciating its transparency. The authors conclude that peer assessment can support formative assessment and group learning when it is designed carefully, but that it can also create conflict, be viewed as unfair, and require safeguards such as clearer rules, confidential submission, accountability for free-riding, and structured feedback. The paper does not provide causal evidence that peer assessment improves academic achievement; its main contribution is a set of implementation recommendations and a report of student attitudes and experiences.

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward peer assessment and group work were mixed. In the survey (n=276 responses from 582 students), 63% reported being comfortable assessing peers and 74% valued peer feedback, but 37% would choose individual work over group work and many cited conflict and unequal contribution as concerns. In the case study (n=27 questionnaires), 82.1% said they enjoyed working in a group with Facebook and 82.1% said peer assessment was impartial, suggesting generally positive but uneven affective responses.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of fairness, comfort with peer assessment, enjoyment of group work, and attitudes toward feedback
finding.study_size: n=276 survey responses; n=12 focus group participants; n=27 case study questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on collaboration, group dynamics, and constructive feedback as durable skills associated with peer assessment. In the case study (n=27), 89.3% of students said they could demonstrate their skills through group work, and the authors argue that peer assessment can help students learn to give constructive feedback and monitor contribution. However, the study also reports persistent problems with freeloading, conflict, and disruptive behavior that can undermine collaboration.
finding.measure: Self-reported collaboration/group-work experience, perceived skill demonstration, and feedback practices
finding.study_size: n=276 survey responses; n=12 focus group participants; n=27 case study questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: The study discusses process efficiency and implementation burden mainly in terms of making peer assessment easier to run and more transparent. Participants preferred online submission and Moodle/ Facebook-based workflows over Word documents, and the authors argue that online, time-bounded, and rule-based implementation could reduce discussion, friendship conflicts, and administrative difficulty. However, no direct workload or time-on-task outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Perceived usability and transparency of online peer-assessment processes
finding.study_size: n=27 case study questionnaires; qualitative focus group data

finding.finding_summary: The paper makes institutional recommendations for how peer assessment should be governed and administered in courses. It argues for transparent scoring mechanisms, clear task allocation, confidential submission, and safeguards against freeloading so that peer assessment can function more fairly within course assessment systems. These are implementation recommendations rather than measured institutional effects.
finding.measure: Recommendations regarding assessment governance, transparency, and monitoring

paper_profiles.title: AI chatbots versus human healthcare professionals: a systematic review and meta-analysis of empathy in patient care
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether large language model (LLM) chatbots are perceived as more empathic than human healthcare professionals in patient-care communication. The authors conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies from 2023–2024 that directly compared AI-generated responses with human clinicians’ responses on empathy-related outcomes.

The review included 15 studies spanning multiple healthcare contexts, including general medical questions, outpatient messaging, dermatology, oncology, thyroid disease, systemic lupus erythematosus, multiple sclerosis, autism-related queries, mental health support, and patient complaints. Most comparisons used text-only interactions and blinded proxy raters such as clinicians, patient proxies, laypeople, or students. Thirteen studies provided data for pooling; the meta-analysis found that ChatGPT-based systems were rated as more empathic than human practitioners overall (pooled SMD=0.87, 95% CI 0.54–1.20), with GPT-4 showing a stronger pooled advantage than GPT-3.5.

The main conclusion is that, in text-based healthcare communication, LLM chatbots are often perceived as more empathic than human clinicians, especially GPT-4, though heterogeneity was high and the evidence is limited by unvalidated measures, proxy raters, and non-real-world interaction formats. The authors caution that these findings should not be overgeneralized to voice or in-person care and note important concerns about clinical accuracy, contamination, and implementation fidelity. They recommend future trials using direct patient evaluations, voice-enabled systems, and clinically supervised AI drafting workflows.

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper is not an education study, it does directly discuss a workflow implication for clinician productivity: AI could draft patient-facing messages and reduce clinician workload while preserving or improving empathic tone. The review does not provide a pooled workload effect size, but it explicitly recommends randomized trials to test impacts on clinician workload and suggests a human-AI collaboration model to free clinician time.
finding.measure: Clinician workload / drafting efficiency (conceptual, not directly pooled)

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI chatbots may be useful for institutional patient-communication systems, but only with clinician oversight, disclosure, and safeguards for accuracy and safety. The paper frames its findings as relevant to healthcare service design and governance, recommending policy-sensitive evaluation of AI disclosure, accuracy, and implementation fidelity.
finding.measure: Institutional implementation implications, disclosure, governance, and service design

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments compare when used as inputs for Generative AI-enhanced feedback in a higher-education engineering course. The core problem is that timely formative feedback is hard to scale in large classes, and the authors explore whether human evaluations can be combined in the AICoFe system to produce more reliable and pedagogically useful feedback.

The study was conducted with 46 final-year undergraduate students in Telecommunication Technology and Service Engineering at Universidad Autónoma de Madrid. Each student gave an individual oral presentation that was scored with a validated 15-item rubric by the teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the student themself; the teacher also assigned an independent overall grade. The analysis focused on agreement, correlations, and score biases across evaluators, rather than on learning gains from an intervention.

Results showed moderate to substantial agreement overall, especially when using Gwet’s AC2 rather than Cohen’s kappa, with peer-peer agreement stronger than teacher-self agreement. Teacher rubric scores correlated strongly with the teacher’s overall grade (r=0.88), peer scores correlated moderately to strongly (r=0.69), and self-assessments were the least aligned but still significant (r=0.59). The teacher was consistently stricter than peers and the teacher’s own global grade, while self-scores were slightly higher than teacher rubric scores. The main conclusion is that peer and self-assessments can be useful, but they should be weighted and interpreted differently rather than simply averaged, motivating a bias-aware GenAI feedback design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on oral presentation performance in engineering education, using a rubric with 15 items covering content, design, and delivery during 10-minute presentations plus 5-minute Q&A sessions. It does not test improvement in speaking outcomes, but it does provide evidence that peer, self, and teacher ratings of oral communication are moderately to substantially aligned (e.g., teacher-self r=0.62; teacher-peer r=0.59; n=46), indicating that the assessment system can capture speaking-related performance reliably.
finding.measure: Rubric-based oral presentation scores (content, design, delivery) and independent teacher overall grade

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examines evaluative judgment, self-assessment, and alignment across teacher, peer, and self ratings, all of which relate to metacognition and reflective judgment. Self-assessments were moderately correlated with the teacher’s overall grade (r=0.59, ρ=0.67), but they were also significantly more lenient than teacher rubric scores (mean difference +0.36 on a 0–10 scale, p=0.037), suggesting partial calibration and some self-perception bias.
finding.measure: Agreement, correlations, and mean differences among teacher, peer, and self-assessments on a validated rubric

finding.finding_summary: A central motivation of the paper is scalability of feedback in large higher-education classes, and the authors propose a GenAI-enhanced workflow to reduce reliance on teacher-only feedback. While no workload experiment was run, the paper explicitly argues that integrating peer and self-assessments with generative AI can support more efficient feedback production and reduce teacher burden while maintaining human oversight.
finding.measure: Design analysis and proposed AICoFe/GePeTo feedback integration approach

paper_profiles.title: DisasterM3: A Remote Sensing Vision-Language Dataset for Disaster Damage Assessment and Response
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (remote sensing disaster imagery / models, not human learners)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces DisasterM3, a large remote sensing vision-language dataset designed for disaster damage assessment and response. The authors argue that existing vision-language models (VLMs) struggle in disaster scenes because of limited disaster-specific training data, cross-sensor mismatch between optical and SAR imagery, and weak counting/reasoning performance in complex scenes.

To address this, the paper curates 26,988 bi-temporal satellite images and 123,010 instruction pairs spanning 36 historical disaster events across five continents. DisasterM3 supports nine disaster-focused tasks covering recognition, counting, referring segmentation, spatial reasoning, and long-form report generation. The dataset combines optical and SAR post-disaster imagery and is split into an instruction-tuning set and a benchmark set.

The authors benchmark 14 generic and remote sensing VLMs and find substantial performance gaps, especially on SAR imagery and fine-grained damage-counting tasks. They then fine-tune four models on DisasterM3 and report consistent improvements across tasks, with gains up to 10.4% in QA accuracy, 2.1 points in report scoring, and 40.8% in referring segmentation. The paper concludes that disaster-specific corpus injection helps narrow the domain gap, though overfitting and cross-sensor limitations remain important concerns.

finding.finding_summary: DisasterM3 is designed to improve AI-assisted disaster assessment workflows, and fine-tuning on the dataset improves model performance on several operational tasks. The authors report stable gains across QA, report generation, and referring segmentation, with up to +10.4% QA accuracy, +2.1 report-score points, and +40.8% referring segmentation performance, suggesting better automated support for damage assessment and response.
finding.measure: QA accuracy, disaster report scoring, referring segmentation mIoU/cIoU
finding.effect_size: up to +10.4% QA; +2.1 report score; +40.8% referring segmentation

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Readability Assessment of German Sentences with Transformer Ensembles
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the GermEval 2022 Workshop on Text Complexity Assessment of German Text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic readability assessment (ARA) for German sentences. The authors ask whether ensembles of fine-tuned transformer language models, specifically GBERT and GPT-2-Wechsel, can predict human judgments of sentence complexity more accurately than models built from a single transformer type, and whether adding traditional linguistic readability features improves performance.

The study uses the GermEval 2022 shared-task dataset of 1,000 German sentences drawn from Wikipedia articles, with 10,650 human ratings on complexity, understandability, and lexical difficulty collected on a 7-point Likert scale. The task is framed as regression on mean opinion scores (MOS) for text complexity/readability. The modeling pipeline includes fine-tuning transformer encoders, adding regression heads, incorporating 154 handcrafted readability features, and evaluating ensemble size and composition with cross-validation and held-out test data.

Results show that larger ensembles generally reduce RMSE and stabilize predictions, with mixed ensembles of GBERT and GPT-2-Wechsel outperforming homogeneous ensembles. On the shared-task test set, the best mixed ensemble achieved RMSE 0.442 (mapped RMSE 0.4355), ranking 2nd. The authors also report that traditional linguistic features slightly improved performance, although the gains were small. Overall, the paper concludes that ensemble composition matters, and that combining transformer representations with handcrafted readability features is beneficial for German readability prediction.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies automatic readability assessment, a literacy-related task, by predicting German sentence complexity/readability from human ratings. Mixed ensembles of GBERT and GPT-2-Wechsel achieved better prediction accuracy than homogeneous ensembles, with the best submitted mixed ensemble reaching RMSE 0.442 on the test set (mapped RMSE 0.4355), and traditional readability features provided a small additional benefit.
finding.measure: Root mean squared error (RMSE) for predicting Mean Opinion Scores of sentence readability/text complexity

paper_profiles.title: Classroom assessment and pedagogy
paper_profiles.venue: Assessment in Education: Principles, Policy & Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that formative and summative assessment should not be treated as separate, disconnected domains, but rather understood within a broader theory of pedagogy. Black and Wiliam contend that classroom assessment is best viewed as an evidentiary process: teachers gather information from student work, dialogue, and testing, then use that evidence to make instructional decisions. The paper reviews major pedagogical frameworks and shows how assessment is embedded in aims, planning, classroom interaction, and review of learning.

The authors focus especially on classroom teaching and learning across K-12 and, to a lesser extent, postsecondary contexts, drawing heavily on prior research, theory, and examples from formative assessment practice. They emphasize that effective formative assessment depends on eliciting evidence from all students, responding contingently, and using feedback to move learning forward. They also argue that summative assessment can sometimes support learning when designed and used well, but that high-stakes accountability and narrow testing can undermine learning by distorting instruction.

A major conclusion is that there should be synergy, not a sharp divide, between formative and summative assessment. The paper highlights persistent tensions: workload, moderation, reliability, comparability, and the risk of superficial or test-driven implementation. It concludes that teacher judgment can play a meaningful role in summative assessment, but only when systems provide training, moderation, and assessment designs that are aligned with broader educational aims.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a conceptual/theoretical review, but it cites evidence that formative assessment and related classroom assessment practices can improve student achievement on standardized tests, while also warning that poorly designed high-stakes summative assessment can narrow the curriculum and distort instruction. No single new effect size is reported in this article; instead it synthesizes prior evidence and examples to argue for synergy between formative and summative purposes.
finding.measure: Student achievement on standardized tests; curricular breadth and assessment validity

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment practices such as feedback, self-assessment, and peer-assessment can support students’ motivation, self-regulation, and willingness to take an active role in learning. It notes that feedback framed as comments for improvement is more likely than grades to promote a belief that ability can improve, although no new quantitative effect is reported here.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-regulation, learner agency

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that classroom assessment supports durable skills such as metacognition, dialogue, collaboration, and the ability to apply learning in new contexts. The authors emphasize dialogue, peer interaction, and self-monitoring as mechanisms for developing learners’ power of critical review, but the article is a theory/review piece and does not report new effect sizes.
finding.measure: Metacognition, dialogue, collaboration, transfer of learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses workload and implementation burdens of formative and summative assessment systems, especially the demands of moderation, portfolio-based assessment, and maintaining reliability and comparability. It reports that in the KOSAP project moderation was viewed as valuable for rigour and confidence, but also implies that the processes require training and consistent support and can be logistically complex.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, moderation burden, assessment reliability/comparability processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses how accountability systems, external testing, moderation, and teacher assessment shape institutional practice. It argues that high-stakes testing can undermine learning and construct validity, while more integrated systems with contextual value-added accountability, teacher judgment, and moderation can better align assessment with educational aims; no new quantitative effect is reported.
finding.measure: Assessment policy, accountability, moderation, validity of teacher assessment systems

paper_profiles.title: Online Diagnostic Assessment in Support of Personalized Teaching and Learning: The eDia System
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the eDia online diagnostic assessment system and explains how it was designed to support personalized teaching and learning through frequent, technology-based formative feedback. The authors motivate the system by arguing that traditional summative assessments provide feedback too slowly and too coarsely to support day-to-day instructional adjustment, especially in heterogeneous classrooms where students differ substantially in prior knowledge and developmental level.

The paper describes the system architecture, including item banking, online delivery, automated scoring, analytics, teacher-assembled tests, adaptive testing options, and multiple feedback formats. It also outlines three-dimensional assessment frameworks for reading, mathematics, and science spanning Grades 1–6, and discusses how technology enables measurement of disciplinary knowledge, application, and psychological/cognitive dimensions. The discussion emphasizes that eDia is intended to help teachers diagnose learning needs, differentiate instruction, and support formative assessment in regular school practice.

Evidence reported in the paper is primarily descriptive and based on the system’s development, piloting, and implementation across more than 1,000 Hungarian partner schools, along with summaries of related research applications in other countries and contexts. The paper concludes that online diagnostic assessment can improve the feasibility, frequency, and richness of feedback, but that assessment alone does not improve learning unless teachers are trained and the information is used to change instruction; it also notes practical limitations, including workload, the need for professional development, and the risk of superficial implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that eDia improves operational efficiency by automating scoring, data processing, scaling, feedback generation, and test assembly, reducing the time and human resources needed for frequent diagnostic assessment. The system is reported to support regular school use across more than 1,000 schools, with immediate results available after testing; however, no quantitative effect size for workload reduction is reported.
finding.measure: assessment administration, automated scoring, data processing, and feedback turnaround

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports broad institutional adoption and infrastructure development: eDia had been piloted and operated in experimental mode since 2015 and was in use in over 1,000 partner schools in Hungary, with additional applications in other countries and in higher education. The system is presented as a platform for scaling diagnostic assessment and supporting schoolwide and longitudinal data collection, but the paper does not report a quantitative institutional impact estimate.
finding.measure: system adoption, school participation, implementation scale

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes reading assessments within the eDia system, including diagnostic frameworks for Grades 1–6 and implementations in multiple language-related studies. It reports that the system can capture reading-related skills and provide differentiated feedback, but it does not present a single pooled effect of the assessment system on reading achievement.
finding.measure: reading assessment performance and diagnostic feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes mathematics as one of the three core domains of eDia and notes that the system supports diagnostic assessment of mathematical learning from Grades 1–6, including application, disciplinary, and psychological dimensions. It also references related studies in reasoning and problem-solving, but does not report a numerical effect on mathematics achievement from the system itself.
finding.measure: mathematics diagnostic assessment and related reasoning/problem-solving measures

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies science as a core diagnostic domain in eDia and describes science-related frameworks and items designed to assess reasoning, application, and disciplinary knowledge. It mentions feasibility and implementation across schools and related scientific inquiry studies, but does not provide a quantitative effect size for gains in scientific reasoning attributable to eDia.
finding.measure: science diagnostic assessment and scientific reasoning/inquiry tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that eDia has been used for English and German as foreign language assessments, including listening, reading, and vocabulary tasks, and that authentic audio can be used to assess listening. It presents these as expanded assessment capabilities rather than as outcome evaluations, so no effect size or pre-post gain is reported.
finding.measure: foreign language reading, listening, and vocabulary assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses motivation and other affective variables as part of the eDia platform’s broader assessment scope, including mastery motivation and self-regulated learning strategy questionnaires. It argues that regular personalized feedback and optimally challenging tasks may support intrinsic motivation, but it does not report quantitative evidence that the system increased motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: mastery motivation and self-regulated learning questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the paper is devoted to assessing reasoning and problem-solving skills, including inductive reasoning, combinatorial reasoning, dynamic problem-solving, collaborative problem-solving, and creativity. These are presented as measurable constructs within eDia and as examples of what technology-based assessment enables, but the paper does not report a single causal estimate of improvement in these skills from using the system.
finding.measure: inductive reasoning, combinatorial reasoning, dynamic problem-solving, collaborative problem-solving, creativity

paper_profiles.title: Asesmen Pembelajaran Sekolah Dasar dalam Kurikulum Merdeka
paper_profiles.venue: Pena Anda Jurnal Pendidikan Sekolah Dasar
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses assessment practices in Indonesian elementary schools within the Merdeka Curriculum (Kurikulum Merdeka). The authors aim to clarify what assessment means in learning, why it matters for understanding students’ needs and progress, and how formative and summative assessment are positioned in current policy and classroom practice.

The paper is a documentary/historical review based on government documents and related literature, rather than an empirical study of student outcomes. It explains that formative assessment is used at the beginning of learning and during instruction to identify student readiness, learning difficulties, and ongoing progress, while summative assessment is used at the end of learning units or at the end of the school year to determine achievement, promotion, and graduation decisions.

The article focuses on elementary-school teachers and the implementation context of the Merdeka Curriculum in Indonesia. It outlines assessment principles, examples of instruments such as rubrics, checklists, anecdotal notes, and portfolios, and a suggested assessment cycle that begins with planning, includes diagnostic/formative assessment at the start of lessons, teacher adjustment of plans, instruction, and end-of-lesson assessment. The main conclusion is that assessment should be integrated with instruction and used formatively to support differentiated and student-centered learning, but the paper does not report original data, effect sizes, or comparative evidence on learning gains.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure operational efficiency empirically, but it argues that formative assessment is intended to support teachers’ planning, adjustment, and reflection during instruction. It presents assessment as part of a practical instructional cycle (plan, assess at the start, modify, teach, assess at the end), but reports no data on workload, efficiency, or implementation costs.
finding.measure: not_reported
