finding.finding_summary: The article substantively addresses the Merdeka Curriculum’s assessment policy and how assessment should be implemented in elementary schools under Indonesian regulations. It describes official standards, assessment principles, and examples of instruments, but it does not evaluate policy outcomes empirically or compare institutions.
finding.measure: policy/document review of assessment regulations and curriculum guidance

paper_profiles.title: Kurikulum Merdeka dalam Perspektif Pedagogik
paper_profiles.population: Educators (K-12 teachers in the context of Indonesian elementary and secondary education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses Indonesia’s new “Kurikulum Merdeka” (Independent Curriculum) from a pedagogical perspective. The author frames the curriculum reform as a response to persistent concerns about uneven educational quality and low student literacy/numeracy, and asks what teacher competencies need to be strengthened so the curriculum can be implemented effectively.

Using a literature review approach, the paper analyzes the curriculum’s major pedagogical changes: competency-based learning outcomes organized by developmental phase, project-based learning tied to the Pancasila Student Profile, and a stronger emphasis on formative assessment over summative assessment. The article argues that these shifts require teachers to deepen their understanding of constructivist learning theory, adopt more suitable approaches for interdisciplinary projects (including socio-scientific approaches), and expand the use of formative assessment practices in everyday instruction.

The paper does not report original empirical data; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and policy documents to identify implementation needs and likely challenges. Its main conclusion is that successful implementation of Kurikulum Merdeka depends heavily on teacher pedagogical readiness, especially in designing meaningful projects, facilitating active learning, and using assessment formatively rather than relying primarily on end-of-unit summative testing.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment and project-based implementation under Kurikulum Merdeka require teachers to develop new pedagogical competencies and may increase preparation demands. It does not provide original effect sizes, but it explicitly notes that teachers must expand their assessment practices and use platform-based independent training to support implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher pedagogical readiness and assessment implementation demands (literature-based discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The article presents Kurikulum Merdeka as a policy response to low literacy/numeracy and uneven educational quality in Indonesia, arguing that the reform is intended to improve curriculum relevance and school-level autonomy. The paper does not test policy outcomes empirically, but it strongly emphasizes system-level curriculum change, teacher preparation, and institutional implementation conditions.
finding.measure: Curriculum reform and implementation readiness in Indonesian schools

paper_profiles.title: The future of self-assessment in classroom practice: Reframing self-assessment as a core competency
paper_profiles.population: Compulsory schooling (K-12), with examples spanning primary, middle school, and secondary students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that student self-assessment should be understood less as a formal assessment practice and more as a teachable component of self-regulated learning. Drawing on prior research and reviews, the authors review concerns about the validity and reliability of student self-evaluations, noting that students’ judgments often diverge from teacher ratings, test scores, and rubric-based criteria.

The article synthesizes literature on forms of self-assessment used in classrooms, including self-estimation, self-rating, rubric-based judgments, self-correction, and computer-assisted prompts. It concludes that self-assessment can improve achievement and self-regulation when it is explicitly taught, sequenced developmentally, and implemented in psychologically safe settings. The authors propose a curriculum progression: start with simple, concrete self-estimates for younger or lower-performing students, then move toward scaffolded, criterion-based, and eventually rubric-based self-assessment.

The paper emphasizes tradeoffs and implementation risks: superficial uses such as smiley-face scales, public disclosure of self-ratings, or using self-assessments for grading/accountability may undermine validity and may even be harmful. It also highlights workload considerations, suggesting that well-designed self-assessment can reduce teacher burden, but only if teachers and students receive training and if implementation is structured around accuracy, feedback, and student justification of judgments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that student self-assessment can contribute to improved academic performance when it is systematically taught and used as part of instruction. It summarizes prior studies showing that self-assessment training and structured self-evaluation are associated with better achievement outcomes, but notes that the effects are highly variable and depend on realism, feedback, and developmental fit.
finding.measure: Academic performance / achievement, including external examinations, graded work, and task performance

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that self-assessment supports self-regulation, motivation, engagement, and efficacy. The authors state that teaching students to set targets, evaluate progress, and adjust strategy use improves self-regulatory skills and can reduce dependence on the teacher.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, motivation, engagement, efficacy, and self-evaluative capability

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats self-assessment as a durable skill, specifically a metacognitive competence within self-regulated learning. It reports that students can improve metacognitive monitoring and evaluation through instruction, especially when they learn to apply criteria, justify judgments, and compare performance against standards or prior work.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-monitoring, judgment accuracy, and criterion-based reflection

finding.finding_summary: The article notes that self-assessment may reduce teacher workload by shifting some tracking and feedback responsibility to students. However, it qualifies this claim by emphasizing that such efficiency gains depend on training, structure, and avoiding superficial implementation that undermines accuracy.
finding.measure: Teacher assessment workload / responsibility for feedback and progress tracking

paper_profiles.title: Challenges in addressing student difficulties with quantum measurement of two-state quantum systems using a multiple-choice question sequence in online and in-person classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a research-validated multiple-choice question sequence (CQS) can improve students’ understanding of quantum measurement in an upper-level undergraduate quantum mechanics course. The authors focus on a topic that is known to be conceptually difficult: distinguishing the action of an operator from the act of measurement, identifying measurement outcomes and probabilities, handling basis changes, understanding state collapse, working through successive measurements, and beginning to reason about expectation values.

The intervention is a short sequence of clicker questions designed to scaffold common misconceptions, provide immediate feedback, and support productive struggle. It was implemented over three consecutive years in a mandatory junior/senior quantum mechanics course at a large U.S. research university, with one online administration and two in-person administrations. The in-person sections included peer discussion; the online section largely lacked peer interaction and relied more on individual polling and instructor-led discussion.

Across all implementations, post-test performance improved on nearly every concept, with larger gains for items that were initially difficult and smaller gains for items students already handled well after lecture. The authors conclude that the CQS was beneficial in both online and in-person settings and appears robust across instructors and textbooks. They also report evidence of retention: on a later midterm in one in-person class, students performed very well on analogous questions after solutions had been posted, suggesting that the structured struggle and feedback supported durable learning. The paper notes persistent difficulty on some core misconceptions and acknowledges that modality, instructor, and online assessment conditions may affect the results.

finding.finding_summary: The clicker question sequence improved understanding of quantum-measurement concepts in an upper-level quantum mechanics course. Across three implementations (online n=30; in-person n=23; in-person n=28), post-test scores increased on nearly every item, with medium-to-large Cohen’s d in many cases (e.g., question 1: d=0.78 online, 0.84 in-person 1; question 2a: d=0.62 online, 0.73 in-person 1, 1.04 in-person 2).
finding.measure: Pretest/post-test scores on conceptually focused quantum measurement questions and item-level correctness
finding.effect_size: d=0.22 to 1.04 (item-level); normalized gains up to 1.00 on later retention items

finding.finding_summary: The intervention supported transfer and retention-like outcomes through successive-measurement and far-transfer items, and later midterm performance suggested students retained or further consolidated the concepts. For the in-person class with follow-up testing (n=28), analogous midterm questions reached nearly 100% correctness on several items, including 2b and 4b, with normalized gains of 1.00 on those retained items.
finding.measure: Performance on successive-measurement/far-transfer items and delayed midterm questions; evidence of transfer/retention of conceptual reasoning
finding.effect_size: d=0.16 to 0.80 on delayed items; normalized gain=1.00 for some retained items

paper_profiles.title: Online Assessment in Higher Education: A Systematic Review
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; graduate; postgraduate; MOOC learners in higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how online assessment is designed and used in higher education and what benefits and success factors have been reported in the research literature. Rather than testing a single intervention, the authors systematically review empirical studies on online assessment to synthesize evidence about assessment modes, formats, types, feedback practices, and implementation conditions.

The review screened 4,290 records and included 114 empirical publications from 2010–2022. Across the studies, the authors identify four main assessment modes: peer, teacher, automated, and self-assessment. These modes were implemented in formative, summative, or mixed formats across tasks such as quizzes, essays, e-portfolios, projects, short-answer questions, and interactive activities.

The review concludes that online assessment has promising potential to support learning outcomes and learning processes in higher education, especially when it is formative, aligned with course goals, and accompanied by clear criteria, rubrics, timely feedback, and instructional support. It also highlights that automated assessment is most often used formatively, peer and teacher assessment are often combined with rubrics and written feedback, and self-assessment is mainly used for reflection. The paper emphasizes design tradeoffs and risks, including the need for strong implementation support, transparency, and attention to academic misconduct, infrastructure, and student access.

finding.finding_summary: Across 114 higher-education studies, online assessment was associated with improved academic performance and other learning outcomes in many cases, but the review does not report a pooled effect size. Formative quizzes, peer feedback, e-portfolios, and automated feedback were repeatedly linked to better final learning outcomes, higher-order thinking, and improved task performance, though the evidence is heterogeneous and largely study-specific.
finding.measure: Academic performance, final learning outcomes, task performance, course completion, writing accuracy, higher-order thinking outcomes
finding.study_size: n=114 publications (review sample); individual study ns vary and are not pooled

finding.finding_summary: The review found that online assessment was frequently studied for effects on motivation, engagement, self-regulation, reflection, and satisfaction. Reported findings generally suggest that formative quizzes, peer assessment, portfolios, and gamified feedback can increase motivation and engagement and support self-regulation and reflection, but the review does not provide pooled estimates.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, self-regulation, reflection, satisfaction, sense of community
finding.study_size: n=114 publications (review sample); individual study ns vary and are not pooled

finding.finding_summary: The review reports repeated links between online assessment and durable skills such as critical thinking, metacognition/reflection, collaboration, and deeper learning. E-portfolios were often associated with reflection and higher-order thinking, peer assessment with collaborative learning and deep learning, and some studies reported gains in critical thinking, but no pooled effect size is given.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflection/metacognition, collaboration, deep learning, higher-order thinking
finding.study_size: n=114 publications (review sample); individual study ns vary and are not pooled

finding.finding_summary: Several studies in the review suggest online assessment can improve operational efficiency by allowing assessment of larger groups, enabling automated marking or reports, and reducing some workload through technology-supported feedback. However, the review also notes implementation costs, the need for instructional support, and higher initial investment as tradeoffs; no quantitative synthesis is reported.
finding.measure: Assessment scalability, automated scoring/feedback, reporting, implementation workload and efficiency
finding.study_size: n=114 publications (review sample); individual study ns vary and are not pooled

paper_profiles.title: Is Online Assessment in Higher Education Institutions during COVID-19 Pandemic Reliable?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether online assessment in higher education institutions during the COVID-19 pandemic can be reliable and practical, and what strategies educators can use to manage assessment remotely. It is motivated by the rapid shift to online learning caused by pandemic-related campus closures and the need to preserve learning while reducing disruptions.

The authors conducted a scoping literature review of papers, reviews, and reports on online assessment methods used in higher education before and during COVID-19. They summarize common online assessment formats such as quizzes, multiple-choice tests, automated essay scoring, discussion forums, e-portfolios, and online viva-voce or clinical examinations, with a particular focus on medical education. The article also discusses psychometric considerations, assessment validity, feedback, cheating prevention, institutional readiness, and student diversity (including internet access and English as a second language).

The main conclusion is that online assessment can be useful and feasible in higher education, especially when aligned with learning objectives and supported by clear feedback, training, and institutional infrastructure. However, the paper emphasizes practical limitations such as cheating, technical instability, workload, and equity concerns, and recommends simple low-cost safeguards like using free software, mock exams, and mobile-phone video monitoring during exams. It is primarily a conceptual and practice-oriented synthesis rather than an empirical effectiveness study, and it urges educators to evaluate assessment methods and their impact on learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that online assessment can save time and costs through reduced printing, travel, and venue requirements, and that automated scoring and free software can streamline administration. However, it also notes added workload for educators in setting up platforms, monitoring exams, checking plagiarism, and managing technical support, with no quantitative effect size reported.
finding.measure: Perceived cost, time, and administrative burden of online assessment methods

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that successful online assessment depends on institutional readiness, including internet coverage, IT support, policies, and faculty/student training, and that these factors shape feasibility during pandemic disruption. It does not report an empirical institutional outcome estimate, but synthesizes evidence that institutions must address infrastructure, cheating prevention, and learner diversity to implement assessment at scale.
finding.measure: Institutional readiness, policy, infrastructure, and implementation feasibility

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames online quizzes, discussion forums, feedback, and blended assessment as supporting self-directed learning, engagement, collaboration, and real-life application of knowledge. These claims are presented as literature-based assertions rather than directly measured outcomes, and no quantitative effect size or sample is reported.
finding.measure: Self-directed learning, collaboration, engagement, and higher-order learning support

finding.finding_summary: The review notes that students may experience psychological stress, reduced personalized engagement, and varying acceptance of online assessment, while also valuing timely and personalized feedback and practice quizzes. These are synthesized perceptions from prior studies rather than directly pooled outcomes, so no effect size or study size is reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions, stress, acceptance, and engagement with online assessment

paper_profiles.title: The Design of Curriculum, Assessment and Evaluation in Higher Education with Constructive Alignment
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Education and e-Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses constructive alignment in higher education, focusing on how curriculum design, learning activities, assessment, and feedback should be coordinated to support intended learning outcomes. The author argues that formative assessment is a central mechanism within this alignment because it provides feedback that can help students monitor progress, identify weaknesses, and improve learning.

The paper is a literature-based conceptual discussion rather than an empirical evaluation. It emphasizes that assessment should not merely measure achievement at the end of a course, but should be integrated throughout teaching to support deep learning, self-regulation, employability, and inclusive practice for diverse learners, including students with disabilities and international students. The author also notes practical constraints such as time, workload, institutional conservatism, and the risk that assessment becomes superficial if feedback is weak or alignment is poorly implemented.

Overall, the paper concludes that constructive alignment requires coherence among learning outcomes, teaching methods, assessment, and feedback. It presents formative assessment as beneficial in principle for higher education, but does not provide original data, comparative effect sizes, or a systematic review of outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment and feedback support metacognitive skills, planning, critical thinking, and self-regulated learning in higher education. It does not report original quantitative effects, but presents these skills as key intended benefits of constructive alignment and assessment-for-learning practices.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims formative feedback can improve motivation and help students become self-regulated learners, especially when feedback is timely and comprehensible. These claims are discussed conceptually rather than tested empirically, and no sample size or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper highlights that designing constructive alignment and effective formative assessment requires substantial time, effort, and staff responsiveness, which can be difficult under heavy academic workloads. At the same time, it argues that feedback can help teachers identify student difficulties and realign instruction, implying potential efficiency gains if implemented well.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes institutional-level effects of constructive alignment, including curriculum design, assessment policy, inclusivity, accessibility for students with disabilities, and alignment with higher-education standards. It argues that institutions should adopt flexible assessment practices and reasonable adjustments, but provides no empirical evaluation of policy outcomes.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: The benefits of debriefing as formative feedback in nurse education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper critically reviews the nursing education literature on debriefing as a form of formative feedback, asking where debriefing is used, what effect it has on learning, and what features characterize best practice. The authors searched peer-reviewed English-language studies from 2000 to May 2010 and identified 17 nursing studies, most of which embedded debriefing within simulation, case-based learning, or other experiential teaching activities.

The review finds that debriefing is widely used in undergraduate, postgraduate, and professional nursing education, especially for clinical skills, communication, emergencies, teamwork, and simulation-based training. However, the evidence base is thin: only one nursing study isolated debriefing as a variable with outcome data, and most studies measured broader simulation packages rather than debriefing alone.

Overall, the paper concludes that structured, facilitated debriefing is an important and potentially powerful learning strategy, but its independent effect on learning remains uncertain because of confounding with simulation and other instructional components. The authors argue that effectiveness depends heavily on facilitator skill, timely constructive feedback, and a structured process (preparation, dialogue, closure), and they caution that further research is needed to determine impact on clinical practice and patient care.

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests debriefing/simulation packages generally improved communication, confidence, team functioning, and reflective practice in nursing learners, but the effect of debriefing alone was largely not isolated. One randomized trial in registered nurses (n=65) found verbal debriefing improved CPR performance, with greater gains in compression depth and rate (36%; p=.005) than automated machine feedback; most other included studies reported positive learning outcomes without separate debrief-only estimates.
finding.measure: CPR performance quality; confidence, critical thinking, team communication, reflective practice, and perceived skill in simulation-based nursing education
finding.study_size: n=65 for the only isolated debriefing trial; n=17 studies total in the review
finding.effect_size: 36% improvement in CPR performance depth/rate reported in one trial; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Across the included nursing studies, students and staff commonly reported improved confidence, self-efficacy, and reduced anxiety when debriefing was embedded in simulation or feedback-based learning. For example, one quasi-experimental study of baccalaureate students (n=112) reported significant increases in self-reported confidence and self-efficacy after simulation with debrief, and another study found improved confidence that persisted four months later in nurse practitioner students.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence, self-efficacy, and perceived skill
finding.study_size: n=112 in one study; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports positive learning outcomes for clinical knowledge and procedural skill in nursing education contexts such as ECG interpretation, postpartum care, blood transfusion practice, infection control, emergency response, and clinical reasoning. Most studies showed gains after simulation plus debriefing, but because debriefing was usually bundled with simulation, the authors conclude that the independent contribution of debriefing to achievement is uncertain.
finding.measure: Clinical knowledge, procedural skill, clinical reasoning, and performance in simulation-based nursing tasks
finding.study_size: n=17 studies total; individual studies ranged from n=6 to n=1237

finding.finding_summary: A small number of team-based studies suggest debriefing and brief-debrief routines may improve workflow-related outcomes such as team cohesion, communication, and patient safety in clinical settings. The review notes that structured debriefing can help identify recurring problems and support more effective team functioning, but it does not provide pooled estimates or isolate workload effects.
finding.measure: Team communication, team cohesion, patient safety processes, and functioning of clinical teams

paper_profiles.title: Development of an Instructional System Design Model as a Guideline for Lecturers in Creating a Course Using a Blended Learning Approach
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical instructional design problem: how lecturers can systematically create high-quality blended-learning courses. The authors note that blended learning is often described too loosely as simply mixing face-to-face and online instruction, and argue that lecturers need a clearer instructional system design (ISD) model to decide what content, activities, and delivery modes best support learning outcomes.

Using a formative research approach, the study developed and iteratively refined an ISD model called PEDATI for higher-education lecturers in Indonesia. The model includes four steps: formulating course learning outcomes, mapping and organizing content, determining appropriate learning activities, and designing synchronous/asynchronous learning activities through a learning path framework (LDAE: learning, deepening, applying, evaluating). The model was reviewed by experts, revised using qualitative feedback, and then tested in field trials with lecturers who used it to design blended courses.

The paper reports that experts generally judged PEDATI to be relevant, systematic, easy to follow, and operational. Performance in course design improved across three field tests: initially most lecturers scored fair or poor, then shifted to mostly good/excellent by the third test. The authors conclude that PEDATI is feasible and usable as a guideline for lecturers designing blended-learning courses in Indonesian higher education, while noting limits to generalizability beyond that context and the need for further testing in broader implementation settings.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that the PEDATI instructional design model improved lecturers’ ability to design blended-learning courses. In field test 1, 52.2% of lecturers scored fair and 29.2% poor; by field test 3, 60.5% scored excellent and only 5.9% poor, indicating substantial improvement in course-design performance across iterative trials (n=235 lecturers).
finding.measure: Rubric-based performance assessment of lecturers’ course designs

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that experts judged the PEDATI model to be relevant to learning theory and e-learning concepts, systematic, and operational enough to serve as an institutional guideline for higher-education lecturers. The model was designed specifically for Indonesian higher education, suggesting institutional usefulness for course design practice, although no formal policy or organizational outcome measures were reported.
finding.measure: Expert review ratings and implementation feasibility/usability judgments
finding.study_size: 7 instructional design and e-learning experts; 235 lecturers

paper_profiles.title: Student Explanation Strategies in Postsecondary Mathematics and Statistics Education: A Scoping Review
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 27th Annual Conference on Research in Undergraduate Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This scoping review examines how student explanation strategies are used in postsecondary mathematics and statistics education and how the literature can be organized. The authors reviewed 46 peer-reviewed English-language studies published from 2014 to 2024, identifying three main forms of student explanation: self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others.

The paper does not test a new intervention itself; instead, it synthesizes prior studies to clarify the theoretical bases, implementation patterns, and reported benefits and limitations of these strategies. Across the reviewed literature, self-explanation and explaining to fictitious others were described as supporting individual generative learning and long-term understanding, while peer explanation added collaborative benefits but also introduced risks such as domination by more knowledgeable students, spread of misconceptions, and uneven explanation quality. The review concludes that effects vary by implementation, duration, and context, and that explanation to fictitious others may avoid some of the drawbacks of live peer interaction. Because this is a scoping review rather than a quantitative meta-analysis, it provides synthesis and patterning of evidence rather than pooled effects.

finding.finding_summary: The review focuses centrally on mathematics and statistics learning outcomes across 46 postsecondary studies. It reports that self-explanation, peer explanation, and explanation to fictitious others can improve academic achievement, conceptual learning, proof comprehension, and problem-solving, but the results vary by implementation, duration, context, and prior knowledge. No pooled effect size is reported because this is a scoping review.
finding.measure: Academic achievement, conceptual learning, proof comprehension, and problem-solving performance in mathematics/statistics

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed peer-explanation studies reported motivational and affective benefits, including higher motivation, increased social presence, and improved self-efficacy. The review also notes that peer explanation can reduce anxiety in some contexts, but these outcomes are synthesized narratively rather than pooled quantitatively.
finding.measure: Motivation, social presence, self-efficacy, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly frames student explanation as promoting generative thinking, retrieval, organization, integration, and metacognitive processing. It also notes collaborative dimensions of peer explanation, such as peer discussion and explanation quality, and emphasizes that these skills depend on implementation conditions and prior knowledge.
finding.measure: Generative thinking, metacognition, explanation quality, and collaborative learning processes

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pre-existing social relationships between students influence the accuracy, fairness, and perceived value of peer assessment in an e-learning course. The motivation is practical: peer assessment is often used to reduce instructor workload and scale evaluation, but social ties among students may introduce grading bias, especially in settings where students know one another.

The authors implemented a Moodle plugin (PeerForum) in a Master’s-level multimedia course at the University of Lisbon. Students completed relationship nominations (liked/disliked peers), were trained with rubrics, and then peer-assessed forum submissions in a single-anonymized setup where the reviewer knew the author but not vice versa. Each post was typically graded by five peers, and the study analyzed 2,681 peer assessments (2,238 with known relationship data), along with questionnaire responses from 53 students.

Results show that peer assessment was reasonably reliable and accurate when posts received at least three peer assessments: the average peer grade correlated moderately with professor grades (rs=.56 for raw averages; rs=.49 for rounded final peer grades), and inter-rater reliability was moderate to poor depending on the number of graders. Social relationships did matter statistically: students who liked an author tended to score them slightly higher, while disliked peers were scored slightly lower. However, these differences were small (generally under half a grade point) and had little effect on the final aggregate peer grade. Students generally perceived peer assessment as useful and fair, and most did not believe their relationships affected the grades they gave or received. The authors conclude that peer assessment can replace traditional evaluation in this type of e-learning context, especially when combined with training, rubrics, and careful reviewer assignment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer assessment can reduce instructor workload by replacing part of traditional evaluation, and reports that the mechanism worked operationally in the course context. Students also described the process as quick and manageable, and no respondent reported that peer grading increased workload; however, this is based on perceptions rather than a workload time study.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of workload; use of peer assessment as replacement for instructor grading
finding.study_size: n=53 questionnaire respondents; course total n=69

finding.finding_summary: Students reported increased perceived usefulness and fairness of peer assessment after the course, and many indicated that the activity helped them learn, stay engaged, and improve their work. Post-course survey results showed 54.7% agreed peer assessment was helpful and 52.8% agreed it was fair; 30.2% agreed it was difficult, suggesting moderate acceptability and engagement benefits rather than strong motivational gains.
finding.measure: Likert-scale questionnaire on perceived usefulness, fairness, difficulty, engagement, and learning value

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests peer assessment supports reflective judgment and feedback-related collaboration, as students said it helped them learn the material, notice issues in their own work, and give useful feedback to peers. However, the study did not directly measure critical thinking or metacognitive gains with a standardized instrument; evidence comes from student reports and the nature of the peer-review task.
finding.measure: Student reports on learning, feedback quality, and perceived help in completing course skills

finding.finding_summary: The study concludes that peer assessment can function as a viable replacement for traditional evaluation in this e-learning setting, particularly when at least three peer assessments are collected and reviewer assignment is balanced across relationship types. The authors note that this could support institutional scaling of assessment, although they also caution that the finding may not generalize to high-stakes assessment or other contexts.
finding.measure: Feasibility of replacing traditional evaluation; aggregate peer-grade agreement with professor grading; student acceptance
finding.study_size: n=64 analyzed students; 588 posts for accuracy analysis; 2,681 peer assessments

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Peer Grading: A Systematic Literature Review of Reviewer Assignment Strategies and Quantity of Reviewers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how peer-grading systems should be designed to improve grading accuracy, fairness, learning value, and workload balance. Specifically, it synthesizes evidence on reviewer-assignment strategies and the number of peer reviewers per submission, with attention to trade-offs such as reliability versus student burden and the risks of superficial grading.

The review systematically screened 626 records and included 87 studies published from 2010 to 2024. The studies span traditional classrooms and MOOCs, and the review identifies four reviewer-assignment strategies: random, competency-based, social-network-based, and bidding-based assignment. Random assignment is the most common and is scalable, but the review reports recurring concerns about uneven reviewer quality, fairness, and inconsistent grading. Competency-based assignment is presented as a more robust approach for improving accuracy and fairness, though direct empirical comparisons remain limited; social-network and bidding approaches are promising but under-tested.

A second focus is reviewer quantity. Across the literature, three reviews per submission is the modal practice, and the review concludes that roughly three to five reviews often provide a good balance among accuracy, learning, and workload. Accuracy generally improves as the number of reviewers increases, but gains diminish after about five to six reviews, while larger numbers can increase disengagement, fatigue, or rushed reviews. Overall, the paper argues that peer-grading systems should prioritize preventive design choices—especially better reviewer allocation and moderate review counts—rather than relying only on post hoc correction methods.

finding.finding_summary: The review focuses on peer grading as a form of academic assessment rather than on subject-matter learning in a specific discipline. It synthesizes evidence that reviewer-assignment strategy and number of reviewers affect grading accuracy and fairness, with the strongest evidence favoring competency-based assignment and 3–5 reviewers per submission for balanced performance.
finding.measure: Peer grading accuracy, fairness, and validity of assessment scores

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that peer grading can support engagement and perceived educational value, but excessive review demands can reduce motivation or lead to rushed, low-effort work. In the review, requiring more than five reviews per student was repeatedly associated with disengagement or burnout risk, whereas three to five reviews was described as a workable balance.
finding.measure: Student engagement, perceived workload, and motivation during peer review

finding.finding_summary: The paper links peer assessment to learning-oriented skills such as evaluating work from multiple perspectives and using feedback to improve understanding. It reports that diverse and competency-based reviewer assignments can enhance the educational value of feedback, though the evidence is synthesized qualitatively rather than through a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, feedback quality, and engagement with peer review

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that reviewer allocation and reviewer count strongly affect the efficiency of peer-grading workflows. Random assignment is simple and scalable, but competency-based and dynamic allocation methods can improve fairness and reduce grading error; meanwhile, assigning about 3–5 reviews per submission balances accuracy with student workload, and benefits diminish beyond 5–6 reviews.
finding.measure: Reviewer workload, grading reliability, assignment efficiency, and time/effort required for peer review

paper_profiles.title: A review of problem- and team-based methods for teaching statistics in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: Teaching Mathematics and its Applications: An International Journal of the IMA
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews problem-based learning (PBL) and team-based learning (TBL) as collaborative, active-learning approaches for teaching statistics in higher education, with particular attention to introductory undergraduate statistics and some discussion of more advanced courses. The authors aim to synthesize evidence on whether these methods improve student learning compared with traditional lecture-based instruction and to offer practical guidance for implementation.

The review argues that statistics is well suited to group-based, problem-centered instruction because it can be taught through authentic problems, data analysis, and interpretation tasks. The paper describes the structure of classic PBL and TBL, including group formation, readiness tests, facilitator roles, assessment formats, and classroom setup. It then summarizes prior evidence showing that TBL and other collaborative methods are generally associated with better end-of-module performance and higher student engagement, whereas evidence for PBL is weaker and more mixed.

The strongest and most consistent academic gains were reported for cooperative/collaborative variants such as TBL, while inquiry-based approaches such as PBL did not consistently improve achievement in statistics. The review also notes that long-term retention evidence is sparse and, where available, does not show clear durable gains. Practical limitations highlighted include high staff demands for PBL, the need for careful group formation and facilitation, potential student resistance, risks of coasting or intimidation in teams, and the importance of not introducing group-based learning in a superficial way without adequate support and explanation.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that group-based learning can improve end-of-module statistics achievement, but the benefits depend on the instructional model. A cited meta-analysis (Kalaian and Kasim, 2014) found cooperative/collaborative methods such as TBL to be effective, while inquiry-based methods such as PBL showed no evidence of improved academic achievement; individual studies also reported improved grades after TBL and some PBL implementations.
finding.measure: End-of-module assessments, exam marks, and statistics achievement

finding.finding_summary: Beyond statistics content knowledge, the paper emphasizes gains in applied problem solving and interpretation of statistical methods in context. These outcomes are discussed as part of students’ ability to tackle real-world or case-based statistical tasks, but the review does not report a single pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Problem-solving and interpretation of statistical methods in applied tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review finds broadly positive student reactions to both PBL and TBL, including enjoyment, engagement, and attendance. However, it also notes that some students may coast in teams, weaker students may feel intimidated, and some learners may initially resist group-based learning, indicating that affective responses are positive on balance but not uniform.
finding.measure: Student enjoyment, engagement, attendance, and perceptions of group-based learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that collaborative learning supports durable skills such as teamwork, communication, and problem solving, which are especially relevant in statistics education and later professional practice. Evidence cited in the review suggests that group-based learning helps students develop these softer skills, although no pooled quantitative estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Collaborative skills, communication, teamwork, and problem-solving development

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses implementation tradeoffs rather than direct productivity outcomes. Traditional PBL is described as staff-intensive because it requires a facilitator for each group, whereas TBL is presented as more scalable for large classes; the paper also notes that online tools and lecture recordings can reduce workload and improve manageability.
finding.measure: Staffing demands, scalability, and ease of implementation

paper_profiles.title: Systematic Review of Approaches to Improve Peer Assessment at Scale & Possible Research Questions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative survey of research on peer assessment at scale, with an emphasis on MOOCs and university settings. It does not test a single intervention experimentally; instead, it synthesizes prior work on three related problem areas: automated grading and peer-assessment tools, methods for handling rogue or low-quality peer reviews, and NLP-based approaches to improving the quality and usefulness of peer feedback.

The review draws heavily on systems and studies from higher education, especially programming, writing, and open-response assignments in MOOCs and campus courses. It discusses tools such as PeerStudio, Critique-Kit, SWoRD-related systems, and automated grading methods, highlighting how they support rapid feedback, rubric-based review, comment scaffolding, reviewer selection, and review-quality analysis. The paper concludes that peer assessment can be improved through better tooling, score aggregation, reviewer grouping, and NLP support, but that complex assignments remain difficult, many approaches are domain-specific, and reviewer workload and shallow implementation are persistent concerns.

Rather than providing new causal evidence, the paper identifies recurring limitations across the literature: many systems work best for programming or other structured tasks, many still require reviewers to answer every rubric item, and some implementations fail to produce multiple drafts or sustained revision. It also argues that rogue reviews, sparse or biased scoring, and time-consuming review workflows limit the scalability and pedagogical value of peer assessment, especially in large online courses and resource-constrained settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer-assessment tools and automated grading can improve scalability and speed of feedback, but it does not report a single pooled effect. Across cited systems, benefits include rapid or incremental feedback and reduced grading burden, while limitations include time-consuming rubric-by-rubric review and the need for reviewer effort that can reduce student interest.
finding.measure: Tool functionality, grading speed, and reviewer workload as reported across reviewed systems

finding.finding_summary: The review highlights peer assessment as a mechanism for improving feedback quality, critique, and revision-related skills, especially through scaffolding and iterative feedback. It cites studies showing that adaptive guidance and rapid feedback were perceived as more helpful, but the paper does not synthesize a quantitative effect on collaboration, metacognition, or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Feedback quality, revision support, and reviewer performance in peer review activities

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed systems focus on writing and open-response feedback, including essay grading, peer review of writing, and NLP-based feedback localization. The paper notes that these approaches can support improvement of written feedback and revisions, but it does not provide a meta-analytic estimate of gains in writing achievement or literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing quality, peer comments, and revision-oriented feedback in open-response and essay tasks

paper_profiles.title: Automatic assessment of text-based responses in post-secondary education: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on automatic assessment of text-based student responses in post-secondary education. The authors focus on AI- and NLP-based systems used to grade short answers, classify open-ended responses, provide automated feedback, evaluate writing, and support multimodal assessment, motivated by the burden of manually grading open-ended work in large classes.

Using a PRISMA-based search across ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, Education Source, and ASEE conference proceedings, the review screened 838 records and synthesized 93 studies published from 2017–2023. The paper organizes systems through an input-process-output framework and finds that automatic grading systems are most common, followed by classifiers and feedback systems. Most studies emphasize model performance metrics rather than direct learning outcomes, and the review concludes that automated assessment can support efficiency and some learning tasks, but evidence for educational impact is limited and future work should better connect model design to pedagogy, teacher support, and student learning.

The review is especially relevant to higher education and STEM contexts, where large enrollments and open-ended assessment create workload challenges. It also highlights use in language learning and writing evaluation. The authors emphasize that automated systems should complement, not replace, human judgment, and that they are most promising when used for rapid feedback, preliminary scoring, and identifying misconceptions while preserving instructor oversight.

finding.finding_summary: Across 93 reviewed studies, the central motivation and most common reported benefit of text-based automatic assessment systems was reducing grading time, effort, and errors in post-secondary settings. The review reports that 19 studies explicitly addressed reducing grading time/effort, and many systems aimed to automate grading, review, and feedback for large courses (>50 students), though the paper does not aggregate a single effect size across studies.
finding.measure: Reported reductions in grading time, effort, and error; system automation of grading/feedback workflows
finding.study_size: n=93 studies reviewed; 19 studies directly coded for reduced grading time/effort

finding.finding_summary: The review includes automated writing evaluation systems and English grammar/writing support tools that were designed to improve writing quality and grammatical accuracy. Reported study-level results included significant improvement in an English grammar achievement test for an IRF-based assistant and one Arabic essay scoring system reporting 73% overall score accuracy, but the review does not pool effects across studies.
finding.measure: Essay quality, grammar achievement, automated essay scoring accuracy, writing proficiency

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed systems focused on language learning and writing support, including English language learner placement/diagnostic feedback and systems for Arabic essay evaluation. The review suggests these tools can support language learning and diagnostic feedback, but it does not report a pooled effect on speaking or listening and the main evidence is on written language performance rather than oral fluency.
finding.measure: Language proficiency, diagnostic feedback for English language learners, essay scoring in English/Arabic

finding.finding_summary: A notable subset of studies used automated feedback or classification to support scientific argumentation, conceptual understanding, and physics/science explanations. Examples include systems that classified student scientific arguments or provided feedback on science classroom argumentation; however, the review mainly summarizes model performance and does not provide a synthesized learning effect size.
finding.measure: Scientific argumentation quality, conceptual understanding, physics/science constructed responses

finding.finding_summary: The review covers automatic assessment in domains beyond literacy and science, including engineering, computer science, and business/teacher self-assessment surveys. These systems generally aimed to classify responses, grade short answers, or summarize open-ended feedback, but the paper does not report a pooled academic outcome across these heterogeneous domains.
finding.measure: Constructed-response grading, topic classification, course/evaluation response analysis in non-literacy domains

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly frames automated feedback systems as supporting deeper learning, conceptual understanding, critical thinking, problem-solving, and metacognition. Evidence is qualitative and study-level rather than pooled, but the authors identify feedback/review as the most frequent learning concept (28 codes) and report that some systems improved student recall, test scores, or reasoning support.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, recall
finding.study_size: n=93 studies reviewed; learning-impact outcomes explicitly reported in 6 studies

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies addressed student engagement, motivation, and personalization through automated feedback and conversational systems (e.g., quiz/chat bots and scaffolding tools). The review indicates these systems were intended to improve engagement and motivation, but it reports limited direct outcome evidence and no pooled quantitative estimate.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, personalization, student interaction with feedback tools

paper_profiles.title: Scaling Success: A Systematic Review of Peer Grading Strategies for Accuracy, Efficiency, and Learning in Contemporary Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of designing peer-grading systems that are accurate, fair, scalable, and educationally useful in large or online courses. The authors conduct a systematic review of 122 peer-reviewed studies spanning 1981–2024 and build a taxonomy of peer grading along two dimensions: evaluation approaches (summative rating, ranking, categorization, and formative feedback) and reviewer weighting strategies (calibration, back-evaluation, consensus, and reputation).

Across the reviewed literature, the paper compares how different peer-grading designs affect grading accuracy, reliability, fairness, student learning, and workload. The review concludes that simple numeric ratings are often noisy and biased, while ranking, categorical judgments, and weighting strategies can improve reliability under the right conditions. Formative feedback is highlighted as pedagogically valuable but underused in grade synthesis, and no single weighting strategy is universally best.

The reviewed studies are drawn largely from higher education, MOOCs, computer science, engineering, pharmacy, and related settings, with some work in K–12-adjacent or mixed educational contexts. Rather than testing one intervention directly, the paper synthesizes evidence on peer grading mechanisms and implementation conditions. Its main contribution is a comparative framework showing that effective peer grading generally requires hybrid, staged designs and that trade-offs remain around transparency, initial setup cost, student burden, and the risk of superficial or strategic implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Across 122 studies, peer grading mechanisms showed mixed effects on the quality and accuracy of scored work: raw ratings were often noisy and biased, while ranking, categorization, and several weighting strategies improved agreement with instructor or TA grades. The review reports examples such as average rating error of 42% (n not reported), inter-rater agreement of 0.32, and consensus-based weighting improving exact match to 60.7% vs. 56.4% for arithmetic average.
finding.measure: Peer-assigned grades compared with instructor/TA grades; inter-rater agreement; error rates; RMSE; exact match rate

finding.finding_summary: The review indicates that formative feedback, back-evaluation, and transparent review processes can increase student motivation, accountability, and engagement with peer assessment. Reported findings include 80% of participants feeling more motivated to write useful feedback when they knew reviews would be evaluated, and students rating a review-of-review process 3.9/5 for motivating careful and constructive reviewing.
finding.measure: Student motivation, engagement, perceived accountability, attitudes toward peer review

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that peer grading can support critical thinking, reasoning, and metacognitive judgment, especially when students provide rankings or formative comments rather than only numeric scores. It cites studies where ranking encouraged deeper critical engagement and justification, and where calibration/training helped weaker students accurately evaluate higher-performing peers, indicating gains in evaluative judgment and understanding of quality.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, justification quality, evaluative judgment, reasoning skills, metacognitive understanding

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion is that peer grading can substantially reduce instructor workload and scale assessment in large or online courses, though some methods impose cognitive burden on students. The review notes that consensus-based systems can handle 100+ essays without manual calibration, calibration can work with only 10 TA-graded submissions for 1,000 students, and automated/autograder support reduced grading error by up to 82.77% in one study.
finding.measure: Instructor grading burden, scalability, student grading workload, automation of grade aggregation

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that peer grading is an institutional solution for large-scale and online education, particularly MOOCs and large classes where instructor-only grading is difficult to sustain. It highlights that hybrid systems combining calibration, consensus, reputation, and challenge mechanisms may improve fairness, transparency, and trust at the system level, but also warns about equity risks when historical performance or reputation is used to weight grades.
finding.measure: Scalability, fairness, transparency, trust, and institutional feasibility of peer-grading systems

paper_profiles.title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical scoping review of inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME) in tertiary settings. The authors examine whether the common claim that students learn mathematics better when they discover ideas with minimal direct instruction is supported by cognitive science and educational psychology evidence. They focus on the instructional logic of inquiry-based learning, its relation to active learning, and whether it can plausibly improve deep understanding, transfer, and equity outcomes for university mathematics learners.

The review synthesizes theoretical arguments and prior empirical studies, especially meta-analytic evidence and controlled experiments comparing unassisted discovery/inquiry with explicit instruction, worked examples, and guided discovery. The authors conclude that the broad reform agenda promoted by IBME advocates is not justified: novice learners generally do worse with unassisted discovery, while explicit instruction and guided support produce better achievement and transfer. They also argue that the benefits of inquiry are conditional, depending on prior knowledge, scaffold quality, and cognitive load; superficially implemented inquiry can impose heavy working-memory demands and be less efficient than direct teaching.

The paper is centered on undergraduate mathematics education, though it draws on evidence from other educational levels and domains to support its claims. It is written for researchers, instructors, and reformers interested in whether inquiry-based approaches should replace or complement explicit instruction in tertiary mathematics. The main takeaway is not that all inquiry is harmful, but that minimal guidance is inappropriate for novices and that the strongest evidence favors explicit, well-structured instruction before more open-ended problem solving.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed evidence, unassisted inquiry/discovery was less effective than explicit instruction for learning novel mathematics. The paper cites a meta-analysis of 108 studies (580 comparisons) reporting an average effect of d = -0.38 (95% CI [-0.50, -0.25]) in favor of explicit teaching over unassisted discovery, and notes that a study of 129 students found principle-oriented explanations outperformed procedure-oriented explanations on both application and transfer tests.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning outcomes, application tests, and transfer tests in explicit instruction vs. inquiry/discovery comparisons
finding.study_size: n=580 comparisons from 108 studies; individual studies cited included n=129 and n=80

finding.finding_summary: In the cited randomized study on control of variables strategy (CVS), direct instruction produced substantially more mastery than discovery learning for elementary students learning scientific reasoning. The paper reports that 77% of students in the direct-instruction condition became CVS masters versus 23% in the discovery condition; among low-performing students, 69% versus 15% became masters respectively. Transfer to evaluating science-fair posters was similar for learners who mastered the skill, regardless of condition.
finding.measure: Mastery of the control-of-variables strategy and performance on a science-fair poster evaluation transfer task

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that inquiry/discovery can support transfer and deeper understanding only when learners already have relevant schemas and receive strong guidance, and it emphasizes self-explanation and principle-oriented explanations as beneficial scaffolds. However, the main pattern from the cited studies is that generative and transfer-related outcomes improve more reliably with explicit, principle-focused support than with unguided exploration.
finding.measure: Transfer performance, application tests, self-explanation engagement, and depth of processing

paper_profiles.title: AI and Machine Learning for Next Generation Science Assessments
paper_profiles.venue: Machine learning, natural language processing and psychometrics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter reviews how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are changing science assessment, especially for the shift from traditional conceptual recall to three-dimensional, knowledge-in-use assessment aligned with the Framework for K-12 Science Education and NGSS. The central problem is that conventional multiple-choice tests do not adequately capture scientific practices such as modeling, explanation, and argumentation, while performance-based tasks are more authentic but costly and slow for teachers to score.

The chapter surveys ML-based automatic scoring approaches for science assessments, including supervised, unsupervised, semi-supervised, pre-trained models (e.g., BERT), zero-shot methods, and fine-tuned ChatGPT-style models. It focuses on how these methods can provide timely feedback, reduce teacher workload, and support scalable scoring of written and drawn student responses. The chapter also presents a framework for understanding machine-human scoring agreement and summarizes factors that influence scoring accuracy, including assessment design, construct complexity, examinee characteristics such as grade level and ELL status, training/validation choices, and algorithmic features.

The population and context are science learners and educators in K-12 and related instructional settings, with examples drawn from middle school, high school, and some broader assessment contexts. The chapter’s main conclusion is that ML can make next-generation science assessment more feasible and efficient, but accuracy, fairness, generalizability, class imbalance, and responsible use remain major challenges. It emphasizes that current evidence is strongest for task-specific automatic scoring models, while broader transfer across tasks and populations is still limited.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that ML-based performance assessments can better capture scientific reasoning than multiple-choice tests by scoring written, drawn, and constructed responses tied to modeling, explanation, and argumentation. It cites prior studies showing satisfactory automatic scoring accuracy for scientific practices, including a domain-specific GPT-3.5 model that improved average accuracy by 9.1% over fine-tuned BERT across six science assessment tasks.
finding.measure: Machine-human scoring agreement and automated scoring accuracy on science assessment tasks involving argumentation, explanation, investigation, and modeling
finding.effect_size: 9.1% accuracy increase (GPT-3.5 vs. fine-tuned BERT); other studies report Cohen's kappa values and machine-human agreements
finding.confidence_interval: p < 0.05 for the 9.1% improvement; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion of the chapter is that automatic scoring can substantially reduce teacher workload and speed feedback on complex performance tasks. The chapter gives a concrete example that scoring one middle school science task could take about 1 minute per student, or about 100 minutes for a teacher with 100 students, and argues that ML systems can provide timely and objective feedback while alleviating this burden.
finding.measure: Teacher scoring time, workload, and timeliness of feedback for performance-based science assessments

paper_profiles.title: Use of Analogies in Science Education, A Systematic Mapping Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a systematic mapping study of the literature on analogies as a didactic strategy in science education. Its goal was not to test a single intervention, but to identify, classify, and synthesize research on how analogies are used, what instructional models and resources are most common, what research designs have been used, and how learning outcomes have been assessed.

The authors searched five education-related databases for English-language publications from the last twenty years and ultimately included 28 studies. The reviewed literature spans primary, secondary, and undergraduate settings, with most studies focused on secondary education. Across the mapped studies, analogies were commonly used through teacher verbal explanation, images/illustrations, and sometimes videos; effectiveness was typically evaluated with multiple-choice tests, oral responses, interviews, pre/post tests, delayed posttests, and student-generated analogies.

The paper concludes that analogies are widely treated as a useful strategy for helping learners understand scientific concepts and promoting meaningful learning and conceptual change, but that their effectiveness depends on how they are designed and implemented. The review highlights several instructional models, including teacher-generated and student-generated analogies, multiple analogies, and explicit mapping of source-to-target features. It also emphasizes the need to clearly explain the limits of analogies and to use them carefully because they can also generate misconceptions or alternative conceptions if implemented superficially.

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 included studies, the review reports that analogies generally support understanding of scientific concepts and meaningful learning, but can also produce alternative conceptions when students map them incorrectly. The paper does not report a pooled effect size; instead, it synthesizes evidence that effectiveness depends on the analogy model, explicit mapping, and whether teachers clarify where the analogy breaks down.
finding.measure: Science concept learning, conceptual change, and understanding of scientific ideas assessed with multiple-choice tests, oral tests, interviews, and student-generated analogies
finding.study_size: n=28 studies (reviewed); primary-study sample sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review includes studies using analogies across science subjects and textbook analyses, indicating broad support for learning science content rather than a single narrow skill. The paper’s synthesis suggests analogies are used to improve comprehension of unfamiliar scientific domains and support meaning-making in science classes, especially when paired with instructional guidance and appropriate resources.
finding.measure: Science content understanding across textbook analyses and classroom studies
finding.study_size: n=28 studies (reviewed); primary-study sample sizes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Several mapped studies reported that analogies can increase student interest, motivation, and engagement, particularly when students generate analogies themselves. The review notes that self-generated analogy instruction was described as a metacognitive strategy that can promote autonomy, interest, and motivation, though no pooled estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Interest, motivation, perceived usefulness, and self-reported engagement

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies analogy use as supporting inferential reasoning, conceptual restructuring, and cognitive mapping between source and target domains. Evidence from the included studies shows that explicit mapping, student-generated analogies, and tasks requiring explanation or analogy creation were used to assess deeper reasoning rather than recall alone, but the paper does not provide a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Inferential reasoning, conceptual restructuring, analogy generation, and causal/mechanistic reasoning tasks
finding.study_size: n=28 studies (reviewed); primary-study sample sizes not_reported

paper_profiles.title: A Survey on Offline Reinforcement Learning: Taxonomy, Review, and Open Problems
paper_profiles.venue: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This survey reviews the emerging field of offline reinforcement learning (offline RL), a paradigm that learns policies solely from static datasets of previously collected interactions rather than from ongoing environment interaction. The paper is motivated by the high cost, danger, and impracticality of online data collection in domains such as education, healthcare, robotics, and autonomous driving, and it argues that offline RL could be especially useful for real-world decision-making settings.

The authors propose a taxonomy that organizes offline RL methods into major classes, including policy-constraint methods, importance sampling methods, regularization methods, uncertainty-estimation methods, model-based methods, one-step methods, imitation learning methods, and trajectory optimization. They also review seminal and recent algorithms, benchmark datasets, and the properties and shortcomings of offline RL evaluation settings. A major theme is the tradeoff between conservatism and performance: methods that stay close to the behavior policy can be safer but overly pessimistic, while more flexible methods may achieve higher performance but risk out-of-distribution actions and compounding errors.

The paper does not report a new empirical study in education; instead, it synthesizes algorithmic evidence from the offline RL literature and discusses open problems such as off-policy evaluation, reliable workflows, and dynamically adjusting conservatism. Its main conclusion is that offline RL is promising for domains where direct interaction is costly or risky, but robust progress depends on better benchmarks, stronger evaluation, and algorithms that balance distributional shift control with the ability to exploit good actions in the data.

paper_profiles.title: Perspective of Software Engineering Researchers on Machine Learning Practices Regarding Research, Review, and Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM/IEEE International Conference on Software Engineering
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how software engineering (SE) researchers think about and use machine learning (ML) across three contexts: research, peer review, and education. The authors aim to identify the ML practices that are actually used in SE papers, the practices SE researchers believe are best practices, the challenges they face when applying ML, and what should matter when teaching or reviewing ML in SE contexts.

The study combines analysis of SE research articles with surveys and follow-up interviews of SE researchers. The paper examines 117 SE conference articles from ASE, FSE, and ICSE (2011–2022) and surveys 769 authors, receiving 58 responses. It also surveys 38 influential ML-for-SE researchers and interviews 14 of them. The analysis uses grounded-theory style open and axial coding to extract practices, challenges, reviewer concerns, and teaching perspectives.

Main findings are descriptive rather than experimental. The authors report that SE papers commonly include model training, evaluation, train-test splitting, data collection/reuse, baselines, and data cleaning, but rarely address deployment. They also find a gap between what researchers describe as best practices and what is commonly reported in papers; commonly named best practices such as hyperparameter tuning, human expertise in evaluation, exploratory data analysis, and non-functional evaluation appear in fewer than 20% of articles. The study concludes that data handling and evaluation are major challenges, reviewers need better guidance for ML-specific concerns, and hands-on activities dominate ML teaching in SE while traditional methods remain common.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not an intervention study, but it does substantively examine operational aspects of ML-in-SE work such as data collection, data cleaning, model training, evaluation, and deployment. It reports that SE researchers commonly use practices related to training and functional evaluation, while deployment is rarely considered; it also highlights that data handling and evaluation beyond accuracy are major challenges. No effect sizes or causal estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Reported ML practices, challenges, and workflow stages in SE research and teaching contexts
finding.study_size: n=117 SE articles; n=58 author survey responses; n=14 interviews

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses reviewing and teaching practices for ML in software engineering, proposing that existing guidelines are insufficient for ML-specific SE concerns. It reports that reviewers should consider process quality, result validity, non-functional aspects, qualitative assessments, and human-expert involvement, and that teaching should emphasize hands-on activities while still using traditional instruction; these are descriptive findings without experimental impact estimates.
finding.measure: Reviewer concerns, teaching perspectives, and guideline gaps identified via qualitative coding of surveys/interviews
finding.study_size: n=14 interviews; n=19 survey respondents from influential researchers

paper_profiles.title: A Systematic Review of Generative AI for Teaching and Learning Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews the emerging literature on generative AI (GenAI) in higher education (HE), focusing on how these tools are being used for teaching, learning, assessment, and related institutional practices. The authors ask two broad questions: what the publication landscape looks like in this area, and what major themes are emerging in the literature. They do not test a single intervention; instead, they systematically analyze 355 Scopus-indexed journal articles and conference papers published between 2017 and 2023 using bibliometric analysis and latent Dirichlet allocation (topic modeling).

The review finds a rapid rise in GenAI scholarship in 2023, driven largely by ChatGPT. The most common themes are GenAI implications, GenAI for education and research, support systems, bias and inclusion, intelligent tutoring systems, machine learning/AI applications, exam-question performance evaluation, GenAI for writing, ethical and regulatory concerns, and deep learning/AI models. Across these themes, the literature is described as emphasizing potential benefits such as personalized learning, feedback, engagement, exercise generation, and administrative support, while also highlighting concerns about hallucinations, academic integrity, plagiarism, privacy, bias, and superficial or unethical use.

Because this is a descriptive systematic review of GenAI research rather than an outcome study, it does not provide causal estimates for achievement, retention, or transfer. Instead, it synthesizes the current state of the field and recommends future interdisciplinary, comparative, and experimental studies, especially outside medical education and beyond English-language publications.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that GenAI is frequently discussed as a support system for teaching and learning workflows, including exercise/question generation, administrative support, chatbot-based student services, and assistance with drafting and writing. These are presented as plausible productivity gains for educators and institutions, but the paper does not report a pooled effect size or causal estimate.
finding.measure: Reported use cases and thematic prevalence in the reviewed literature (e.g., exercise generation, administrative support, chatbot services, drafting/writing assistance)

finding.finding_summary: A major conclusion is that GenAI is reshaping higher-education policy, assessment, and governance discussions, especially around academic integrity, ethics, privacy, and regulation. The review notes a growing need for institutional guidelines, curriculum updates, and cross-disciplinary collaboration, but it does not evaluate policy outcomes quantitatively.
finding.measure: Frequency and content of themes related to policy, regulation, academic integrity, ethics, and curriculum reform

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly highlights concerns and opportunities related to critical thinking, prompt engineering, and analytical skill development. It suggests GenAI may support reflection and case-study work, but also warns that overreliance can impair critical and analytical thinking and other soft skills; no empirical effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Thematic discussion of critical thinking, analytical skills, and prompt engineering across the reviewed literature

paper_profiles.title: Research-based assessment affordances and constraints: Perceptions of physics faculty
paper_profiles.venue: Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how physics faculty and department chairs perceive research-based assessments (RBAs) and what they need in order to use them more effectively. The authors ask what assessment resources faculty want, how those wants vary by institutional context and faculty role, and what barriers prevent wider use of RBAs in physics teaching and program evaluation.
