Across the 146 included studies, the authors conclude these systems can perform assessment and evaluation tasks at very high accuracy and efficiency levels, with many classification models outperforming logistic regression; however, this is a synthesis of heterogeneous studies rather than a single effect estimate.
finding.measure: Accuracy, classification performance, and workload-related automation in AI applications (e.g., automated grading, prediction, feedback, administrative decision support)

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies focused on engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related learner behaviors. The review reports positive preliminary results in many studies, but also notes one delayed post-test study where the experimental group using a dialogue-based computer-assisted language system scored lower than the control group, and it highlights that most studies were short-term and vulnerable to novelty effects.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related behavioral indicators in learning environments

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a substantial set of automated essay scoring and writing-feedback studies. These systems generally showed strong agreement with human raters and were intended to support revision and reduce grading time, although the review also notes ongoing concerns about feedback quality and appropriateness for some writing contexts.
finding.measure: Automated essay scoring, writing quality/feedback, and reading-comprehension strategy support

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of ITS and adaptive-system studies addressed mathematics and related quantitative content. The review summarizes these studies as generally producing positive or satisfactory preliminary results, but it does not provide a pooled quantitative estimate and notes that most implementations were short-term pilot studies.
finding.measure: Mathematics and quantitative-course learning outcomes in intelligent tutoring/adaptive systems

finding.finding_summary: The review covers AI applications across a wide range of non-literacy, non-math academic domains including computer science, medicine, business statistics/accounting, engineering, and second-language learning. Across these studies, results are described as mostly positive or satisfactory at the pilot level, though the authors stress the lack of longer-term evidence and the limited pedagogical framing.
finding.measure: Subject-matter learning outcomes across higher-education courses (e.g., computer science, medicine, business, engineering, second language learning)

finding.finding_summary: The review includes English-as-a-second-language and second-language learning studies, especially around automated writing feedback and tutoring. The authors report generally positive pilot results, but they also note concerns about the suitability and usefulness of detailed automated feedback for beginning language learners, making the evidence mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Second-language learning and writing feedback outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Some included studies targeted collaboration, self-regulation, and metacognitive support through intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive learning environments. The review characterizes these studies as generally promising, such as systems that supported self-regulatory processes or collaborative problem solving, but again the evidence base was short-term and not longitudinal.
finding.measure: Collaboration, self-regulation, and metacognitive/strategic learning support

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the review is institutional and administrative AI uses such as admission decisions, course scheduling, drop-out prediction, retention, advising, career services, and institutional decision support. The authors report that these systems can predict admissions and attrition with high accuracy and can support institutional planning, but they also note very limited critical reflection on privacy, ethics, and governance.
finding.measure: Institutional prediction and decision-support applications, including admissions, retention, advising, and career-service matching

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; primarily a conceptual/practitioner guide for K-12 and higher education educators
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in ways that are aligned with core pedagogical principles. Rather than treating LLMs as generic productivity tools, the authors organize their discussion around an established formative assessment framework: clarifying where learners are going, diagnosing where learners are, and moving learners forward through feedback.

The paper is a narrative review and practical guide. It synthesizes examples of prompting and classroom use cases, including rewriting learning objectives into student-friendly language, co-constructing success criteria, generating sample work for critique, and producing formative questions or feedback. The discussion spans generic LLMs, domain-specialized systems, and LLM-integrated educational platforms, with an emphasis on accessible tools educators can use without specialized technical infrastructure.

Because the paper is not an empirical study, it does not test an intervention on a sample of learners or teachers and does not report outcome data, effect sizes, or statistical estimates. Its main conclusion is that LLMs can augment formative assessment at scale, but only when educators apply them with strong pedagogical judgment, careful prompting, and attention to the risks of overreliance, inaccurate outputs, and poor alignment with formative purposes. The authors also argue for better evaluation metrics and future research that connects AI capabilities more directly to formative assessment theory.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator workload by automating or streamlining tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating formative questions, creating sample work, and drafting feedback. However, this is a conceptual claim supported by examples rather than empirical testing, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Not reported; conceptual discussion of task efficiency and teacher workload

finding.finding_summary: The authors repeatedly emphasize that well-designed LLM-supported formative assessment can promote critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation, and transferable skills, especially when students evaluate exemplars or use feedback to reflect on next steps. These claims are theoretical and illustrative rather than based on a direct empirical study.
finding.measure: Not reported; conceptual discussion of critical thinking, metacognition, and self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses support for academic tasks such as writing student-friendly learning objectives, constructing method-section exemplars, and generating discipline-specific formative assessment materials. The examples are framed as instructional supports rather than measured learning outcomes, and no quantitative effects are reported.
finding.measure: Not reported; examples include learning objectives and methods writing support

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment could be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessment with timely feedback should improve learning and potentially support stronger performance on end-of-semester summative exams.

The paper combines a conceptual discussion of formative assessment with a small survey of Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) students about continuous assessment and Blackboard-based online tests. The implementation described includes weekly or fortnightly online quizzes with immediate automated feedback and teacher explanations. Students responded positively overall, especially to the idea of breaking course work into small topic assessments, receiving immediate feedback, and using Blackboard for convenience and flexibility.

The study is not an outcomes trial measuring achievement gains; rather, it reports student perceptions and descriptive statistics from questionnaire data. The main conclusion is that Blackboard-supported formative assessment is seen as workable and potentially beneficial for keeping students engaged across the semester, helping them identify strengths and weaknesses, and possibly improving later summative performance, though this latter claim is presented as expectation rather than demonstrated causal evidence.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally supported frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based testing because they believed it would help them stay on track, receive immediate feedback, and keep in touch with the subject throughout the semester. The paper reports survey-based perceptions rather than achievement outcomes; no effect size or pre/post comparison was reported (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, feedback, and Blackboard test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames formative assessment as supporting metacognition and self-monitoring, and students said the approach would help them measure strengths and weaknesses and understand whether they were on track. This is based on questionnaire responses about perceived benefits of feedback and self-checking, not a measured skill gain (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, reflection, and understanding strengths/weaknesses

finding.finding_summary: Students favored splitting coursework into many small topic assessments and using Blackboard tests, primarily because it made learning seem stepwise, improved checking of learning, and was viewed as helpful for the summative semester examination. The evidence is descriptive survey data and open-ended responses; no direct academic performance outcome was measured (n=not_reported).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of formative assessment and anticipated usefulness for course learning/summative exams

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Peer Grading: A Systematic Literature Review of Reviewer Assignment Strategies and Quantity of Reviewers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a design question in peer grading: how reviewer assignment strategies and the number of reviewers per submission affect grading quality, fairness, workload, and learning-related outcomes. The authors argue that while peer assessment is widely used in classrooms and MOOCs, its effectiveness depends heavily on how reviewers are allocated and how many reviews each submission receives.

To investigate this, the paper conducts a systematic literature review of 87 studies published between 2010 and 2024. It categorizes reviewer-assignment approaches into random, competency-based, social-network-based, and bidding-based strategies, and synthesizes findings on review cardinality. The review finds that random assignment is common but can create fairness and reliability problems, whereas competency-based assignment more consistently improves accuracy and fairness; evidence for social-network and bidding approaches remains limited. Across studies, three to five reviews per submission is presented as a practical balance between accuracy and workload, with accuracy generally improving as the number of reviewers increases but with diminishing returns beyond about five to six reviewers.

Because this is a review rather than a primary causal study, the paper does not report one new intervention effect, but instead synthesizes prior evidence across classroom and MOOC settings. Its main conclusion is that peer grading systems should prioritize preventive design choices—especially competent reviewer matching and moderate review counts—rather than relying only on post-hoc grade correction methods.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, requiring more than five reviews per student was often associated with disengagement, rushed grading, or lower willingness to participate, while three to five reviews was repeatedly described as a workable balance. Some studies also reported that peer reviewing could improve student attitudes toward the process and support engagement, but the review emphasizes trade-offs rather than a uniformly positive effect.
finding.measure: Student engagement, attitudes toward peer review, and perceived workload

finding.finding_summary: The review synthesizes evidence that peer grading can support learning-related durable skills by exposing students to multiple perspectives and encouraging more thoughtful evaluation of work. It reports that increasing the number of reviews generally improves the educational value of reviewing and that competency-based reviewer assignment can make feedback more complementary, supporting critical comparison and reflection.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes, perceived educational value, and engagement with feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies reviewer assignment efficiency and review-count design in peer grading systems. It concludes that random assignment is scalable but can produce fairness and reliability problems, while competency-based and dynamic allocation strategies can improve accuracy and timeliness; it also identifies three to five reviews per submission as a common and efficient balance between grading quality and workload. No single primary effect size is reported because this is a systematic review of 87 studies.
finding.measure: Review distribution efficiency, grading accuracy, fairness, timeliness, and reviewer workload

finding.finding_summary: The review has institutional-level implications for how peer assessment systems should be designed and governed in classrooms and MOOCs. It argues that design choices such as reviewer matching, anonymity-related structures, and review cardinality influence fairness, trust, and scalability, and it calls for larger comparative studies to guide platform design and institutional implementation.
finding.measure: Peer assessment system design implications, fairness, and scalability across classroom and MOOC contexts

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging Peer, Self, and Teacher Assessments for Generative AI-Enhanced Feedback
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teacher, peer, and self-assessments align within the AICoFe collaborative feedback system and how those assessments could be better used to support Generative AI (GenAI)-enhanced feedback in higher education. The core problem is that formative feedback is difficult to scale in large classes, and current AI-supported feedback systems often treat all human evaluators as equally reliable, without accounting for differences in strictness, bias, or perspective.

The study was conducted with 46 final-year undergraduate engineering students at Universidad Aut�f3noma de Madrid. Each student gave an individual oral presentation that was evaluated with a 15-item validated rubric by the teacher, two randomly assigned peers, and the student themself; the teacher also assigned an independent overall grade. The authors analyzed inter-rater agreement, correlations with the teacher's overall grade, and score differences across evaluator groups. Results showed moderate-to-substantial agreement when using Gwet's AC2, strong correlations between teacher rubric scores and the teacher's overall grade, lower but still significant alignment for peer scores, and the weakest alignment for self-assessments. Peers and students tended to score slightly higher than the teacher, while the teacher's rubric scores were stricter than her holistic overall grades.

The paper does not test a new GenAI intervention experimentally; instead, it uses the findings to propose a design improvement for the GePeTo model inside AICoFe. The proposed enhancement adds weighted integration of evaluator inputs, bias detection, and context-aware generative reasoning. The main conclusion is that peer and self-assessment can be useful formative data when guided by a shared rubric, but AI feedback systems should not aggregate all sources uniformly because different evaluators show systematic differences in scoring behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The paper studies oral presentation assessment in engineering education, which is an academic performance task outside the literacy/mathematics/science categories. Using 46 full evaluation sets, the study found moderate-to-substantial agreement across teacher, peer, and self ratings (Gwet's AC2 = 0.58-0.66) and significant positive correlations between rubric scores and the teacher's overall grade (teacher rubric r = 0.88; peers r = 0.69; self r = 0.59).
finding.measure: Rubric-based oral presentation scores and teacher's overall grade for engineering presentations

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines evaluative judgment, self-assessment, and peer assessment, all of which relate to metacognition and self-regulated learning. Self-assessments were moderately aligned with the teacher's overall grade (r = 0.59; Spearman ρ = 0.67), and the authors interpret this as evidence that students can use rubric-based reflection to calibrate judgment, though with some bias.
finding.measure: Self-assessment rubric scores, peer assessment rubric scores, agreement statistics, and correlations with teacher grade

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the AICoFe workflow and proposed GenAI enhancement are intended to improve the scalability and efficiency of formative feedback in large higher-education classes. However, the study itself reports agreement and bias patterns rather than direct workload outcomes, so the efficiency claim is design-oriented rather than experimentally demonstrated.
finding.measure: Feedback workflow design and use of GenAI-assisted aggregation of rubric-based evaluations

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Social Relationships on Peer Assessment in E-Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether pre-existing social relationships between students influence peer assessment quality and perceptions in an e-learning course. The authors focus on a practical concern in formative assessment: when students know one another, does friendship or dislike bias the grades they give, and can structured reviewer assignment plus rubrics reduce that bias?

To study this, the authors built a Moodle plugin called PeerForum and deployed it in a Master’s course in Information Systems and Computer Engineering at Instituto Superior Técnico. Students first nominated peers they liked most and least, then completed peer assessments of forum posts in a single-anonymized setting where only the reviewer knew the author’s identity. The system curated reviewer assignment using relationship data, required rubric-based training before grading, and compared peer grades with professor ratings across 69 enrolled students (64 active peer graders in the analyzed sample).

The main findings are that peer assessment was generally reliable and accurate when at least three peer assessments were available per post: average-measures ICC was .698 for posts with three peer assessments and Spearman correlations between professor and peer grades were moderate to strong (e.g., rs=.558 for posts with at least three peer assessments). Social relationships did affect individual grades in the expected direction: liked peers received slightly higher grades and disliked peers slightly lower grades, but the differences were small and had little effect on the final aggregate peer grade. Students also reported that peer assessment was useful and fair, and most disagreed that their relationships affected the grades they gave or received.

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment reduced reliance on professor-only grading by enabling students to assess forum submissions, and the authors conclude it can replace traditional evaluation in this e-learning setting. The system also showed that a minimum of three peer assessments was sufficient for acceptable reliability and accuracy, which supports practical scalability for course workflow.
finding.measure: Peer assessment reliability/accuracy and feasibility of replacing traditional evaluation; number of peer assessments needed per post
finding.study_size: n=588 posts for accuracy; n=625 posts with at least three peer assessments; 64 active peer graders

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer assessment supports learning-related durable skills by helping students give feedback, learn course criteria, and improve their work. Student questionnaire responses indicated that many perceived peer grading as helpful for learning and engagement, and the discussion links the activity to collaboration and feedback practice.
finding.measure: Student perception questionnaire items about usefulness of peer assessment, feedback usefulness, and learning/helpfulness

finding.finding_summary: Students’ perceptions of peer assessment became more positive over the semester: 54.7% agreed it was helpful after the course versus 43.4% before, and 52.8% agreed it was fair after the course versus 24.5% disagreeing. Most students also disagreed that relationships influenced the grades they gave or received, suggesting relatively positive attitudes and confidence in the process.
finding.measure: Pre/post questionnaire ratings of usefulness, fairness, difficulty, and relationship influence

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment grades were close to professor grades overall, but slightly higher on average. For posts with at least three peer assessments, the final peer grade correlated moderately with professor ratings (rs=.49, p<.001 for rounded final peer grade; rs=.56, p<.001 for average peer grades), and agreement was strongest at three assessments (ICC average measures=.698, 95% CI [.617, .764]).
finding.measure: Professor rating vs. final peer grade; inter-rater reliability of peer grades
finding.study_size: n=588 posts (accuracy analysis); n=199 posts with 3 peer assessments for ICC average measures
finding.confidence_interval: ICC 95% CI [.617, .764] for 3-assessment posts; correlation CI not_reported
finding.std_deviation: Professor rating SD=.92; final peer grade SD=.61; average peer grades SD=.57

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests an institutional design approach for peer assessment systems: use relationship-aware reviewer assignment, rubrics, and prior training rather than full anonymity. The authors conclude that this can help peer assessment function as a viable replacement for traditional evaluation in a course setting, while keeping relationship bias small enough not to affect final aggregate grades much.
finding.measure: Policy/design implication derived from relationship-aware reviewer assignment and peer assessment performance
finding.study_size: n=64 active peer graders; course-level implementation

paper_profiles.title: The Study of Peer Assessment Impact on Group Learning Activities
paper_profiles.venue: FECS'21 (The 17th Int'l Conf on Frontiers in Education: Computer Science and Computer Engineering)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how peer assessment affects group learning activities in undergraduate computer science modules, with a particular focus on fairness, contribution transparency, feedback, and group dynamics. The authors are motivated by concerns that peer assessment can be viewed as unfair or unreliable, especially when students perceive freeloading, conflict, or unequal contribution within group work.

The study uses a mixed-methods design: a preliminary survey of 582 students (276 responses), focus group interviews with 12 participants, and a case study of an HCI coursework group project using Facebook for collaboration and evidence of contribution. The approach emphasizes online/social-media-supported peer assessment as a way to make contribution more visible and assessment more transparent.

Findings are largely descriptive and perception-based rather than causal. Students reported concerns about fairness and conflicts in groups, but the case study suggested that many students enjoyed group work with Facebook support, felt they could demonstrate their skills, and viewed peer assessment as more impartial when contribution was visible. The paper concludes that peer assessment can be improved by identifying freeloaders, rewarding deserving students, teaching constructive feedback, and making assessment processes more transparent and accessible online.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaboration, group dynamics, and feedback practices in peer-assessed group work. Survey results showed that 37% of students would choose individual work over group work, while 56% would assist other members after completing their own work and 72% would consult other members for solutions; however, conflicts, unequal contribution, and disruptive behavior were reported as major barriers to effective collaboration.
finding.measure: Survey responses and focus-group comments on group work, peer assessment attitudes, and group dynamics
finding.study_size: n=276 survey responses; n=12 focus group participants; n=28 case-study students

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses strongly on student attitudes, perceptions of fairness, comfort with giving/receiving feedback, and enjoyment of group work. In the case study, 82.1% of 28 students said they enjoyed working in a group with Facebook, and 82.1% agreed that peer assessment was an impartial method when Facebook evidence showed self-contribution; however, many survey respondents also reported discomfort with negative feedback and concerns about fairness.
finding.measure: Questionnaires, surveys, and exit questionnaire items about fairness, comfort with feedback, and enjoyment of group work
finding.study_size: n=276 survey responses; n=28 case-study students

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively addresses assessment-process design at the course/institution level, proposing changes to peer assessment procedures such as online submission, transparency, privacy, random timing, and clearer task allocation. These recommendations are intended to improve fairness, reduce conflict, and make peer assessment more workable in higher education modules.
finding.measure: Implementation recommendations derived from surveys, focus groups, and a coursework case study

paper_profiles.title: Randomized Controlled Trials without Data Retention
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological and privacy problem in randomized controlled trials (RCTs): how to obtain valid causal inferences when researchers are not allowed to retain individual-level data for the full duration of the study. The motivating idea is data minimization, where records should be deleted or anonymized shortly after collection rather than stored until analysis is complete.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or learner outcome. Instead, it develops statistical algorithms for online or recursive estimation in RCTs, including recursive least squares, online bootstrap inference, cluster bootstrap variants, and a federated approach for cluster-robust standard errors. These methods are presented as ways to estimate treatment effects, variances, and confidence intervals while minimizing data retention and preserving privacy.

The context is general digital experimentation and causal inference, with examples drawn from A/B testing, cluster-randomized trials, and federated computation. The main conclusion is that accurate inference from RCTs can be achieved without storing raw records, and that recursive/federated methods can support privacy-preserving experimentation under strict retention or anonymization constraints.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that recursive estimation and online bootstrap methods can reduce the data-retention burden of RCT analysis by allowing records to be discarded or anonymized immediately after being incorporated into running estimates. It does not report an empirical effect size; the contribution is methodological, showing that treatment effects and uncertainty can be computed with minimal storage in principle.
finding.measure: Data retention feasibility / ability to compute causal estimates without storing individual records

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes privacy-preserving experimentation workflows aligned with data minimization, GDPR-like retention constraints, and federated computation. Its main claim is that institutions can maintain causal inference capabilities while changing data governance practices to delete or anonymize records shortly after collection.
finding.measure: Privacy-preserving causal inference under retention/anonymization policies

paper_profiles.title: ‘Getting out of the closet’: Scientific authorship of literary fiction and knowledge transfer
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether scientists who write literary fiction use those books as a mechanism of knowledge transfer. The authors ask three related questions: whether fiction can convey scientists’ research topics directly, whether publishing fiction creates opportunities for indirect knowledge transfer through interactions with cultural audiences, and whether the experience can generate reverse knowledge transfer by prompting new research ideas.

The study develops a conceptual framework positioning literary fiction as a form of non-formal knowledge transfer: it is written in spare time, involves copyrights, and sits outside standard formal or informal university technology transfer channels. Empirically, the paper uses a mixed-methods design in two Spanish regions (Catalonia and the Valencian Community), combining manual coding of a sample of 541 fiction books published in 2015, regression analysis, and interviews with 15 scientific authors. Scientists were identified through affiliation and evidence of research activity, then classified by academic vs. non-academic status and by scientific field.

The findings suggest that scientific authorship of literary fiction is uncommon overall (11% of fiction authors in the sample), but when scientists do write fiction, direct knowledge transfer is more likely among non-academic scientists than academic scientists. The regression results show that being an academic scientist is negatively associated with direct knowledge transfer (Heckman probit coefficient = -0.66, p<0.05), while Other Humanities is positively associated relative to the benchmark field. Qualitative interviews further suggest that academic constraints, disciplinary norms, and format-content interference in Linguistics and Literature shape how knowledge is transferred through fiction. The paper concludes that literary fiction can function as a meaningful, though unusual, knowledge transfer mechanism, especially for non-academic scientists and some humanities fields.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that literary fiction can operate as a non-formal knowledge transfer mechanism and that institutional/academic logics shape whether scientists use it that way. In the sample of 541 fiction books, 11% had scientific authors, and the authors conclude that universities and research systems may need to recognize this form of transfer more explicitly.
finding.measure: Scientific authorship of literary fiction; classification of knowledge transfer channels; interviews and regression analysis

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central empirical focus is literary fiction as a channel for non-standard dissemination of disciplinary knowledge, especially in the humanities and social sciences. Direct knowledge transfer was more likely in Other Humanities than in the benchmark field, but the effect was not uniform across fields because Linguistics and Literature showed format-content interference that complicated external detection of transfer.
finding.measure: Direct knowledge transfer via whether the fiction plot/theme matched the author’s research lines
finding.study_size: n=541 books (with scientist-authored subset analyzed for DKT1)
finding.effect_size: Heckman probit coefficient = -1.59 for Linguistics and Literature relative to Other Humanities; Other Humanities is the benchmark

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether fiction books transfer scientific knowledge from authors’ research to the public. In externally coded direct knowledge transfer (DKT1), 32% of scientific-authored books were judged to include the author’s research topics; in the Heckman probit, academic scientist status was negatively associated with direct transfer (coefficient = -0.66, p<0.05).
finding.measure: Direct knowledge transfer (DKT1) judged from book plots/summaries against authors’ research lines
finding.study_size: n=61 scientific-authored books for DKT analysis; n=541 total books
finding.effect_size: Heckman probit coefficient = -0.66 for academic scientist; DKT1 prevalence = 32% among scientific-authored books

finding.finding_summary: A secondary qualitative finding is that writing fiction may help academics reduce inhibition, cope with tension between academic and literary work, and gain personal satisfaction. Interviewees described fiction as a hobby, evasion, and a way of ‘getting out of the closet,’ suggesting improved self-expression and reduced constraint, although this was not measured as a formal outcome.
finding.measure: Interview responses about motivations, self-perception, and personal effects of writing fiction

paper_profiles.title: Online Peer-Assessment Datasets
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a set of online peer-assessment datasets collected from five undergraduate computer science courses at the University of Trento. The paper’s main purpose is not to test a causal intervention, but to describe how the peer-assessment system worked, what data were captured, and why open datasets are useful for future research in learning analytics, automated scoring, and performance prediction.

The platform was used over multiple semesters (2013–2016) in Italian undergraduate courses. Students participated in weekly cycles that included submitting questions, rating questions, answering selected questions, and evaluating answers; teachers only minimally supervised the process by filtering questions each week. The datasets include questions, answers, peer ratings/coins, and final course scores, enabling research on student modeling, prediction of success, and properties of peer-assessment data.

The paper argues that automation can reduce teacher workload and improve the scalability and analyzability of peer-assessment, but it does not report an experimental comparison of outcomes against a control condition. Instead, it provides a data resource and a description of the system design, noting that participation was optional and that completion rates declined over time. The main conclusion is that openly available peer-assessment datasets can support future studies on validity, reliability, student progress, and predictive modeling.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that moving peer-assessment online substantially reduces teacher workload and makes large-scale peer assessment more scalable. No direct effect size or controlled comparison is reported; the claim is based on system design and qualitative reasoning rather than an experiment.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / scalability of peer-assessment processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses peer-assessment as a context for student modeling, performance prediction, and monitoring progress, which are related to metacognition and self-regulation. However, no direct causal estimate of durable-skill improvement is reported; the evidence is limited to the availability of data and references to prior predictive work.
finding.measure: Student progress / performance prediction proxies

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that peer-assessment participation was optional and that active participation dropped toward the end of each course, suggesting engagement challenges in the platform. It does not evaluate an intervention effect on motivation or persistence, but it does document participation patterns across the courses.
finding.measure: Participation/completion rates in weekly peer-assessment tasks

paper_profiles.title: Engaging Software Engineering Students in Grading: The effects of peer assessment on self-evaluation, motivation, and study time
paper_profiles.venue: Conference paper (venue not specified in provided text)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether introducing peer assessment into a software engineering course changes students’ self-evaluation accuracy, motivation, and study time. The authors are interested in peer assessment not just as a grading mechanism, but as a learning activity that may help students develop reflective and lifelong learning skills.

The study was conducted in a third-year bachelor Electronics/ICT course at KU Leuven. Data from two academic years were compared: 2018–19 as a baseline without peer assessment (n=25) and 2019–20 with obligatory peer assessment added (n=27). Students completed self-assessments using a shared rubric, filled out a follow-up survey on motivation and perceived self-grading ease/accuracy, and tracked their project study time.

Results suggest that peer assessment was associated with better alignment between student and teacher grades for some rubric criteria, especially Complexity and UI, but not for all criteria. Students also reported slightly higher motivation and slightly easier/more accurate self-evaluation in the peer-assessment year, while overall study time changed little. The authors conclude that peer assessment can improve self-evaluative skills and may strengthen motivation, though the evidence is based on two-year observational comparisons rather than a causal experiment.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported higher motivation in the year when peer assessment was introduced. Mean self-reported motivation increased from 3.58 (s.d. 0.659) in 2018–19 (n=25) to 3.96 (s.d. 0.774) in 2019–20 (n=27) on a 1-5 Likert scale, though the authors note this cannot be attributed to peer grading alone.
finding.measure: Self-reported motivation (Likert 1-5)

finding.finding_summary: Peer assessment was associated with improved self-evaluation accuracy for several rubric criteria, especially Complexity and UI. Correlations between self and teacher grading increased from 0.202 to 0.666 for Complexity and from 0.376 to 0.713 for UI, while Design showed no meaningful improvement (0.331 to 0.105).
finding.measure: Correlation between self-grades and teacher grades across rubric criteria

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that self-evaluation became easier and more accurate after peer assessment was introduced. On a 1-5 scale, perceived ease of grading rose from 3.25 to 3.42 and perceived accuracy from 3.25 to 3.62 across the two years.
finding.measure: Self-reported ease and accuracy of self-evaluation (Likert 1-5)

finding.finding_summary: The relationship between motivation and study time increased in the peer-assessment year, suggesting motivated students invested more time once peer evaluation was in place. The correlation between time spent and motivation rose from 0.005 in 2018–19 to 0.331 in 2019–20.
finding.measure: Correlation between study time and motivation

finding.finding_summary: Overall study time changed little after peer assessment was introduced. Mean hours spent on the project decreased slightly from 39.63 (s.d. 18.999) in 2018–19 to 36.61 (s.d. 18.892) in 2019–20, and the authors state there was no significant change in workload visible between the two years except a slightly larger deadline rush.
finding.measure: Self-reported project study time (hours)

paper_profiles.title: Continuous monitoring of delayed outcomes in basket trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical design problem in early-phase oncology basket trials: how to conduct interim analyses when treatment response is delayed and not yet observed for many enrolled patients. The authors note that continuous monitoring can help identify futile baskets earlier, but existing Bayesian basket-trial methods either have high computational cost or do not handle delayed outcomes well.

To solve this, the paper adapts an empirical Bayesian basket-trial design and adds missing-data handling through multiple imputation under a Weibull time-to-response model. The proposed framework compares several interim-analysis strategies: naive imputation, observed-data-only analysis, complete-data suspension, and two multiple-imputation variants (with and without basket covariates). The study population is not patients in an educational setting but simulated adult oncology trial participants in 2- and 3-basket basket trials, with response windows modeled at 3 months.

The paper’s main evidence comes from extensive simulation studies across accrual rates, basket response-rate configurations, basket counts, sample sizes, and interim-analysis schedules. Results show that naive imputation tends to overestimate early termination, while observed-data and multiple-imputation approaches generally track the complete-data benchmark more closely, especially when accrual is slow and missing data are limited. The authors conclude that the covariate-adjusted multiple-imputation approach is the most robust overall in heterogeneous basket scenarios with fast accrual, but that simpler observed-data analysis may be adequate when accrual is slow and missingness is low.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates operational consequences of different interim-analysis strategies using simulation, including probability of early termination (PET), expected sample size (ESS), and expected trial duration (ETD). Compared with the complete-data benchmark, naive imputation generally increases PET and reduces ESS, while observed-data and multiple-imputation methods usually produce smaller deviations; continuous monitoring with delayed outcomes is feasible without substantially increasing ETD relative to complete-data suspension.
finding.measure: Probability of early termination (PET), expected sample size (ESS), expected trial duration (ETD) across simulated basket-trial scenarios

paper_profiles.title: Garbage Collection Makes Rust Easier to Use: A Randomized Controlled Trial of the Bronze Garbage Collector
paper_profiles.venue: ICSE ’22 (44th International Conference on Software Engineering)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether adding an optional garbage collector to Rust can make the language easier to use for novice programmers, especially when working on tasks that require complex aliasing and mutable shared data. The authors introduce Bronze, a library-based garbage collector for Rust, and test it in a randomized controlled trial embedded in a sophomore-level programming languages course.

Students in a required university course completed a multi-part Rust assignment covering basics, ownership/borrowing, and a more difficult aliasing task. Participants were randomly assigned to use either traditional Rust or Bronze for the post-basics tasks. The study analyzed both performance data and surveys from 333 experiment participants (428 total study participants including non-random-assignment respondents). The assignment was designed so that Bronze mainly simplified the aliasing portion while still requiring learners to engage with core Rust concepts.

The main finding is that Bronze improved productivity on the most aliasing-heavy task: Bronze users were more likely to complete the aliasing task within the time limit and did so much faster among completers (median 4 hours vs. 12 hours). However, Bronze did not reduce total project time because Bronze participants had to redo the aliasing task without GC afterward. Survey data showed that students found ownership, lifetimes, borrowing, and references difficult, and that many came to believe GC made programming easier after experiencing both versions. The paper concludes that optional GC can simplify architecture and improve short-term task completion for novices learning Rust, though it does not necessarily increase overall enjoyment of the language.

finding.finding_summary: Bronze improved task efficiency on the most aliasing-heavy programming task. Students using Bronze were more likely to complete the aliasing task within the time limit (odds ratio approximately 0.41 favoring Bronze; p≈.006), and among those who finished, Bronze users completed it much faster with a median of 4 hours versus 12 hours for Traditional Rust users (Wilcoxon W=561, p<.001).
finding.measure: Task completion rate and self-reported hours spent on the aliasing programming task
finding.study_size: n=301 for completion analyses; n=149 for completion-time analyses among students who finished all tasks
finding.effect_size: odds ratio ≈ 0.41; median time 4 hours vs 12 hours

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that experiences with Bronze changed students’ beliefs that garbage collection makes programming easier. On a 0–4 Likert scale, Bronze participants’ median agreement increased from 2 after Basics to 4 after the later no-GC aliasing task, and an ordinal regression showed a significant shift (p<.001, odds ratio 21.4). The study also reports no significant difference between conditions in how much participants liked Rust by the end of the assignment.
finding.measure: Likert-scale survey responses about whether GC makes writing programs easier, and liking Rust
finding.study_size: n=89 responding Bronze participants for the GC-helpfulness item; condition-comparison liking analyses used experiment participants after assignment completion
finding.effect_size: odds ratio 21.4 for increased belief that GC makes programming easier

finding.finding_summary: The assignment and survey results indicate that Bronze reduced architectural complexity for a hard programming task, which the authors interpret as improving learners’ ability to manage complex aliasing problems. Qualitative responses suggest students struggled with references, lifetimes, ownership, interior mutability, and dynamic borrowing, and that Bronze simplified the structure design needed for the aliasing task. This is more indirect than the operational-efficiency result, but the paper does substantively analyze how the intervention affected students’ programming problem-solving experience.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of free-response survey answers and performance on multi-part Rust programming tasks
finding.study_size: n=1143 coded comments; experiment data from n=333

paper_profiles.title: Foundations for AI-Assisted Formative Assessment Feedback for Short-Answer Tasks in Large-Enrollment Classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether natural language processing (NLP) can support scalable formative assessment for short-answer tasks in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The motivation is that short-answer “write-to-learn” activities can improve learning, but scoring and giving timely feedback becomes difficult when class sizes are large.

Using de-identified responses from 1,935 post-secondary students across 29 class sections from 16 courses at 15 institutions, the authors examine scoring reliability among multiple trained human raters and compare it with an automated short-answer scoring model (SFRN) and an LSTM-based baseline. They also explore whether learned text representations can support clustering of student responses for potential feedback workflows.

The main findings are that human raters showed substantial agreement (pairwise QWK about 0.79-0.83; Fleiss’ kappa 0.70), the algorithm also agreed substantially with human raters (pairwise QWK about 0.74-0.82; four-way Fleiss’ kappa 0.68), and the SFRN classifier outperformed the LSTM baseline in accuracy (83% vs. 72%). For clustering, the study found a tradeoff between representations that work well for classification and those that yield more consistent clusters, suggesting that automated scoring is feasible for formative assessment support but further work is needed to make feedback meaningful and instructionally useful at scale.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly evaluates whether NLP can reduce the burden of scoring short-answer formative assessment at scale. Human raters achieved substantial agreement (pairwise QWK = 0.79-0.83; Fleiss’ kappa = 0.70), and the SFRN algorithm showed similarly strong agreement with humans (pairwise QWK = 0.74-0.82; four-way Fleiss’ kappa = 0.68), suggesting feasible automated or semi-automated scoring workflows for large classes.
finding.measure: Inter-rater and algorithm-human scoring reliability; classification accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The paper is situated in introductory statistics and short-answer task scoring, so it substantively concerns academic performance in a disciplinary context, though it does not test student learning gains directly. The automated model classified responses with 83% accuracy versus 72% for the LSTM baseline, indicating improved support for evaluating students’ written statistical reasoning.
finding.measure: Automated short-answer classification accuracy; correctness labels (incorrect/partial/correct)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that short-answer responses and feedback support students’ ability to communicate statistical ideas and reason about concepts, which aligns with durable skills such as written communication and critical thinking. However, the study itself does not measure these student outcomes; it only provides infrastructure evidence that could enable such formative assessment at scale.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ViR: Towards Efficient Vision Retention Backbones
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable / computer vision models (no human education population studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces Vision Retention Networks (ViR), a new family of computer vision backbones designed to address the compute and memory bottlenecks of Vision Transformers. The central problem is that standard self-attention scales quadratically with input length, which makes high-resolution image processing slow and memory-intensive, especially at inference time.

The proposed approach replaces self-attention with a retention mechanism that can be computed in parallel, recurrently, or in a hybrid chunkwise form. The authors also extend the formulation to 2D to better preserve shift equivariance across image rows and columns. The model is evaluated on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation benchmarks using ImageNet-1K/ImageNet-21K, MS COCO, and ADE20K, respectively.

Results show that ViR and hybrid ViR variants achieve competitive accuracy while improving throughput and memory efficiency relative to several ViT and hybrid CNN/Transformer baselines. The paper also reports ablations showing that 2D retention is beneficial for higher-resolution fine-tuning and downstream dense prediction tasks, while chunkwise inference enables substantially better scalability at large image sizes. Overall, the contribution is methodological for efficient vision modeling, not educational intervention research.

paper_profiles.title: Mapping research in student engagement and educational technology in higher education: a systematic evidence map
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and postgraduate higher education students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broad problem that research on student engagement and educational technology in higher education is fragmented, theoretically inconsistent, and unevenly distributed across countries, fields, and study designs. The authors ask how studies define and theoretically ground engagement, which engagement/disengagement indicators appear in the literature, and what learning scenarios, delivery modes, and technologies are most often studied.

To answer these questions, the paper conducts a systematic evidence map of 243 studies published between 2007 and 2016. The corpus is drawn from peer-reviewed English-language journal articles in higher education that examined students, engagement, and educational technology. The review does not test a single intervention; instead, it maps patterns across the field, including country distribution, methods, theoretical frameworks, engagement indicators, learning scenarios, delivery modes, and technology types.

The population is primarily undergraduate higher education students, although postgraduate students are also represented. The dominant contexts are universities in the United States, United Kingdom, Australia, Taiwan, and China, and the most common learning scenarios are social-collaborative learning and self-directed learning. The review concludes that student engagement is usually not defined, theoretical grounding is often absent, and engagement is most often behavioral, while disengagement is less frequently reported. It also finds that text-based tools, LMSs, and discussion forums are the most common technologies, and that some tools (especially assessment and website-creation tools) are associated with more disengagement indicators. Overall, the paper argues for clearer definitions, stronger theory, more diverse methodologies, and more research outside the main English-speaking and STEM-heavy contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Across 243 higher-education studies, the review found that educational technology was most often associated with behavioral engagement, followed by affective and then cognitive engagement. Specifically, 209 studies documented behavioral engagement, 163 affective engagement, and 136 cognitive engagement; however, the review is descriptive and does not estimate a causal effect size for any one intervention.
finding.measure: Student engagement indicators and disengagement indicators coded from included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review repeatedly identifies durable-skill indicators such as critical thinking, self-regulation, learning from peers, and positive self-perception as engagement outcomes in the literature. For example, self-regulation appeared in 39 studies, critical thinking in 25, and learning from peers in 54, but the paper is a map of reported indicators rather than a test of intervention effects.
finding.measure: Coded engagement indicators from studies using educational technology

finding.finding_summary: The paper is substantively focused on higher-education educational technology across disciplines, with frequent reporting of achievement as an engagement indicator. Achievement was identified in 106 studies, but the review does not pool outcomes or provide intervention-level causal estimates; it maps how often achievement is mentioned alongside technology use.
finding.measure: Achievement coded as a student engagement indicator

paper_profiles.title: Students’ Satisfaction with Online Learning Experiences during the COVID-19 Pandemic
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This survey study examines undergraduate students’ satisfaction with emergency online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic in one private, non-profit Saudi higher education institution. The authors ask two main questions: how satisfied students were with the online teaching/learning approaches used during the pandemic, and which online platforms students perceived as most effective for their learning.

The study uses a researcher-developed questionnaire administered in May 2020 to 283 students across multiple majors. The survey covers student satisfaction with the online learning environment, satisfaction with institutional support, and preferences for online platforms and future delivery modes. Descriptive statistics (mean scores, standard deviations, skewness/kurtosis, Cronbach’s alpha) and a simple regression/correlation analysis were used; no experimental manipulation or comparison group was included.

Findings indicate generally positive student satisfaction with instructor support, alternative assessment plans, online course delivery, and school support services. Students reported the highest satisfaction with Google Hangouts for lecture delivery, with Google Classroom and Moodle also viewed favorably for course management and assessment. However, students preferred blended learning over fully online instruction, suggesting that online delivery was valued as an emergency response but not as the ideal replacement for face-to-face learning in this context.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported satisfaction with the online delivery arrangements, including platform selection, grading system, assessment options, training workshops, and technical support. In the descriptive results, the average satisfaction scores for online course delivery-related items were all above the agreement threshold, with the highest mean for instructors’ follow-up (M=3.99, SD=1.040; n=283) and overall online learning environment satisfaction around M=3.89-3.95 across items.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction survey items about online learning environment, course delivery, assessment plans, and instructor follow-up

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on institutional responses to COVID-19, including the coordinated use of specific platforms, grading systems, assessment options, training workshops, and online technical support. Students were satisfied with school support services such as technical help, academic advising, webinars, seminars, and facilities (e.g., staff responsiveness to technical support M=3.64, SD=1.009; academic advisor follow-up M=3.66, SD=1.034; n=283).
finding.measure: Student satisfaction with school support, facilities, advising, webinars, seminars, and technical support

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive satisfaction with the online learning experience and course engagement, suggesting favorable effects on engagement and perceived learning experience during emergency remote teaching. The study reports mean agreement levels above 3.5 on items such as course engagement (M=3.90, SD=1.045), gained knowledge and skills (M=3.89, SD=1.049), and online classes helping achieve learning outcomes (M=3.90, SD=1.057) for the 283 respondents.
finding.measure: Survey items on engagement, satisfaction, perceived knowledge/skills, and perceived achievement of course learning outcomes

finding.finding_summary: The study frames online learning as supporting collaborative and self-directed participation, and students were satisfied with instructor approaches that encouraged self-exploring, peer collaboration, and group work. Although not measured as a direct skill test, the reported satisfaction with engagement and collaborative online practices suggests positive perceptions of collaboration and self-regulated participation in the emergency online context.
finding.measure: Survey items referencing peer collaboration, group collaboration, self-exploring, and engagement

paper_profiles.title: Exploring Design Elements for Online STEM Courses: Active Learning, Engagement & Assessment Design
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined which design elements in fully online STEM courses at a large public four-year university were associated with students’ perceptions of learning and course satisfaction. The authors were interested in three broad design dimensions: course activity (including active learning), interactivity, and assessment/evaluation. They used a survey instrument adapted from the DETA toolkit and analyzed responses from 537 students enrolled in 15 fully online STEM courses in spring 2016.

Students reported frequent use of major projects, readings, websites, quizzes/exams, and slides, while active learning tasks such as using course-related software, solving real-world problems, and analyzing case studies were also common. However, the key correlational finding was that students’ perceptions of assessment design were strongly and significantly associated with both perceived learning and learning satisfaction, whereas activity and interactivity were not significant predictors of perceived learning in the overall sample. For some subgroups, assessment remained the only significant correlate; for female students, interactivity also related to satisfaction. The authors conclude that clear, timely, and formative assessment practices, along with UDL-informed course design, may improve the online STEM experience for diverse learners.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the online STEM courses reported that course activities helped them better understand concepts, get better grades, and think more deeply about course materials. These were self-reported perceptions rather than objective achievement outcomes, based on a survey of n=537 students in 15 online STEM courses.
finding.measure: Student self-reported perceived learning in online STEM courses

finding.finding_summary: Perceptions of assessment design were strongly and significantly associated with students’ self-perceived learning and learning satisfaction. Assessment explained 34% of the variance in perceived learning (adjusted R2=0.34; F(1,475)=241.31, p=.000) and 41% of the variance in satisfaction (adjusted R2=0.41; F(1,475)=337.43, p=.000).
finding.measure: Perceived learning and learning satisfaction survey scales
finding.study_size: n=537 (analysis subsets reported n=475 for regressions)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that online activities helped them think more deeply about course materials, and the course design included active learning tasks such as real-world problem solving and case analysis. The study is correlational and does not report objective gains in critical thinking, but it directly targets deeper thinking and related course engagement processes.
finding.measure: Self-reported deeper thinking about course materials; active learning activity frequencies

paper_profiles.title: Instructional strategies and course design for teaching statistics online: perspectives from online students
paper_profiles.population: Graduate students in educational technology; mostly K-20 instructors taking an online statistics course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks which instructional strategies and online course design features students perceive as effective in a fully online statistics course. The motivation is the challenge of teaching applied STEM content online, especially statistics, where students often need concrete demonstrations, application opportunities, and support for understanding procedures and concepts.

The study examines one online graduate-level statistics course at a U.S. university, delivered in Moodle with no face-to-face meetings. The course used multiple instructional strategies: case studies, SPSS video demonstrations, instructor notes, mini-projects, discussion forums, self-tests, and learning reflections. Course design features emphasized consistent module structure, aligned objectives and assessments, multiple resources, and application-focused content.

Data came from student reflections and end-of-semester course evaluations from 39 K-20 instructors/teachers enrolled across multiple offerings of the course (2013, 2014, 2016). Using qualitative coding, the author found that students viewed the course as effective overall, with case studies rated most helpful, followed by video demonstrations, instructor notes, mini-projects, and discussion forums. Students also valued the consistent structure, variety of resources, and practical application focus. The main conclusion is that online STEM courses, especially statistics, benefit from a carefully structured design that combines active application, worked examples, feedback, and opportunities for interaction and self-directed review.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the online statistics course helped them learn statistical concepts and procedures, especially through case studies, SPSS video demonstrations, instructor notes, and mini-projects. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes, but reflections indicate improved understanding of concepts such as t-tests, ANOVA, confidence intervals, and SPSS procedures among n=39 participants.
finding.measure: Student reflections and course evaluations about learning statistics concepts and procedures

finding.finding_summary: Students described gains in critical thinking, self-reflection, and ability to compare their understanding with peers and the instructor, particularly through case studies and discussion forums. The course also encouraged self-directed problem solving, collaborative discussion, and iterative work on mini-projects, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student reflections describing critical thinking, self-reflection, collaboration, and self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: Students frequently reported increased confidence, reduced intimidation about statistics and SPSS, and stronger engagement with the course because of the instructional design. The discussion forum, structured videos, and consistent module layout were described as helping students feel more comfortable and motivated, but the paper provides no quantitative effect size.
finding.measure: Student reflections and course evaluations regarding confidence, motivation, and engagement

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating Diagnostic Competences in Higher Education—a Meta-Analysis in Medical and Teacher Education
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate; graduate/postsecondary professional students in medical and teacher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis examines how instructional support can facilitate diagnostic competences in higher education, focusing on two professional domains: medical education and teacher education. The authors frame diagnostic competence as the ability to gather, integrate, and interpret case-specific information in order to make accurate professional decisions, and they ask which instructional supports are most effective, for whom, and under what contextual conditions.

The review synthesizes 35 empirical studies and analyzes the effects of problem-solving, examples, prompts, roles, and reflection phases, along with moderators such as prior professional knowledge and diagnostic context. Across studies, instructional support had a moderate positive effect on diagnostic competence (g = .39, 95% CI [.22, .56], n = 3472 across 35 studies). The meta-analysis found that problem-solving is effective independent of learners’ prior knowledge, but scaffolding works best when matched to knowledge level: more guided scaffolds help less advanced learners, while more self-regulatory scaffolds help advanced learners.

The included studies are mostly experimental interventions with medical students, preservice teachers, and in-service teachers, using outcome measures such as diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, professional vision, and knowledge related to formative assessment. The review concludes that instructional support can meaningfully improve diagnostic competences in postsecondary professional education, and that effectiveness depends on how much structure and self-regulation the scaffold affords as well as on the learner’s existing knowledge base and the diagnostic context.

finding.finding_summary: Across 35 empirical studies (n=3472), instructional support for diagnostic competence produced a moderate positive overall effect (g=.39, 95% CI [.22, .56], p=.001). The review directly targets higher-education professional learning in medical and teacher education, including outcomes such as diagnostic accuracy, clinical reasoning, professional vision, and formative assessment knowledge.
finding.measure: Diagnostic competence, clinical reasoning, diagnostic accuracy, professional vision, formative assessment-related knowledge/performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies diagnostic competence as a higher-order professional skill involving problem identification, evidence evaluation, hypothesis generation, and decision-making. Problem-solving and scaffolding generally improved these complex reasoning processes, with moderation by prior knowledge: low-guidance supports favored advanced learners, while high-guidance supports favored less advanced learners.
finding.measure: Diagnostic reasoning processes; epistemic-diagnostic activities; strategic and conditional knowledge

finding.finding_summary: Although not the primary focus, some included studies measured related motivational variables such as interest, and the review discusses engagement-like elements of scaffolding (e.g., prompts, reflection, role-taking) that can support learning. However, the meta-analysis does not synthesize a central social-emotional outcome, so this category is only marginally applicable.
finding.measure: Interest / self-reported engagement-related measures in a subset of primary studies

paper_profiles.title: Personalized and Adaptive Learning
paper_profiles.venue: Innovative Learning Environments in STEM Higher Education (SpringerBriefs in Statistics)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter provides an overview of personalized and adaptive learning in higher education, with an emphasis on how these approaches can be used in STEM courses. Rather than testing a single intervention, the chapter explains definitions, common technologies, pedagogical principles, implementation considerations, and challenges for adaptive learning systems such as intelligent tutoring, learning analytics, and machine-learning-driven courseware.

The chapter uses a hypothetical undergraduate nursing student and instructor to illustrate how adaptive courseware can diagnose prior knowledge, deliver individualized content and feedback, and support formative assessment, remediation, and self-regulated learning in a large physiology course. It argues that adaptive learning may improve student success, engagement, and course completion, while also reducing faculty burden through automation of assessment and early identification of at-risk students.

The chapter is largely conceptual and practitioner-oriented, drawing on prior literature and examples from higher education implementations rather than reporting a new empirical study. Its main conclusion is that adaptive learning has promise for STEM higher education, but successful adoption depends on fit with course context, faculty buy-in, infrastructure, and adequate support for content development and implementation.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter argues that adaptive learning systems can support STEM learning by diagnosing prior knowledge, delivering sequenced content, and using formative assessment and remediation to promote mastery of concepts. No new study is reported, but the authors cite prior work suggesting improved learning outcomes when adaptive courseware is integrated into STEM instruction.
finding.measure: STEM course learning/mastery through formative assessments and course performance

finding.finding_summary: The chapter claims adaptive learning can promote engagement, autonomy, self-regulation, and motivation by giving students immediate feedback, individualized pacing, and progress tracking. These assertions are supported by literature cited in the chapter, but the chapter itself does not present new quantitative evidence.
finding.measure: Engagement, autonomy, self-regulation, motivation, and persistence

finding.finding_summary: The chapter emphasizes metacognition and retrieval practice as important mechanisms in adaptive learning, noting that systems may include metacognitive prompts and practice opportunities that help learners monitor their progress. The paper does not report original effect sizes, but it presents these skills as central to how adaptive learning supports student learning.
finding.measure: Metacognition and progress monitoring

finding.finding_summary: The chapter states that adaptive learning systems can reduce faculty workload by automating grading, providing immediate feedback, and supplying real-time formative data that instructors can use to target intervention. It also notes that such systems may reduce the need for instructor remediation and allow more efficient use of class time, but no original workload study is reported.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, grading efficiency, and time to identify at-risk students

finding.finding_summary: The chapter discusses institution-level adoption, including APLU initiatives, courseware selection tools, faculty buy-in, and support structures needed to implement adaptive learning at scale in higher education. The main finding is conceptual: successful institutional adoption depends on contextual fit, infrastructure, and governance supports rather than technology alone.
finding.measure: Institutional adoption, implementation support, and courseware selection processes

paper_profiles.title: Experiential Learning in Second-Language Classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article argues for incorporating experiential learning into second-language classrooms, with a particular focus on how reflective phases can turn classroom activity into meaningful learning. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes prior work on experiential education, second-language acquisition, communicative teaching, motivation, and investment to build a theoretical rationale for an experiential-communicative syllabus.

The paper describes a four-phase model—exposure, participation, internalization, and dissemination/transfer—and explains how each phase can be used to structure ESL instruction. It uses examples from ESL contexts, including adult, pre-university, and university-bound learners, and discusses how experiential projects can support collaboration, learner ownership, self-evaluation, and real-world language use.

The central claims are that experiential methods can strengthen motivation, investment, confidence, and communicative competence, especially when students work on meaningful projects and reflect on their experiences. The article also cautions that experiential teaching can be difficult to assess and may conflict with standardized testing demands, but argues that it can complement form-focused instruction rather than replace it. Overall, it is a conceptual and practitioner-oriented discussion, not an empirical comparison of interventions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that experiential, project-based ESL instruction can improve oral language use by giving learners authentic opportunities to speak, negotiate meaning, and present products publicly. It does not report original effect sizes or a controlled comparison, but it cites prior work suggesting that collaborative language production tasks and project work support communicative competence and oral proficiency.
finding.measure: Oral proficiency; communicative language use; speaking tasks

finding.finding_summary: A major claim of the article is that experiential learning increases motivation, investment, confidence, and positive self-perception in second-language learners. The author describes these outcomes as recurring observations in project-based ESL settings, but the paper is conceptual and does not provide original quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Motivation, investment, confidence, self-perception, anticipation of success

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes durable skills developed through experiential projects, including collaboration, teamwork, leadership, self-evaluation, and critical reflection. These are presented as core benefits of the communicative-experiential syllabus, with no original numeric effect estimates reported.
finding.measure: Teamwork, leadership, self-evaluation, critical reflection, collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that experiential projects can improve broader ESL learning outcomes beyond isolated language forms, including performance on communicative tasks and portfolio-based assessment of oral proficiency and employability-related language skills. The discussion is instructional and theoretical rather than empirical, so no study-level statistics are reported.
finding.measure: Communicative task performance; portfolio/rubric-based assessment; oral proficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that experiential learning has implications for curriculum design and assessment policy, arguing that it can complement standardized, form-focused instruction and be integrated with portfolio and formative assessment. These institutional implications are discussed as recommendations rather than evaluated outcomes.
finding.measure: Curriculum design and assessment approach

paper_profiles.title: Subjective data, objective data and the role of bias in predictive modelling: Lessons from a dispositional learning analytics application
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how response-style bias in self-report questionnaires and overconfidence bias in confidence judgments affect predictive models in higher education learning analytics. The authors ask whether questionnaire data, trace data from digital learning systems, and course performance measures can be decomposed into bias-related and bias-corrected components, and whether doing so changes the explanatory power of models of learning and performance.

The study is situated in a large first-year introductory mathematics and statistics course in a Dutch business and economics program. Students completed multiple validated questionnaires on achievement emotions, epistemic emotions, motivation, goals, and related dispositions; the course also produced LMS and e-tutorial trace data, diagnostic entry tests, and final performance measures. The authors use regression-based instrumental-variable style decompositions to estimate response-style effects (especially extreme response style) and a subjective-vs-objective confidence difference.

Main findings are that response-style bias explains a substantial share of variation in several self-report constructs and even some course performance variables, while overconfidence contributes much less. Trace process data were least affected by response-style patterns. In models of achievement and epistemic emotions, correcting for response styles meaningfully changes coefficients and explained variance, whereas correcting for overconfidence has limited impact. The paper concludes that so-called bias in survey data may still carry predictive value in educational models, but trace data are comparatively more robust to these response-style effects.

finding.finding_summary: The study’s core context is an introductory mathematics and statistics course, and course performance outcomes include mathematics exam and quiz measures.
