Response-style bias and questionnaire-derived predictors substantially explain variation in math-related achievement emotions that in turn predict mathematics performance, but direct evidence of improvement from any intervention is absent. For course outcomes, overconfidence explained less than 1% of variation in Grade and MathExam, indicating little practical effect (n=1080).
finding.measure: Final course grade, mathematics exam score, mathematics quiz score, statistics exam score, statistics quiz score

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly models achievement emotions and epistemic emotions, including learning anxiety, boredom, hopelessness, enjoyment, confusion, curiosity, and related motivation/disposition scales. Response styles accounted for substantial variation in these constructs, with the largest bias components for anxiety and hopelessness (e.g., LAX R2=.430; LHL R2=.415), while overconfidence effects were much smaller (typically at most about 10% explained variance).
finding.measure: Self-report scales of achievement emotions, epistemic emotions, motivation/engagement, and related dispositions

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly analyzes constructs such as cognitive and metacognitive processing, goal-setting, and control/value beliefs, treating them as antecedents and correlates in predictive models. Response-style bias showed meaningful associations with these durable-skill-related questionnaire scales, while trace process variables were comparatively independent of response styles, suggesting these measures are more robust than self-reports for modeling metacognitive or strategic learning behavior.
finding.measure: Questionnaire scales for approaches to learning, cognitive and metacognitive strategies, goal-setting, and related self-regulation constructs

finding.finding_summary: The study includes LMS and e-tutorial trace measures such as clicks, attempts, time on task, hints, worked examples, and mastery, with the analytic goal of determining which data types are more stable and predictive. The authors find that process-type trace data stand out as being independent of response-style bias, implying these data may be more operationally useful for prediction and monitoring than self-report data; however, the paper does not evaluate an efficiency intervention per se.
finding.measure: BlackBoard clicks; e-tutorial attempts, time on task, hints, worked examples, mastery

finding.finding_summary: The paper also models statistics-related course performance alongside mathematics, including statistics exam and quiz scores, within the same introductory STEM course. As with mathematics outcomes, response-style bias is present in some performance variables, but overconfidence contributes little to explaining variance; the main practical finding is that performance metrics are not free of bias-related associations even when they are objectively scored.
finding.measure: Statistics exam score and statistics quiz score

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment might be implemented through an e-learning platform (BlackBoard) in a university setting. The authors frame the problem as improving assessment practices in a tech-savvy higher-education context, arguing that frequent low-stakes assessments with timely feedback can support learning better than relying mainly on summative end-of-semester exams.

The paper proposes weekly or fortnightly online tests in BlackBoard with immediate, detailed feedback, and describes a 10-item Java online test (multiple choice and true/false) as an example. The study then reports a student questionnaire on continuous assessment and BlackBoard testing, including reliability estimates and some between-stream differences (Business, Engineering, IT) in attitudes toward open-book continuous assessment and the BB test option.

Overall, students were generally supportive of the approach, especially because it broke content into smaller topics and provided immediate teacher feedback. The authors conclude that formative assessment delivered through e-learning is workable and likely beneficial for keeping students engaged with the subject, reducing delay in feedback, and potentially improving summative grades, though the evidence presented is based on perceptions rather than achievement outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable attitudes toward frequent internal assessments and the BlackBoard test format because it provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and helped them stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester. The survey found that a majority supported continuous assessment, and 60% favored good learning with more marks over less learning and more marks, suggesting positive effects on motivation and engagement rather than direct achievement gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, motivation, stress/pressure, and perceived usefulness of feedback from questionnaire responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on formative assessment as a way to support metacognition and self-monitoring: students can see their score, identify strengths and weaknesses, and check whether they are on track. Respondents said the approach would help them learn topics progressively and correct mistakes without delay, indicating perceived benefits for self-regulation and metacognitive learning.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, understanding strengths and weaknesses, and correcting mistakes through detailed feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on formative assessment in a university course context and reports that students generally supported splitting course work into 10-12 weekly Blackboard assessments. The main perceived benefit was that smaller topic assessments with immediate feedback made learning more manageable and supported preparation for the summative semester examination, but no direct exam-score data were reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and perceived preparation for semester-end tests

finding.finding_summary: The proposed Blackboard implementation was presented as a practical way to deliver frequent formative assessments with immediate, detailed feedback and flexible administration. Students favored the online test option over classroom tests mainly because of immediate feedback and convenience, indicating perceived gains in assessment delivery efficiency, though the paper does not measure staff workload or time savings directly.
finding.measure: Student ratings and preferences for Blackboard test option versus classroom test option

paper_profiles.title: Turing’s Children: Representation of Sexual Minorities in STEM
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines representation gaps for sexual minorities in STEM using nationally representative U.S. survey data. The authors ask whether lesbian, gay, bisexual, and queer people are underrepresented in STEM degree attainment and STEM occupations, and whether those gaps differ by gender.

The study uses two large observational datasets: the 2009-2018 American Community Survey (ACS) and the 2013-2018 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS). In the ACS, sexual minority status is proxied by being in a same-sex couple; in the NHIS, respondents directly report sexual orientation. Outcomes are STEM degree completion and STEM occupation, with analyses stratified by sex and adjusted for age, race/ethnicity, and location. The paper is not an intervention study; it is a descriptive and regression-adjusted population analysis.

The main findings are that men in same-sex couples are substantially less likely than men in different-sex couples to have a STEM bachelor’s degree and, to a lesser extent, to work in a STEM occupation. The ACS shows a 12 percentage point raw gap in STEM degrees for men (22.8% vs. 34.8%) and a 1.1 percentage point gap in STEM occupation; regression-adjusted results remain large and significant (e.g., -0.108 for STEM degree, -0.014 for STEM occupation). For women, the paper finds little to no gap in STEM degrees and mixed/near-null differences in STEM occupations. The authors conclude that sexual minorities, especially men, are underrepresented in STEM and that more inclusive policies and data collection are needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies STEM degree attainment as a postsecondary academic outcome. In the ACS, men in same-sex couples were 12 percentage points less likely than men in different-sex couples to have earned a STEM bachelor’s degree (22.8% vs. 34.8%; n=69,641 vs. 5,237,089), and this gap remained large after adjustment (0.108 lower probability, p<.01; mean dependent variable 0.345, n=1,850,340 vs. 2,063,090). For women, the STEM degree gap was essentially zero in the raw means (14.0% vs. 13.9%) but became slightly positive after adjustment (0.012, p<.01).
finding.measure: STEM bachelor’s degree completion
finding.study_size: n=10,809,885 coupled adults in ACS; regression sample n=2,063,090 women and n=1,850,340 men

finding.finding_summary: The paper also studies STEM occupational representation as a labor-market/institutional outcome. In the ACS, men in same-sex couples were 1.1 percentage points less likely than men in different-sex couples to be in STEM occupations (8.4% vs. 9.5%; p<.01), and the adjusted gap remained negative (-0.014, p<.01; n=4,992,047 men and 4,664,190 women in the occupation regressions). The NHIS replication showed a similar pattern for gay men, who were 2.3 percentage points less likely than heterosexual men to work in STEM occupations (6.5% vs. 8.8%; p<.01).
finding.measure: STEM occupation representation
finding.study_size: ACS: n=9,656,237 coupled adults for raw occupation comparisons; NHIS: n=69,972 women and n=61,890 men

paper_profiles.title: Faster Consensus via a Sparser Controller
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a control-theoretic question: when distributed consensus systems with communication delays are allowed to vary their controller architecture, which network topology yields the fastest convergence? The authors focus on single-integrator agents with delayed feedback and assume that communication latency increases with the number of hops or links in the controller architecture.

The approach analyzes the convergence rate of delayed consensus dynamics under different graph architectures and optimizes both feedback gains and architecture. The paper derives stability and monotonicity properties of the characteristic roots, then shows how to decouple gain optimization from architecture selection. It compares uniform and optimized gains across several initial graph families, including regular graphs and random graphs, using numerical experiments with N=100 agents.

The main conclusion is that, contrary to the common assumption that denser or fully connected architectures always perform best, sparse architectures can minimize convergence time when delays grow with network density or hop count. The optimal architecture depends on the delay growth rate and the feedback-gain design strategy, but in the reported experiments the best-performing controller is often not fully connected. This is a theoretical and simulation-based engineering paper about distributed control; it does not study educational interventions or learners.

paper_profiles.title: Koopman-based control using sum-of-squares optimization: Improved stability guarantees and data efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of stabilizing unknown nonlinear control-affine dynamical systems using data-driven methods. The authors combine Koopman operator theory with SafEDMD to learn a bilinear surrogate model with certified error bounds, then design a rational state-feedback controller via sum-of-squares (SOS) optimization that accounts explicitly for bilinearity and model uncertainty.

The approach is developed first for discrete-time bilinear systems with known dynamics and then extended to continuous-time unknown nonlinear systems using sampled-data feedback and lifted-state representations. The paper’s main claim is that explicitly retaining bilinearity, rather than over-approximating it as in prior robust Koopman-based control methods, reduces conservatism and yields larger guaranteed regions of attraction, better feasibility, and improved data efficiency.

The empirical evidence consists of numerical examples: a perturbed zone-temperature building-control system and an inverted pendulum with data-driven Koopman lifting. In both examples, the proposed SOS-based controller is reported to outperform comparison methods in terms of feasibility and guaranteed stability region, but the paper does not report educational outcomes or human-subject data.

paper_profiles.title: Encrypted control for networked systems: An illustrative introduction and current challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This tutorial-style paper surveys the emerging area of encrypted control for networked dynamical systems. The core problem addressed is how to preserve confidentiality when control computation and communication are outsourced to cloud or distributed platforms that may be curious, compromised, or exposed to eavesdropping and manipulation. Rather than focusing on a single empirical study, the article explains the threat model, summarizes relevant cryptographic primitives, and maps them onto control formulations.

The paper reviews how standard linear controllers, model predictive controllers (MPC), and distributed control schemes can be reformulated so that computations are carried out on encrypted data. It contrasts multiple implementation strategies, including homomorphic encryption (e.g., ElGamal, Paillier), secret sharing, and secure multi-party computation, and discusses practical issues such as quantization, communication cost, and computational overhead. The audience is technical readers in control/cryptography; no student or educator population is studied.

Overall, the article concludes that encrypted control is feasible for several classes of controllers, but that there is a persistent trade-off between privacy and efficiency. Homomorphic approaches are flexible but computationally expensive, while secret-sharing and multi-party approaches can be more efficient when the architecture allows multiple non-colluding parties. The paper frames open challenges and future directions rather than reporting new experimental effectiveness results.

paper_profiles.title: Individual Risk in Mean Field Control with Application to Automated Demand Response
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a control problem in automated demand response for large power grids: how to use many flexible electrical loads to track a grid-level reference signal while also protecting the service quality of each individual load. The authors argue that prior mean-field control work achieved good aggregate tracking but did not address the risk that some individual loads would receive systematically poor service over time.

The paper proposes a mean-field and linear time-invariant approximation for an individual load’s quality-of-service (QoS) dynamics, then uses this model to estimate the mean and variance of QoS under randomized control. A key contribution is a simple local "opt-out" mechanism: when a load’s QoS is about to exceed prespecified bounds, it temporarily refuses grid control commands to keep service quality within limits.

The empirical section uses simulated pool-pump loads as the example population. Across simulations, QoS without local control is approximately Gaussian and can drift far from acceptable bounds, while opt-out control truncates the QoS distribution and guarantees strict bounds with only a modest reduction in grid-level ancillary service capacity. The paper concludes that individual risk can be quantified and substantially reduced without materially harming tracking performance at the grid level.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that a local opt-out controller improves individual-load service quality by truncating the QoS distribution to the target interval while preserving near-perfect grid-level tracking. In simulation with 10^5 pool pumps, the QoS variance in the moving-window metric dropped by more than a factor of three, and no more than 3% of loads opted out at any time in the baseline experiment.
finding.measure: Quality-of-service (QoS) / moving-window operation-hours metric and discounted QoS, plus opt-out frequency and grid tracking performance
finding.std_deviation: approximately 23 without local control; approximately 6.5 with local control (variance estimates)

paper_profiles.title: Passive iFIR filters for data-driven control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-engineering problem: how to design passive iFIR controllers for passive plants using data-driven methods, without requiring an accurate plant model or large datasets. The motivation is to retain the simplicity and integral action of PID control while making the controller more flexible through a finite impulse response (FIR) component.

The proposed approach builds on virtual reference feedback tuning (VRFT), which turns controller design into a least-squares fitting problem from measured open-loop input-output data. The novelty is to add passivity constraints to the tuning problem using three alternative formulations: a KYP/LMI-based method, an infinite Toeplitz formulation, and a finite sampled-frequency positive-realness formulation. These constraints are intended to ensure closed-loop stability for passive plants while preserving the data-driven fitting objective.

The paper is theoretical and algorithmic, illustrated with simulation examples on passive FIR filter identification and on velocity control of a compliant two-cart mechanical system, including a nonlinear variant. The examples compare computational cost and closed-loop performance across the three formulations and against a PID controller tuned with VRFT. The main conclusion is that the proposed passive iFIR design can achieve strong tracking performance while guaranteeing stability by construction, and that the finite Toeplitz / positive-realness approaches scale better than the KYP formulation for larger filters.

paper_profiles.title: Stem Cells: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual/theoretical treatment of stem cell and cancer stem cell network theory rather than an empirical study. The author argues that healthy stem cells and cancer stem cells are often governed by topologically similar developmental control networks, and that differences in phenotype arise from where and when these networks are activated, plus additional non-network genetic changes that enable metastasis.

The paper proposes that a normal linear stem cell network can become dangerous if a second feedback loop mutation converts it into an exponential network, leading to explosive proliferation. It also argues that higher-order metastatic stem cell networks are progressively more dangerous and that the most effective therapeutic strategy is to identify, disable, or edit the cancer network itself—potentially using genome-editing tools such as CRISPR. The paper is framed as a computational/theoretical roadmap for modeling, diagnosing, and eventually curing cancers, but it does not report original empirical data or experimental evaluation.

Because it is written as a theoretical exposition with figures and references to prior modeling work, the paper is best understood as an argument about developmental/cancer network structure and its implications for therapy, not as a study of a student, educator, or school-based intervention. The context is adult biomedical research, especially cancer systems biology and computational biology.

paper_profiles.title: On the relationship between control barrier functions and projected dynamical systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a theoretical question in control systems: how control barrier function (CBF)-based safety controllers relate to projected dynamical systems (PDSs). The authors show that, under stated regularity assumptions, the vector field generated by a CBF quadratic program can be viewed as a Krasovskii-like perturbation of a differential inclusion that represents a PDS, with a bound on the perturbation that shrinks as the CBF tuning parameter increases.

The paper then uses this relationship to discuss controller design. In a simple continuous control setting with a nominal stabilizing controller and a convex safe set, it argues that choosing the quadratic-program cost matrix to match the Lyapunov matrix of the nominal system, and selecting a sufficiently large tuning parameter, can preserve asymptotic stability while enforcing safety and avoiding undesired equilibria or limit cycles.

A small numerical example on a two-dimensional control system illustrates the point: with the correct cost matrix, the CBF controller safely stabilizes the origin; with an incorrect cost matrix, it creates an undesired stable equilibrium on the safety boundary. The paper is primarily theoretical and focuses on continuous control and projected-dynamics methods, not educational interventions or learners.

paper_profiles.title: On Controller Design for Systems on Manifolds in Euclidean Space
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-theoretic problem: how to design feedback controllers for dynamical systems whose state evolves on a manifold rather than in ordinary Euclidean space. The author argues that many such systems are easier to control if the manifold is embedded into a Euclidean ambient space, the dynamics are extended off-manifold, and an additional transversal-stabilizing term is introduced so the manifold becomes an attractive invariant set.

The main methodological contribution is a general framework for controller synthesis in ambient Euclidean coordinates, followed by restriction back to the original manifold. The paper develops the theory and then works through two benchmark mechanical systems: a fully actuated rigid body on SO(3) × R^3 and a quadcopter model with attitude and position dynamics. For both systems, the author derives linearized tracking controllers in ambient space and shows exponential convergence of tracking errors under the proposed designs, with numerical simulations illustrating performance and robustness to disturbance.

The work is methodological rather than educational: it does not study learners, classrooms, or instructional interventions. Its conclusions are that embedding-plus-transversal-stabilization can simplify controller synthesis, avoid coordinate singularities, and produce intrinsic tracking laws on manifolds while still leveraging standard Euclidean linear control tools.

paper_profiles.title: Data-Driven Control of Nonlinear Systems: Beyond Polynomial Dynamics
paper_profiles.venue: Proc. IEEE Conference on Decision and Control (CDC)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of designing stabilizing controllers for unknown continuous-time nonlinear systems using only measured input-state data, without assuming a known model. The authors focus on systems with rational dynamics and, more broadly, nonlinear systems that are linear in non-polynomial basis functions. Their central challenge is to obtain closed-loop stability and performance guarantees despite measurement noise and model uncertainty.

The proposed approach rewrites rational dynamics into a polynomial equation that is linearly parameterized in unknown coefficients, enabling a data-driven system parametrization from one open-loop trajectory subject to bounded noise. Using this parametrization, the paper derives sum-of-squares (SOS) and linear-matrix-inequality-based conditions for robust state-feedback controller synthesis. The method guarantees stability for all systems consistent with the measured data and the assumed noise bound, and it is extended to robust quadratic performance specifications such as L2-gain.

The paper is methodological and theoretical, with numerical examples illustrating feasibility on a small academic rational system, a drug-distribution model, and a pendulum after polynomialization of non-polynomial basis functions. It does not study human learners, schools, or instructional interventions. As a result, its educational relevance is indirect: it is best characterized as an AI/controls research paper rather than an education outcomes study.

paper_profiles.title: Faster Consensus via a Sparser Controller
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a control-theoretic question: when the communication latency in a distributed consensus system depends on the density of the controller architecture, what network structure and feedback gains minimize the convergence rate? The authors consider discrete-time single-integrator agents connected by an undirected communication graph, with delayed state feedback whose delay increases with the number of communication hops/links allowed in the architecture.

The main methodological contribution is an optimization analysis of the convergence rate for delayed consensus dynamics. For a fixed architecture, the paper derives stability conditions and shows how to optimally scale feedback gains; for architecture selection, it compares controllers built from increasingly dense graphs under delay functions that grow with architecture complexity. The study is entirely theoretical and uses numerical experiments on networks with 100 agents to illustrate the optimization results under linear and quadratic delay growth.

The paper concludes that denser communication is not always better: when delays increase sufficiently fast with added links, the fastest consensus can be achieved by sparse controller architectures rather than fully connected ones. The optimal architecture depends on how gains are chosen and on the delay-growth function, with numerical examples showing that sparse or moderately sparse architectures can outperform denser ones under architecture-dependent latency.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that, under architecture-dependent communication delays, a sparser distributed controller can yield faster convergence than a fully connected one. In numerical experiments with N=100 agents, the optimal architecture was often sparse (e.g., n*=1, 2, 5, or 7 depending on the delay law and gain design), indicating improved control efficiency measured by the convergence rate of consensus.
finding.measure: Convergence rate Rn of delayed consensus dynamics
finding.study_size: n=100 agents (numerical experiments); theoretical analysis over architectures

paper_profiles.title: Encrypted control for networked systems: An illustrative introduction and current challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tutorial-style introduction to encrypted control for networked dynamical systems. It addresses the problem of how to compute control decisions over encrypted data so that sensitive system states, controller parameters, and model data remain confidential even when computation and communication are outsourced to third-party clouds or distributed agents.

The paper surveys and organizes the field around three main controller classes: linear controllers, model predictive control (MPC), and distributed/multi-party control. It explains the cryptographic primitives that make encrypted computation possible, especially homomorphic encryption, secret sharing, and secure multi-party computation, and then shows how standard control formulations can be re-expressed to work with these tools. The paper uses examples from cloud-based industrial and networked control contexts, but it is not an empirical evaluation study with human participants.

The main conclusion is that encrypted control is feasible for several important control problems, but practical deployment requires careful co-design of control formulations and cryptographic methods to balance privacy, computation cost, communication load, and quantization error. The paper highlights that fully homomorphic approaches are still too expensive for many embedded or real-time applications, while more efficient schemes based on additively homomorphic encryption or secret sharing can be practical under narrower assumptions. It ends by identifying open research problems and future directions for making encrypted control more efficient and broadly usable.

paper_profiles.title: Passive iFIR filters for data-driven control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a control-engineering problem: how to design feedback controllers that are both data-driven and provably passive, while retaining the simplicity of PID-style controllers. The authors argue that standard virtual reference feedback tuning (VRFT) can fit desired closed-loop behavior from data, but by itself does not guarantee stability. They propose a new controller class, iFIR controllers, which combine an integrator with a finite impulse response (FIR) filter, making them more flexible than PID controllers while preserving passivity-related benefits.

The main contribution is a model-free design framework that augments VRFT with passivity constraints. Three formulations are developed: a KYP/LMI-based approach, a Toeplitz-matrix-based approach, and a frequency-sampled positive-realness approach. These methods use only input-output data and do not require an accurate plant model or large datasets. The paper argues that enforcing passivity separates closed-loop stability from performance matching: stability is guaranteed by construction for passive plants, while the data determine how closely the controller matches a desired reference model.

The examples are entirely in control-systems contexts, including fitting passive FIR filters and velocity control of a compliant two-cart mechanical system, plus a nonlinear passive plant variant. Results show that the proposed passive iFIR controllers can closely match target reference models, and that the Toeplitz and positive-realness formulations scale much better computationally than the KYP/LMI approach for larger filter orders. The paper concludes that passive iFIR design is a promising one-shot or low-iteration alternative to conventional data-driven controller tuning, especially when stability guarantees are important.

paper_profiles.title: Guaranteed Safe Spacecraft Docking with Control Barrier Functions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies a control problem in spacecraft guidance: how to guarantee safe rendezvous, landing, and docking when the vehicle must satisfy tight terminal tolerances in the presence of bounded matched and unmatched disturbances. The authors note that standard robust control barrier functions can keep trajectories safe, but may also prevent the system from approaching close enough to the boundary of the safe set to complete a docking maneuver.

To address this, the paper develops a modified robust control barrier function construction that adds a tunable margin, allowing trajectories to remain safe while still reaching a docking state in finite time. The framework is built for systems with relative-degree-2 safety constraints and input bounds, and the authors prove conditions under which landing or docking occurs with prescribed terminal velocity bounds.

The paper is entirely methodological and theoretical, with simulation demonstrations on two spacecraft scenarios: landing on the asteroid Ceres and docking in low Earth orbit under the Hill-Clohessy-Wiltshire dynamics. The simulations show that the proposed controller satisfies safety and input constraints while achieving the specified terminal tolerances in finite time. The work is relevant to aerospace control and safety-critical autonomy, but it does not study educational populations, instructional interventions, or learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Koopman-based control using sum-of-squares optimization: Improved stability guarantees and data efficiency
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of stabilizing unknown nonlinear control-affine systems using data-driven methods with formal guarantees. The authors focus on reducing conservatism in Koopman-based controller synthesis, where prior methods approximate the lifted dynamics too coarsely and can yield small guaranteed regions of attraction or require more data than desirable.

The proposed approach combines SafEDMD, which learns a bilinear surrogate model with certified approximation-error bounds from input-state data, with a new sum-of-squares (SOS) controller design. For the bilinear surrogate, the controller is a rational state-feedback law whose coefficients are obtained from a convex SOS program and which explicitly accounts for bilinearity and model uncertainty rather than over-approximating them. The paper then extends the same design to continuous-time nonlinear systems via sampled-data feedback in the lifted Koopman space.

The empirical validation consists of numerical examples, including a perturbed discrete-time bilinear building-control model and an unknown nonlinear inverted pendulum. In both cases, the SOS-based design is reported to be less conservative than prior LMI-based or robust bilinear-control methods: it achieves a larger guaranteed region of attraction and remains feasible for larger error-bound constants, implying improved data efficiency. The paper’s main conclusion is that exploiting bilinear structure directly in SOS optimization yields more robust and less conservative Koopman-based control than existing alternatives.

paper_profiles.title: Implicit predictors in regularized data-driven predictive control
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines a theoretical question in data-driven predictive control (DPC): when a controller uses collected trajectory data and regularization rather than an explicit system model, what predictive behavior is implicitly being assumed? The authors introduce the concept of an "implicit predictor," defined as a predictor that can be inserted as an equality constraint without changing the minimizers or optimal value of the optimal control problem.

The paper focuses on regularized DPC schemes, especially common squared 2-norm regularization and a projection-based variant, and derives the corresponding implicit predictors under a full-row-rank data assumption. It shows that, without output constraints, both regularizations yield the same implicit predictor: a linear predictor that interpolates between the subspace predictive control (SPC) predictor and zero depending on the regularization weight. With output constraints, the predictor becomes piecewise affine and can deviate substantially from the unconstrained predictor when the unconstrained prediction is infeasible.

The context is postsecondary/graduate-level control engineering research rather than an intervention study with learners. The main conclusion is that regularization in DPC does not merely improve numerical behavior; it effectively specifies the model class through the structure of the implicit predictor, and constraints can significantly alter that predictive behavior. The work is conceptual/theoretical and uses a small numerical example for illustration, not an empirical education study.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessments with immediate, detailed feedback can support learning better than a purely summative approach, and they frame this as a way to build a “culture of success.”

The implementation described uses Blackboard to deliver weekly or fortnightly online tests, with options for multiple-choice and true/false questions, randomized ordering, and detailed feedback after submission. The paper also reviews theoretical and prior empirical support for formative assessment, emphasizing feedback, scaffolding, metacognition, and student self-monitoring.

To gauge reception, the authors surveyed university students about continuous assessment and the proposed Blackboard testing approach. Students generally supported the idea, especially because it broke content into smaller topic-based assessments and provided immediate teacher feedback; some concern was expressed about stress and overemphasis on learning/assessment load. The paper concludes that e-learning can effectively support formative assessment and may improve student understanding and, potentially, summative exam performance, though the evidence presented is primarily perceptual rather than outcome-based.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the Blackboard-based formative assessment approach was useful for learning smaller topic units and for supporting preparation for semester-end exams. The study does not report achievement test gains, but respondents believed the method would help them learn progressively and improve their standing in the subject.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard online tests; open-ended survey responses about learning and exam preparation

finding.finding_summary: Students largely endorsed frequent formative assessment because it provided immediate feedback and helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses, but some also reported stress and pressure from too many tests. The paper presents these as perception-based findings from a university survey rather than measured changes in motivation or well-being.
finding.measure: Survey ratings and open-ended comments on continuous assessment, feedback, and test frequency

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment with immediate feedback supports metacognition and self-monitoring, and students said it helped them check whether they were on track. This is based on attitudes toward the assessment model, not direct measurement of metacognitive skill gains.
finding.measure: Survey responses about teacher feedback, self-checking, and tracking strengths/weaknesses

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review/article aimed at educators; no empirical participant sample reported)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical review of how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in education. The authors frame formative assessment around three core questions—where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward—and argue that LLMs can be aligned to each of these functions when used with sound pedagogy and careful prompting.

The paper does not report a new empirical study, intervention, or participant sample. Instead, it synthesizes prior work and provides classroom-oriented examples of prompting LLMs to rewrite learning objectives into student-friendly language, generate discussion prompts for co-constructing success criteria, create sample work of varying quality, and produce formative questions and feedback. The review emphasizes that LLM outputs are useful only when educators critically adapt them to context, accuracy, and learning goals.

A major conclusion is that LLMs can potentially scale formative assessment and reduce teacher workload, but they should augment rather than replace teacher expertise. The authors also highlight limitations in current evaluation metrics, risks of overreliance on AI, and the need for future research on robust feedback metrics, AI-aware assessment design, and culturally/contextually grounded prompting resources. Because the article is conceptual and illustrative rather than empirical, it does not provide subgroup effects or outcome estimates for student populations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce educator time and effort by helping generate student-friendly learning objectives, formative questions, feedback, and sample work. However, this is presented as a conceptual/practical claim rather than a measured empirical effect; no sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time-saving potential in creating formative-assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that LLM-supported formative assessment may strengthen metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by making learning goals explicit, prompting reflection, and asking students to critique AI-generated exemplars. These claims are illustrative and pedagogical, not based on direct outcome measurement in this paper.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking/collaboration through formative-assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows how LLMs can support writing-related formative tasks such as simplifying learning objectives, generating sample methods sections, and helping students critique exemplar text. No student performance data are reported; the evidence consists of illustrative prompts and generated examples rather than a study of outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing support / quality of sample work and writing-related formative materials

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the importance of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering education and explains how technology has made it easier to collect and act on student responses during class. The central problem addressed is that, while formative assessment is theoretically and empirically supported, it is often underused or only partially effective because instructors may not respond appropriately to the feedback, may not know how to adapt instruction in real time, or may rely on questions that do not reveal student thinking.

The paper discusses technology-facilitated approaches such as clickers, cell-phone polling, and especially open-format questions submitted with digital ink or text. It uses examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course with third-year engineering physics majors to illustrate how real-time student responses can reveal misconceptions, gaps in calculus fluency, and failure to transfer prior solution work to a new task. The paper is primarily a conceptual/practice-oriented overview rather than a controlled study; its evidence base is illustrative and drawn from prior literature and classroom examples.

The main conclusion is that embedded formative assessment can improve learning by engaging students, increasing metacognition, and informing instruction, but its effectiveness depends on high-quality questions and especially on timely, adaptive instructor response. The authors also argue that open-format responses provide richer insight into student thinking than multiple-choice items, and that current technology can reduce clerical burden enough to make such practices more feasible in large engineering classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment supports metacognition and critical thinking by making student thinking visible and prompting learners to reflect on what they know and do not know. In the classroom examples, open-format prompts revealed students’ struggles with explaining reasoning, choosing methods, and transferring prior derivations to new problems, but no formal effect sizes or experimental estimates are reported.
finding.measure: Observed student written responses to open-format formative assessment questions; qualitative indications of metacognition, reasoning, and problem-solving approach

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by streamlining collection and immediate review of responses. It describes clickers, mobile polling, and InkSurvey as tools that make real-time feedback feasible in large classes, but does not provide quantitative productivity data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Instructor ability to collect and review student responses in real time; perceived reduction in clerical burden

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course showing that open-format formative questions can expose students’ understanding of Gauss’s law, symmetry arguments, integral setup, and transfer of derivations to graphing tasks. Students’ responses revealed misconceptions and incomplete reasoning, but the paper does not report a controlled improvement in scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Student solutions to open-format electromagnetics problems involving Gauss’s law and electric-field graphs

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student-produced videos can serve as an effective formative assessment tool in high school physics. The authors argue that conventional tests and questionnaires capture only a narrow slice of understanding, while video production can reveal students’ conceptual grasp, misconceptions, planning processes, and collaborative skills.

The approach was implemented in a Brazilian high school (Colégio Pedro II) with students aged roughly 14–17 across three grade levels. After formal instruction, students worked in self-selected groups of up to five to create short videos on physics topics studied during the term, along with a brief written explanation. The teacher reviewed the products, analyzed them across content, format, and general qualities, and then used class discussions to provide feedback and support learning.

The paper reports descriptive analyses of 55 videos from 232 students in 2011. Most videos were at least partially correct in physics content, and the authors note a strong association between technical quality and conceptual quality. They conclude that student video production is a useful and reliable formative assessment method because it surfaces misconceptions and understanding in ways that traditional assessments may miss, while also fostering planning, collaboration, and active participation.

finding.finding_summary: Student-produced videos were used to assess physics understanding and revealed substantive information about conceptual accuracy and misconceptions. Among 55 videos produced by 232 students, 35% were judged correct and 45% partially correct; the authors also report that 47% presented ideas clearly and 87% had a logical sequence.
finding.measure: Teacher analysis of physics content in student videos (correctness, clarity, logical sequence, and connection between proposal and product)

finding.finding_summary: The activity was framed as supporting metacognition, planning, and collaboration, and the authors observed that students often chose more elaborate production forms requiring careful planning and implementation. The paper does not provide a quantitative effect size, but it concludes that video production elicited project-completion and cooperative-work skills alongside content learning.
finding.measure: Observed characteristics of video planning/production; teacher qualitative analysis of collaboration and planning

finding.finding_summary: In addition to physics content, the paper evaluates the quality of the produced videos as artifacts, including technical format and alignment between the task prompt and final product. The authors report that 75% of videos showed a satisfactory connection between proposal and product, 42% were technically very well done, and technical quality was strongly correlated with conceptual correctness.
finding.measure: Video production quality (technical quality, format, and alignment with task)

paper_profiles.title: Foundations for AI-Assisted Formative Assessment Feedback for Short-Answer Tasks in Large-Enrollment Classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of providing timely, individualized formative assessment feedback for short-answer tasks in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The authors argue that while write-to-learn tasks can support learning, manually scoring many open-ended responses is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. Their goal is to establish whether natural language processing (NLP) methods can reliably assist human raters in scoring short-answer student responses and, in turn, support clustering of similar responses for scalable feedback.

Using de-identified extant data from a prior study, the authors analyzed 6 short-answer tasks completed by 1,935 post-secondary students across 29 class sections at 15 institutions. Four human raters with different levels of statistics-teaching experience scored responses with a detailed rubric, and agreement was evaluated with quadratic weighted kappa and Fleiss’ kappa. The study also compared two NLP approaches for automated scoring, finding that the Semantic Feature-Wise Transformation Relation Network (SFRN) outperformed an LSTM-based baseline in classification accuracy and achieved substantial agreement with human raters.

Beyond scoring accuracy, the paper explored whether learned text representations could support clustering of student answers into semantically coherent groups for instructors to interpret. The results suggest that high-dimensional representations used for classification can achieve strong agreement, while lower-dimensional static representations may be better for clustering consistency. Overall, the paper concludes that human-machine collaboration using NLP is promising for scalable formative assessment in large classes, though the work is primarily foundational and does not test downstream learning effects of feedback on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that NLP can support scalable scoring of short-answer formative assessment in large classes. The best model (SFRN) achieved 83% classification accuracy versus 72% for an LSTM baseline, and pairwise agreement with human raters was substantial (QWK range 0.74-0.82; four-rater Fleiss’ kappa = 0.68).
finding.measure: Classification accuracy; quadratic weighted kappa; Fleiss’ kappa

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on short-answer response scoring in introductory statistics, a discipline-specific academic task. Human raters showed substantial agreement on the correctness of student responses (QWK 0.79-0.83 among three raters; Fleiss’ kappa 0.70), and the automated scorer also aligned well with these academic response categories.
finding.measure: Scores of short-answer statistics responses (incorrect/partial/correct)

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that combines classroom response system technology with question-driven instruction, dialogical whole-class discussion, and formative assessment. The central problem is teacher change: how educators adapt to a demanding instructional approach, what kinds of tensions they encounter, and what professional development supports meaningful adoption.

The intervention is a five-year professional development and research project with approximately 39 teachers across four sites in western Massachusetts. Teachers received an intensive summer workshop, weekly or biweekly follow-up support, and were observed through multiple data sources including logs, surveys, video, interviews, journals, and PD transcripts. The paper uses four detailed teacher narratives (Tracy, Kim, Renee, Gina) to illustrate different learning trajectories and then synthesizes cross-case patterns.

The main conclusions are that TEFA is difficult for teachers to learn, but teachers can make substantial progress within a year and continue to refine their practice over time. Common growth areas included using classroom response technology, crafting better questions, facilitating richer discussion, and using formative assessment information to adjust instruction. The paper emphasizes that teacher learning is highly individualized, that effective professional development must be responsive to teachers’ contexts and evolving needs, and that formative assessment can become an integrated part of teaching even when teachers modify TEFA substantially from its original form.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is not an outcomes study of student math achievement, but it does report mathematics teachers’ growing use of TEFA and their perceptions that it helped students review for exams, surface misunderstandings, and support learning. In Gina’s case, TEFA became a daily review tool for the statewide math exam, and Kim reported that it changed how she planned and discussed mathematical ideas, but no standardized math achievement results or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported use of TEFA in mathematics instruction; formative understanding of student learning; exam review practice
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers total; mathematics subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Because TEFA was developed and studied in science classrooms as well as math classrooms, the paper substantively focuses on how teachers use question-driven instruction and dialogical discourse to develop students’ conceptual understanding and reasoning. Tracy and Renee, both science teachers, reported that TEFA helped elicit student thinking and deepen discussion, but the paper provides no direct student achievement measures or quantified effect estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher reports and classroom observations of discussion, questioning, and formative assessment in science classes
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers total; science subset not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports changes in student participation, engagement, and classroom climate as teachers adopted TEFA. For example, Kim observed that students boldly shared opinions in whole-class discussion after using a PD-developed question, and Renee reported that participation rose dramatically after changing the way histograms were shown; however, these are qualitative observations rather than measured student affect or motivation outcomes.
finding.measure: Teacher observations of student participation, engagement, and classroom atmosphere

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the development of durable teaching and learning-related skills such as metacognition, collaborative discussion, and adjusting practice based on evidence. Teachers increasingly used formative information to make real-time instructional changes, designed better questions, and fostered more student-to-student discussion; the paper reports these as observed changes across cases and video analyses, but not with numeric effect sizes.
finding.measure: Classroom video, interviews, journals, and PD records documenting teacher orchestration of discussion, question design, and use of formative feedback
finding.study_size: n=approximately 39 teachers; first-site longitudinal data and four focal cases

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly notes that TEFA increased teachers’ preparation burden and sometimes consumed valuable class time, especially for crafting good questions and conducting discussion. At the same time, teachers also reported becoming more efficient over time at using the technology and at gathering information about student thinking, suggesting a tradeoff between added workload and instructional usefulness.
finding.measure: Teacher reports of preparation time, class time use, and ease of implementing TEFA

finding.finding_summary: The study discusses implementation across schools and districts, including site recruitment, on-site PD, and the challenge of scaling TEFA in different institutional contexts. It does not evaluate policy or district-level outcomes directly, but it does conclude that the professional development model may be adaptable and that implementation feasibility depends strongly on school context and infrastructure.
finding.measure: Implementation feasibility across multiple school sites and districts

paper_profiles.title: Sentence-level Feedback Generation for English Language Learners: Does Data Augmentation Help?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the task of generating sentence-level feedback comments for English language learners, specifically for preposition errors in writing. The authors ask whether data augmentation via pseudo-data improves a T5-based feedback comment generation system. They compare a baseline T5-Large model against multi-stage and combined fine-tuning setups using in-domain pseudo data from ICNALE and out-of-domain pseudo data from W&I+LOCNESS.

The study uses learner essay data from ICNALE, a corpus of English essays written by Asian learners, with train/dev/test splits of 4,868/170/215 sentences. Pseudo data is created by automatically identifying preposition errors with ERRANT and then generating comments from the model itself. The paper evaluates systems with BLEU and shared-task human judgments. Results show that fine-tuning on pseudo data yields only small automatic gains overall, with in-domain pseudo data performing better than larger out-of-domain pseudo data, and combined fine-tuning slightly outperforming multi-stage fine-tuning.

The main conclusion is that data augmentation can help feedback comment generation, but only modestly and only when pseudo data is carefully constructed. Human evaluation suggests a somewhat larger benefit than BLEU alone, but the authors caution that the task is narrow, heavily template-driven, and limited to preposition errors on two essay topics. They therefore argue the results are useful as an early step toward better feedback generation systems, but not yet evidence of general grammatical error feedback capability.

finding.finding_summary: The system was trained and evaluated on sentence-level feedback comment generation for writing, a literacy-related task. Compared with the official baseline, T5-based models improved test BLEU by over 12 points, and the best model reached 47.25 BLEU on the test set versus 33.40 for the baseline; human evaluation F1 also improved from 31.16 to 61.90 in the best combined-fine-tuning condition (n=215 test sentences).
finding.measure: BLEU on test set; human evaluation F1 of generated feedback comments
finding.study_size: n=215 test sentences (human evaluation reported for three systems)

paper_profiles.title: Concept-based Rubrics Improve LLM Formative Assessment and Data Synthesis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether concept-based rubrics can improve large language model (LLM) performance for automated formative assessment of open-ended STEM student responses, and whether those same rubrics can help LLMs generate useful synthetic training data for lightweight supervised classifiers. The motivation is to support timely feedback in large STEM classes, where human grading is costly and slow.

The authors evaluate GPT-4o-mini and supervised PLMs across five student-response datasets spanning short-answer science, statistics, and essay-like prompts, including Beetle, SciEntsBank, ASAP-SAS, ISTUDIO, and CLASSIFIES. They compare prompting with no examples, few-shot examples, and question-specific rubrics; they also test LLM-generated synthetic training data for RoBERTa/Longformer classifiers and a small feedback study on explanatory comments.

Results show that supervised PLMs remain the strongest scorers on the original human-labeled data, but concept-based rubrics substantially boost LLM accuracy, especially on ISTUDIO and CLASSIFIES, outperforming example-based prompting by about 8–10 percentage points. The same rubric-guided prompting can generate synthetic data that, after re-annotation and diversity enhancement, trains lightweight models that approach or match LLM performance. The paper concludes that concept-based rubrics are a practical way to improve LLM-based formative assessment and to reduce reliance on expensive human training data.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates automated scoring of constructed responses in STEM/statistics tasks that require scientific/statistical reasoning. Across datasets, concept-based rubrics improved GPT-4o-mini performance on ISTUDIO by about 10 percentage points and on CLASSIFIES by about 8 percentage points compared with example-based prompting, while supervised PLMs remained strongest overall (e.g., ISTUDIO PLM-L accuracy 86.59%, GPT-4o-mini 79.63%).
finding.measure: Automated assessment accuracy and F1 on student constructed-response items in STEM/statistics tasks
finding.study_size: multiple datasets; e.g., ISTUDIO, CLASSIFIES, Beetle, SciEntsBank, ASAP-SAS; exact n varies by dataset

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is reducing the need for large human-labeled training sets by using LLMs to synthesize labels and responses for training lightweight PLMs. With diversity-enhanced synthetic data, RoBERTa-large reached performance close to GPT-4o-mini, and the authors note that approximately 3,000–4,000 synthetic samples were enough to approach that level, indicating a substantial efficiency gain in model development.
finding.measure: Classifier training performance using synthetic versus original training data; number of synthetic samples needed to reach target accuracy
finding.study_size: approximately 10,000 synthesized answers per dataset for ISTUDIO and CLASSIFIES; sensitivity analysis around 3,000–4,000 samples

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes preliminary analysis of explanatory feedback quality, finding that most LLM explanations aligned with rubrics when the LLM score matched human labels (ISTUDIO 96%, CLASSIFIES 76%). This suggests potential support for feedback that can help students interpret and improve their answers, though the study does not directly measure student learning gains.
finding.measure: Human annotation of LLM feedback explainability, preference, and subjectivity
finding.study_size: 50 partially correct samples per dataset for explainability; 50 disagreement cases per dataset for preference/subjectivity

paper_profiles.title: Disability, Job Satisfaction, and Workplace Accommodations: Evidence from the Healthcare Industry
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how disability status relates to job satisfaction, perceptions of workplace experiences, requests for accommodations, and whether accommodations moderate those relationships. The authors ask whether workers with disabilities differ from workers without disabilities in accommodation-seeking and in indicators such as turnover intentions, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, workplace inclusion, and relationships with managers and coworkers.

The study uses a novel survey of 993 employees from a large university-based healthcare system. Respondents reported disability status, disclosure to employers, prior accommodation requests, whether requests were granted, and multiple job-experience measures. The authors estimate descriptive differences and multivariable regressions with interactions between disability and accommodation disposition. The context is a healthcare employer with formal disability inclusion policies and a broad range of occupational roles.

The main finding is that workers with disabilities report substantially worse workplace experiences on many measures, especially turnover intentions, organizational support, inclusion, and manager/coworker relations, though not consistently lower overall job satisfaction. Workers with disabilities are more likely to request accommodations, but not more likely to have requests granted than workers without disabilities. When accommodations are fully granted, many disability-related gaps in work experience shrink or disappear, although turnover intentions remain higher for workers with disabilities. The paper concludes that fully granting accommodations can meaningfully reduce disability-related disparities in job experiences, even if it does not eliminate all adverse outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that workplace accommodations and disability disclosure are associated with changes in workplace experiences, and that fully granted accommodations often reduce or eliminate disability gaps in job satisfaction and related perceptions. In the regression models, disability-related disadvantages are largely attenuated when accommodation requests are granted, though turnover intentions remain higher for workers with disabilities even when accommodations are fully granted (0.096, p<0.10).
finding.measure: Job satisfaction; accommodation request status and disposition; indices of workplace experiences (organizational commitment, support, inclusion, manager/coworker relations, treatment of people with disabilities)

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies work outcomes tied to employee functioning and retention, including job satisfaction, turnover intentions, job autonomy, and workplace support. Descriptively, workers with disabilities have higher turnover intentions (0.420 vs 0.323, p<0.01), and regression results show that denied or partially granted accommodations are associated with worse job satisfaction and several negative work-experience measures.
finding.measure: Turnover intentions, job satisfaction, job autonomy, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, and related workplace-experience indices

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Curiosity Using Interactive Simulations Combined with Real-Time Formative Assessment Facilitated by Open-Format Questions on Tablet Computers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether interactive simulations combined with real-time formative assessment can stimulate and reveal student curiosity in an undergraduate engineering physics course. The authors argue that in lecture settings, curiosity is often not visible because only a few students ask questions, and they propose using open-format questions submitted through InkSurvey on tablet computers as students explore simulations.

In the study, junior-level engineering physics students used several online simulations and responded in real time to prompts such as what they observed, what the simulation illustrated, and what they were curious about. The authors then categorized the resulting questions into curiosity types: incongruous, congruous, modifying, generalizing/analogy, causal/creative, and informational. Across the four simulation activities, most questions were congruous (focused on understanding or calculating the model), with smaller proportions in other categories; the authors interpret this as evidence that students were actively engaging with the material and generating meaningful questions even without extrinsic incentives.

The paper is primarily descriptive and conceptual rather than an experimental comparison study. Its main conclusion is that real-time open-response formative assessment can surface and potentially nurture curiosity, metacognition, and deeper discussion in STEM classrooms. The authors suggest the approach may be broadly useful across science and engineering courses, but they do not report subgroup analyses by prior achievement, English learner status, or disability status.

finding.finding_summary: Students produced many curiosity-driven questions while using interactive simulations with real-time formative assessment, and the authors conclude that the approach made students appear more curious than they do in lecture. Across four activities, students submitted numerous questions even without extrinsic incentives (e.g., 68 questions from 40 students; 53 from 31 students; 35 comments from 35 students; 32 questions from 31 students), suggesting increased engagement and intrinsic motivation.
finding.measure: Student curiosity/questions submitted via open-format prompts in InkSurvey during simulation activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the activity promoted metacognition and question-generation skills, and that categorizing and discussing student questions helped students become aware of different ways to be curious. The responses also provided springboards for critical thinking and for connecting models across contexts, indicating gains in higher-order thinking practices rather than content mastery alone.
finding.measure: Categorized student questions and qualitative instructor interpretation of metacognitive/critical-thinking behavior

finding.finding_summary: Students used simulation-based prompts to ask about physical models, calculations, assumptions, and limitations, indicating engagement with scientific reasoning processes. In the four simulations, the dominant questions concerned applying and interpreting models (e.g., charge distribution, field calculations, inductance geometry, quantum state behavior), with the authors interpreting these as productive supports for understanding scientific concepts and model limits.
finding.measure: Student question categories and content during physics simulation tasks

paper_profiles.title: A Chain-of-Thought Prompting Approach with LLMs for Evaluating Students’ Formative Assessment Responses in Science
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be used to automatically score and explain middle school students’ short-answer formative assessment responses in a science curriculum. The central problem is that teachers spend substantial time grading open-ended formative assessments and providing feedback, especially in science where reasoning and explanations matter and responses are highly variable.

The authors develop a human-in-the-loop prompting pipeline for GPT-4 that combines few-shot examples, chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, and one round of active learning. The approach was tested on three middle school Earth science formative assessment questions from the SPICE curriculum, with student responses manually scored and used to build prompts. They compare zero-shot, few-shot, few-shot plus CoT, and CoT plus active learning across multiple subscores and total scores using Macro F1 and quadratic weighted kappa.

Results show that the LLM often aligned well with human scorers, and in several cases the full CoT + active learning approach achieved strong or near-perfect agreement with human scores. However, performance was uneven across subscores: CoT and active learning sometimes improved concept scoring but sometimes hurt reasoning subscores, and the authors note overfitting risks, especially on simpler items and ambiguous prompts. The paper concludes that human-in-the-loop prompting can support automated scoring and explanation for science formative assessments, but rubric clarity, prompt design, and careful balancing are critical.

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main substantive focus is on scoring middle school science formative assessments that include scientific reasoning subscores. Across the three questions and multiple prompt configurations, GPT-4 often achieved strong agreement with human scorers, with several subscores reaching QWK >= 0.90 and many reaching QWK >= 0.80; however, performance sometimes dropped when chain-of-thought prompting was added and then improved again with active learning. The results are mixed because CoT + active learning improved some reasoning subscores (e.g., Q3 Runoff Direction Reasoning QWK = 0.94) but reduced others (e.g., Q2 Arrow Direction Reasoning QWK fell to 0.30 in CoT + AL).
finding.measure: Agreement between GPT-4 and human scoring on science reasoning subscores and total scores, using Macro F1 and Cohen’s quadratic weighted kappa (QWK)
finding.study_size: n=270 students; held-out test sets by question (exact test n not separately reported)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that automated scoring and explanation can reduce the teacher workload associated with frequent formative assessment grading and feedback generation. The system was designed to support efficient scoring of open-ended responses and to provide interpretable explanations tied to rubric criteria, which the authors position as a way to make formative assessment more feasible at scale. No direct time-savings metric or workload effect size was reported, so the evidence is qualitative and design-oriented rather than a measured productivity outcome.
finding.measure: Potential teacher workload reduction and scoring efficiency from automated grading/explanation; no direct workload measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The study centers on students’ scientific reasoning and the generation of explanations that can help students understand why responses receive particular scores. The authors frame the approach as supporting students’ self-evaluation and giving actionable feedback, but they do not measure durable skills directly (e.g., metacognition, persistence, or critical thinking) with a separate instrument. Any claim here is therefore indirect: the system is intended to support reasoning-related skill development through feedback, not to empirically test those skills.
finding.measure: Scientific explanation quality and rubric-aligned feedback intended to support self-evaluation; no direct durable-skills measure reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s assessment tasks require students to interpret diagrams and answer open-ended Earth science questions, so the work also directly concerns science content understanding beyond reasoning alone. GPT-4 with CoT + active learning produced strong agreement with human scorers on several conceptual subscores, including concept-based arrow direction and arrow size items, with many QWK values in the strong-to-almost-perfect range (for example, Q3 Arrow Size QWK = 0.83 and Q2 Arrow Size QWK = 0.83 under CoT + AL). These results suggest the approach can score science conceptual knowledge accurately, though the paper is not an instructional efficacy study for content learning.
finding.measure: Agreement on science conceptual knowledge subscores (e.g., arrow direction, arrow size)
finding.study_size: n=270 students; held-out test sets by question (exact test n not separately reported)

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding in Teacher–Student Interaction: A Decade of Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews a decade of research on scaffolding in teacher–student interaction, focusing on how scaffolding has been conceptualized, how it appears in classroom practice, and whether it is effective. The authors note that scaffolding is widely used but inconsistently defined across studies, and they argue for three core characteristics: contingency, fading, and transfer of responsibility.

The review synthesizes 66 articles published between 1998 and 2009, mostly descriptive studies in primary and secondary education, with a smaller number of effectiveness studies. The reviewed work spans literacy, mathematics, science, and a few affective or motivation-related contexts, but much of the empirical evidence comes from small-scale classroom or tutoring studies. The authors propose a framework distinguishing scaffolding means (e.g., questioning, modeling, explaining) from intentions (e.g., cognitive structuring, direction maintenance, recruitment).

Overall, the review concludes that scaffolding appears effective, especially for supporting metacognitive and cognitive outcomes, but that the evidence base is limited by weak and inconsistent measurement. The authors emphasize that future research needs better instruments that capture the dynamic, interactive nature of scaffolding and that include both teacher and student behavior. The paper is primarily a conceptual and methodological review rather than a single primary empirical study.

finding.finding_summary: The review concludes that scaffolding is most fully developed and frequently studied in literacy, and the cited descriptive and effectiveness studies generally indicate beneficial effects on literacy-related tasks such as text comprehension, reading discussions, and early literacy instruction. However, the review does not report a single pooled effect size for literacy outcomes; it synthesizes multiple small studies with varied measures and designs.
finding.measure: Literacy outcomes such as text comprehension, reading/literacy performance, and literacy discussion behaviors

finding.finding_summary: Math-focused studies in the review suggest positive effects of scaffolding on problem solving and representation development. For example, in Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998), fourth- and fifth-grade students receiving contingent support solved significantly more long-division problems than peers in other conditions, though the review does not provide an effect size.
finding.measure: Math problem-solving performance, including long-division tasks and balance-scale reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several science-related effectiveness studies and reports that scaffolding generally improved students’ scientific learning and reasoning. For instance, Mercer et al. (2004) found that students in the scaffolded 'Thinking Together' condition were better able to use talk for reasoning and made greater gains on non-verbal reasoning, while Azevedo et al. (2005) found greater knowledge gains and more self-regulated learning in adaptive scaffolding conditions.
finding.measure: Science learning, reasoning, mental models, and knowledge gains in topics such as chemical equilibrium, the circulatory system, light, and sound

finding.finding_summary: The review finds positive associations between scaffolding and student engagement, motivation, enjoyment, and self-regulation, although results are somewhat mixed. Turner et al. (1998) reported that classrooms with more intrinsic support and transfer of responsibility had higher student involvement, and Azevedo et al. (2005) observed more self-regulating behaviors under adaptive scaffolding. Pratt and Savoy-Levine (1998) found no differences in enjoyment across scaffolded conditions, except that the no-support control scored lower than the other groups.
finding.measure: Student involvement, engagement, self-regulated learning behaviors, and enjoyment/motivation ratings

finding.finding_summary: A central conclusion of the review is that scaffolding supports durable skills such as metacognition, reasoning, collaboration, and transfer of responsibility. The strongest effectiveness findings in the review show gains in reasoning-together, constructive interaction, and transfer performance, with students in interactive/scaffolded conditions taking greater responsibility for learning and performing better on transfer questions.
finding.measure: Metacognitive and collaborative discourse, reasoning quality, transfer questions, and constructive student responses

paper_profiles.title: Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills
