paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This thesis examines whether the Dynamic Indicators of Basic Early Literacy Skills (DIBELS), a formative early literacy assessment, is a valid and reliable tool for assessing reading skills in special education students. The central question is whether scores from DIBELS align with scores from a more established standardized measure, the Woodcock-Johnson III (WJ III), and whether repeated ratings of DIBELS show acceptable reliability.

The study was conducted with 30 students receiving special education services at one elementary school in Fresno Unified School District. Students in grades 3–6 were administered four DIBELS subtests (Initial Sound Fluency, Letter Naming Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Nonsense Word Fluency) and two WJ III reading subtests (Letter-Word Identification and Word Attack). Two trained raters scored the DIBELS measures to examine interrater reliability.

Results showed strong interrater reliability for DIBELS and significant correlations between three of the four DIBELS subtests and the WJ III reading measures. Letter Naming Fluency, Phoneme Segmentation Fluency, and Nonsense Word Fluency were associated with WJ III scores, while Initial Sound Fluency was not consistently related to the WJ III subtests. The author concludes that DIBELS is a valid and reliable formative assessment for special education students, though Initial Sound Fluency appears weaker than the other probes.

finding.finding_summary: DIBELS showed significant concurrent validity with WJ III reading measures in a sample of special education students (n=30). Letter Naming Fluency correlated with WJ III Letter-Word Identification (r=.331, p=.074) and Word Attack (r=.455, p=.011); Phoneme Segmentation Fluency correlated with Letter-Word Identification (r=.341, p=.065) and Word Attack (r=.482, p=.007); and Nonsense Word Fluency correlated with Word Attack (r=.328, p=.077) but not Letter-Word Identification (r=-.074, p=.698). Initial Sound Fluency was weakly related to both WJ III measures (r=.071 and r=.145).
finding.measure: DIBELS subtests (ISF, LNF, PSF, NWF) compared with WJ III Letter-Word Identification and Word Attack

paper_profiles.title: The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper updates the PRISMA reporting guideline for systematic reviews. It addresses the problem that the 2009 PRISMA statement had become incomplete relative to advances in systematic review methods, terminology, registration, search methods, risk-of-bias appraisal, and evidence certainty assessment.

The work is not an evaluation of an educational intervention or AI tool; instead, it is a methodological guideline paper developed through review of existing guidance, an online survey of methodologists and journal editors, an in-person consensus meeting, and iterative drafting. The authors produced the PRISMA 2020 27-item checklist, an abstract checklist, and updated flow diagrams to improve how systematic reviews are reported.

The paper is aimed at authors, editors, peer reviewers, guideline developers, policy makers, health care providers, patients, and other stakeholders who use or produce systematic reviews. Its main conclusion is that adoption of PRISMA 2020 should improve transparency, completeness, and accuracy of systematic review reporting, but it does not present empirical effects on student outcomes or educational subgroup effects.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that PRISMA 2020 should improve the transparency, completeness, and accuracy of systematic review reporting and thereby benefit users of reviews, including guideline developers, policy makers, health care providers, patients, and other stakeholders. This is a guideline/development paper rather than an outcomes study, so no effect size or participant-level empirical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Adoption and use of reporting guideline in systematic review reporting

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment II. Indications of Effectiveness in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.venue: arXiv (companion conference paper referenced as WIPTTE 2013)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the use of InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment, across several educational settings and subject areas. The central question is whether collecting open-ended student responses on pen-enabled devices can help instructors quickly diagnose understanding, repair misconceptions, and improve learning in diverse classrooms.

The paper is a collection of seven vignettes from physics, mathematics, chemical engineering, food science, and biology courses in the United States and Mexico. Across these settings, instructors used open-format questions and digital ink responses to make student thinking visible in real time, then adjusted instruction immediately. Evidence reported includes summative assessment gains, improved quiz performance, stronger problem-solving skills, increased student participation, and favorable student/instructor perceptions.

The paper is not a controlled study of subgroup effects; rather, it synthesizes observational evidence from multiple implementations. It suggests that InkSurvey can support learning gains and engagement in varied contexts, including some indications that female students in one high school Algebra I setting showed greater gains than males, and that students of different learning styles benefited. However, the paper provides limited quantitative detail and does not directly analyze prior achievement, English learner status, or disability status.

finding.finding_summary: In a high school Algebra I setting, students using InkSurvey showed greater mastery of fundamental concepts on standards-based assessments than students not exposed to the intervention. The paper reports that female students in particular demonstrated much greater learning gains than the control group, but no effect size or sample size for the Algebra I comparison is provided.
finding.measure: Standards-based assessments of Algebra I concepts

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, chemical engineering, and related STEM contexts, InkSurvey was used to diagnose misconceptions, guide instruction, and improve understanding of concepts and problem solving. Examples include a triple-integrals misconception that persisted for only 1 of 87 students on a later exam after an InkSurvey-based lesson, improved problem-solving scores over a semester, and chemistry/chemical engineering concept understanding increasing from about 1.8 to about 3.1 on a 4-point scale when InkSurvey-guided exploration was added.
finding.measure: Summative exam questions, problem-solving strategy scores, and concept understanding ratings
finding.study_size: n=87 for one physics vignette; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In Food Chemistry and related undergraduate/graduate courses, students showed improved performance on summative quizzes after formative assessment was incorporated with InkSurvey and Tablet PCs. The paper reports mean improvements of 0.6 points in an undergraduate course and 0.5 points in a graduate course, both out of 10 possible points, compared with performance from four years earlier before the instructional revisions.
finding.measure: Summative quiz scores

finding.finding_summary: Student attitudes toward InkSurvey were generally favorable, with many students reporting increased engagement, motivation, and sense of understanding. In one anonymous survey of 63 junior-level undergraduate physics students, 54 (86%) agreed that InkSurvey helped the instructor understand what they did and did not understand, and 48 (76%) said the responses helped them better understand the material or realize what they did and did not understand.
finding.measure: Student survey responses on engagement, understanding, and metacognitive awareness

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in problem-solving, self-assessment, and metacognitive awareness associated with InkSurvey use. In one engineering physics course, scores on problem-solving skill responses improved steadily over the semester; in another survey, 76% of students said the tool helped them better understand what was covered or what they did not understand, indicating improved metacognition.
finding.measure: Problem-solving skill scores and student metacognition/self-assessment survey responses
finding.study_size: n=63 for survey; other studies not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that real-time formative assessment via InkSurvey helps instructors identify misconceptions quickly and tailor instruction immediately, improving classroom efficiency and responsiveness. Reported benefits include immediate feedback, faster detection of common difficulties, and more efficient use of class time because instructors can revise instruction before misconceptions become entrenched.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported instructional responsiveness and classroom feedback process

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the value of formative assessment in higher education and explores how it can be implemented through an e-learning platform, Blackboard Learning System. The authors argue that frequent low-stakes assessments paired with immediate, detailed feedback can support learning better than relying only on end-of-semester summative exams.

The study is based on a survey of university students at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus). Students responded to questionnaire items about continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online testing. The paper also describes a proposed implementation of weekly or fortnightly online tests with immediate feedback, including the use of Blackboard tools such as discussion forums and virtual classrooms.

Results were largely perceptual rather than achievement-based. Students generally supported formative assessment and preferred the Blackboard testing option because it provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and easier study of smaller content chunks. A statistically significant difference was found across Business, Engineering, and IT students in their views of continuous assessment and the Blackboard option, with Engineering students more strongly favoring it. The paper concludes that formative assessment, especially when delivered electronically with timely feedback, may help students stay engaged and could improve summative performance, though no direct learning gains were experimentally measured.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that frequent online formative assessments were helpful because they provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and a sense of continual progress. Survey responses indicated general support for continuous assessment and concern only that too many tests might create stress; however, no direct achievement effect was measured.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online tests (questionnaire survey)

finding.finding_summary: The paper frames formative assessment as supporting students' metacognition and self-monitoring by helping them identify strengths and weaknesses and keep track of whether they are on track. These claims are supported by student survey perceptions rather than direct skill assessments.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of self-monitoring, feedback use, and progressive learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on course-level learning in university subjects delivered through Blackboard rather than a specific content domain such as literacy or mathematics. Students preferred splitting coursework into smaller weekly assessments and believed this would help them learn subject topics progressively and perform better on semester examinations.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness of frequent internal assessments for subject learning and semester exam preparation

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical guide that reviews how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize the discussion around the classic formative assessment functions of clarifying where learners are going, determining where they are now, and helping them move forward, and they also discuss prompting techniques and the strengths/limitations of LLM-generated feedback.

The article is not an empirical intervention study; rather, it synthesizes prior work and provides illustrative prompt examples and classroom applications. It focuses on how educators can use accessible LLMs to rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate sample work, create formative questions, and produce process-level feedback. The context is broad K-12 and higher-education usage, with examples drawn from high school biology and undergraduate fMRI classes.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment formative assessment by saving teacher time and supporting scalable, adaptive feedback, but they do not replace pedagogical expertise. The authors emphasize that educators must check outputs for accuracy, align prompts to learning goals, and remain aware of risks such as over-reliance, weak evaluation metrics, and the need for AI-aware assessment design.

paper_profiles.title: Using InkSurvey with Pen-Enabled Mobile Devices for Real-Time Formative Assessment I. Applications in Diverse Educational Environments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the instructional value and broad applicability of InkSurvey, a free web-based tool for real-time formative assessment that lets students submit open-ended responses using pen-enabled mobile devices. The central problem addressed is that conventional formative assessment can be slow, cumbersome, and limited in the kinds of student thinking it reveals; InkSurvey is presented as a way to capture student reasoning instantly and allow instructors to respond immediately to misconceptions.

The paper is organized as seven classroom vignettes spanning mathematics, high school algebra, physics, biology, food chemistry, chemical engineering, and creativity-in-physics courses in the United States and Mexico. In each setting, instructors used tablets or similar devices to pose open-format questions, collect digital-ink responses, and use those responses to guide discussion, scaffold learning, and make immediate pedagogical adjustments.

The evidence presented is descriptive rather than experimental: the paper summarizes observed classroom use and instructor impressions, and explicitly notes that a companion paper contains data and conclusions about effectiveness. The main conclusion is that InkSurvey appears flexible across subjects, devices, and educational levels, and that open-ended real-time formative assessment can improve instructors' ability to diagnose misconceptions and support active learning, though this paper does not provide controlled outcome data.

finding.finding_summary: In the university honors calculus vignette (n=87 initially, 83 responding on the key item), InkSurvey was used to diagnose and then address misconceptions about setting up inequalities for triple integrals. On the first question, 32 of 83 responses showed all constant bounds; after immediate class discussion and a follow-up question, all students responded and none showed all-constant bounds, suggesting improved understanding within the session.
finding.measure: Student responses to inequality setup questions for triple integrals in calculus

finding.finding_summary: Across physics, biology, food chemistry, and chemical engineering vignettes, InkSurvey was used to elicit and refine student reasoning about scientific concepts in real time. The paper reports that open-format responses revealed misconceptions, supported immediate instructor feedback, and helped students connect ideas and repair understanding, but no standardized outcome measures or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Open-ended conceptual responses and instructor-observed misconception correction in STEM classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly reports increased student engagement, motivation to participate, and willingness to share responses when InkSurvey is used instead of or alongside clickers. In the biology vignette, for example, students were described as engaged in their learning and motivated to participate in interspersed discussions; however, these are observational descriptions rather than quantified measures.
finding.measure: Observed engagement and participation in class discussions

finding.finding_summary: InkSurvey is presented as supporting metacognition, independent thinking, and collaborative idea generation, especially in the creativity-in-physics vignette. The paper describes students generating ideas, questions, positive and negative critiques, and criteria for solutions, which the authors argue enhances metacognition and constructive collaboration, but no formal skill assessment is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognitive questioning, idea generation, and collaborative critique processes

finding.finding_summary: A major claimed benefit of InkSurvey is improved instructional efficiency: instructors can rapidly scan responses, detect misconceptions, and adjust instruction in real time rather than waiting until later or interacting with only a few students. The high school algebra vignette explicitly contrasts feedback from 25 students at once with prior practice of hearing from only 2 or 3 students, indicating more efficient collection and use of formative assessment information.
finding.measure: Instructor ability to collect, review, and act on student responses in real time

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that lowering the cost barrier of pen-enabled devices and using free software like InkSurvey can broaden access to real-time formative assessment across diverse institutions and countries. This is presented as an implementation and adoption argument across K-12, community college, private university, public engineering university, and graduate settings, not as a measured institutional outcome.
finding.measure: Cross-setting adoption and applicability across institutions

paper_profiles.title: Work from Home and Job Satisfaction: Differences by Disability Status among Healthcare Workers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether work from home (WFH) is associated with higher job satisfaction and better work experiences, and whether that association differs by disability status. The authors focus on a longstanding gap in job satisfaction and workplace experiences between workers with and without disabilities, asking whether remote work functions as a helpful accommodation or whether its benefits are unevenly distributed.

Using an original survey of 1,405 employees from a large healthcare system (analytic sample n=993), the study estimates multivariable regressions linking disability status, WFH frequency, and their interaction to job satisfaction and ten indices of workplace experience. The analysis includes direct job satisfaction, job autonomy, turnover intentions, organizational commitment, organizational citizenship behaviors, perceived organizational support, openness to differences, climate for inclusion, treatment of people with disabilities, and relations with managers and coworkers.

The main findings show that workers with disabilities reported more negative workplace experiences than workers without disabilities on most measures, though not significantly lower overall job satisfaction on the single direct item. WFH was generally associated with better job experiences for all workers, especially those working from home three or more days per week, but the positive associations were typically smaller for workers with disabilities. The authors conclude that remote work helps, but does not close disability-related gaps in workplace experiences because the gains are even larger for workers without disabilities; additional disability-targeted accommodations and efforts to reduce social isolation are needed.

finding.finding_summary: Working from home was associated with more favorable work experiences, especially higher job autonomy and lower turnover intentions. In regressions with n=993, WFH <3 days/week and 3+ days/week were positively associated with job autonomy (b=0.226 and 0.294) and job satisfaction (b=0.124 and 0.195), while 3+ days/week was associated with lower turnover intentions (b=-0.162).
finding.measure: Job autonomy, turnover intentions, and direct job satisfaction in survey/regression models

finding.finding_summary: WFH was associated with better organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, and more positive workplace attitudes, though the gains were smaller for workers with disabilities than for workers without disabilities. For example, WFH 3+ days/week was associated with higher organizational commitment (b=0.176) and perceived organizational support (b=0.253) in the full sample, and the disability interaction for organizational commitment was negative (b=-0.117), indicating attenuated benefits for disabled workers.
finding.measure: Organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, climate for inclusion, and related work-experience indices

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds a robust disability gap in workplace experiences and shows that WFH improves many outcomes for all employees but does not close those gaps. Disability gaps persisted in turnover intentions, organizational commitment, perceived organizational support, openness to differences, climate for inclusion, and relations with managers and coworkers; the disability-by-WFH interactions were often negative, meaning the benefits of WFH were smaller for workers with disabilities.
finding.measure: Regression-adjusted disability gaps and disability-by-WFH interaction effects across workplace experience indices

paper_profiles.title: Contributions from Cognitive Research to Mathematics and Science Education
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Workshop on Research in Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This invited talk argues that cognitive research can inform mathematics and science education by shifting teaching away from information transmission and toward helping students construct knowledge. The paper frames cognitive science through constructivism, emphasizing that prior knowledge, context, and active processing shape learning, and that educators need to understand how students think in order to communicate effectively and interpret their responses.

The talk synthesizes existing cognitive research rather than reporting a new empirical study. It reviews findings on misconceptions, novice–expert differences, chunking, hierarchical knowledge structures, cognitive load, metacognition, and developmental stages of expertise, drawing primarily from physics and related domains. It then translates these ideas into pedagogical guidance, such as using multiple representations, fostering interconnections among concepts, extending context to refine concepts, and using comparisons, contrasts, and multiple-pass learning to support deeper understanding.

The intended audience is educators in mathematics and science, especially those teaching at secondary and higher levels, and the paper positions classrooms as sites where cognitive models can be tested and refined. Its main conclusion is that effective teaching depends on interactive communication and on instructional designs that help learners build structured, transferable, and context-sensitive knowledge rather than merely memorize facts or procedures.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that mathematics learning is improved when instruction helps students build structured conceptual knowledge, connect representations, and revisit ideas across contexts. However, it is a conceptual synthesis rather than a new outcome study, so no effect size, sample size, or statistical estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding and problem-solving in mathematics

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes cognitive research showing that science learning is improved by addressing misconceptions, supporting expert-like qualitative analysis, and building hierarchical conceptual knowledge. It cites prior studies of novice–expert differences and problem categorization in physics, but reports no original quantitative effect in this paper.
finding.measure: Conceptual understanding, problem categorization, and problem-solving in science/physics

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that motivation, self-confidence, persistence, and expectation of success are important for progressing from novice toward proficient problem solving. It presents these as theoretically important factors in learning and expertise development, but does not provide original quantitative evidence in this paper.
finding.measure: Motivation, self-confidence, self-motivation, persistence

finding.finding_summary: The paper strongly foregrounds metacognition, reflection, self-monitoring, and expert-like qualitative analysis as central to learning and problem solving. It argues that instructional practices such as requiring students to explain reasoning and compare cases can improve students' ability to organize and use knowledge, but no new effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, reflection, qualitative analysis, concept integration

paper_profiles.title: Modernizing use of regression models in physics education research: A review of hierarchical linear modeling
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in physics education research: many studies analyze student outcomes with single-level regression models even when the data are hierarchically structured, such as students nested within courses. The authors argue that ignoring this nesting can bias coefficients, standard errors, and statistical significance, which in turn can distort conclusions about teaching practices and student learning.

The paper is primarily a review/tutorial on hierarchical linear modeling (HLM), comparing disaggregation, aggregation, and HLM conceptually and with equations. It then reanalyzes a real multi-institution dataset from 5,959 students in 112 introductory physics courses at 17 institutions, using both multiple linear regression (MLR) and HLM to predict student gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI) and compare findings about lecture, collaborative learning, and learning assistants (LAs).

The main conclusion is that HLM is the more appropriate approach for multilevel education data because it accounts for course-level clustering and yields more reliable estimates. In the reanalysis, MLR produced artificially small standard errors and overstated the benefit of collaborative learning without LAs, while HLM showed that this effect was not statistically significant. The paper’s broader recommendation is that physics education researchers should use multilevel models whenever student data are nested within courses or similar higher-level units.

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively studies student conceptual learning in introductory physics as measured by gains on the Force Concept Inventory (FCI). In the reanalysis of 5,959 students across 112 courses, HLM and MLR produced different estimates for course types: collaborative learning without LAs had a much smaller coefficient in HLM (γ02=3.26, p=0.283) than in MLR (β=12.99, p<0.001), indicating that ignoring nesting inflated the apparent effect. The unconditional HLM model also showed that course-level effects explained 13% of the variance in gains.
finding.measure: Force Concept Inventory (FCI) pretest-posttest gains / conceptual understanding

finding.finding_summary: The central contribution is methodological and institutional: the paper argues that educational research findings and policy-relevant conclusions can be biased if hierarchical data are analyzed with single-level regression instead of HLM. In the empirical reanalysis, MLR overstated differences between instructional contexts and produced standard errors about half the size of those from HLM, demonstrating that analytic choice can materially change conclusions used by instructors, administrators, and policy makers. The paper recommends broader adoption of HLM for multilevel education datasets.
finding.measure: Comparative model fit and coefficient/standard error differences between MLR and HLM in a multi-institution physics dataset

paper_profiles.title: How to define and test an Indirect Moderation model: the missing link in regression-based path models.
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a methodological problem in regression-based path models: how to distinguish a case where moderation is indirect from the more familiar model of mediated moderation. The authors argue that existing mediation-moderation frameworks focus on extending mediation, leaving a gap for situations in which an apparent moderator (Z) is only acting as a proxy for a true moderator (W).

To address this, the paper introduces an “indirect moderation” model and proposes a four-step decision tree using ordinary least squares regression to test whether moderation disappears once the true moderator is included. The paper is primarily methodological and tutorial in nature, with a simulation study evaluating Type I error, power, and model behavior across sample sizes (N=100, 250) and correlations between the proposed and true moderator.

The simulation results show that including a correlated non-moderating variable as a moderator can substantially inflate Type I error and reduce power to detect the true moderator. The authors conclude that researchers should consider possible confounding moderators in addition to covariates, and that indirect moderation and mediated moderation are statistically and conceptually distinct models that can answer different research questions.

paper_profiles.title: Inquiry-Based Mathematics Education: a call for reform in tertiary education seems unjustified
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a critical scoping review of the inquiry-based mathematics education (IBME/IBL) movement in tertiary education. The authors ask whether minimally guided, inquiry-based approaches should replace more explicit instruction in undergraduate mathematics, and whether the common arguments for IBME—better learning, deeper conceptual understanding, and improved equity—are supported by evidence.

Rather than reporting a new experiment, the paper synthesizes prior findings from cognitive science, educational psychology, and mathematics education. It argues that novices generally learn novel mathematics better with explicit instruction, worked examples, explanations, and guidance than with unassisted discovery or pure inquiry. The paper also discusses a small number of experimental studies and meta-analyses, including Alfieri et al. (2011), Klahr and Nigam, and other work on explanation quality and transfer, to support the claim that direct instruction tends to outperform discovery learning on learning and transfer outcomes.

The review focuses on undergraduate mathematics contexts, though it draws heavily on broader evidence from schooling and other domains. Its main conclusion is that the case for a wholesale reform toward IBME in tertiary mathematics is not justified by the empirical literature. The authors further argue that claims that inquiry-based classrooms are inherently better for equity are not supported by the evidence reviewed.

finding.finding_summary: Across the evidence reviewed, unassisted discovery/inquiry learning in mathematics was consistently less effective than explicit instruction for novice learners. The paper cites a meta-analysis of 108 studies (580 comparisons) showing a mean effect of d = -0.38 (95% CI [-0.50, -0.25]) favoring explicit teaching over unassisted discovery, and reports additional studies where explanation-based instruction improved application and transfer.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes in mathematics instruction, including application and transfer tests
finding.study_size: n=108 studies / 580 comparisons (meta-analysis); also n=80 and n=129 in cited experiments

finding.finding_summary: The review discusses an experiment on the control-of-variables strategy (CVS), a core scientific reasoning skill. In the cited randomized study (N = 112), direct instruction produced far more CVS masters than discovery learning (77% vs 23%); the advantage held for low-performing students as well (69% vs 15% among low initial scorers).
finding.measure: Mastery of the control-of-variables strategy; transfer task evaluating science-fair posters

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally argues that explicit instruction better supports cognitively demanding learning processes such as generating, organizing, and integrating schemas, which it frames as the basis of conceptual understanding and transfer. It cites studies where principle-oriented explanations outperformed procedure-oriented explanations on application and transfer, implying better learning-related metacognitive processing and deeper understanding than minimally guided discovery.
finding.measure: Transfer tests and application tests as proxies for conceptual understanding and deep processing
finding.study_size: n=80; n=129 in cited experiments; plus meta-analysis of 108 studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates the broader reform claim that tertiary mathematics should shift toward inquiry-based instruction and concludes that a major institutional reform agenda is not justified by the evidence. It also states that the general claim that IBME helps address equity issues in mathematics classrooms is not supported by the reviewed literature.
finding.measure: Evidence-based assessment of the IBME reform agenda and equity claims

paper_profiles.title: Dynamic Models of Learning and Education Measurement
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a foundational question in education measurement: why normalized gain on pre/post tests often appears uncorrelated with students’ pretest scores, and what that statistic actually captures. Using physics education as the context, the author develops a probabilistic dynamic model of learning in which student score change is generated by three types of transitions: α-processes (instruction acting on incorrect or missing knowledge), β-processes (instruction acting on already-correct knowledge), and γ-processes (associative interactions between correct and incorrect knowledge).

The paper is primarily theoretical, but it uses published physics education data as illustrative evidence. It argues that when learning is dominated by α-processes and α is unrelated to pretest score, normalized gain will not correlate with pretest score; when γ-processes or non-constant α are important, gain should correlate positively with pretest score. The author also discusses how random measurement error can induce negative correlations and how data patterns may differ for high-ability versus lower-ability student groups, using examples from conceptual physics testing such as the FCI and CSE.

The population of interest is students in college-level, calculus-based physics courses, with comparisons across different university populations including honor students and high-achieving groups. The paper’s main conclusion is that normalized gain can be interpreted as an estimate of instructional/learning effectiveness under specific assumptions, but its relationship to prior achievement depends on the learning process and population composition. It does not evaluate an AI intervention or a formative assessment program; rather, it proposes a measurement framework for interpreting pre/post learning data and subgroup differences.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on modeling student learning and interpreting normalized gain in physics concept inventories, especially the FCI and CSE, which are measures of scientific/physics reasoning and conceptual understanding. It argues that normalized gain is positively related to learning effectiveness (α, β, γ coefficients) and may correlate with prior scientific reasoning ability, but the relationship depends on whether learning is α-dominant or γ-dominant and on population characteristics; no new experimental effect size is reported in this theoretical paper.
finding.measure: Physics concept inventory pre/post scores and normalized gain; examples include the Force Concept Inventory (FCI), Conceptual Survey in Electricity (CSE), and Lawson Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning

paper_profiles.title: Are Educational Escape Rooms More Effective Than Traditional Lectures for Teaching Software Engineering? A Randomized Controlled Trial
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a virtual educational escape room is more effective than a traditional lecture for teaching software engineering content, specifically software modeling with UML diagrams. The authors position the study as addressing a gap in the escape-room literature, which has had relatively little randomized evidence and few direct comparisons with conventional teaching.

The intervention was a fully virtual escape room delivered face-to-face through the Escapp web platform, compared against a traditional lecture covering the same software modeling material. The study used a cluster randomized controlled trial with 326 second-year undergraduate software engineering students at Universidad Politécnica de Madrid: 164 in the escape-room group and 162 in the lecture group. Students completed a pretest, the assigned activity, and then a post-test; students in the escape-room condition also completed a perceptions questionnaire.

Results showed significant learning gains in both groups, but the escape-room group outperformed the lecture group on post-test knowledge acquisition after controlling for pretest scores (ANCOVA, p < 0.001, r = 0.25). Students in the escape-room condition reported very positive perceptions, including strong enjoyment, engagement, usability of the platform, and preference for the escape room over traditional lectures. The paper concludes that educational escape rooms can improve software modeling learning and are well received by students, while noting that findings are limited to this topic and immediate post-intervention outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: Students who learned software modeling through the educational escape room significantly outperformed those in the traditional lecture condition on the post-test after adjusting for pretest scores. The ANCOVA comparison was statistically significant (p < 0.001) with a small-to-medium effect (r = 0.25) in favor of the escape room, indicating better knowledge acquisition in the intervention group.
finding.measure: Software modeling knowledge test (10-item multiple-choice pretest/post-test on UML use case, class, sequence, activity, and state machine diagrams)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported very positive perceptions of the escape-room activity, including strong enjoyment, immersion, acceptance, and preference over a traditional lecture. The questionnaire (n=164 in the experimental group) showed high ratings for overall opinion, recommendation, perceived learning, and platform usability; internal consistency was good (Cronbach’s α=0.80).
finding.measure: Perceptions questionnaire with closed-ended and Likert items on enjoyment, acceptance, perceived learning, and platform usability

finding.finding_summary: The escape room was designed to require team-based problem solving and collaboration, and the authors argue that this format supports soft skills such as communication, teamwork, and leadership. However, these skills were not directly measured; the evidence is indirect and based on the team-based structure and students’ positive perceptions rather than a specific collaboration outcome measure.
finding.measure: Team-based participation and student perceptions of the activity

paper_profiles.title: Complexity in Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual chapter; no empirical sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This encyclopedia chapter surveys the role of complexity theory in mathematics education. It argues that complexity has become influential in the field as an epistemological lens for understanding learning as nested, adaptive, and emergent; as an historical discourse connecting mathematics education to the development of dynamical systems and computational modeling; as a disciplinary discourse motivating the inclusion of nonlinear, computational, and agent-based modeling content in school mathematics; and as a pragmatic discourse offering guidance for classroom organization and pedagogy.

The chapter does not report a single empirical study or intervention. Instead, it synthesizes scholarship on complexity, including radical constructivist, sociocultural, embodied, and critical theories, and draws on examples such as participatory simulations, agent-based modeling, and computational modeling in K–12 mathematics and science. Its main conclusion is that complexity-oriented approaches can support richer mathematical understanding, interdisciplinary connections, and classroom environments that foster collaboration, emergent insight, and more authentic engagement with contemporary mathematics.

Because the piece is conceptual and review-like rather than empirical, it does not provide direct effect estimates or participant-level results. Its primary contribution is theoretical: it reframes mathematics education as an area where complex adaptive systems thinking can inform curriculum, pedagogy, and the design of learning environments.

paper_profiles.title: The Analysis of Summative Assessment and Formative Assessment and Their Roles in College English Assessment System
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Language Teaching and Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the roles of summative and formative assessment in college English teaching, with a particular focus on distinguishing their functions and arguing for a combined assessment system. The authors frame assessment as a decision-making process that should support both evaluation of outcomes and improvement of teaching and learning. They contrast standardized, end-of-term tests with classroom-based formative practices, emphasizing that a single assessment mode cannot capture students’ real English proficiency.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and practice-based discussion grounded in the authors’ teaching experience in Chinese universities. It describes common summative measures such as final examinations and multiple-choice tests, and formative practices such as drama performance, student interviews, and feedback. The context is college English instruction for university students in China, including learners with varied backgrounds and English use profiles.

The main conclusion is that summative assessment remains necessary for efficient, reliable overview of student learning, but it is insufficient on its own because it underrepresents speaking ability, critical thinking, and individual differences. Formative assessment is presented as a complementary approach that can diagnose learning problems, motivate students, support self-assessment, and provide richer feedback for instruction. The paper argues that the best practice is to combine the two approaches to achieve a more comprehensive and fair evaluation of student English learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that summative assessment captures some aspects of English proficiency well, but does not adequately measure real communicative ability, especially speaking. In the authors' classroom observations, some students with high paper-and-pencil test scores had poor speaking participation, while others with better speaking ability scored lower on written tests; no quantitative effect size is reported.
finding.measure: English proficiency assessments, especially speaking ability, classroom participation, and paper-and-pencil test performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims formative assessment can increase motivation, confidence, and students' willingness to improve by providing encouragement and supportive feedback. These claims are based on classroom experience rather than quantified outcomes; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, confidence, and response to feedback in classroom formative assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that formative assessment activities such as drama performance and interviewing encourage critical thinking, cooperation, reflection, and problem solving. The paper provides descriptive examples of these processes but no experimental or statistical evidence; no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, collaboration, reflection, problem solving, and self-assessment during formative assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: In the context of college English learning, the paper states that formative assessment can better capture students' overall language use and supports a more comprehensive evaluation of English achievement than summative tests alone. The evidence is illustrative and practice-based rather than empirical; no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Overall college English achievement / English level as assessed through a combined assessment system

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims summative assessments such as multiple-choice tests are efficient to administer and score, reducing teacher bias and saving time through machine grading. It also suggests formative assessment provides useful diagnostic information for adjusting instruction, but no quantitative workload or productivity data are reported.
finding.measure: Assessment efficiency, grading speed, and instructional feedback utility

paper_profiles.title: The Relationship between Formative Assessment and Summative Assessment in Primary Grade Mathematics Classrooms
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether an internet-based formative assessment in primary-grade mathematics is related to student performance on a state summative mathematics assessment. The authors also ask whether this relationship differs by grade level and by average classroom achievement, with a focus on number sense concepts such as counting and decomposing numbers.

The study used data from 77 teachers in one southeastern U.S. school district who had completed an 80-hour professional development program on formative assessment and number sense. Two groups of classrooms used different AMC Anywhere formative assessment components: hiding (Grade 1 and Grade 2; n=258 students) and counting (Kindergarten and Grade 1; n=471 students). The summative assessment was a state-developed measure aligned to grade-level mathematics content. Analyses included Pearson correlations, MANOVA, and two-level hierarchical linear modeling.

Results showed positive relationships between formative assessment scores and summative assessment scores in both assessment strands. The association was stronger in classrooms with lower average performance for the hiding assessment, suggesting formative assessment may be particularly useful for lower-achieving classrooms. For the counting assessment, the formative-summative relationship was stronger in first grade than in kindergarten. Overall, the paper argues that formative assessment can provide useful evidence of student learning and may have greater value in classrooms where students are struggling, while also noting that the observed relationships may reflect alignment between the formative and summative measures rather than causal effects.

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment scores on AMC Anywhere were positively associated with state summative mathematics scores. For the hiding assessment, the zero-order correlation with summative scores was r=.44 (p<.01; n=258), and for the counting assessment it was r=.29 (p<.01; n=471). In multilevel models, a one-unit increase in individual formative score predicted a 0.17-point increase in summative score for hiding and a 0.21-point increase for counting, with classroom achievement also positively related to summative performance (b=.81 and b=.43, respectively).
finding.measure: Mathematics formative assessment scores (AMC Anywhere hiding/counting) and state summative mathematics assessment scores

paper_profiles.title: Positive Impact of Utilizing More Formative Assessment over Summative Assessment in the EFL/ESL Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary: This paper discusses the role of assessment in EFL/ESL classrooms and argues that formative assessment is preferable to relying primarily on summative assessment. The author frames assessment as a broader process that includes testing, observing, judging, and making decisions, and contrasts formal/summative practices with informal/formative practices. A central concern is that students often experience summative assessment as punitive and delayed, while formative assessment can provide timely feedback that supports learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that greater use of formative assessment supports students’ oral language development and confidence in using a second/foreign language. The main basis for this claim is qualitative/theoretical synthesis rather than a new empirical comparison; no study sample or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Oral language use, language fluency, and confidence in using the target language

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that formative assessment improves students’ motivation, confidence, and willingness to use the target language because of timely constructive feedback. No direct quantitative measurement is reported in the paper, and no sample size or effect estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Student confidence, motivation, and perceptions of feedback/assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that summative assessment is more convenient for teachers to score and report, whereas formative assessment requires more effort and training. It does not report empirical workload data, but it does substantively discuss teacher practice implications and the relative practicality of the two approaches.
finding.measure: Teacher scoring/reporting convenience and instructional workload

paper_profiles.title: Formative vs. summative assessment: impacts on academic motivation, attitude toward learning, test anxiety, and self-regulation skill
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether formative assessment or summative assessment has greater effects on Iranian EFL learners’ academic motivation, attitude toward learning, test anxiety, and self-regulation skill. The authors frame the work around the distinction between assessment used primarily to measure learning versus assessment used to support ongoing learning through feedback.

The study used 72 intermediate male Iranian EFL learners from a language institute in Ahvaz, Iran. Participants were assigned to a formative-assessment group, a summative-assessment group, or a control group. After pretesting, the formative group received instruction with self/peer assessment and detailed feedback, the summative group received midterm and final exams with limited feedback, and the control group received instruction without preplanned assessment. The treatment lasted 15 sessions within a 23-session study period.

Results from one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni tests showed that both formative and summative assessment improved outcomes relative to the control group, but formative assessment produced the strongest gains in test anxiety, motivation, and self-regulation. The attitude questionnaire also indicated positive attitudes toward both assessment approaches. Overall, the paper concludes that formative assessment is more effective than summative assessment for these psychosocial outcomes in EFL instruction.

finding.finding_summary: Both formative and summative assessment improved academic motivation compared with the control group, but the formative group improved more. On the motivation post-test, the formative group (M=127.83, n=24) outperformed the summative group (M=115.79, n=24) and control group (M=92.87, n=24); ANOVA showed a significant group effect (F=29.12, p=.00).
finding.measure: Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB) motivation scores

finding.finding_summary: Test anxiety decreased more under formative assessment than summative assessment or no assessment. Post-test means were 49.50 for the formative group, 37.91 for the summative group, and 29.95 for control (n=24 each), with a significant group effect (F=20.02, p=.00). Bonferroni comparisons showed the formative group scored significantly better than both the summative group (mean difference=11.58) and control group (mean difference=19.54).
finding.measure: Test anxiety scores from the adapted Science Anxiety Scale (SAS)

finding.finding_summary: Self-regulation skill improved substantially in both assessment groups, with the formative group showing the largest gains. Post-test means were 147.25 for formative, 130.04 for summative, and 80.12 for control (n=24 each); the group difference was significant (F=76.60, p=.00). Bonferroni tests indicated the formative group outperformed the summative group by 17.20 points and the control group by 67.12 points.
finding.measure: Self-Regulatory Strategies Scale (SRSS) scores

finding.finding_summary: Students reported positive attitudes toward the effectiveness of both formative and summative assessment. The one-sample t-test on the attitude questionnaire was significant (t=63.72, df=16, p<.001), with a mean difference of 4.52 above the test value.
finding.measure: Researcher-developed attitude questionnaire about formative and summative assessment

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors frame formative assessment as diagnostic assessment used during instruction to give students and teachers feedback, contrasting it with summative assessment that occurs after instruction. They argue that formative assessment should be integrated with, rather than opposed to, summative assessment, and that it may help students perform better on end-of-semester exams.

The proposed implementation involves weekly or fortnightly Blackboard online tests, including multiple-choice and true/false items, with immediate scoring and detailed feedback after each attempt. The paper describes features such as randomized questions, open-book possibilities, and use of Blackboard discussion/forum tools to extend feedback. The context is Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus), where Blackboard was used to deliver lecture materials and online assessments.

Empirically, the paper reports a student survey (16-item questionnaire) on continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported frequent small assessments and valued immediate teacher feedback, convenience, and the ability to study topic by topic. The authors conclude that e-learning-supported formative assessment can promote ongoing learning, help students identify strengths and weaknesses, and potentially improve summative performance, though they also note concerns about pressure from too many tests.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that the proposed frequent Blackboard-based formative assessments were supportive of ongoing learning and helped them stay engaged with the subject throughout the semester. The most valued features were immediate feedback and the sense that learning occurs in steps rather than only for final exams, although some students also reported stress/pressure from too many tests.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire on perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online tests

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that frequent formative assessments supported metacognitive processes by helping students check whether they were on track, identify strengths and weaknesses, and reflect on mistakes using immediate detailed feedback. Students also felt the approach helped them learn individual topics progressively, which the authors interpret as supporting self-monitoring and learning how to learn.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback usefulness, self-checking, and progressive topic learning

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports positive student perceptions of frequent internal assessments delivered as Blackboard online tests, with students favoring small-topic, weekly or fortnightly assessments over classroom tests because they made studying easier and provided immediate feedback. The authors argue that this formative approach may improve learning across the course and help prepare students for summative semester examinations, but no direct achievement outcome is measured in the paper.
finding.measure: Student questionnaire on acceptance of frequent internal assessments and Blackboard test option

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review and practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback in education. The authors frame formative assessment using an established pedagogical model: clarifying where learners are going, where learners currently are, and how to move them forward. They argue that many current AI-for-education applications do not sufficiently align with these core formative principles, and that evaluation metrics often miss distinctions among task-level, process-level, and self-regulatory feedback.

Rather than testing a single intervention empirically, the paper surveys and synthesizes ways LLMs might be used for student-friendly learning objectives, co-constructing success criteria, generating exemplars or sample work, automating question generation, and producing feedback. It includes prompt examples, classroom-oriented suggestions, and cautionary notes about limitations such as output variability, over-reliance on AI, and the need for educator judgment and domain expertise.

The intended users are primarily educators and researchers, with examples spanning classroom teaching, lesson planning, and assessment design. The paper concludes that LLMs can augment, but not replace, expert pedagogy, and that future work should develop more formative-assessment-sensitive benchmarks and AI-aware assessment strategies that support deeper learning and transferable skills.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by accelerating tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating exemplars, creating questions, and drafting feedback. However, this is presented as a conceptual/practical claim rather than an empirically tested effect, and no effect size or study sample is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time-saving potential in formative assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes that AI-supported formative assessment can foster student self-regulation, metacognition, and critical thinking, especially when learners use exemplars, co-construct success criteria, and critique AI-generated outputs. These are presented as pedagogical benefits supported by cited prior work and examples, not new empirical results from this paper.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, metacognition, critical thinking, and reflection in formative-assessment activities

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM support for academic writing-related tasks, especially generating student-friendly learning objectives and sample method sections, and simplifying complex syllabus language. The examples are intended to improve clarity and understanding of academic tasks, but the paper does not report original empirical outcomes for writing performance.
finding.measure: Writing-related academic task support and objective clarity

paper_profiles.title: Computing with CodeRunner at Coventry University: Automated summative assessment of Python and C++ code
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes Coventry University’s use of CodeRunner, an open-source Moodle plugin that automatically marks student programming code, for summative assessment in first-year undergraduate computer science modules. The authors frame the need for CodeRunner as arising from large cohort sizes, limited staff capacity, and a desire for a more authentic assessment of programming ability than multiple-choice quizzes or written exams could provide.

The intervention is not a controlled experiment but a practice report of implementing CodeRunner in two first-year modules: one teaching Python 3 and another translating programming knowledge to C++14. The system allows students to submit code through Moodle, run it against unit tests, and receive partial credit, syntax feedback, and limited retry opportunities; for C++ it additionally uses introspection techniques to award partial marks when compilation would otherwise fail on minor errors.

The paper reports institutional outcomes after adoption, including lower average marks and pass rates than the multiple-choice tests CodeRunner replaced, alongside higher written-exam performance in one module and improved student satisfaction in the Python module. The authors argue that the lower marks likely reflect more valid assessment of programming competence rather than worse learning, and conclude that CodeRunner is a promising approach for authentic, scalable summative assessment, especially when paired with mechanisms that better support partial credit in compiled languages.

finding.finding_summary: CodeRunner was adopted to make large-cohort mid-term programming assessment feasible under tight feedback deadlines and staffing constraints. The paper reports that the tool enabled auto-marked summative tests for about 280 first-year students, reducing reliance on hand-marking while preserving exam integrity and allowing partial automation of feedback and marking.
finding.measure: Instructor workflow and feasibility of automated summative assessment in large classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports institutional-level changes in assessment practice: CodeRunner replaced prior multiple-choice mid-term tests in two first-year modules and was used within Moodle under university summative-assessment regulations. The authors also note that it altered assessment policy and implementation, including exam-board-approved retrospective application of C++ partial-credit scoring.
finding.measure: Assessment policy/practice change and institutional adoption of CodeRunner in degree modules

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how formative assessment is defined, why it matters in undergraduate engineering education, and how technology has changed its classroom use. The authors argue that formative assessment is often used loosely in the literature and narrow the definition to in-class, embedded activities that provide immediate feedback to both students and instructors for adjusting instruction.

The paper is primarily a conceptual/practice-oriented discussion rather than an experimental study. It reviews the role of embedded formative assessment in engineering classrooms, emphasizing sociocultural and constructivist rationales, the importance of instructor response, and the limitations of multiple-choice clicker use when the goal is to reveal student thinking. The authors then argue for open-format questions, which can elicit richer evidence of reasoning and misconceptions, and illustrate their use with examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course (about 60 third-year engineering physics majors) using Tablet PCs and InkSurvey.

The main conclusion is that technology-facilitated formative assessment can reduce clerical burden and support real-time feedback, but its instructional value depends on how well questions surface thinking and how responsively instructors use the information. The paper does not report a controlled evaluation of outcomes; instead, it makes a case that open-format, embedded formative assessment is likely to better support active learning, metacognition, and conceptual understanding than using technology solely for attendance or simple polling.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment, especially open-format questioning, can support conceptual understanding in undergraduate engineering by making student thinking visible and prompting refinement of understanding. In the illustrated electromagnetics example (n=60), student responses showed misunderstandings about Gauss’s law, limits, symmetry, and dot products, which the instructor used to diagnose and address misconceptions, but no controlled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Student written responses to open-format formative assessment questions in an undergraduate electromagnetics course; conceptual understanding of Gauss's law and electric field reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly claims that formative assessment increases student metacognition and supports critical thinking by helping students recognize what they know and do not know. In the course example, open-format questions revealed gaps in reasoning and shortcuts in problem solving, suggesting the approach can strengthen reflective and analytical habits, but no quantitative effect estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Metacognition, critical thinking, and quality of problem-solving reasoning observed in student responses

finding.finding_summary: A central claim is that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by streamlining the collection and analysis of student responses. The paper does not provide a formal productivity measure, but describes clickers, mobile polling, and InkSurvey as enabling real-time feedback and easier classroom implementation compared with manual methods.
finding.measure: Instructor clerical burden / efficiency of collecting and viewing student responses

paper_profiles.title: Efficacy of a hybrid take home and in class summative assessment for the postsecondary physics classroom
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a hybrid assessment format can improve the accuracy and student experience of summative testing in an introductory college physics course. The authors argue that conventional in-class exams can be confounded by test anxiety, which may depress grades and obscure what students actually know. They propose a hybrid take-home/in-class exam intended to preserve academic integrity while reducing anxiety and better capturing mastery.

The study was conducted in three sections of Physics II: Introduction to Electricity and Magnetism at Lafayette College during fall 2022. One cohort (n=31) took traditional in-class exams, while another cohort (n=59) received hybrid exams: the questions were released one week in advance, but students completed the final written exam in class without calculators or outside resources. After each of the second, third, and final exams, students completed surveys about stress, preparation, and perceived mastery. The analysis compared control and experimental groups using ordinal survey responses and nonparametric tests.

Results suggest that the hybrid format reduced reported stress during the exam and increased self-reported mastery of physics. The experimental cohort reported that completing the exam was less stressful than a typical exam in other classes (p=0.019) and agreed more strongly that both preparing for and completing the exam increased their mastery of physics topics (p=0.031 and p=0.035, respectively). The authors conclude that hybrid take-home/in-class exams may be a promising alternative to traditional summative assessments in introductory physics, though the study is limited by small sample sizes, self-reported outcomes, and possible response bias toward higher-performing students.

finding.finding_summary: The hybrid exam format reduced perceived test stress during the exam and did not significantly increase stress during preparation. Students in the experimental cohort rated completing the exam as less stressful than a typical exam in other classes (Q10 mean 2.41 vs 3.05 in control; pMW=0.019), while preparation stress was similar across groups (Q7 mean 3.44 vs 3.63; pMW=0.492).
finding.measure: Student self-reported stress on 1-5 Likert survey items about preparation and exam completion
finding.study_size: n=90 surveyed students total (control n=31, experimental n=59); response rates 44% and 36%
finding.effect_size: rMW≈0.236 for Q10; rMW≈0.071 for Q7
finding.std_deviation: Q7: 1.22 control, 1.28 experimental; Q10: 1.24 control, 1.31 experimental

finding.finding_summary: Students in the hybrid cohort reported greater perceived mastery from both preparing for and completing the exam. For Q14, the experimental group agreed more strongly that preparation increased mastery (mean 4.07 vs 3.61; pMW=0.031), and for Q15 they also reported higher mastery gains from completing the exam (mean 3.00 vs 2.41; pMW=0.035).
finding.measure: Student self-reported mastery of physics topics on 1-5 Likert survey items
finding.study_size: n=90 surveyed students total (control n=31, experimental n=59)
finding.effect_size: rMW≈0.224 for Q14; rMW≈0.214 for Q15
finding.std_deviation: Q14: 1.05 control, 0.98 experimental; Q15: 1.30 control, 1.25 experimental

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centered on assessment of physics knowledge and whether the hybrid test better captures student understanding. Students in the experimental cohort more strongly agreed that their exam performance represented their knowledge of the subject matter (Q11 mean 3.48 vs 2.98; rMW=0.191, pMW=0.061), but this result was not statistically significant at the 0.05 level and is reported as suggestive rather than conclusive.
finding.measure: Self-reported representativeness of exam performance for subject-matter knowledge; physics exam context
finding.study_size: n=90 surveyed students total (control n=31, experimental n=59)

paper_profiles.title: COMPARE: A Taxonomy and Dataset of Comparison Discussions in Peer Reviews
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatically identifying and classifying comparison-related discussion in peer reviews of machine learning papers. The authors argue that meaningful comparison with prior work is a key factor in research quality and paper acceptance, yet existing peer-review datasets and analyses do not exhaustively capture the different ways reviewers discuss comparisons. To support this, they propose COMPARE, a taxonomy of comparison discussions with four high-level aspects—dataset, baseline, task, and metric—and 13 subcategories.

The approach studied is a manually curated dataset of 117 peer reviews from ICLR papers submitted between 2017 and 2020, containing about 1,800 sentences labeled as comparison or non-comparison and further annotated with fine-grained comparison categories. The paper also evaluates several sentence-encoding and traditional machine-learning classifiers, including USE, BERT, SciBERT, and two RoBERTa variants pretrained on scientific abstracts and peer reviews. The best reported performance for comparison-sentence classification is F1 = 0.49 using MLRoBERTa with chunk representations. Results suggest that chunk-based representations generally outperform full-sentence representations, but performance remains limited due to the small and imbalanced dataset.

The main conclusion is that comparison discussions in peer reviews are structured but diverse, and a taxonomy can help characterize whether a paper meaningfully compares itself against datasets, baselines, tasks, and evaluation metrics. The authors suggest the dataset and models could support reviewer assistance and downstream systems that summarize or generate comparison-oriented feedback, but the paper itself is primarily a dataset/taxonomy and classification study rather than an educational intervention study.

paper_profiles.title: Student’s Video Production as Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: ICPE 2013 – International Conference on Physics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether student-produced videos can serve as a reliable formative assessment tool in high school physics, and how such videos compare to more traditional assessments. The authors argue that video production can reveal students’ understanding, misunderstandings, and reasoning in ways that tests and questionnaires often do not, while also capturing broader skills such as cooperation, planning, and persistence.

The approach studied was an extra-class activity in which high school students in Rio de Janeiro worked in groups of up to five to produce short videos on physics topics covered during the term. Students also submitted a brief written explanation of what they made and the physics involved. Teachers then reviewed the videos and texts, discussed them in class, and analyzed the products across categories including physical correctness, clarity, technical format, coherence, and the relationship between production quality and conceptual quality.

The paper reports descriptive results from 55 videos produced by 232 students in 2011. Most videos were at least partially correct, and the authors claim the activity exposed misconceptions and learning difficulties that would be hard to detect in conventional assessments. They conclude that student video production is a useful and reliable formative assessment approach in physics, with an observed correlation between technical quality and conceptual quality, though the paper does not present inferential statistics or a comparison group.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that student-produced videos often revealed whether students understood physics concepts correctly, with 35% of videos judged correct and 45% partially correct. Teachers could identify misconceptions and reasoning problems in topics such as elementary dynamics, and the authors argue the activity helped diagnose learning while it was still possible to adjust instruction.
finding.measure: Teacher analysis of video physics content for correctness, clarity, and conceptual reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper explicitly frames video production as requiring and revealing durable skills such as planning, replanning, collaborative work, and metacognitive regulation. The authors note that students often chose technically more demanding production forms and that this reflected careful planning and implementation, although no standardized skill measure was used.
finding.measure: Analysis of collaboration, planning, and metacognitive characteristics inferred from video production process and products

finding.finding_summary: Because the content area is physics, the paper substantively focuses on academic learning in a non-literacy/non-numeracy domain. Across the sample, 75% of videos had a satisfactory connection between the proposal and the product, and 87% showed a logical sequence, suggesting the task supported learning and presentation of physics content.
finding.measure: Teacher ratings of physics video products for connection to task, logical sequence, and conceptual correctness

paper_profiles.title: Foundations for AI-Assisted Formative Assessment Feedback for Short-Answer Tasks in Large-Enrollment Classes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how natural language processing (NLP) can support formative assessment for short-answer tasks in large-enrollment introductory statistics courses. The authors frame the problem as a scalability challenge: short-answer, write-to-learn activities can better reveal student thinking than selected-response items, but they are difficult for instructors to score and provide feedback on quickly when class sizes are large.

Using de-identified responses from 1,935 post-secondary students across six short-answer tasks, the study first evaluates agreement among four trained human raters scoring responses with a detailed rubric. It then compares two automated scoring approaches, including a semantic feature-wise transformation relation network (SFRN), against human ratings, and finally explores whether learned text representations can be clustered to support scalable formative feedback. The main results show substantial human-human reliability (pairwise QWK > 0.74; Fleiss’ kappa around 0.68–0.70), strong human-machine agreement for SFRN (pairwise QWK 0.74–0.82; four-way Fleiss’ kappa 0.68), and promising clustering behavior, especially with lower-dimensional static representations. The study concludes that AI-assisted short-answer scoring and clustering could help instructors provide timely formative feedback at scale, though further work is needed to turn these tools into effective feedback workflows.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that NLP-assisted scoring can support scalable formative assessment in large classes by reducing the burden of manually evaluating short-answer responses. The SFRN algorithm achieved 83% classification accuracy and substantial agreement with human raters (pairwise QWK 0.74–0.82; four-way Fleiss’ kappa = 0.68) on 653 test responses, suggesting the approach could make feedback more efficient at scale.
finding.measure: Algorithm classification accuracy; inter-rater agreement (quadratic weighted kappa, Fleiss’ kappa) for short-answer scoring
finding.study_size: n=1,935 students; 7,258 unique task-responses; test set n=653

paper_profiles.title: Teaching Predictive Control Using Specification-based Summative Assessments
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and evolution of a predictive control course taught at Imperial College London from 2018 to 2021, with a particular focus on how student learning in model predictive control (MPC) was assessed. The authors argue that traditional written or exam-based summative assessment was not well suited to evaluating whether students could design robust MPC controllers, so they developed a specification-based assessment framework in MATLAB/Simulink.
