The course served Masters-level students (MSc and final-year MEng) and combined lectures, laboratory activities, checkpointing assignments, and two larger controller-design assessments. The assessments asked students to design controllers for an overhead gantry crane under a range of constraints and obstacle configurations, using either linear MPC, nonlinear MPC, or custom implementations. The paper also compares how the course and assessment changed across years, including the shift from linear to nonlinear MPC and from in-person to virtual laboratories during COVID-19.

The main contribution is a detailed account of the assessment framework and lessons learned from several years of use. The authors report that the specification-based format gave students substantial freedom and produced diverse controller designs, but also created challenges: ambiguous specifications led to loopholes, and automated marking required extensive error handling for student code. Overall, the paper concludes that specification-based summative assessment can better capture applied MPC understanding and robustness than a conventional written exam, but the assessment specifications must be very carefully written and the grading infrastructure must be robust.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that the MATLAB/Simulink and MATLAB Grader-based framework automated the assessment of controller designs across more than 30 test cases, reducing reliance on a traditional written exam and enabling scalable marking of student submissions. The framework also generated individual reports with trajectories and specification violations, streamlining feedback and grading, although the authors note that substantial error handling was needed to keep the automated system running reliably.
finding.measure: Assessment automation, marking workflow, and ability to evaluate many test cases automatically

finding.finding_summary: The assessment was intentionally designed to require students to design, implement, debug, and justify MPC controllers, which the authors argue assessed deeper understanding, robustness thinking, and problem-solving beyond formula recall. Student solution diversity in 2018 and 2021 suggests the tasks elicited authentic controller-design reasoning rather than a single prescribed procedure.
finding.measure: Variety of student controller designs, design choices, and qualitative observation of student engagement with controller design

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that students engaged with and enjoyed the in-person laboratory components, indicating positive engagement with the course activities. However, they also observed that the freedom in the final assessment sometimes led students to spend excessive time experimenting and debugging advanced methods, suggesting mixed effects on persistence and time management.
finding.measure: Observed student engagement and time spent completing final summative assessments

finding.finding_summary: This paper directly studies students' ability to learn and apply model predictive control, including linear MPC, nonlinear MPC, optimization-related implementation choices, and controller robustness. Across cohorts, student submissions showed competence in core MPC design, but many students still relied on linear models and quadratic costs even after the course shifted toward nonlinear MPC, indicating partial but not complete uptake of advanced concepts.
finding.measure: Student controller submissions, design option frequencies, and course assessment performance on MPC tasks

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper reports on a five-year project studying how secondary science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy built around classroom response systems (“clickers”). The paper asks how teachers change over time, what tensions they experience when adopting TEFA, and how a sustained professional development (PD) program can support that change.

The intervention combines clicker technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive PD model delivered on-site to groups of teachers in three school districts in western Massachusetts. The authors describe the teacher participants, the longitudinal staggered-site research design, multiple data sources (PD transcripts, journals, logs, surveys, classroom video, and interviews), and four teacher change narratives that illustrate different learning trajectories.

The paper’s main conclusion is that TEFA is hard to learn but can be learned through sustained, responsive PD and iterative classroom experimentation. Across cases, teachers generally became more comfortable with technology, improved question design and discourse orchestration, and used formative assessment information to adjust instruction. The paper emphasizes that teachers often move from seeing TEFA as an externally imposed method to using it as a flexible instructional tool, though tensions around time, class management, and PD fit often remain.

finding.finding_summary: In the math-teacher cases, TEFA was used to support mathematical understanding, question discussion, and review for the state-wide math exam. The paper is largely descriptive and does not report standardized achievement effect sizes, but it does indicate that teachers used TEFA to probe student thinking in math and adjust instruction based on responses (n not reported).
finding.measure: Teacher-reported and video-observed use of TEFA for mathematics instruction and assessment; student understanding as inferred from classroom discussion and teacher reflection

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on science teachers using TEFA to elicit student reasoning, compare ideas, and develop scientific understanding through question-driven discussion. The authors report that teachers gained better information about how students were thinking about concepts and changed lessons accordingly, but they do not report quantitative achievement effects (n approximately 39 teachers total, student sample not reported).
finding.measure: Teacher and student classroom discourse about scientific concepts; teacher-reported formative assessment of student thinking
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; student sample not reported

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported and the authors observed increases in student participation, engagement, and willingness to discuss ideas during TEFA question cycles. In the case narratives, TEFA was also used to improve classroom climate, motivation, and student confidence, but the evidence is qualitative and descriptive rather than statistical.
finding.measure: Student participation in whole-class discussion, class engagement, and teacher perceptions from logs, interviews, surveys, and video

finding.finding_summary: A central finding is that TEFA supported development of durable skills such as metacognition, discussion, collaboration, and reasoning. Teachers reported increased student-to-student interaction, richer discourse, and greater attention to students' thinking; several case narratives explicitly describe gains in metacognitive awareness and instructional agility (n not reported).
finding.measure: Classroom discourse quality, student-to-student interactions, metacognitive talk, and teacher adjustments based on formative feedback

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that TEFA and its PD are time-intensive: teachers repeatedly struggled with preparation time, class time, and technology glitches, especially early on. At the same time, teachers became more efficient with the technology over time and used TEFA to streamline management and instruction in some contexts, so the overall operational effect is mixed rather than uniformly positive.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, preparation time, class time devoted to TEFA, and technology reliability as reported in logs, surveys, and interviews

paper_profiles.title: Vision Mamba: A Comprehensive Survey and Taxonomy
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys the emerging family of Mamba- and state-space-model-based architectures for computer vision. It asks how Mamba can be adapted from language sequence modeling to visual tasks, and organizes the literature into a taxonomy spanning general vision, multi-modal learning, and vertical-domain applications such as remote sensing and medical imaging.

The paper is not an intervention study; rather, it synthesizes prior work on model design choices including selective scanning, bidirectional scanning, cross-scan modules, and hybrid CNN-Mamba/Transformer-Mamba blocks. It reviews how these variants are applied to image classification, detection, segmentation, restoration, point cloud analysis, video understanding, and vision-language tasks, and compares reported benchmark results across representative papers and tables.

The main conclusion is that Mamba’s linear-time selective state-space modeling can be competitive with or superior to transformer-based approaches in many vision benchmarks, while often offering better efficiency. The survey also highlights open problems such as direction sensitivity, stability at scale, and the need for better scanning strategies and multimodal integration. No education-specific population or formative-assessment-related study is presented in the paper.

paper_profiles.title: The Stochastic Parrot on LLM’s Shoulder: A Summative Assessment of Physical Concept Understanding
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models (LLMs) truly understand physical concepts or merely reproduce memorized language patterns, framed as a test of the “stochastic parrot” hypothesis. Using educational measurement ideas from summative assessment and Bloom’s taxonomy, the authors introduce PHYSICO, a benchmark of 52 high-school-level physics concepts with paired low-level and high-level tasks designed to separate memorization from deeper conceptual understanding.

The intervention/approach is a benchmark and evaluation protocol rather than an instructional treatment. Low-level tasks ask models to identify or generate physical concepts from natural-language definitions and images, while high-level tasks use abstract grid representations inspired by ARC to test whether models can map patterns to physical concepts and apply knowledge beyond memorization. The study evaluates several commercial and open-source LLMs, including GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Llama-3, Mistral, InternVL, and LLaVA, and compares them with human annotators.

Results show a large gap between low-level and high-level performance: models do very well on natural-language concept recognition and generation, but perform near chance or well below humans on the abstract reasoning tasks. Humans achieve high accuracy on the core tasks, while LLMs remain substantially weaker even when given multimodal inputs, chain-of-thought prompting, in-context learning, or fine-tuning on related grid-format data. The authors conclude that current LLMs exhibit a stochastic-parrot-like pattern: they can recall and verbalize concepts, but struggle to demonstrate deeper understanding in controlled abstract settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly tests understanding of physical concepts, using concept selection/generation and abstract grid-based classification as measures of scientific reasoning. LLMs performed near ceiling on low-level natural-language concept tasks (e.g., GPT-3.5 97.3% and GPT-4 95.0% accuracy on text concept selection) but dropped sharply on high-level abstract tasks, where even top models were around 28%-53% depending on setting, while humans reached 89.5%-92.0% on CORE tasks.
finding.measure: Accuracy on physical concept selection, generation, and abstract grid-based classification tasks (PHYSICO-CORE, PHYSICO-ASSOCIATIVE)
finding.study_size: n=400 CORE grid instances for development/test, n=200 ASSOCIATIVE instances; human study n=3 annotators per item
finding.std_deviation: text tables report std. dev. for some model runs, e.g. GPT-4 1.3 on CORE-Dev; overall effect size not reported

paper_profiles.title: Concept-based Rubrics Improve LLM Formative Assessment and Data Synthesis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines automated formative assessment for open-ended STEM student responses, asking whether concept-based rubrics can improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) and also improve the quality of synthetic data used to train smaller supervised models. The authors frame the work around formative assessment as a way to provide timely feedback in large STEM classes, where human scoring is costly and difficult to scale.

The study compares fine-tuned pretrained language models (RoBERTa and Longformer) with GPT-4o-mini and, in some analyses, other LLMs, across five datasets: Beetle, SciEntsBank, ASAP-SAS, ISTUDIO, and CLASSIFIES. The datasets vary in domain, response length, rubric availability, and whether questions are standalone or scenario-based. The core intervention is prompting LLMs with concept-based, question-specific rubrics rather than examples; the paper also tests LLM-based data synthesis methods and rubric-guided feedback generation.

Results show that fine-tuned supervised PLMs remain strongest overall on the human-labeled datasets, but concept-based rubrics substantially improve LLM assessment accuracy, narrowing the gap with supervised models. The rubric effect is strongest for ISTUDIO and CLASSIFIES, where rubrics are tightly aligned with underlying concepts; it is weaker or inconsistent for ASAP, whose rubrics are more general and less concept-specific. The paper also finds that rubric-guided synthetic data, especially with diversity enhancement and re-annotation, can train lightweight PLMs to approach LLM-level performance, and that LLMs can sometimes generate useful explanatory feedback, though explanations may drift toward subjective criteria when scores disagree with human labels.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates automated assessment of undergraduate statistics responses and finds that concept-based rubrics improve GPT-4o-mini performance on the statistics-focused ISTUDIO dataset. With rubrics, GPT-4o-mini accuracy improved by about 10 percentage points over example-based prompting, reaching 79.63% accuracy and 70.27% F1 in the data-synthesis comparison, while rubric-based prompting also outperformed prompting with multiple examples for assessment.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy and F1 for scoring short-answer statistics responses

finding.finding_summary: The paper also studies STEM constructed-response assessment more broadly, including science/electronics datasets such as SciEntsBank and Beetle. For these datasets, fine-tuned PLMs performed strongly, and rubric use showed limited or inconsistent gains for PLMs; however, for LLM prompting the concept-based rubric approach improved assessment relative to example-based prompting, with performance on SciEntsBank around 81% accuracy and F1 near 81–82% for the supervised baseline.
finding.measure: 3-way answer classification accuracy and F1 on STEM short-answer assessment datasets

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is reducing the need for expensive labeled training data and manual rubric engineering for automated assessment. The paper shows that LLM-generated synthetic data, especially after diversity enhancement and re-annotation, can train lightweight PLMs to near GPT-4o-mini performance (e.g., 80.70% accuracy / 80.33% F1 on ISTUDIO and 68.76% / 69.05% on CLASSIFIES), while avoiding human data effort.
finding.measure: Accuracy/F1 of lightweight PLMs trained on synthetic data; need for human labeling and training data

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether LLM explanations can justify score assignments in ways aligned with rubrics, which relates to interpretive judgment and feedback usefulness. When the LLM’s score matched human labels, explanations were judged explainable in 96% of ISTUDIO cases and 76% of CLASSIFIES cases, suggesting that rubric-guided explanations can support feedback-oriented assessment.
finding.measure: Human annotation of LLM explanatory feedback for explainability and subjectivity
finding.study_size: n=50 per dataset for aligned-score explainability samples; n=50 per dataset for disagreement samples

paper_profiles.title: Conditions Under Which Assessment Supports Students’ Learning
paper_profiles.venue: Learning and Teaching in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article asks under what conditions assessment supports student learning in higher education. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it synthesizes prior research and arguments about assessment practices, emphasizing how different assessment designs influence study behavior, motivation, feedback use, and the amount/type of learning students undertake.

The paper focuses on undergraduate contexts and on assessment arrangements such as the timing, quantity, nature, and stakes of assignments, as well as feedback and alignment between assessment and intended learning. Its central claim is that assessment has strong effects on learning, but these effects are conditional: assessment can encourage deep learning when it is frequent, low-stakes or formative, and aligned with learning goals, but can also drive surface learning, strategic behavior, and workload overload when poorly designed.

Because the paper is primarily a conceptual/review piece rather than an empirical study, it does not report a new sample, effect sizes, or experimental comparison. Its contribution is to distinguish assessment conditions that support learning from those that do not, and to argue for assessment designs that channel students’ effort toward intended educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that assessment conditions can influence student motivation, anxiety, and engagement. It reports that frequent, low-stakes, and well-aligned assessment can encourage regular study and engagement, while high-stakes or excessive assessment can increase surface approaches, anxiety, and strategic behavior; no new sample or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, anxiety, engagement, and study approach (conceptual synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: A central focus is on how assessment shapes metacognition, self-regulation, and critical engagement with learning tasks. The paper contends that formative-like assessment conditions support reflection and deeper processing, whereas assessment that is too infrequent or too heavily weighted can reduce opportunities for self-monitoring and thoughtful revision; no new quantitative estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking, and depth of processing (conceptual synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses assessment workload and efficiency for both students and staff. It argues that some assessment designs create excessive marking and student workload without improving learning, while better-aligned and strategically timed assessment can make learning effort more productive; however, the article does not report a new empirical workload effect.
finding.measure: Student workload and teacher marking/workload (conceptual synthesis)

paper_profiles.title: Classroom Video Assessment and Retrieval via Multiple Instance Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of supporting human classroom assessment by automatically retrieving classroom video segments that are likely to be informative for assessment. The authors argue that classroom video contains semantic cues relevant to frameworks such as the Classroom Assessment Scoring System (CLASS), but that these cues are difficult to detect directly because they are expressed through low-level audio and visual signals. To bridge this semantic gap, they propose the Classroom Evaluation and Video Retrieval (CLEVER) system, a multiple instance learning approach that maps CLASS assessment concepts to video/audio features and uses those features to rank or filter clips.

The system is built around classroom video clips from two junior-level Systems Engineering classes at the University of Virginia. The paper describes a feature extraction pipeline using computer vision and speech-analysis features such as motion intensity, teacher position, gesture, pose orientation, silence detection, pitch, and dialog-talking events. Clips are segmented into micro-clips and grouped into principal shots, which are then used as instances in a multiple instance learning framework.

The empirical study is formative and involves 10 expert CLASS coders who label 40 three-minute clips from the two courses as positive or negative based on whether each clip would be useful for CLASS assessment. The authors report substantial disagreement among coders (Fleiss’ kappa = 0.146 for Course A and 0.125 for Course B), but also show that CLEVER can predict individual coder labels with accuracy well above chance, with reported accuracies varying by coder and course (e.g., up to 0.994 for one coder on Course B). They conclude that the approach has potential to reduce human viewing load and support productivity in classroom assessment, though the paper is an early formative experiment rather than a validation of student learning outcomes or assessment effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: CLEVER substantially improved the efficiency of screening classroom video for assessment-relevant clips compared with random ordering. In a formative experiment with 10 expert CLASS coders labeling 40 three-minute clips, the system achieved above-chance label prediction and the authors' productivity simulations suggested it could reduce human viewing load by a factor of 2 or more by reordering clips to maximize positive clips viewed during a fixed 10-minute window.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy on coder labels; simulated productivity measured as expected frequency/number of positive clips viewed after reordering

paper_profiles.title: FOKE: A Personalized and Explainable Education Framework Integrating Foundation Models, Knowledge Graphs, and Prompt Engineering
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes FOKE (Forest Of Knowledge and Education), a conceptual framework for intelligent education that combines foundation models, knowledge graphs, and prompt engineering. The authors argue that existing LLM-based educational tools struggle with personalization, interactivity, and explainability, and they present FOKE as a way to address these gaps through structured knowledge representation, multi-dimensional learner profiling, and prompt templates that generate tailored guidance.

The paper describes four core modules: a hierarchical knowledge forest, user profiling, structured prompt representation, and graph embedding. These components are intended to support personalized learning support, interactive tutoring, explainable recommendations, and adaptive instruction. The authors illustrate the framework through three application scenarios—interactive programming education, learning path planning, and intelligent homework/writing assessment—and also describe a real-world system called Scholar Hero built on top of FOKE.

The paper is primarily a framework and system description rather than an empirical evaluation study. It does not report a controlled experiment or comparative study with outcome data; instead, it argues for the potential value of the approach and gives illustrative workflows and example prompts/feedback. The main conclusion is that combining foundation models with knowledge graphs and prompt engineering may enable more personalized, interactive, and explainable educational AI systems, though the authors note that rigorous evaluation is still needed.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses writing assessment as one of three illustrative application scenarios, but it does not report empirical results on writing performance. No sample size, effect size, or pre/post outcome data are provided; the paper only presents example feedback on thesis statements, evidence, and counterarguments.
finding.measure: Writing assessment quality / feedback on essay components

finding.finding_summary: The framework is positioned as a way to automate and streamline homework and writing assessment by generating objective, detailed feedback and adaptive prompts. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim and illustrative system capability rather than a measured productivity outcome, so no effect size or study sample is reported.
finding.measure: Homework/writing assessment workflow efficiency and automation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that FOKE and Scholar Hero have been piloted in university settings and may improve student engagement, academic performance, and personalized support at the institutional level. These claims are not backed by comparative evidence in the paper, and no formal institutional outcome measures are reported.
finding.measure: Pilot deployment and institutional educational service delivery

paper_profiles.title: Towards a low-cost universal access cloud framework to assess STEM students
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the practical problem of assessing university STEM students remotely during pandemic-era and otherwise constrained learning conditions, with special attention to preserving exam integrity for coding-based assessments. The authors argue that traditional on-campus computer labs are costly, inflexible, and inaccessible for some students, and that remote assessment must still provide identity verification, proctoring, secure access to tools, and backup/recovery of student work.

To meet this need, the paper describes a cloud-based assessment framework built on Google Cloud Platform, Kubernetes, JupyterHub, OpenLDAP, Moodle, and the Respondus LockDown Browser. The system is designed so students can complete a theory quiz and then a practical programming section from home, while the proctoring tool restricts access and the cloud environment provides a scalable, authenticated coding workspace. The authors compare this setup against two alternative remote assessment configurations previously used by the university: a small-group video-proctored exam and a more complex multi-camera recording workflow.

The paper reports a case-study style deployment in an undergraduate Introduction to Computer Science course with about 30 students. The main conclusions are that the cloud setup reduced student configuration burden, required fewer teachers for supervision, and eliminated the need for additional IT intervention, while also improving flexibility and access for students with mobility or sensory impairments. The authors also conclude that cloud deployment can support low-stakes testing, collaborative coding, and other educational uses beyond summative exams, though the paper is primarily descriptive and does not present controlled learning-outcome data.

finding.finding_summary: The cloud-based proctored assessment workflow reduced staffing and setup burden compared with the two alternative remote exam setups. For a similar 30-student exam, setup A required four teachers for surveillance, setup B required extensive pre-exam configuration and generated IT support issues, while the proposed setup C required only one teacher, minimal student configuration, and no extra IT intervention once the exam started.
finding.measure: Teacher supervision required, student setup/configuration burden, and IT support issues during remote assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the cloud deployment improves institutional flexibility, accessibility, and cost control for online assessment. The authors report that the system was cheaper and more flexible than equivalent on-premise installations, could be integrated with university authentication and proctoring systems, and could support broader institutional uses such as labs, collaborative coding, and potentially reduced need for physical computer labs.
finding.measure: Deployment cost, flexibility, accessibility, and institutional integration/adoption characteristics

paper_profiles.title: Learn Like Feynman: Developing and Testing an AI-Driven Feynman Bot
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether a generative AI bot built around the Feynman learning technique can improve self-regulated learning compared with passive study methods. The authors argue that many current AI study tools support memorization or question-answer practice, but do not sufficiently promote higher-order, discussion-based explanation and peer-like questioning. To fill this gap, they developed the Feynman Bot, which uses a large language model with retrieval-augmented generation and prompt engineering to conduct a two-way, question-answer-driven conversation about user-provided study materials.

The bot was tested in a controlled experiment over three days with 14 working adults (ages 21-29) enrolled in Harvard’s online Justice course. Participants were randomly split into a passive-learning control group and a Feynman Bot group; both studied two lectures on utilitarianism, but the experimental group reviewed transcripts through 25-minute conversations with the bot. Learning was measured with formative and summative assessments, and self-efficacy/comfort was measured with a Likert survey for the bot group.

The authors report that the Feynman Bot group achieved higher mean learning gains than the passive group (3.83 vs 2.17) and slightly higher summative scores (M=6.8, SD=1.3 vs M=6.5, SD=1.9). They also report improved comfort and confidence with the material among bot users, with over 80% preferring the bot over rereading or rewatching lectures, and a preference for typing over speech as the interaction mode. The paper concludes that the bot is a promising tool for self-regulated learners, though it is limited by a small sample and a narrow subject context in a humanities course.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that the Feynman Bot group achieved higher learning gains than the passive-learning group on the course assessments. Mean summative score was slightly higher for the bot group (M=6.8, SD=1.3) than for the passive group (M=6.5, SD=1.9), and mean learning gain was also higher (FB=3.83 vs CG=2.17) across 14 adult participants.
finding.measure: Formative and summative assessment scores on two lectures from Harvard's Justice course (10 MCQs each, plus 2 open-ended questions); learning gain calculated as summative minus formative score
finding.std_deviation: FB learning gain SD=1.32; Passive Learners SD=1.94

finding.finding_summary: Participants using the Feynman Bot reported greater comfort and confidence with the study material after the intervention. Over 80% preferred the bot to passive study methods, all bot users reported increased comfort discussing the material with peers, and 85.7% said it was useful for new topics.
finding.measure: Self-efficacy survey (5-point Likert items) focused on comfort with study material and using the bot
finding.study_size: n=7 in bot group (survey administered only to Feynman Bot Learners)

finding.finding_summary: The bot appeared to support deeper explanation and application of ideas, which the authors interpret as stronger comprehension and higher-order reasoning. In open-ended responses, Feynman Bot learners more often provided scenario- or case-based explanations, whereas passive learners gave short theoretical answers without elaboration.
finding.measure: Open-ended assessment responses analyzed with thematic analysis

paper_profiles.title: Assessing m-Learning Adoption in Higher Education
paper_profiles.venue: 10th International Conference on Engineering and Computer Education (ICECE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to assess mobile learning (m-learning) adoption in higher education institutions. Rather than evaluating a specific instructional intervention, it proposes an M-Learning Maturity Model (MLMM) based on the Capability Maturity Model (CMM) to help universities determine how advanced their m-learning adoption is and what conditions must be met to progress to higher stages of adoption.

The model defines five maturity levels—Preliminary, Established, Defined, Structured, and Continuous Improvement—using nine critical success factors and a rating methodology. The paper then applies the model to two universities (University A and University B), each with eight complete survey responses from administrators/faculty/staff, and uses Likert-scale questionnaire ratings to determine their maturity levels. Both universities were classified at the "Established" level.

The study also examines inter-rater agreement using Cohen’s/Fleiss’ kappa to check consistency across respondents within each university, finding moderate agreement in both cases. Overall, the paper concludes that the MLMM can support university management in evaluating and improving m-learning implementation, but it is an institutional assessment framework rather than a student-outcome study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and validates an M-Learning Maturity Model (MLMM) for assessing institutional adoption of m-learning in higher education. Applied to two universities, the model classified both as being at the "Established" maturity level based on questionnaire ratings and threshold rules, suggesting the framework can differentiate institutional stages of adoption and support planning for improvement.
finding.measure: M-learning maturity assessment using a Likert-scale questionnaire, number of achieved statements (NAS), and passing threshold (80%) across maturity levels
finding.study_size: n=2 universities; 17 respondents total (8 from University A, 9 from University B)

finding.finding_summary: The MLMM is presented as a tool to help university management evaluate m-learning projects more systematically and to guide upgrade strategies and implementation planning. The paper argues that the framework can improve decision-making and refinement of procedures and policies, but it does not measure direct efficiency gains or workload reductions empirically.
finding.measure: Institutional assessment utility of the maturity model; qualitative application to two university case studies

paper_profiles.title: Enhancing Precision of Automated Teller Machines Network Quality Assessment: Machine Learning and Multi Classifier Fusion Approaches
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of unreliable ATM status detection in banking networks, focusing on false alarms and missed alarms that lead to unnecessary maintenance, higher costs, and reduced service availability. The authors frame ATM service-state detection as a binary classification problem: in-service versus out-of-service. Ground-truth labels are derived from detailed ATM journal files, while more compact operational features come from ATM status files and transaction records.

The study evaluates several machine learning and ensemble approaches, including SVM, decision tree, bagging, Random Forest, LightGBM, CatBoost, dynamic classifier selection, dynamic ensemble selection, and a stacking classifier. Because the data are highly imbalanced, the authors apply SMOTE to balance the classes before training. They also test a transaction-gap feature using an exponential inter-arrival assumption supported by a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. On this proprietary banking dataset, the stacking model performed best overall, reaching 99.29% accuracy, with Random Forest close behind at 99.26%.

The main conclusion is that ensemble and fusion-based methods, especially when combined with SMOTE, substantially improve detection of out-of-service ATMs and reduce false alarms. The paper is presented as a practical operational solution for banks seeking better monitoring, lower maintenance costs, and improved customer satisfaction. However, it is not an educational study and does not involve student learning outcomes; its relevance here is limited to the sub-question about distinguishing formative assessment from related practices only in the broad sense that it evaluates classifier-based monitoring systems rather than assessment in education.

finding.finding_summary: The proposed machine-learning and fusion framework improved ATM status monitoring by reducing false alarms from 3.56% to 0.71% and achieving 99.29% overall accuracy with the stacking classifier (n=not_reported). Random Forest also performed strongly at 99.26% accuracy, and SMOTE substantially improved minority-class detection across models.
finding.measure: ATM status classification accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, false alarm rate

finding.finding_summary: The study reports institutional benefits for banking operations, including reduced unnecessary maintenance, better resource allocation, and improved decision-making for ATM network management. These outcomes are based on proprietary bank data and the comparison of multiple status-detection models, with the best model reaching 99.29% accuracy.
finding.measure: Operational decision-making, maintenance burden, ATM network reliability indicators

paper_profiles.title: Assessing the Performance of Diagnostic Classification Models in Small Sample Contexts with Different Estimation Methods
paper_profiles.population: N/A (simulation study; classroom-sized samples modeled after K-12 contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how diagnostic classification models (DCMs), which are often discussed as tools for formative assessment, behave when used in small-sample classroom-like contexts. The core question is whether respondent classification and item parameter estimation remain accurate when sample sizes are typical of classrooms, and how performance changes across estimation methods (maximum likelihood, Bayesian, and nonparametric), DCM families (DINA, DINO, RRUM, CRUM, LCDM), item quality, number of items, number of attributes, and Q-matrix misspecification.

The authors conduct a large simulation study using classroom-sized samples (N=20, 40, 160), 20 or 40 items, and 4 or 5 attributes, with controlled levels of item discrimination and Q-matrix misspecification. They evaluate classification accuracy using element-wise and pattern-wise attribute classification rates, and item recovery using bias and RMSE for slip/guessing parameters. For Bayesian estimation, they use weak priors and MCMC; for ML, marginal maximum likelihood via GDINA; and for nonparametric estimation, NPCD where applicable.

The main findings are that item quality, item count, and Q-matrix accuracy matter substantially for classification, while small sample size especially harms item-parameter recovery. High-discrimination items and more items generally improve classification, but Q-matrix misspecification can sharply reduce pattern-wise accuracy. Bayesian estimation tends to do slightly better for parsimonious models (DINA/DINO), while ML performs slightly better for more complex models (RRUM/CRUM/LCDM); nonparametric methods are competitive for DINA/DINO. However, item-parameter estimates are often unreliable in classroom-sized samples, and the paper highlights method-specific problems such as ML boundary estimates and unstable Bayesian posteriors for some slip parameters.

paper_profiles.title: Bayesian Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (Bayesian-KANs): A Probabilistic Approach to Enhance Accuracy and Interpretability
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper proposes Bayesian Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (Bayesian-KANs), a neural network architecture that combines Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks with Bayesian inference to improve prediction accuracy, interpretability, and uncertainty quantification. The central problem addressed is that standard deep learning models are often opaque and do not represent predictive uncertainty, which limits their usefulness in high-stakes decision settings.

The proposed method replaces deterministic spline functions with probabilistic splines and uses variational inference to learn posterior distributions over model parameters. The paper evaluates the approach on two adult medical classification benchmarks: the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset (n=768) and the Cleveland/Heart Disease dataset (n=303). Bayesian-KANs are compared against logistic regression, random forest, support vector machine, and traditional neural network baselines.

Results reported in the paper indicate that Bayesian-KANs achieve the best predictive performance on both datasets, with improved accuracy, F1 score, AUC-ROC, and tighter uncertainty intervals than the comparator models. The model is also presented as more interpretable because it identifies clinically meaningful predictors such as glucose, BMI, cholesterol, age, and resting blood pressure. Overall, the paper argues that combining Bayesian inference with KAN architecture yields a more reliable and transparent model for medical decision support, while noting computational cost and scalability limitations.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates a new machine-learning architecture on two medical classification benchmarks rather than educational outcomes. Bayesian-KANs outperformed baseline models on the Pima Indians Diabetes dataset (accuracy 80.1%, F1=0.78, AUC-ROC=0.87; n=768) and the Heart Disease dataset (accuracy 85.7%, F1=0.84, AUC-ROC=0.91; n=303).
finding.measure: Classification accuracy, F1 score, and AUC-ROC on medical diagnosis datasets
finding.confidence_interval: [0.78, 0.82] and [0.83, 0.88] for uncertainty intervals reported in tables

paper_profiles.title: On the Security & Privacy in Federated Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys the security and privacy literature on federated learning (FL) and proposes a unifying threat model plus taxonomies for attacks and defenses. The authors aim to resolve inconsistent terminology and fragmented categorization across prior work by organizing the FL attack surface, adversarial actors, capabilities, and goals according to confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA).

The paper is a systematic review of prior FL security research rather than an experiment on a learner population. It synthesizes published work on poisoning, backdoor, free-rider, evasion, membership inference, property inference, model inversion, model extraction, and defenses such as cryptographic methods, differential privacy, pruning, server cleaning, adversarial training, robust aggregation, and GAN-based defenses. The review also extracts common evaluation metrics, experimental settings, and relationships between attacks and defenses.

Its main conclusion is that FL security is highly fragmented and that no single defense fully addresses the evolving attack surface. The authors emphasize that cryptographic methods do not fully prevent inference, differential privacy trades off with model accuracy, robust aggregation and server-cleaning methods are often attack-specific, and adaptive attacks can evade many proposed defenses. The paper frames several open challenges and calls for more generalizable, comparative evaluation of defenses across attack types and data settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper systematically reviews and organizes the FL security/privacy literature, proposing a threat model and unifying taxonomies for attacks and defenses. It does not evaluate an intervention on learner outcomes, but it does have a strong field-level impact by standardizing how researchers compare attacks, defenses, metrics, and experimental setups.
finding.measure: Conceptual synthesis of prior federated learning security and privacy studies

paper_profiles.title: Assessing Mobile Learning System Performance in Indonesia: Reports of the Model Development and Its Instrument Testing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of clear, instrumented studies evaluating mobile learning system performance from the end-user perspective in Indonesia. The authors argue that prior work on m-learning has often focused either on technical aspects or on psychological/social perspectives, but rarely integrates these views or explains how a research model is developed and operationalized into survey items.

The study develops a mobile learning success model by adopting the DeLone and McLean information systems success model and combining it with mobile-learning-specific constructs, especially learning content and user motivation. The model is broken down into 31 indicators, and a questionnaire is administered online to about 50 respondents using snowball purposive sampling. The paper’s main contribution is methodological: it reports the conceptual model, indicator development, and preliminary instrument testing using PLS-SEM in SmartPLS, rather than testing the substantive causal effects of the model.

The respondents are mostly students in Indonesia, with the sample dominated by high school pupils and users of commercial mobile learning providers such as Ruang Guru, Zenius, and Quipper. The instrument testing reports that 10 indicators were rejected and 21 were retained as reliable and valid. The authors conclude that the model-building and instrument-testing process is transparent and useful for novice researchers, but they caution that the findings are preliminary and not broadly generalizable.

finding.finding_summary: The study does not evaluate an intervention’s effect on operational efficiency; instead, it develops and tests a survey instrument for assessing m-learning system success. The closest efficiency-related measure is the net benefits construct, but results are limited to reliability/validity testing, with 10 of 31 indicators rejected and 21 retained; no effect size or outcome impact is reported (n=50).
finding.measure: Instrument reliability/validity for m-learning success constructs, including net benefits indicators

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes user motivation and user satisfaction as constructs in the proposed model, but it does not test their substantive relationships or any causal effect on learner motivation or engagement. The reported results concern only psychometric testing of indicators (e.g., 10 rejected items out of 31), so no effect size on motivation-related outcomes is provided (n=50).
finding.measure: Instrument reliability/validity for user motivation and user satisfaction indicators

paper_profiles.title: AI Powered Road Network Prediction with Multi-Modal Data
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of automatic road network prediction from remote sensing data, focusing on whether lower-resolution satellite imagery can be improved by fusing GPS trajectory data. The authors argue that prior road-extraction work largely relied on expensive high-resolution imagery, and that fusion-stage choices, loss functions, and evaluation metrics have not been systematically compared in the low-resolution setting.

The study evaluates U-Net, ResUnet, and D-Linknet on Sentinel-2 imagery from Istanbul and Montreal, with GPS trajectories rasterized to match image resolution. It compares baseline satellite-only models to early fusion and two late-fusion variants, along with three loss functions (MSE, BCE, focal loss) and two metrics (IoU and Boundary-IoU). The work also builds and uses a benchmark dataset covering two cities to test generalization across geographic domains.

Results show that ResUnet generally performs best, and that adding GPS trajectories usually improves road extraction, especially in late fusion Type-2 with concatenation and MSE loss. The authors also report that MSE outperforms BCE and focal loss overall, while BCE can degrade performance with average and maximum fusion. Cross-city generalization is limited, and early fusion appears to generalize better than late fusion even when absolute scores are lower. The paper concludes that low-resolution multimodal fusion is promising for road extraction and that Boundary-IoU provides useful shape-sensitive complement to IoU.

paper_profiles.title: A Domain-Agnostic Approach for Characterization of Lifelong Learning Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement and evaluation problem in lifelong learning (LL): how to characterize whether deployed machine learning systems can continuously learn, transfer knowledge across tasks, and scale over long operational lifetimes. The authors argue that prior work often assessed these capabilities in isolation and within domain-specific benchmarks, making it hard to compare systems or understand trade-offs such as catastrophic forgetting versus transfer.

To address this, the paper proposes a domain-agnostic evaluation framework built around three conditions of lifelong learning: continuous learning, transfer and adaptation, and scalability. It defines five metrics—performance maintenance, forward transfer, backward transfer, relative performance to single-task experts, and sample efficiency—and pairs them with scenario and protocol guidance for constructing evaluations. The paper then applies this framework to five DARPA L2M system groups across embodied AI, autonomous driving, open-world exploration, and game-play environments, showing how the metrics reveal different strengths, weaknesses, and trade-offs across systems and task-ordering scenarios.

The paper is not an education study in the K-12 sense; its population is adult technical users and researchers developing AI systems. Its main contribution is methodological rather than intervention-based: it offers a standardized way to evaluate lifelong learning systems and interpret performance trade-offs across diverse environments. The case studies suggest the framework can distinguish systems that mitigate forgetting from those that learn more quickly, and can detect when preservation mechanisms help or hurt performance depending on task structure.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies efficiency-related properties of lifelong learning systems, especially sample efficiency and resource-scalable learning over long lifetimes. Across the case studies, systems differed substantially: for example, SG-UPenn’s META-KFO improved sample efficiency (SE=3.40±0.46) relative to DF-CNN (SE=1.61±0.12), while some configurations showed better stability but lower learning efficiency. These results indicate clear trade-offs between learning speed, retention, and scalability rather than a single uniformly superior approach.
finding.measure: Sample efficiency (SE), relative performance to single-task expert (RP), and metric-based evaluation of learning under limited resources
finding.study_size: multiple system evaluations across five case studies; individual reported n varies by case (e.g., n=33, n=30, n=15)
finding.std_deviation: reported in source as metric means ± standard deviations; exact SDs vary by configuration

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s primary contribution is a framework for standardizing how lifelong learning systems are evaluated across domains and research groups. It proposes explicit conditions, scenarios, protocols, and metrics intended to support reproducibility, comparability, and program-level assessment, which the authors report was useful for the DARPA L2M program and for identifying strengths and weaknesses of systems in a uniform way.
finding.measure: Evaluation framework adoption/use across five DARPA L2M system groups; comparison of systems under shared scenarios and metrics
finding.study_size: 5 system groups; multiple evaluation runs per group

paper_profiles.title: TrueImage: A Machine Learning Algorithm to Improve the Quality of Telehealth Photos
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical telehealth problem: patient-submitted dermatology photos are often too blurry, poorly lit, or poorly framed for clinical assessment, which creates workflow delays and can reduce the usefulness of teledermatology visits. The authors argue that photo quality is an understudied bottleneck in telehealth and propose an automated method to detect low-quality images and provide corrective guidance to patients.

The proposed system, TrueImage, is a lightweight machine-learning pipeline that first segments skin regions, then computes interpretable features for blur, lighting, and zoom/crop problems, and finally applies logistic regression classifiers to label overall quality and specific failure modes. The paper evaluates the method on a small dermatology image dataset assembled from web images, Stanford clinic photos, and artificially augmented poor-quality examples, plus a small set of additional poor-lighting photos. Performance is reported using ROC curves and threshold tradeoffs; the system can reject about 50% of poor-quality images while retaining about 80% of good-quality images, or reject about 10% of poor-quality images while retaining more than 95% of good-quality images, suggesting utility for reducing clinician time spent triaging unusable photos. The authors conclude that automated photo-quality screening is feasible and could improve teledermatology workflow, though they note limitations in data size, label subjectivity, and skin-tone diversity.

finding.finding_summary: TrueImage is intended to reduce clinician time spent manually triaging poor-quality teledermatology photos and prompting retakes. In evaluation on a 362-image dermatology dataset, the system could reject about 50% of poor-quality images while retaining about 80% of good-quality images, or reject about 10% of poor-quality images while retaining more than 95% of good-quality images, suggesting workflow gains for teledermatology screening.
finding.measure: ROC-based classification of good vs poor-quality dermatology photos; rejection/retention tradeoff for image triage
finding.std_deviation: 1 standard deviation confidence band shown on ROC curve, exact value not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Stealth Assessment: Measuring and Supporting Learning in Video Games
paper_profiles.venue: The John D. and Catherine T. MacArthur Foundation Reports on Digital Media and Learning / MIT Press
paper_profiles.population: K–16 students (primarily K–12 and undergraduate examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This report argues that traditional classroom assessments are often detached from learning, limited in validity, and poorly suited to measuring complex twenty-first-century competencies such as persistence, creativity, collaboration, and conceptual understanding. The authors propose stealth assessment as an alternative approach: embedding assessment deeply inside digital games so that evidence about student learning can be captured unobtrusively during gameplay and used immediately to support learning.

The report is primarily conceptual and methodological, but it is grounded in examples and prior studies of educational games and assessment-for-learning systems. It discusses evidence-centered design as the framework for building game-based assessments, then illustrates the approach with a Newtonian physics game (Newton’s Playground) intended to assess creativity, conscientiousness/persistence, and conceptual physics understanding. The paper also reviews existing studies showing that game-based or feedback-supported systems can improve learning, including an adaptive feedback system for high-school geometry, undergraduate programming instruction with NIU-Torcs, cancer education with Re-Mission, and middle-school science learning with Quest Atlantis: Taiga Park.

Overall, the report concludes that well-designed games can both assess and support learning in real time, but that designers must address construct-irrelevant demands, accessibility, feedback effects, and dependency among actions. It does not present a single new empirical study of stealth assessment efficacy; rather, it synthesizes prior evidence and lays out design principles and challenges for future research.

finding.finding_summary: In the ACED study described in the report, 268 high-school students using an assessment-for-learning system with elaborated feedback showed significantly greater learning of geometric sequences than a control group receiving only correct/incorrect feedback. The report states that the feedback did not impair assessment quality and improved content learning, but it does not report the exact effect size in the excerpted text.
finding.measure: Learning of geometric sequences

finding.finding_summary: In the Taiga Park study, middle-school students in a controlled experiment scored significantly higher than the classroom comparison group on a posttest of core science concepts (including erosion and eutrophication), with p < 0.01. The treatment group also outperformed the control group on a delayed posttest measuring retention and transfer of water-quality content, with p < 0.001.
finding.measure: Posttest and delayed posttest of science concepts/water-quality understanding

finding.finding_summary: In the NIU-Torcs evaluation, undergraduate mechanical engineering students using the game-based instructional approach (n=38) scored significantly higher than students in four control classrooms (n=48) on a concept map assessment tied to programming/control-algorithm learning. The gains were especially evident on deeper knowledge indicators such as hierarchy depth and connections among branches, although the report does not provide a numerical effect size.
finding.measure: Concept map assessment of programming/control-algorithm understanding

finding.finding_summary: The report argues that digital games can support persistence, conscientiousness, and engagement, and it cites evidence that game play may improve persistence by requiring players to persevere through failure and frustration. However, the report’s own empirical support here is indirect and largely drawn from prior literature and design rationale rather than a newly reported experiment on persistence.
finding.measure: Persistence / conscientiousness indicators and related game-play behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that digital games can measure and support durable skills such as creativity, problem solving, collaboration, and systems thinking, and it presents these as target constructs for stealth assessment. The strongest empirical support in the report is indirect, coming from prior game-based learning studies and the authors’ planned Newton’s Playground application rather than from a completed stealth-assessment trial.
finding.measure: Creativity, systems thinking, problem solving, collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Competency-Based Education in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This RAND report examines whether and how competency-based education models were implemented in three Project Mastery pilot initiatives funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. The core question is not a direct test of formative assessment alone, but a broader evaluation of competency-based schooling features such as flexible pacing, student choice, and proficiency-based evaluation, with attention to implementation challenges, student experiences, and student outcomes.

The projects were carried out in five public secondary-school settings across Colorado, New Hampshire, Texas, and Pennsylvania: Adams County District 50, four Asia Society partner schools, and the School District of Philadelphia. The initiative funded technology-enriched curricula, online learning management systems, performance rubrics, and project-based or blended-learning materials during 2011–2012, followed by implementation in 2012–2013. RAND used site visits, interviews, student surveys, and several nonexperimental outcome analyses tailored to each site's data and design constraints.

Findings suggest that implementation varied substantially across sites, with recurring tensions around awarding credit for out-of-school learning, maintaining common proficiency standards, sustainability of technology systems, and equity for lower-performing students. Student survey responses were broadly positive and fairly uniform across sites, with DCIS showing the strongest reported engagement, choice, and flexible pacing. Outcome results were mixed: Adams 50 showed a statistically significant decline in mathematics performance of about 0.22 SD relative to pre-transition trends, Newfound showed a small nonsignificant reading gain of about 0.1 SD, DCIS and Sharpstown outperformed demographically similar peers but causality is uncertain, DCIS-M was similar to peers, and Philadelphia showed no clear achievement gains but modest attendance benefits and stronger outcomes for students in the optional badge program. The authors conclude that competency-based systems may offer promise, but effects depend on implementation, context, and support for equity and persistence.

finding.finding_summary: Philadelphia students performed below comparison students on the fall language arts assessment after about three months of exposure, but were about the same as peers on the winter assessment after about five months of exposure. In the Newfound Regional High School analysis, reading performance increased by about 0.1 student SD relative to the synthetic comparison group, but the estimate was not statistically significant and power was low.
finding.measure: Language arts assessment; reading test scores
finding.effect_size: About -0.22 SD in Philadelphia fall language arts; about +0.1 SD in Newfound reading

finding.finding_summary: In Adams County District 50, conversion to a competency-based model was associated with lower mathematics performance on the state accountability test in the five years after the transition. The report states this decline was about 0.22 student SD in 2013 and was significant at the 10-percent level.
finding.measure: State accountability mathematics test scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes non-literacy, non-math achievement outcomes in multiple schools, especially state accountability performance and promotion. DCIS and Sharpstown outperformed demographically similar peers, while DCIS-M performed similarly to peers; however, the authors caution that causal attribution is limited because these were school-choice contexts and the research design was observational. In Philadelphia, Project Mastery students were about the same as peers in promotion to tenth grade, while students in the optional badge program had higher promotion rates by 6.6 percentage points.
finding.measure: State accountability outcomes; promotion to 10th grade
finding.effect_size: Higher promotion by 6.6 percentage points in badge participants; other site estimates not reported in extract

finding.finding_summary: Student survey data indicated broadly positive perceptions of school value, engagement, flexible pacing, choice, and technology use across sites, with DCIS standing out as having the highest reports of engagement and flexible pacing. In Philadelphia, attendance rates were 1.4 percentage points higher than comparison students, and students in the optional filmmaking badge program had attendance rates 3.0 percentage points higher than non–Project Mastery students.
finding.measure: Student surveys of engagement/enjoyment; school attendance
finding.effect_size: +1.4 percentage points attendance in Project Mastery; +3.0 percentage points in badge participants

finding.finding_summary: The report emphasizes student choice, self-directed projects, flexible pacing, and project-based work as central features of the competency-based models, but direct durable-skill outcomes were not the main focus. Evidence is therefore indirect and mostly descriptive, based on student survey responses and implementation accounts rather than a dedicated measure of critical thinking or collaboration.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of choice/self-directed work; project-based learning features

finding.finding_summary: The report documents implementation and institutional effects of competency-based reforms, including adoption and upgrading of learning management systems, new performance rubrics, curriculum modules, and district-level policy tensions around credit, proficiency, and sustainability. It also concludes that competency-based systems require policy flexibility for accountability timing and infrastructure support for technology use.
finding.measure: Implementation of LMSs, curriculum modules, rubrics, and policy/process changes

paper_profiles.title: Instructionally Embedded Assessment: Theory of Action for an Innovative System
paper_profiles.population: K-12 students with the most significant cognitive disabilities (alternate assessment population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that traditional statewide summative assessments often provide feedback too late, at too coarse a grain size, and with too little instructional usefulness to support teachers’ day-to-day decision-making. It also responds to policy shifts toward innovative assessment systems that are intended to serve both instructional and accountability purposes.

The article presents a conceptual theory of action for the Dynamic Learning Maps Instructionally Embedded assessment system, an operational through-year alternate assessment used in five states. The system is described as integrating a cognitive model, rigorous academic standards, accessible-by-design item and platform features, teacher training, and flexible blueprints so teachers can select and administer short instructionally relevant assessments after instruction. Fine-grained diagnostic results are then aggregated into summative performance reports for accountability.

The paper’s population focus is students with the most significant cognitive disabilities, along with the educators who teach and assess them. It argues that when assessments are aligned to a strong cognitive model, administered accessibly and with fidelity, and paired with teacher training and instructional professional development, educators can better use assessment data to inform instruction and hold higher expectations for student learning. Because the article is a conceptual theory-of-action paper rather than an empirical evaluation, it does not report causal effects on student achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that an instructionally embedded through-year assessment system can serve both instructional and accountability purposes, replacing traditional summative-only testing with more flexible reporting and use of results. It claims the system is designed to improve stakeholder behavior and institutional decision-making, including state/district accountability reporting and educational program monitoring, but it does not present empirical effect sizes.
finding.measure: Assessment system design, reporting uses, and institutional decision-making model

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims the system reduces testing burden by spreading short administrations throughout the year and using diagnostic scoring to generate useful information with fewer items than traditional subscores. It suggests this can reduce time spent testing and support quicker instructional use of results, but provides no empirical estimate of workload reduction.
finding.measure: Testing time / administration burden / usefulness of assessment reporting

finding.finding_summary: The central academic focus is access to and progress in rigorous subject-area standards for students with significant cognitive disabilities, across multiple content areas rather than one narrow subject. The paper argues that aligning instruction, assessment content, and diagnostic reporting to a cognitive model can support student progress toward grade-level and postsecondary-aligned expectations, but it does not report empirical achievement outcomes.
finding.measure: Academic content mastery / progress toward rigorous standards

paper_profiles.title: Effect of Differentiated Instruction on Reading Comprehension of Third Graders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether differentiated instruction improves reading comprehension for third-grade students in rural eastern New Mexico. The problem motivating the study is persistently low reading performance among elementary students, especially the transition from learning to read to reading to learn, and the need for classroom practices that better support struggling readers.

The study compares two instructional conditions: differentiated instruction versus nondifferentiated instruction. Using a cross-sectional quasi-experimental causal-comparative design, the author analyzed archival PARCC reading comprehension scores for 128 third-grade students (64 in each group) across three school years (2015, 2016, and 2017). Teachers were classified using classroom observation and evaluation systems, and the dependent outcome was students’ PARCC reading comprehension scores.

The dissertation reports that differentiated instruction significantly improved PARCC reading scores in all three years examined. The findings are interpreted as supporting the use of differentiated instruction and related professional development to help elementary teachers better meet diverse learning needs and improve literacy outcomes for third graders.

finding.finding_summary: Differentiated instruction significantly improved third-grade students’ reading comprehension as measured by PARCC reading scores across all three years analyzed (2015, 2016, and 2017). The study used archived reading assessment data from N=128 students (64 differentiated instruction, 64 nondifferentiated) and found a consistent advantage for the differentiated group, but the dissertation text does not report effect sizes, confidence intervals, or standard deviations.
finding.measure: PARCC reading comprehension scores

paper_profiles.title: The Relationship Between Instructional Delivery and Student Engagement in Selected Classrooms: A Cross-Case Analysis
paper_profiles.venue: Doctoral dissertation, The College of William and Mary
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This dissertation examines whether and how instructional delivery practices are associated with student engagement in elementary classrooms, in the context of Miami-Dade County Public Schools (MDCPS). The problem motivating the study is that, despite district-wide alignment efforts through the Framework for Effective Instruction (FEI) and the IPEGS evaluation system, differences in student proficiency and learning gains persisted across schools. The author frames student engagement as a key nonacademic indicator that may be useful for understanding and improving classroom instruction and student achievement.

The study used a convergent mixed-methods, cross-case design to observe 16 teachers in four MDCPS elementary schools, focusing on fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms. Classroom observations were conducted using the Differentiated Classroom Observation Scale and IPEGS-related indicators to document instructional delivery behaviors and student engagement ratings. The analysis explored frequencies of instructional strategies, levels of student engagement, and correlations among instructional delivery indicators, student engagement indicators, and holistic engagement ratings.

The main conclusions are that teacher questioning was the most common instructional strategy observed, and some instructional delivery practices showed positive correlations with engagement-related indicators, especially high-order learning tasks with authentic learning and explicit instruction with connecting to prior knowledge and providing feedback. However, correlations involving student engagement were generally weak or varied, suggesting that the relationship between instructional delivery and engagement was not uniform across observed classrooms. The dissertation argues for continued professional development in explicit instruction, questioning, feedback, and technology use, and recommends further research to identify instructional strategies that better predict student engagement.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined student engagement in fourth- and fifth-grade classrooms and found that engagement levels varied across classrooms and were only weakly correlated with several student engagement indicators. Observations suggested some positive associations between instructional delivery and engagement-related measures, but the overall pattern was inconsistent rather than strongly positive.
finding.measure: Classroom observation ratings of student engagement using IPEGS student engagement indicators and a holistic learning director rating

finding.finding_summary: The dissertation focused on instructional practices such as higher-order learning tasks, authentic learning, questioning, and providing feedback, which are aligned with durable skills like critical thinking and metacognition. The reported findings indicate positive correlations between some instructional delivery indicators and these practices, but the evidence is correlational and not strong enough to show consistent effects.
finding.measure: Correlations among IPEGS instructional delivery indicators and observed instructional activity types

paper_profiles.title: The social and emotional foundations of learning
paper_profiles.venue: UNESCO MGIEP / International Science and Evidence-based Education Assessment (ISEEA) chapter
paper_profiles.population: PreK-12 and young people across the lifespan
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This chapter reviews the social and emotional foundations of learning (SEL) and argues that learning is inherently social, relational, and affective. It synthesizes interdisciplinary research from educational psychology, neuroscience, sociology, and developmental science to explain how emotions, relationships, motivation, and self-regulation shape learning, achievement, and well-being.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the chapter provides a conceptual and evidence-informed overview of SEL across development, from birth through adolescence and young adulthood. It describes how social-emotional capacities develop in dynamic cultural contexts, why school climates and adult relationships matter, and how assessment, instruction, play, creativity, and supportive school systems can foster SEL.

The chapter concludes that effective SEL should be responsive to context and culture, aligned with neurobiological development, and attentive to the social and emotional capacities of educators as well as learners. It emphasizes that social-emotional experiences influence academic performance, school engagement, and life outcomes, but it does not present a new empirical study or direct causal estimate of a specific SEL program.

finding.finding_summary: The chapter synthesizes evidence that emotions, motivation, self-determination, self-regulation, and relatedness are central to learning and well-being. It reports that positive emotions can support interest, motivation, and deep learning, while anxiety, hopelessness, and boredom can undermine learning; effects vary by emotion, task, and context rather than being uniformly positive or negative.
finding.measure: Synthesized findings on emotions, motivation, self-regulation, engagement, and well-being

finding.finding_summary: The chapter cites evidence that early playful experiences and middle-childhood social play are associated with literacy-related outcomes. It specifically notes that social play with peers at ages 7-9 predicts standardized literacy test outcomes, even after accounting for family economic circumstances, language ability, phonological skills, and general IQ.
finding.measure: Standardized literacy tests

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports consistent negative associations between math anxiety and achievement. In PISA 2012, student anxiety and achievement in mathematics correlated negatively in all 64 participating countries, with all but one correlation significant; no pooled effect size is reported in the chapter.
finding.measure: Mathematics achievement and math anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The chapter links SEL-related experiences such as play, creativity, trust, perspective-taking, and collaboration to durable skills including problem-solving, creativity, and cooperation. It argues that supportive relationships and creative environments foster curiosity, risk-taking, and divergent thinking, but the chapter does not report a single quantitative effect estimate.
finding.measure: Creative thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and perspective-taking

finding.finding_summary: The chapter states that play and creative approaches are associated with a range of learning outcomes beyond literacy and math, including language ability, social and emotional regulation, and causal reasoning. These claims are based on cited prior studies and synthesis rather than a new empirical analysis in the chapter itself.
finding.measure: Language ability, social and emotional regulation, causal reasoning

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper discusses formative assessment and argues for its use in higher education, especially through an e-learning platform (BlackBoard). The authors frame formative assessment as a way to provide frequent quizzes, immediate feedback, and continuous monitoring of student learning, with the goal of improving understanding and eventual summative exam performance.

The paper describes an implementation concept at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) using weekly or fortnightly online tests with detailed feedback. A survey of university students was administered to gauge perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard-based testing. Students generally supported the approach, especially because it broke content into smaller topic assessments, provided immediate teacher feedback, and helped them track their strengths and weaknesses.

Empirically, the paper reports descriptive survey results and some statistically significant differences in attitudes across Business, Engineering, and IT streams, but it does not report learning gains from the intervention itself. The article concludes that formative assessment, especially when supported by online tools, is viewed positively and is argued to support learning, though the evidence presented here is perception-based rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported favorable attitudes toward frequent formative assessments and Blackboard-based testing because these supported monitoring progress, reduced uncertainty, and provided immediate feedback. The paper does not report a causal effect on achievement, but survey responses suggest the approach improved motivation and perceived control over learning (n not reported).
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, teacher feedback, and Blackboard online tests (questionnaire responses)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes formative assessment as supporting learning reflection, metacognition, and students' ability to identify and close gaps in understanding. Survey responses indicated that students believed frequent topic-level assessments and immediate feedback helped them correct mistakes and keep track of their learning over the semester (n not reported).
