The paper compares inter-rater and intra-rater agreement among four human raters and between humans and two NLP classifiers, finding substantial agreement for the best model (SFRN) and high consistency for human raters.

Beyond classification, the study pilots clustering of response representations to explore whether similar answers can be grouped for scalable formative assessment feedback. The main conclusion is that AI-assisted scoring is feasible and can support human-machine collaboration for large-enrollment formative assessment, though the authors note a tradeoff between representations that optimize classification accuracy and those that yield useful semantic clusters.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that NLP-assisted scoring can support scalable formative assessment by reducing the burden of manually scoring short-answer responses in large-enrollment courses. The best algorithm (SFRN) achieved 83% classification accuracy versus 72% for the LSTM baseline, with pairwise agreement with human raters ranging from QWK=0.7403 to 0.8151 and overall four-way Fleiss’ kappa=0.678 on the test set.
finding.measure: Classification accuracy; quadratic weighted kappa (QWK); Fleiss’ kappa for agreement between human raters and the NLP algorithm
finding.study_size: n=1,935 students; 7,258 unique task-responses; test set n=653 responses

paper_profiles.title: Embedded Formative Assessment in the Undergraduate Engineering Classroom
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Annual Conference & Exposition
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues for the value of embedded formative assessment in undergraduate engineering classrooms and explains how technology can reduce the clerical burden of collecting and analyzing student responses. The authors frame formative assessment as a way to make student thinking visible, support active learning and metacognition, and help instructors adjust instruction in real time.

The paper is primarily a conceptual and practice-oriented overview rather than an empirical study. It describes common implementation options such as clickers, text messaging, cloud-based polling tools, and open-format responses, and it highlights the advantages of open-ended questions for revealing student reasoning in engineering contexts. The authors illustrate these ideas with examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course in which students used Tablet PCs and InkSurvey to submit graphical solutions to in-class questions.

The paper concludes that embedded formative assessment is improving undergraduate engineering education by encouraging active learning, increasing student metacognition, and informing instruction. It also argues that technology-facilitated tools make the approach more feasible at scale, but that its full potential depends on instructors responding flexibly to student misconceptions and asking questions that genuinely reveal thinking.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that embedded formative assessment can increase student metacognition and critical thinking by making student reasoning visible and prompting students to focus on the process of solving problems rather than only the final answer. The evidence is illustrative rather than statistical; the paper describes classroom examples from an undergraduate electromagnetics course (n=60) showing that open-format questions revealed students' misconceptions, shortcuts, and difficulty with calculus-based reasoning.
finding.measure: Student written/graphical responses to open-format formative assessment questions; instructor observation of reasoning quality and misconceptions

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents embedded formative assessment as a way to improve understanding of scientific and engineering concepts by probing how students apply principles such as Gauss's law and by exposing misconceptions in real time. In the electromagnetics example (n=60), the instructor observed that students' open-format responses revealed difficulties with derivations, limits, dot products, symmetry arguments, and transferring a derived result to a follow-up graphing task.
finding.measure: Open-format conceptual and derivation questions in an undergraduate electromagnetics course

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims formative assessment can increase engagement, student confidence, and motivation by actively involving students in learning and allowing anonymous responses that reduce embarrassment. These claims are supported descriptively through the classroom examples and discussion of how students become more focused on the 'journey' to a solution, but no quantitative effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: Student engagement, metacognitive awareness, and confidence as observed/argued in classroom use of formative assessment

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that technology-assisted formative assessment reduces the clerical burden on instructors by streamlining collection and analysis of student responses. The authors describe clickers, texting, cloud-based apps, and InkSurvey as enabling real-time feedback and faster turnaround; this is presented as a practical benefit rather than a statistically tested outcome.
finding.measure: Instructor time/clerical burden in collecting and interpreting student responses

paper_profiles.title: Receptive vocabulary and early literacy skills in emergent bilingual Northern Sotho-English children
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether receptive vocabulary knowledge in two languages is associated with early literacy skills among emergent bilingual Grade 1 Northern Sotho-English children in South Africa. The paper addresses a practical question in early literacy research: whether vocabulary size can help identify children at risk of poor literacy development, especially in low-SES contexts where learners may be instructed in either English or Northern Sotho.

The study compared two groups of Grade 1 learners (n=99 total; n=49 English LoLT, n=50 Northern Sotho LoLT) on receptive vocabulary in English and Northern Sotho, letter knowledge, phoneme-grapheme correspondences, and early writing. Measures included the PPVT (English and a translated Northern Sotho version), letter naming, phoneme matching, and name writing. The analyses were correlational and regression-based, with group comparisons and MANCOVA used to assess differences while controlling for vocabulary.

Results showed that English and Northern Sotho receptive vocabulary were both positively related to early literacy skills, with English vocabulary predicting all three literacy outcomes and Northern Sotho vocabulary predicting phoneme-grapheme correspondences and early writing. The language of instruction did not significantly predict early literacy once vocabulary was controlled. The author concludes that vocabulary development in both L1 and L2 is important, and that mother-tongue instruction alone does not guarantee literacy success if vocabulary and broader educational supports are weak.

finding.finding_summary: Receptive vocabulary in both English and Northern Sotho was positively associated with early literacy outcomes in Grade 1 learners (n=99). English receptive vocabulary significantly predicted letter knowledge (F[1,95]=14.37, p=0.000), phoneme-grapheme correspondences (F[1,95]=29.26, p=0.000), and early writing (F[1,95]=10.28, p=0.002); Northern Sotho receptive vocabulary significantly predicted phoneme-grapheme correspondences (F[1,95]=9.51, p=0.003) and early writing (F[1,95]=7.83, p=0.006).
finding.measure: PPVT-based receptive vocabulary; letter naming; phoneme-grapheme correspondence matching; early writing (name/surname writing)

paper_profiles.title: Effectiveness of Computer-Based Scaffolding in the Context of Problem-Based Learning for STEM Education: Bayesian Meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This Bayesian meta-analysis examines whether computer-based scaffolding improves student learning in problem-based learning (PBL) settings for STEM education, and whether effects differ by scaffolding characteristics and instructional context. The authors note limitations of traditional meta-analysis, especially small-study effects and sparse subgroups, and use Bayesian methods to estimate effects across multiple moderator categories.

The study synthesizes 21 studies with 47 outcomes published from 1990 to 2015. It evaluates overall scaffolding effects and six moderator domains: scaffolding intervention type, scaffolding customization, scaffolding customization method, scaffolding strategies, higher-order thinking skill targeted, and discipline. Outcomes were cognitive/higher-order learning outcomes in PBL STEM contexts, analyzed with Hedges’s g and Bayesian credible intervals.

Overall, computer-based scaffolding had a positive effect on cognitive outcomes (g = 0.385, 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802). Effects varied by moderator: metacognitive and strategic scaffolding outperformed conceptual scaffolding; customized scaffolding outperformed no customization, with fading/adding the largest effect; self-selected customization methods showed the largest effects; expert modeling and feedback outperformed question prompts; analysis outcomes improved more than synthesis or evaluation; and effects were larger in engineering, technology, and mathematics than in science or integrated STEM. The paper concludes that computer-based scaffolding is beneficial in PBL STEM settings, but its effectiveness depends strongly on design features and disciplinary context.

finding.finding_summary: Computer-based scaffolding significantly improved cognitive/higher-order learning outcomes in PBL STEM education overall, with g = 0.385 and 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802 based on 20,000 MCMC iterations. The paper’s central outcomes are analysis, synthesis, and evaluation—i.e., higher-order thinking skills—rather than basic achievement measures.
finding.measure: Higher-order cognitive outcomes in problem-based learning STEM tasks (analysis, synthesis, evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis directly examined STEM problem-based learning outcomes and found a moderate positive effect of computer-based scaffolding on cognitive performance in that context. Effects varied by discipline, with larger effects in engineering (g = 0.528), technology (g = 0.379), and mathematics (g = 0.425) than in science (g = 0.146), indicating the intervention benefited scientific/STEM reasoning tasks unevenly across disciplines.
finding.measure: Cognitive learning outcomes in STEM PBL by discipline
finding.effect_size: g = 0.385 overall; discipline-specific g values reported
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CrI 0.022 to 0.802 overall; discipline-specific CrIs reported in text

paper_profiles.title: Teaching children to write: A meta-analysis of writing intervention research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical instructional question in elementary literacy: which writing interventions most effectively improve the writing quality of students in grades 4–6. The authors note that writing instruction in elementary school is often limited and that students in the upper elementary grades still show weak writing performance, so they synthesize experimental and quasi-experimental evidence to identify effective practices.

The study meta-analyzes 32 writing intervention studies (55 effect sizes) conducted in regular classroom settings with students in grades 4–6. Interventions were grouped into ten categories, including strategy instruction, text structure instruction, peer assistance, evaluation, goal setting, feedback, grammar instruction, revision, prewriting activities, and the process approach. The primary outcome was posttest text quality, with effect sizes computed as Hedges’ g.

Overall, writing interventions had a positive average effect on writing quality (g = 0.72, 95% CI [0.49, 0.94]). The largest estimated effects were for goal setting (g = 2.03), strategy instruction (g = 0.96), text structure instruction (g = 0.76), feedback (g = 0.88), and peer assistance (g = 0.59), while grammar instruction (g = -0.37) and the process approach (g = -0.25) showed negative average effects. Moderator analyses suggested that strategy instruction was especially effective in grade 6 and that analytical scoring yielded smaller effects than holistic scoring.

The authors conclude that explicit, targeted writing instruction is generally beneficial for upper-elementary students, with strategy instruction, text structure instruction, goal setting, feedback, and peer assistance emerging as the most promising approaches. They also caution that several categories were small and heterogeneous, so some findings—especially goal setting—should be interpreted cautiously and replicated in additional studies.

finding.finding_summary: Across 32 experimental and quasi-experimental studies (55 effect sizes), writing interventions improved posttest writing quality with an overall Hedges’ g = 0.72 (95% CI [0.49, 0.94]). The meta-analysis found the strongest positive category effects for goal setting (g = 2.03), strategy instruction (g = 0.96), text structure instruction (g = 0.76), feedback (g = 0.88), and peer assistance (g = 0.59), while grammar instruction (g = -0.37) and the process approach (g = -0.25) were negative.
finding.measure: Posttest writing text quality (holistic or analytic ratings of student writing)
finding.effect_size: g=0.72 overall; category effects ranged from g=-0.37 to g=2.03
finding.confidence_interval: overall 95% CI [0.49, 0.94]; category CIs reported in paper

finding.finding_summary: The paper included interventions that explicitly targeted self-regulation-related components, such as strategy instruction with self-regulation and goal setting with feedback. These approaches were associated with large positive writing outcomes, especially strategy instruction/self-regulated strategy development and goal setting, suggesting that self-regulatory supports contributed to improved writing performance.
finding.measure: Writing quality following interventions that included self-regulation, goal setting, and feedback components

paper_profiles.title: Opportunities and challenges of using generative AI to personalize educational assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective article examines how generative AI (GenAI), especially large language models, could be used to personalize educational assessment. The paper asks what opportunities such tools create for assessment design and delivery, and what risks they introduce for validity, reliability, fairness, privacy, and explainability.

Rather than reporting a primary empirical study, the authors synthesize prior work and outline conceptual use cases for GenAI in assessment. They describe potential applications in personalized formative feedback, adaptive item generation, conversational agents, reporting dashboards, and accessibility supports for multilingual and neurodiverse learners. The article also argues that GenAI could improve engagement, performance, and access, but only if carefully constrained by evidence-centered design, human-in-the-loop review, standards, and guardrails.

The context is broad educational assessment, including formative and summative settings, with examples drawn from K-12 and related digital learning environments. The main conclusion is cautiously optimistic: GenAI may make assessments more personalized and inclusive, but its black-box behavior, bias, and lack of control create substantial measurement and equity risks that must be addressed before operational use.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that personalized assessments may increase learner motivation and engagement, which in turn can improve effort during test-taking and make scores more representative of what students know and can do. It does not report original effect sizes, but it cites prior work showing personalized learning can enhance motivation and engagement and frames GenAI as a way to support these outcomes in assessment.
finding.measure: Motivation and engagement during test-taking

finding.finding_summary: The article proposes that GenAI could improve assessment workflow efficiency by generating or modifying items in real time, producing adaptive feedback, and supporting reporting dashboards. No original study is conducted, so no effect sizes or sample sizes are reported; the claim is conceptual and based on anticipated workflow gains.
finding.measure: Assessment content generation, feedback delivery, and reporting efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution is the argument that GenAI may broaden access and personalization for multilingual and neurodiverse learners, but may also threaten validity, reliability, and fairness if used without strong guardrails. The paper does not present empirical institutional outcomes; instead, it synthesizes concerns and opportunities related to assessment governance, standards, and responsible AI use.
finding.measure: Validity, reliability, fairness, access, and responsible-use considerations in assessment systems

paper_profiles.title: Adaptation of Teachers' Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Scale into Turkish Culture and a Structural Equation Modeling
paper_profiles.venue: International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses two related questions: whether the Teachers’ Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Scale (TCPFS) can be translated and adapted for Turkish teachers, and whether the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) can explain teachers’ intentions and self-reported practices of formative assessment. The study is motivated by the need for a validated instrument and a stronger theoretical understanding of why teachers do or do not use formative assessment in classrooms.

The authors translated and culturally adapted the 40-item TCPFS, then administered the Turkish version to 400 primary school teachers in public schools in two Turkish provinces. Psychometric analyses included confirmatory factor analysis and Cronbach’s alpha, followed by structural equation modeling to test the TPB model. After removing three weak items, the adapted scale showed acceptable fit and strong internal consistency. The TPB model fit the data reasonably well and suggested that self-efficacy was the strongest predictor of teachers’ intentions to use formative assessment, while self-efficacy and perceived behavioral control were the strongest predictors of reported formative assessment behavior.

Overall, the paper concludes that the Turkish version of TCPFS is a usable research tool and that TPB is a useful framework for understanding Turkish primary teachers’ formative assessment conceptions and practices. The study is about teacher attitudes, intentions, and self-reported practice rather than student learning outcomes, and it does not examine subgroup effects, prior achievement, disability, or English learner status.

finding.finding_summary: The study provides evidence that the Turkish adaptation of the Teachers’ Conceptions and Practices of Formative Assessment Scale (TCPFS) had acceptable psychometric properties after item removal. Confirmatory factor analysis showed fairly good fit after modification (χ2=1906.27, df=567, RMSEA=.07, CFI=.90, TLI=.87, IFI=.90), and internal consistency was high (Cronbach’s alpha=.95 for the full scale; .83-.93 for subscales).
finding.measure: Psychometric validity and reliability of the adapted TCPFS scale (CFA fit indices; Cronbach’s alpha)

finding.finding_summary: The structural equation model suggests that the TPB framework can help explain teachers’ formative assessment intentions and self-reported practices. The model explained 71% of the variance in intention and 15% of the variance in behavior; self-efficacy was the strongest predictor of intention (β=.55), and self-efficacy (β=.68) and controllability (β=-.52) predicted behavior, while intention was not significant.
finding.measure: Teachers’ intentions and self-reported formative assessment behavior

paper_profiles.title: Automatically Creating Bilingual Lexicons for Machine Translation from Bilingual Text
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of how to automatically expand a machine translation (MT) system’s bilingual lexicon using aligned bilingual text. Rather than learning sentence-level translation templates in the abstract, the author proposes a parse-parse-match approach in which existing MT resources are reused to infer new bilingual lexical entries from pairs of aligned sentences.

The method assumes a bidirectional, lexicalist MT system with parsing and transfer capabilities already in place. Bilingual lexical templates are first extracted from an existing bilingual lexicon and then used to transfer the source sentence parse into a target-side bag of lexical items; this transferred bag is matched against the parse of the target sentence. When the bags unify, new bilingual entries are created from the aligned lexical items and the template structure.

The paper illustrates the approach with an English-Spanish example sentence pair and shows how entries for content words and multiword combinations can be automatically induced. The main conclusion is that, given enough template coverage and a bidirectional MT architecture, the system can bootstrap its own bilingual lexicon with little or no additional external linguistic resources. The paper is methodological and does not evaluate educational outcomes or learner populations.

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper discusses the rationale for formative assessment and reports a small university survey on students’ perceptions of implementing formative assessment through an e-learning system (BlackBoard). The authors frame formative assessment as a way to support learning through frequent low-stakes testing and immediate feedback, arguing that it should help students prepare for end-of-semester summative exams.

The implementation described is a series of weekly or fortnightly online tests in BlackBoard, with automatic scoring and detailed feedback, alongside the option to use discussion forums and virtual classroom tools for follow-up. The paper does not report an experimental comparison of learning outcomes; instead, it presents survey evidence about student attitudes toward continuous assessment, online testing, and feedback. Students generally favored the approach because it broke material into smaller topic-based assessments, provided immediate feedback, and was more flexible than classroom tests.

The survey sampled students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams at Swinburne University of Technology’s Sarawak campus. Students’ responses suggested broad support for frequent assessments and teacher feedback, while also noting concerns about stress and the possibility that learning might be overemphasized relative to grades. The paper concludes that technology-supported formative assessment is workable and potentially helpful for improving learning and summative performance, but it provides no direct causal evidence of achievement gains.

finding.finding_summary: Students generally reported favorable attitudes toward frequent formative assessment and online testing because it provided immediate feedback, flexibility, and helped them monitor strengths and weaknesses. However, open-ended responses also noted stress/pressure from too many tests, so the attitudinal pattern was positive overall but not uniformly so.
finding.measure: Student perception survey on continuous assessment, feedback, and BlackBoard online test implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognitive processes such as reflecting on feedback, recognizing errors, and checking whether one is on track. Survey responses indicated that students valued feedback for identifying strengths and weaknesses and for helping them work through topic-by-topic learning.
finding.measure: Survey items on feedback usefulness, self-monitoring, and perceived learning progress

finding.finding_summary: Students supported frequent internal assessments and believed the approach could help them learn course content progressively and perform better on the semester examination. The paper reports no achievement scores or effect sizes, but respondents perceived the weekly/fortnightly BlackBoard assessments as useful for subject learning and exam preparation.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and anticipated summative exam performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that BlackBoard-based online tests are a practical way to deliver frequent formative assessment with automatic scoring and immediate detailed feedback, reducing delay compared with classroom-based approaches. This is presented as an implementation advantage rather than a measured efficiency outcome.
finding.measure: Implementation feasibility and workflow features of BlackBoard online tests

paper_profiles.title: Crosslingual Structural Priming and the Pre-Training Dynamics of Bilingual Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether multilingual language models develop abstract grammatical representations that are shared across languages, and when such representations emerge during pre-training. The authors use crosslingual structural priming as a causal probe: if a Dutch prime increases the probability of an English target with the same syntactic structure, that suggests shared grammatical structure across languages.

To study this, they pre-train a Dutch-English GPT-2 style language model on a large OSCAR corpus, with Dutch-only exposure in the first half of training and mixed Dutch-English exposure in the second half. They then test priming on Dutch primes and English dative targets, tracking normalized target probabilities across pre-training steps. The model shows crosslingual priming effects that become clearly significant soon after English is introduced, with the effect first significantly differing from the baseline at step 500120, after 120 steps of English training and about 983,040 English tokens.

The main conclusion is that crosslingual structural priming can emerge quickly once the model receives some second-language exposure, implying that shared grammatical representations can arise with fewer than 1M tokens in the new language. The authors discuss implications for low-resource transfer and for interpreting apparent zero-shot crosslingual capabilities, suggesting that small amounts of contamination in training data may be enough to produce crosslingual effects.

paper_profiles.title: A Novel Bilingual Word Embedding Method for Lexical Translation Using Bilingual Sense Clique
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of learning bilingual word embeddings for lexical translation. The authors argue that most existing methods rely on shallow local co-occurrence or require separate projection steps, and they propose a graph-based alternative called Bilingual Sense Clique (BSC), which extracts maximal cliques from a bilingual PMI graph built on parallel corpora.

The approach treats source and target words symmetrically and uses BSCs as latent bilingual sense units, analogous to compact bilingual synsets. The BSC-word relationship is then summarized with three dimension-reduction methods: Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Correspondence Analysis (CA), and a neural network CBOW-style model. The paper evaluates these representations on bilingual lexicon induction/translation tasks using WMT11 Spanish-English and IWSLT14 French-English data.

Across the reported translation experiments, the BSC-based methods generally outperform or match prior bilingual embedding baselines, with particularly strong results for CA and NN on some subtasks. The best gains reported are in top-1 or top-5 translation precision, such as BSC+CA improving P@5 by 5 points on WMT11 En-Sp/Sp-En and BSC+CA improving P@5 by 8 points on IWSLT14 Fr-En. The paper concludes that graph-based bilingual sense units are a promising way to construct cross-lingual representations for lexical translation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates bilingual lexical translation, which is directly tied to cross-lingual language representation rather than classroom language learning. On WMT11 Spanish-English and IWSLT14 French-English tasks, BSC-based embeddings generally improved translation precision over prior baselines; for example, BSC+CA reached P@5=56 on WMT11 En-Sp and 60 on WMT11 Sp-En, and BSC+NN achieved P@1=41 on WMT11 En-Sp.
finding.measure: Bilingual lexicon induction / lexical translation precision (P@1, P@5)
finding.study_size: WMT11: training n=132K sentences, dev n=5K, test n=1K; IWSLT14: training n=178K, dev n=5K, test n=1K

paper_profiles.title: A Generalized Constraint Approach to Bilingual Dictionary Induction for Low-Resource Language Families
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of inducing bilingual dictionaries for low-resource language families when parallel corpora, comparable corpora, and machine-readable dictionaries are scarce. The authors focus on closely related languages and propose a generalized constraint-based framework that expands prior pivot-based bilingual lexicon induction methods by adding an n-cycle symmetry assumption and additional heuristics for identifying cognates and cognate synonyms.

The method models translation connectivity as a tripartite transgraph linking a source language, a pivot language, and a target language. It then formulates the extraction task as a weighted partial MaxSAT optimization problem, using heuristics such as cognate pair coexistence probability, missing contribution rate, polysemy pivot ambiguity rate, and form similarity (LCSR) to rank and add likely edges. The paper evaluates the approach on four case studies spanning one Austronesian low-resource setting and three Indo-European language pairs, comparing against prior constraint-based methods, inverse consultation, and Cartesian-product baselines.

The main conclusion is that the generalized method improves precision and F-score over the authors’ previous constraint-based approaches, with statistically significant gains reported for the proposed methods. The paper argues that the framework is especially useful for low-resource, closely related languages and can complement other bilingual dictionary creation methods, such as word alignment approaches that rely on parallel corpora. This is a computational linguistics paper about bilingual lexicon induction, not an education study, so it does not directly investigate learner outcomes or instructional effects.

paper_profiles.title: BiToD: A Bilingual Multi-Domain Dataset For Task-Oriented Dialogue Modeling
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BiToD, a bilingual (English/Chinese) multi-domain dataset for end-to-end task-oriented dialogue modeling. The paper addresses the lack of bilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks in task-oriented dialogue, which limits development and evaluation of robust multilingual conversational agents.

The dataset is constructed from a bilingual knowledge base covering Hong Kong tourism and services, with 7,232 dialogues and 144,798 utterances across restaurants, hotels, attractions, metro, and weather. Dialogues are generated through a machine-to-machine style pipeline, then paraphrased by crowdworkers to sound natural, and annotated with dialogue states, speech acts, and API calls. The paper evaluates baseline multilingual sequence-to-sequence models (mBART and mT5) on dialogue state tracking and end-to-end task completion under monolingual, bilingual, and cross-lingual settings.

Main findings are about benchmark performance rather than educational outcomes. The authors report that bilingual training can outperform separate monolingual systems in some settings, and that cross-lingual pretraining plus mixed-language pretraining improves low-resource transfer. The paper concludes that BiToD is a useful benchmark for studying multilingual task-oriented dialogue and cross-lingual transfer in low-resource conditions.

paper_profiles.title: How a Bilingual LM Becomes Bilingual: Tracing Internal Representations with Sparse Autoencoders
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how bilingual language models develop internal representations over the course of pretraining. The central question is whether models first learn English and Japanese separately and later align them bilingually, and whether this process differs by layer and model size.

To study this, the authors train sparse autoencoders (TopK-SAEs) on hidden states from multiple checkpoints of LLM-jp bilingual decoder-only models ranging from 150M to 3.7B parameters. They analyze feature activations across training stages, layers, and model sizes using language selectivity, token entropy, semantic entropy, monosemanticity, and span length measures.

The main finding is that bilingual models appear to learn in phases: early training learns language-specific representations, mid-to-late training develops bilingual semantic alignment, and mid-layers are the clearest site of bilingual features. Larger models show stronger bilingual alignment than smaller ones, while lower layers tend to be polysemantic and upper layers capture longer spans rather than token-level semantics. The paper also reports an intervention experiment showing that injecting bilingual features from a fully trained model into a mid-training model improves perplexity and translation-like performance metrics (COMET-22), suggesting that bilingual representations are functionally important for performance.

paper_profiles.title: Creating Reverse Bilingual Dictionaries
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of creating reverse bilingual dictionaries when only a standard bilingual dictionary is available and one of the languages is resource-poor. The authors argue that many languages lack sufficient lexical resources, making dictionary creation difficult, and they propose automated methods to generate reverse dictionaries from existing bilingual dictionaries that involve English and another language.

The paper presents three algorithms: Direct Reversal (DR), Direct Reversal with Distance (DRwD), and Direct Reversal with Similarity (DRwS). DR simply swaps source and sense entries; DRwD expands entries using WordNet distance thresholds; and DRwS uses WordNet synsets, synonyms, hyponyms, and hypernyms to compute similarity and add likely equivalent entries. These methods are tested on several bilingual dictionaries including VIE-ENG, ENG-HIN, and dictionaries involving Assamese, Karbi (AJZ), and Dimasa.

Evaluation was carried out by bilingual human volunteers who rated randomly selected dictionary entries on a 5-point scale. The authors report that DRwS generally produced the best balance of precision and coverage, with higher average entry scores and more entries than simple reversal, especially when using a similarity threshold of beta >= 0.9. The methods worked best for languages and dictionaries with simpler single-word senses, and less well for dictionaries with many complex compound phrases such as Vietnamese entries. The paper concludes that WordNet-based reversal can generate useful reverse bilingual dictionaries without relying on intermediate languages or dictionaries, especially for resource-poor languages.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies the efficiency of automated bilingual dictionary construction. Compared with direct reversal, the WordNet-based DRwD and especially DRwS methods increased the number of usable reverse-dictionary entries while reducing manual effort needed to create such resources. For the AJZ-ENG reverse dictionary, DR produced 4,677 entries and DRwS produced 5,941 entries; the DRwS dictionary had an average human evaluation score of 4.07 on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Number of reverse-dictionary entries generated; human ratings of dictionary entry quality on a 5-point scale

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment: A Significant Facilitator of Student Learning
paper_profiles.population: Not clearly specified; general discussion of students and teachers in K-12 / broader education contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a short conceptual/article-style discussion of formative assessment and its role in supporting student learning. It defines formative assessment, contrasts it with summative assessment, and describes common formative practices such as quizzes, observation records, classroom questioning, feedback, self-assessment, and peer assessment.

The paper argues that formative assessment helps students identify learning gaps, adjust study strategies, increase engagement, strengthen motivation, and develop reflective and critical thinking skills. It also argues that formative assessment helps teachers diagnose prior knowledge, adjust instruction, and improve teaching effectiveness. The paper does not present original empirical data of its own; instead, it summarizes and cites prior work, including a separate study in the same journal issue reporting better conceptual learning when formative assessment was embedded in inquiry-based teaching.

Because the paper is primarily expository and synthesis-oriented, it should be treated as a conceptual overview rather than a direct comparative evaluation of formative assessment against alternative assessment conditions. It is useful for background and theory, but it does not itself provide a new experimental comparison, sample size, or effect estimate.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment can increase students’ engagement, motivation, satisfaction, and confidence by making progress visible and by providing timely, specific feedback. No original study data are reported in this article; the claims are descriptive and supported by cited literature rather than a new experiment.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, satisfaction, confidence (described conceptually)

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that self-assessment and peer assessment within formative assessment can foster reflective and critical thinking abilities. This is presented as a general claim based on prior literature, not as an independently measured effect in the paper.
finding.measure: Reflective thinking and critical thinking (conceptual/descriptive)

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that formative assessment helps teachers diagnose prior knowledge, adjust instruction, and optimize teaching efficacy by using assessment information to modify classroom activities and subsequent content. No quantitative teacher-workload or productivity data are reported.
finding.measure: Teaching efficacy / instructional adjustment (descriptive)

paper_profiles.title: Comparing online quizzes and take-home assignments as formative assessments in a 100-level economics course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether online multiple-choice quizzes can serve as an effective formative assessment alternative to traditional take-home written assignments in an introductory economics course. The authors are motivated by both pedagogical and operational questions: whether formative assessment improves engagement and later exam performance, and whether online delivery offers feedback and cost advantages over manual marking.

Using course records from six semesters of take-home assignments (2001–2003; n=1802) and six semesters of online quizzes (2008–2011; n=1204), the paper compares participation, feedback timeliness, course-weighting fit, and delivery cost. Both formats produced high participation, with similar proportions of students completing most tasks, but online quizzes provided immediate feedback and had near-zero marginal cost, while assignments took up to five weeks for feedback and were expensive to write and mark.

The authors find no evidence that take-home assignments produced better subsequent exam outcomes than online quizzes. In both conditions, passing the formative assessment did not guarantee an exam pass, but failing it strongly signaled lack of engagement and near-certain exam failure. The main conclusion is that online quizzes were as effective as take-home assignments as formative assessments, while being substantially cheaper and providing faster feedback; the paper also argues that the lower 10% quiz weighting fit the course better than the earlier 30% assignment weighting.

finding.finding_summary: The paper found no evidence that on-paper take-home assignments were more effective than online quizzes in supporting later exam performance. Across six semesters of each condition, formative assessment marks were poorly correlated with exam marks; passing the formative assessment did not ensure an exam pass, and only 2%-3% of students passed the exam after failing the formative assessment.
finding.measure: Formative assessment marks versus final exam marks; conditional exam pass rates after passing/failing formative assessments

finding.finding_summary: Both assessment formats were highly effective at generating student participation and sustained engagement over the semester. About 93% of students completed at least four of five assignments and 93% completed at least seven of twelve quizzes, suggesting that low-stakes graded formative assessment can support persistence and engagement.
finding.measure: Participation/completion rates for assignments and quizzes

finding.finding_summary: Online quizzes were far more efficient to administer than take-home assignments. Feedback was immediate and marking took seconds, while assignments took up to five weeks for feedback and required substantial manual marking; the authors conclude that the marginal cost of quizzes was close to zero compared with the high cost of assignments.
finding.measure: Feedback turnaround time and delivery/marking cost

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that recalibrating the formative assessment weight from 30% for assignments to 10% for quizzes produced a better fit within the overall assessment regime without harming course outcomes. The authors argue that the lower weighting was sufficient to incentivize participation and allowed a more balanced assessment structure.
finding.measure: Course assessment weighting, overall course pass rates, and mean marks

paper_profiles.title: Comparing online quizzes and take-home assignments as formative assessments in a 100-level economics course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether two forms of graded formative assessment in an introductory economics course—traditional take-home assignments and online multiple-choice quizzes—differ in their effectiveness for promoting student engagement, feedback timeliness, assessment fit, and delivery cost. The authors compare course data from six semesters using assignments (2001–2003) and six semesters using quizzes (2008–2011), focusing on students in a 100-level undergraduate economics course at Lincoln University.

Both assessment formats were open-book, low-stakes, and intended to function as learning exercises rather than definitive measures of mastery. The study compares participation rates, feedback timing, alignment with the rest of the course assessment system, and administrative cost. The online quizzes provided immediate automated feedback and near-zero marginal cost, whereas assignments produced more detailed feedback but required up to five weeks for turnaround and were expensive to mark.

The main conclusion is that, overall, online quizzes were about as effective as take-home assignments as formative assessments for engagement and subsequent course functioning, while costing substantially less. However, the paper also shows that success on either formative task was only weakly predictive of exam success: passing the formative task did not ensure a pass on the final exam, while failing it was a strong warning sign of likely exam failure. The authors therefore argue that the key value of formative assessment lies in maintaining engagement, and that online quizzes are a more efficient way to do so than written take-home assignments.

finding.finding_summary: Both assignments and quizzes were highly effective at sustaining student engagement, but success on the formative tasks did not translate reliably into exam success. Participation was very high in both conditions (assignments: 93% submitted at least 4 of 5; quizzes: 93% submitted at least 7 of 12), suggesting both formats supported persistence and course engagement.
finding.measure: Participation/completion rates in formative assessments; engagement with course work

finding.finding_summary: Online quizzes were much more efficient to deliver than take-home assignments. Quiz feedback was immediate and automated, while assignment feedback took up to five weeks; the marginal cost of quizzes was close to zero compared with the substantial marking and administration cost of assignments.
finding.measure: Feedback turnaround time and delivery/admin cost

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that reducing formative-assessment weighting from 30% (assignments) to 10% (quizzes) fit better within the overall course assessment structure while maintaining similar course outcomes. The authors conclude that the lower-weight quiz regime produced a better-balanced assessment package and comparable overall course mean/pass rates.
finding.measure: Course assessment balance, total course mean, course pass rate

paper_profiles.title: A Case Study of Using Test-Enhanced Learning as a Formative Assessment in High School Mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Science and Mathematics Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory case study asks whether test-enhanced learning can function as an effective formative assessment strategy in high school mathematics, particularly in a context with a large achievement gap between an urban high-needs vocational school and an elite grammar school in Hungary. The authors are motivated by prior retrieval-practice research and by the limited evidence for its use in authentic mathematics classrooms.

The intervention was implemented in ninth-grade geometry lessons. In the experimental vocational-school group (n=9), students completed a short test at the end of each lesson on that day’s material, received feedback, and those scores contributed to end-of-term grades. Two comparison groups served as controls: another vocational-school group (n=23) and an elite grammar-school group (n=34), where students were taught the same content but the lesson-end problems were explained by the teacher rather than tested. All groups took the same final test, which included theory and problem-solving items, to assess longer-term retention.

Results showed that the experimental group outperformed the vocational-school control group and did not differ significantly from the elite grammar-school group on the final test. The authors interpret this as evidence that retrieval-based formative assessment improved geometry learning and helped reduce the performance gap in long-term retention. They also note important limitations: small group sizes, non-equivalent lesson counts between schools, and non-random teacher assignment, so the findings are promising but preliminary.

finding.finding_summary: The retrieval-based formative assessment condition improved geometry learning outcomes. On the final test, the experimental group (n=9) scored significantly higher than the vocational-school control group and statistically matched the elite grammar-school control group, with total scores showing F(2,63)=11.03, p<0.01, ηp²=0.259. Task-level results also favored the experimental group on theory and problem-solving items, indicating better long-term retention of mathematics knowledge.
finding.measure: Geometry final test scores (theoretical questions and problem-solving tasks)
finding.study_size: n=66 total (experimental n=9, control-vocational n=23, control-grammar n=34)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that repeated successful end-of-class testing may have improved students’ self-efficacy, especially in the experimental vocational-school group, which had been perceived as the weakest group. This claim is discussed qualitatively rather than measured directly; the authors point to strong performance on the end-of-lesson tests (reported as 78%–96% and about 80% average) as suggestive evidence.
finding.measure: Observed test performance and inferred self-efficacy discussion

paper_profiles.title: Procedural Generation of STEM Quizzes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint addresses the inefficiency of creating large, varied, and up-to-date STEM quiz banks in conventional learning management systems (LMS), where question authoring through graphical user interfaces is slow and hard to scale. The paper proposes a procedural, script-based Python API for generating quiz questions and variants, including multiple-choice, numerical, matching, fill-in-the-blank, and dynamically generated content such as formulas, plots, images, and interactive 3D objects.

The core contribution is a proof-of-concept tool for instructors that supports random question generation from lists or key-answer pairs, local preview, and easy maintenance/version control. The author compares the script-based workflow with Moodle’s GUI in a small user study and through timing estimates, arguing that the script-based method substantially reduces authoring time and improves reusability and richness of questions.

The evaluation involved trained computer science instructors and focused on question creation speed rather than student learning outcomes. The paper reports that script-based creation was consistently faster than Moodle for simple questions, and estimates even larger speedups for more complex, reusable question-generation scripts. Overall, the study concludes that procedural generation is a practical way to improve operational efficiency in STEM quiz authoring and maintenance, especially for instructors with some programming experience.

finding.finding_summary: The script-based API substantially reduced quiz authoring time compared with Moodle’s GUI. In a user study with five trained users creating 20 text-based multiple-choice questions, the script-based approach was about 49 seconds faster per question on average, with fitted models estimating T = 0.197n + 12.5 s for the script-based method versus T = 0.19n + 61.3 s for Moodle (n = average characters per question = 265; R² > 0.94).
finding.measure: Question creation/typing time for quiz authoring in Moodle GUI vs script-based Python API

finding.finding_summary: The paper demonstrates that the API can generate numerical and multiple-choice questions involving calculus, quadratic equations, matrices, determinants, and other math content. However, it does not evaluate student learning or test-score gains from these math questions; the evidence is limited to authoring feasibility and example generation rather than learning outcomes.
finding.measure: Feasibility/examples of generated mathematics quiz questions

paper_profiles.title: EFL learners’ motivation in a gamified formative assessment: The case of Quizizz
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether a gamified formative assessment tool, Quizizz, changes young EFL learners’ motivation beyond what is typical in traditional formative assessment. Framed by self-determination theory, the authors ask whether gamified assessment supports students’ internalization of motivation and whether it shifts learners from more controlled forms of regulation toward more autonomous forms of motivation.

The study was conducted with 45 Chinese elementary school EFL learners aged 8–10, split into a control group and an experimental group. Over 20 weeks, both groups completed weekly formative assessments after online instruction; the experimental group used Quizizz while the control group used PDF-based assessments. The researchers used questionnaires, interviews with students and some parents, and Quizizz performance reports, analyzing the data with paired t-tests, correlations, and simple regression. They report that Quizizz increased students’ motivation, engagement, and assessment accuracy, with the experimental group outperforming the control group (accuracy 89.05% vs. 74.01%) and showing stronger internalization of motivation, especially in the later stage when feedback was emphasized over external rewards.

The main conclusion is that gamified formative assessment can support elementary EFL learners’ motivational internalization, engagement, and language-task performance. The authors interpret early gains as linked to competition and rewards, and later gains as tied to feedback and perceived value of learning. They argue that Quizizz helped students move from introjected regulation toward identified regulation, and that a small subset of learners displayed intrinsic motivation characterized by curiosity and enjoyment. The paper does not study long-term retention or transfer directly, but it provides evidence that gamified formative assessment can positively influence engagement-related outcomes in primary EFL classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The study reports improved EFL performance/accuracy in the experimental group using Quizizz compared with the control group using PDF-based formative assessment. Overall accuracy was 89.05% for the experimental group versus 74.01% for the control group (n=45 total; EG n=23, CG n=22), suggesting better language-learning task performance in the gamified condition.
finding.measure: Accuracy on weekly EFL formative assessment items based on THINK Starter vocabulary

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central finding is that gamified formative assessment increased learner motivation and internalization. Post-questionnaire motivation improved from a pre-questionnaire mean of -1.07 to -0.15, and interview data indicated movement from introjected regulation in stage 1 to identified regulation in stage 2; five students were described as reaching intrinsic motivation. The authors also report that motivation correlated with performance and engagement.
finding.measure: Motivation questionnaire, interview-coded self-determination motivation, engagement/attendance during assessment
finding.std_deviation: pre-questionnaire SDs not_reported; interview-coded motivation SDs not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes evidence related to self-regulated behaviors such as reattempting assessments, reviewing mistakes, and time management around Quizizz tasks. In the experimental group, 43.48% of assessments were retaken more than twice, compared with 25% in the control group, and students reported checking feedback and identifying weaknesses, indicating stronger self-monitoring and persistence.
finding.measure: Assessment reattempt rate, reported review of errors, task completion behavior

paper_profiles.title: New Methods for Collaborative Learning for Personalised Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of supporting diverse learner needs in higher education using wireless and mobile technologies. The authors argue that conventional classrooms and assessment approaches often struggle to promote engagement, experiential learning, and personalized formative feedback, especially in resource-constrained settings.

The paper proposes and describes two linked approaches: Dynamic Learning Space (DLS), a technology-enhanced collaborative classroom using wireless learning technologies, and Mobile Collaborative Experiential Learning (MCEL), a mobile, SMS-based simulated learning system that provides automated, personalized formative feedback. The work is framed as a design-based research effort and includes classroom observation, informal participant feedback, and a small pilot survey with postgraduate students at James Cook University Singapore.

Results are exploratory rather than causal. Observations suggest that DLS encouraged active, high-level learning, collaboration, and engagement, while MCEL was viewed by students as usable, fun, technically feasible, and cost-effective. The authors conclude that the approach can extend learning beyond the classroom and support constructive alignment and personalized formative learning, but the evidence is based on a small pilot study without experimental comparison or validated outcome measurement.

finding.finding_summary: The pilot study and classroom observations suggest that the mobile and wireless learning approaches improved student engagement, interest, and sense of ownership over learning. Students reported that the experience was fun, convenient, and that they could continue learning at their own pace; the authors also note that some students replied at midnight, indicating sustained engagement beyond class time.
finding.measure: Student surveys on usability/fun/engagement and classroom observation of participation
finding.study_size: n=22 (pilot); survey responses reported from 6 students

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that the dynamic learning space supported collaborative problem solving, spontaneous group formation, and richer peer-to-peer exchange using texts, audio, images, and video. These observations suggest gains in collaboration and creative problem solving, but no quantitative effect size or validated durable-skills measure was reported.
finding.measure: Observed collaborative interaction, group discussion, and problem-solving behaviors

finding.finding_summary: MCEL was perceived as user-friendly, technically feasible, and cost-effective for delivering formative assessment. Survey ratings were generally high on ease of use, navigation, feedback/communication, and cost acceptability (e.g., user-friendliness items ranged from 3.43 to 4.43 on a 5-point Likert scale), indicating improved process efficiency rather than measured achievement gains.
finding.measure: Student usability/feasibility/cost-effectiveness survey
finding.study_size: n=22 (pilot); 6 questionnaire respondents reported in the results table

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the proposed DLS/MCEL model can extend formative feedback beyond the classroom at low cost and may improve access to education in resource-poor settings. This is presented as an institutional design implication rather than a measured policy outcome, with no quantitative institutional effect reported.
finding.measure: Design-based prototype evaluation and implementation discussion

paper_profiles.title: Examining the Effect of an Online Formative Assessment Tool (OFAT) of Students’ Motivation and Achievement for a University Science Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether an online formative assessment tool (OFAT) can improve university students’ motivation toward science and their achievement in a general science course. The authors situate the work in the broader move toward online and personalized assessment in higher education and argue that formative assessment may be especially useful when it provides immediate feedback, lecturer feedback, and adaptive assignments.

The intervention was implemented with second-year undergraduate students in a primary education bachelor’s program in Spain over four consecutive academic years (2014/15–2017/18). Students used PlayPosit, an OFAT that embedded questions and tasks in short video lessons and provided immediate correctness feedback, lecturer comments, and adaptive assignments based on student performance. The study collected pre- and post-survey data on science motivation/attitudes, standardized achievement data, and platform log records from a total of 311 students.

The authors report positive effects on both motivation and achievement across the four cohorts. Motivation improved on multiple survey items, enjoyment of science increased, and anxiety about science decreased. Achievement also improved on course assessments and final grades, and higher levels of OFAT use were associated with better outcomes. The paper further reports that high-performing students appeared to benefit more than lower-performing students, although the authors note that causal attribution for usage intensity is limited because more motivated students may also have used the tool more. Overall, the study concludes that OFATs can support science learning and motivation in university settings, especially when used intensively and combined with feedback and adaptive assignments.

finding.finding_summary: Students using the OFAT showed improved performance on science-course achievement measures across four cohorts (2014/15–2017/18). The paper reports significant positive results on standardized course assessments and final grades, but does not provide a single overall effect size; gains are described as statistically significant and consistent across years (n=311 total).
finding.measure: Standardized science course achievement, class assessments, lab assessments, and final course grade (pre-/post-test and course grades)

finding.finding_summary: The OFAT improved students’ motivation toward science and attitude toward the course, while reducing science anxiety. Across the repeated cohorts, 12 of 20 motivation items showed significant pre-post change; the paper describes these changes as positive overall, with enjoyment increasing and anxiety decreasing (n=311 total).
finding.measure: Science motivation survey and attitude toward science (20-item Likert questionnaire; pre-test vs post-test)

paper_profiles.title: Fostering the Use of Online Learning Resources: Results of Using a Mobile Collaboration Tool based on Gamification in a Blended Course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether MyMOOCSpace (MMS), a mobile gamified collaboration tool, increases student use of online learning resources in a blended university course that used a SPOC as a complement to face-to-face instruction. The authors motivate the study by noting that students in blended learning environments often do not engage consistently with online materials and that instructors need tools to increase motivation and participation.

The intervention was a voluntary Android mobile app that presented SPOC questions and formative exercises as a team-based game. The quasi-experiment took place in the undergraduate Systems Programming course at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, with 294 students total: 97 in the treatment group (students who requested and used MMS) and 197 in the control group (students who did not use MMS). The study used SPOC database logs, MMS logs, questionnaires, and final grades to compare groups.

The findings indicate that students who used MMS accessed substantially more videos and formative assessment exercises than those who did not, and they also had a higher course passing rate. The paper reports statistically significant differences using Wilcoxon tests for resource consumption and a chi-square test for passing rate. Overall, the study concludes that MMS is correlated with greater engagement with learning resources and better course completion, though the design is non-randomized and the authors note limits to causal interpretation.

finding.finding_summary: Students who used MMS showed greater engagement with SPOC learning resources and reported that the tool supported motivation to use those resources. In the main quantitative results, the MMS group watched more videos (mean 127.75 vs. 51.2) and solved more formative problems (mean 88.87 vs. 36.46) than the non-MMS group; the authors interpret this as increased motivation/engagement in the blended course.
finding.measure: Resource consumption and questionnaire-based motivation/engagement indicators
finding.std_deviation: videos SD: 10.79 (MMS) vs 50.31 (no MMS); problems SD: 4.90 (MMS) vs 34.97 (no MMS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was explicitly designed to foster collaboration and collaborative problem solving in teams of 4-5 students, and the post-experience survey assessed team communication, support behavior, initiative, and leadership. The paper reports that MMS increased interaction with assessment exercises and was intended to improve collaborative work, although no separate numeric outcome for collaboration quality is reported in the excerpt.
finding.measure: Team collaboration / team dimensional training survey; collaborative problem solving questionnaire
finding.study_size: n=294 (with 97 in treatment group; 80% survey response among treatment participants for the final survey)

finding.finding_summary: Use of MMS was associated with greater consumption of formative assessment activities and higher course passing rates. The chi-square test showed a significant association between MMS use and passing the course (Pearson χ2(1)=7.9531, p=0.005), with 34 MMS users passing versus 23 non-users; the authors also report higher engagement with assessment exercises (Wilcoxon z=-13.364, p=0.000).
finding.measure: Formative assessment exercise completion and course passing rate

paper_profiles.title: Sustainability of Developed Self-Regulation by Means of Formative Assessment Among Young Adolescents: A Longitudinal Study
paper_profiles.population: Elementary (PreK-5th) to Early Secondary (transition cohort of sixth graders)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This longitudinal study examined whether a formative assessment intervention in upper primary school has lasting effects on students’ self-regulation, motivation, and self-efficacy after they transition to secondary school. The authors were motivated by the possibility that formative assessment may do more than improve immediate academic performance; it may also help students develop durable self-regulated learning skills that persist across school transitions.

The intervention was delivered to 695 Dutch sixth graders from 17 primary schools over the final seven months of primary school. Students were assigned by school to one of three conditions: self-assessment, peer-assessment, or control. The formative assessment conditions included explicit criteria, checklists/rubrics, opportunities to evaluate work, feedback, and revision in the context of writing tasks. Outcomes were measured at pretest, posttest, and a 10-week follow-up after summer break at the start of secondary education.

Multilevel longitudinal analyses showed that students in the self- and peer-assessment conditions developed higher self-regulation and intrinsic motivation than control students at posttest, and these gains largely persisted at follow-up. External regulation did not differ by condition, extrinsic motivation increased across time for all students, and self-efficacy showed no clear intervention-by-time effect. Overall, the paper concludes that formative assessment can support self-regulation and intrinsic motivation beyond the immediate intervention period, including across the transition to secondary school.

finding.finding_summary: Formative assessment via self-assessment and peer-assessment improved students’ self-regulation compared with the control group. In the 695-student sample, multilevel analyses found significant condition-by-time effects; self- and peer-assessment groups showed gains at posttest that remained at the 10-week follow-up after the transition to secondary school, with no comparable improvement in the control group.
finding.measure: Self-regulation subscale of the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also supported intrinsic motivation. In the same 695-student longitudinal sample, self-assessment and peer-assessment conditions showed significant positive effects at posttest, and the gains did not diminish at follow-up; the control group did not show a similar intervention-related increase.
finding.measure: Intrinsic motivation subscale of the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: External regulation was not affected by the formative assessment intervention. Multilevel models found no significant condition effects and no condition-by-time interactions across the 695 students, indicating that the intervention did not reduce or increase students’ dependence on external sources for regulating learning.
finding.measure: External regulation subscale of the Inventory Learning Style Questionnaire (ILS)

finding.finding_summary: Self-efficacy showed no clear intervention-by-time effect. The paper reports significant main effects of condition and time in some models, but no significant interaction between condition and time, and the authors conclude there was no direct formative-assessment effect on self-efficacy across the transition. The 695-student sample was assessed with a self-efficacy questionnaire at three time points.
finding.measure: Self-Efficacy for Task Performance Questionnaire (STPQ)

paper_profiles.title: Impact of Formative Assessment Practices on Student Motivation for Learning the English Language
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Education and Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether formative assessment practices are associated with higher student motivation in learning English as a foreign language. The authors focus on four classroom assessment practices: student portfolios, self-assessment, peer assessment, and teachers’ strategic questioning. The paper is motivated by the claim that formative assessment should do more than measure achievement; it should also support motivation, autonomy, and self-regulation.

The study was conducted in three high schools in Durres, Albania, using a questionnaire administered to students in public and private schools. Of 300 students, 278 responses were retained for analysis. The design was non-experimental and correlational, with factor analysis and multiple linear regression used to examine relationships between assessment practices and motivation. The regression model found that all four practices were positively associated with motivation, with teachers’ strategic questioning showing the strongest association, followed by self-assessment, peer assessment, and portfolios.

The paper concludes that formative assessment practices are linked to stronger student motivation, greater independence, and more active engagement in learning English. It argues that strategic questioning, self-assessment, peer assessment, and portfolio use can help students recognize strengths and weaknesses, reflect on their learning, and develop autonomy. Because the study is correlational and based on self-report perceptions rather than causal measurement, its findings support association rather than causal impact.

finding.finding_summary: The study found a positive association between formative assessment practices and student motivation for learning English. In a multiple regression model with 278 high school students (n=278), all four practices were statistically significant predictors of motivation, with the model explaining 25.8% of the variance (R2=0.262, adjusted R2=0.258).
finding.measure: Student motivation for learning English, including goal orientation, interest, sense of self as a learner, effort, self-esteem, self-regulation, self-efficacy, and locus of control

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that formative assessment practices were associated with gains in durable skills such as self-regulation, self-assessment, critical thinking, reflection, and autonomy. Students reported that portfolio work changed their way of thinking when facing problems, self-assessment helped them identify strengths and weaknesses, peer assessment supported self-analysis, and strategic teacher questions prompted reflection on knowledge and skills. The study is correlational and relies on student perceptions, so the evidence is descriptive rather than causal.
finding.measure: Questionnaire ratings on self-regulation, self-assessment, reflection, independence/autonomy, and critical thinking-related items

finding.finding_summary: The study focused on learning English as a foreign language and found that formative assessment practices were positively associated with motivation in English learning. Students reported benefits from portfolio use, self-assessment, peer assessment, and teachers’ strategic questions in the context of English class. No direct achievement or fluency score was reported; the outcome was student motivation within English learning.
finding.measure: Motivation for learning English as a foreign language

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All ages / K-12, tertiary, and professional learners (conceptual coverage rather than a studied sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early research and proposes ways LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, personalization, and new educational technologies such as AR/VR-enhanced environments.

The paper discusses potential uses across learner groups—from elementary school through university and professional training—and from teachers’ perspectives, including lesson planning, automated feedback, quiz generation, tutoring, and assessment support. It also highlights risks such as bias, overreliance, plagiarism, privacy/security concerns, sustainability, and inequitable access, arguing that successful adoption requires human oversight, critical thinking, fact-checking, and institutional governance.

Because this is a conceptual position paper, it does not report a direct empirical study of student outcomes. Its main contribution is a framework of opportunities, risks, and mitigation strategies for responsible educational use of LLMs, alongside a brief review of early applications in education research.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by semi-automating grading, generating lesson materials, and producing personalized feedback and quizzes. These claims are illustrated with early studies (e.g., grading effort reduced by up to 85% in one NLP-based feedback system), but the paper itself does not present original causal evidence.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLM-supported activities may improve student engagement, curiosity, and participation, and may help reduce foreign-language learning anxiety. However, these claims are based on cited prior studies and examples rather than new empirical evaluation in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, participation, anxiety/willingness to communicate

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact checking, but the paper also warns they may weaken these skills if learners over-rely on model-generated answers. No direct effect sizes are reported because the paper is a conceptual synthesis rather than an outcomes study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, fact-checking, metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper describes how LLMs can support reading and writing through grammar correction, summarization, outlining, and generation of reading-comprehension questions. These are presented as plausible benefits supported by early examples, not as direct experimental results in this paper.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing quality, summarization, grammar/style support

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs can aid language learning by providing conversational practice, translations, grammar explanations, and vocabulary support. It also notes potential benefits for pronunciation practice and reduced communication anxiety, but provides no original quantitative findings.
finding.measure: Language learning, conversational practice, pronunciation support

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that LLMs can generate math practice problems, quizzes, and math word problems to support mathematics learning. This is an application-oriented claim based on cited examples rather than a direct study of math achievement.
finding.measure: Math practice/problem generation

paper_profiles.title: Developing the theory of formative assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a theoretical account of formative assessment rather than reporting a new empirical study. Black and Wiliam aim to unify the diverse practices commonly labeled formative assessment by grounding them in a framework of teacher, peer, and learner roles across three core processes: where the learner is going, where the learner is now, and how to get there.

The paper argues that formative assessment should be understood as classroom practice in which evidence about student achievement is elicited, interpreted, and used to make better-founded decisions about next steps in instruction. It connects this framework to self-regulated learning, classroom discourse, cognitive acceleration, and dynamic assessment, emphasizing that effective formative interactions depend on how teachers interpret student responses and how feedback is strategically and tactically shaped.

The authors also position formative assessment within broader pedagogic theories and discuss implications for classroom practice, including the development of students as instructional resources for one another and as owners of their own learning. The article is primarily conceptual and synthesis-oriented, drawing on prior research to propose a more coherent theory and to suggest directions for future inquiry and teacher practice.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues, on theoretical and review grounds, that formative assessment can support motivation, interest, and self-regulation when feedback helps students stay on the growth track and develop volitional strategies. However, it also notes that poorly designed feedback or classroom cues can shift students toward well-being-protective responses such as avoidance, withholding effort, or aggression. No direct effect sizes or primary empirical estimates are reported in this conceptual paper.
finding.measure: self-regulation, motivation, interest, volitional strategies, effort/avoidance behaviors

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents a strong theoretical case that formative assessment can foster durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, and learner autonomy. It links peer- and self-assessment to students’ capacity to learn how to learn, and argues that classroom dialogue and reciprocal feedback can make thinking processes more explicit and transferable, but it does not report original quantitative outcome data.
finding.measure: metacognition, collaboration, learner autonomy, self-assessment
