finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that formative assessment can change classroom pedagogy more broadly by reshaping teacher practice, student roles, and the organization of instruction. It argues that formative assessment may be especially effective as a lever for broader changes in classroom learning and teacher professional practice, but provides no direct policy-level or institutional effect estimates.
finding.measure: teacher practice, classroom pedagogy, implementation of formative practices

paper_profiles.title: The effects of self-monitoring and self-reflection in A1 adult learners in an English blended learning environment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This master’s thesis examines whether self-monitoring and self-reflection, used as self-assessment strategies in a blended English course, affected the learning experience of A1 adult learners. The study is framed by formative assessment, learner autonomy, and self-regulation, and asks to what extent these strategies influence participants’ language learning experience.

The intervention was implemented in an English blended-learning course for adult tutors at Universidad Nacional Abierta y a Distancia (UNAD) in Bucaramanga, Colombia. The course was a pilot, non-credit offering with no completion requirements beyond attendance/certification. Data came from checklists, surveys, and student journals, and the analysis is presented as qualitative/action research.

The findings suggest that self-assessment strategies had positive effects on participants’ learning experience. Learners reported greater awareness of the language-learning process, increased involvement in their own progress, better identification of areas for improvement, and more goal-setting and monitoring of learning. Participants also responded positively to scaffolded instruction and expressed favorable views of both self-assessment and the blended-learning format. The study does not report quantitative effect sizes, and its evidence is best interpreted as descriptive and context-specific rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased involvement in their individual learning process and progress after using self-monitoring and self-reflection. The study concludes that the self-assessment strategies positively affected learners by helping them identify areas for improvement, monitor progress, and set learning goals, but it does not report quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Checklists, surveys, and students’ journals capturing perceptions of involvement, awareness, and progress

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly addresses metacognitive and self-regulatory processes, especially awareness, monitoring, planning, and reflection. Findings indicate that learners developed greater awareness of the language-learning process and used self-monitoring to track progress and set goals, suggesting improvement in metacognitive self-regulation rather than measured academic achievement.
finding.measure: Checklists, surveys, and journals documenting self-monitoring, reflection, and goal-setting

finding.finding_summary: The course focused on learning English in a blended environment, and participants reflected on their progress in language skills across face-to-face and online sessions. The thesis reports positive learner perceptions and increased awareness of their English learning process, but it does not provide test-score data, effect sizes, or specific performance outcomes for speaking/listening.
finding.measure: Learners’ reflections and self-reports about English language learning progress

finding.finding_summary: The intervention aimed at improving participants’ ability to self-assess their own language learning process in an English course, rather than directly measuring conventional achievement outcomes. The study reports that learners identified strengths and weaknesses and responded positively to scaffolded instruction and the blended modality, indicating improved language-learning process awareness.
finding.measure: Self-assessment artifacts and reflective journals related to English learning process

paper_profiles.title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether a GenAI-powered formative assessment tool called Socratic Mind improves student engagement, perceived learning, higher-order thinking, and academic performance in an introductory online computing course. The tool uses adaptive Socratic questioning to prompt students to explain reasoning, identify misconceptions, and reflect on their thinking, rather than simply providing answers.

The study was conducted in a large, fully online undergraduate CS1301 course at a U.S. research university. Using a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design, the authors analyzed system logs, surveys, open-ended reflections, and course performance data from 171 students who completed one of two extra-credit AI assignments. Results showed high engagement and positive UX ratings, strong perceived learning, and qualitative reports of gains in problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection. On actual performance, the tool did not produce large achievement gains, but it did buffer the typical decline in quiz scores over time, with stronger benefits for lower-performing students. The evidence suggests the tool may support deeper engagement and some academic resilience, though perceived learning was not always aligned with measured performance.

finding.finding_summary: Students who completed the GenAI-based formative assessment showed a smaller decline in quiz performance over time than comparison students. In the difference-in-differences model, the post*treatment interaction was positive and significant for quizzes (β=0.107, p<.05), corresponding to an estimated 3.30-point reduction in the typical post-intervention quiz drop; this effect was stronger for students with lower baseline scores (Pre*Treatment B=-0.217, p<.05).
finding.measure: Quiz scores from unit assessments in an introductory computing course
finding.effect_size: β=0.107; B=3.300 (quiz DiD interaction); B=-0.217 (baseline moderation)

finding.finding_summary: The tool was associated with consistently high engagement and positive user experience, including affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement. Across all students (n=171), mean engagement ratings were high (affective M=3.96, SD=0.76; behavioral M=4.07, SD=0.61; cognitive M=3.96, SD=0.68), and engagement was strongly correlated with perceived learning (e.g., AE r=.76, BE r=.66, CE r=.58).
finding.measure: Self-reported affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement; UX ratings
finding.effect_size: r=.76; r=.66; r=.58; Cohen's d not central

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported perceived gains in higher-order thinking skills, especially problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, after using Socratic Mind. In thematic analysis of 141 open-ended responses, 69% reported positive change in problem-solving, 62% in critical thinking, and 60% in self-reflection; 38% reported positive change in verbal communication.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses about problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication

paper_profiles.title: Formative vs. summative assessment: impacts on academic motivation, attitude toward learning, test anxiety, and self-regulation skill
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether formative assessment has benefits beyond immediate achievement for EFL learners, focusing on academic motivation, attitude toward learning, test anxiety, and self-regulation. The authors note that most prior assessment research emphasizes language achievement, while psychosocial outcomes and learner self-regulation have received less attention.

The study used a quasi-experimental three-group design with 72 Iranian intermediate EFL learners from a language institute in Ahvaz, Iran. Participants were assigned to formative-assessment, summative-assessment, and control groups. Over 15 treatment sessions, the formative group received ongoing feedback, self- and peer-assessment opportunities, and flexible correction; the summative group received midterm and final exams with limited feedback; the control group received instruction without preplanned assessment. Pre- and post-tests measured test anxiety, motivation, and self-regulation, and an attitude questionnaire was administered to the two treatment groups.

Results from one-way ANOVA and Bonferroni tests showed that both formative and summative assessment improved motivation, reduced test anxiety as reported in the paper's framing, and increased self-regulation relative to the control group, with formative assessment generally producing the strongest post-test performance. Learners also reported positive attitudes toward both assessment types. The paper concludes that formative assessment is especially useful in EFL contexts because it provides feedback, supports learner monitoring, and may help students identify weaknesses and take greater responsibility for their learning.

finding.finding_summary: Both formative and summative assessment groups improved on academic motivation relative to the control group, with the formative group showing the strongest post-test scores. The motivation post-test means were 127.83 for formative, 115.79 for summative, and 92.87 for control; the omnibus ANOVA was significant (F=29.12, p=.00, n=72).
finding.measure: Attitude/Motivation Test Battery (AMTB) motivation scores

finding.finding_summary: The study reports a highly significant difference in test anxiety post-tests across groups (F=20.02, p=.00, n=72), but the direction of the scale scoring is not fully described in the text. The authors interpret the findings as formative and summative assessment being effective, with the formative group showing the strongest post-test performance (mean=49.50) compared with summative (37.91) and control (29.95).
finding.measure: Test anxiety scores from a modified Science Anxiety Scale

finding.finding_summary: Formative and summative assessment both improved self-regulation compared with the control group, and the formative group performed best. The self-regulation post-test ANOVA was significant (F=76.60, p=.00, n=72), with means of 147.25 (formative), 130.04 (summative), and 80.12 (control).
finding.measure: Self-Regulatory Strategies Scale (SRSS) scores

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats self-regulation as a core learner capability and argues that formative assessment strengthens learners' ability to monitor, reflect on, and take responsibility for learning. Empirically, self-regulation improved significantly in the experimental groups, especially the formative group (F=76.60, p=.00, n=72), indicating gains in metacognitive/self-regulatory functioning beyond content achievement.
finding.measure: Self-Regulatory Strategies Scale (SRSS) scores

paper_profiles.title: Investigating Effects of Perceived Technology-enhanced Environment on Self-regulated Learning: Beyond P-values
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether a technology-enhanced learning environment is associated with students’ self-regulated learning, and specifically whether web-based self-assessment tools and perceived technology beliefs explain post-intervention self-regulation beyond simple significance testing. The authors frame the work within self-regulated learning and technology acceptance theory, arguing that self-efficacy, perceived usefulness, and perceived ease of use may shape how students use ICT and self-assessment supports.

The study was conducted with 262 eighth-grade students in Northern Taiwan during an eight-lesson, two-month science unit on socio-scientific issues related to energy policy and argumentation. Students used tablets and Google to search for evidence and also used web-based self-assessment standards to monitor and evaluate the quality of their decision-making and arguments. The researchers analyzed pre/post self-regulation, self-efficacy, and perceptions of ICT and self-assessment tools using maximum likelihood SEM and Bayesian SEM.

The main conclusion is that post-intervention self-regulation was strongly predicted by students’ initial self-regulation and by perceptions of the web-based self-assessment system, especially perceived usefulness; perceived ease of use showed weaker or mixed evidence. Self-efficacy had no direct effect on post-intervention self-regulation, but it had meaningful indirect effects through pre-intervention self-regulation and perceptions of the self-assessment tools. By contrast, simply having access to ICT for online information retrieval did not improve self-regulation. The paper argues that technology must be purpose-built to support monitoring and self-regulation, rather than merely added to instruction.

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with improved self-regulation from pre- to post-test in a sample of 262 eighth-grade students. Pre-intervention self-regulation significantly predicted post-intervention self-regulation (ML-SEM β=.22, p=.006; Bayesian median posterior=.24, 95% CI [.09, .39]), and post-test self-regulation mean increased from 4.11 to 4.41.
finding.measure: Metacognitive self-regulation scale adapted from the MSLQ, administered pre- and post-intervention

finding.finding_summary: The study found that technology-enhanced self-assessment supports were linked to self-regulation outcomes, but ordinary ICT access for searching information was not. Perceived usefulness of web-based self-assessment standards strongly predicted post-intervention self-regulation (ML-SEM β=.62, p<.001; Bayesian median posterior=.58, 95% CI [.37, .80]), while ICT perceived usefulness and ease of use did not significantly predict post-test self-regulation.
finding.measure: Perceived usefulness/ease of use of ICT and web-based self-assessment standards; post-intervention self-regulation
finding.effect_size: beta=.62 for SASPU → PostSR; ICT paths not significant
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI [.37, .80] for SASPU → PostSR; ICT paths not significant

paper_profiles.title: Responding to student feedback: Individualising teamwork scores based on peer assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical assessment problem in engineering design courses: how to fairly assign marks in team-based projects when a single group product can mask unequal individual contributions and enable free riding. The authors introduced a peer-assessment process to individualise team marks in response to student complaints that group grades were unfair and did not reflect actual contribution.

The intervention was implemented in engineering design/project courses at RMIT University in Australia across undergraduate and postgraduate cohorts. Students completed online peer assessments after each assessment task, and the resulting peer ratings were used to proportionally adjust each student’s share of the team mark. The study compares course evaluation feedback before implementation (n=151 students, 27 teams) and after implementation (n=129 students, 23 teams).

The paper reports improved student perceptions after peer assessment was introduced: appreciation of teamwork aspects increased from 24% to 34%, complaints about free riding decreased from 26% to 7%, and course evaluation measures improved (mean Good Teaching Scale rose from 4.04±0.47 to 4.34±0.46; Overall Satisfaction Index from 4.00 to 4.12). The authors conclude that peer assessment can support fairer individualisation of group marks and is associated with better teamwork experience, engagement, and perceived teaching quality in project-based engineering courses. However, the evidence is observational and based on pre/post course evaluation data rather than a controlled causal design.

finding.finding_summary: After peer assessment and mark individualisation were introduced, student course feedback indicated improved teamwork experience and engagement. Positive comments about teamwork increased from 24% pre-intervention to 34% post-intervention, while complaints about free riding fell from 26% to 7% in course evaluation responses.
finding.measure: Course Evaluation Survey (CES) written feedback on teamwork appreciation and course improvement needs
finding.study_size: n=280 total feedback observations across pre (n=151) and post (n=129) cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The peer-assessment process was associated with better group processing, cooperation, communication, and teamwork skill development. Qualitative comments after implementation emphasized learning to work in teams, assign tasks, provide feedback, and manage group cooperation; the paper interprets this as improved collaborative skill development.
finding.measure: Qualitative course feedback on teamwork, cooperation, communication, and group processing
finding.study_size: n=280 total feedback observations across pre (n=151) and post (n=129) cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The peer-assessment system was intended to improve the efficiency and fairness of team-mark allocation by individualising group marks according to contribution and reducing administrative ambiguity around free riding. The paper reports that the process was implemented through an online system (SparkPlus) and used to finalise individual marks after each task, but it does not provide direct workload or time-savings measures.
finding.measure: Peer-mark individualisation process and online assessment workflow
finding.study_size: n=280 total feedback observations across pre (n=151) and post (n=129) cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved institutional course evaluation indicators used for teaching-quality monitoring. Mean Good Teaching Scale scores increased significantly from 4.04±0.47 to 4.34±0.46 (P<0.018), and the Overall Satisfaction Index rose from 4.00 to 4.12 after implementation of peer assessment.
finding.measure: Good Teaching Scale (mGTS) and Overall Satisfaction Index (OSI) from the Course Evaluation Survey
finding.study_size: n=280 total feedback observations across pre (n=151) and post (n=129) cohorts

paper_profiles.title: Technology-enhanced pre-instructional peer assessment: Exploring students’ perceptions in a Statistical Methods course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether technology-enhanced peer assessment can be used as a pre-instructional activity to support learning in a university statistics course. The author is interested in whether having students review peers’ work before a lesson begins can help them prepare for new content, reflect on their own understanding, and build motivation for the upcoming class.

The study was conducted in a Statistical Methods course at a private university in Yogyakarta, Indonesia with 34 prospective mathematics teachers. Three class meetings used Moodle-based peer assessment before instruction on ANOVA and related statistical topics. Students submitted work, reviewed two peers’ submissions using a rubric, received feedback, and then reflected on the scores and comments.

Data came from student reflections, a questionnaire, interviews with three students, and LMS logs. The study is descriptive and qualitative, supplemented by simple descriptive statistics. The main conclusion is that students generally perceived the activity positively: it helped them prepare for new content, encouraged reflection and critical thinking, and served as a source of motivation. Students also valued peer feedback, though they raised concerns about grading fairness, credibility, and the need for clearer assessment criteria and more flexible grading. The paper concludes that technology-enhanced pre-instructional peer assessment has promise as a lesson-introduction strategy, but its effectiveness depends on training, feedback quality, and careful design.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that technology-enhanced pre-instructional peer assessment helped them prepare for new statistical content and review prerequisite knowledge before the main lesson. In the statistics course (n=34), the activity was used before one-way and two-way ANOVA tasks and was perceived as supporting learning performance for the following lesson, but the paper provides no test score effect sizes or pre/post achievement data.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of learning preparation and learning performance in a Statistical Methods course; LMS reflections, questionnaire, and interview data

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived the peer assessment process as motivating and engaging, with the activity described as a source of motivation for improving learning performance. Questionnaire results also suggested moderate pressure during assessment (M=3.03 on a 5-point scale) and high perceived benefit (M=4.21), indicating generally positive motivational responses rather than measured causal effects.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and perceived pressure/benefit from peer assessment

finding.finding_summary: The paper centers on durable skills such as reflection, critical thinking, evaluative judgment, and collaboration/discussion during peer assessment. Students said the activity helped them reflect on mistakes, compare and contrast their work with peers’, ask for help when uncertain, and think critically about others’ solutions; however, these are self-reported perceptions rather than measured skill gains.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of reflection, critical thinking, evaluative judgment, and peer discussion/collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The peer assessment system was presented as efficient and transparent for course administration, with automated submission, scoring, and feedback management in Moodle. The paper does not report workload metrics, but students described the online process as efficient, and the author notes that technology can reduce administrative burden in peer assessment.
finding.measure: Perceived efficiency/transparency of the LMS-based peer assessment process; LMS log timing

paper_profiles.title: AI-driven formative assessment and adaptive learning in data-science education: Evaluating an LLM-powered virtual teaching assistant
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents VITA (Virtual Teaching Assistants), an adaptive distributed learning platform for data-science education that embeds an LLM-powered chatbot (BotCaptain) inside Moodle and an xAPI/LRS analytics pipeline. The central problem addressed is how to provide scalable, personalized, formative support in hybrid and distributed courses while also preserving academic integrity and giving instructors actionable learning analytics.

The system combines prompt-engineered conversational tutoring, Socratic questioning, automated formative assessment, and adaptive pathways that route learners to progression, reinforcement, or remediation content. The paper also describes dashboards and xAPI-based logging intended to help instructors monitor learner activity, identify outliers, and intervene just in time.

The paper is primarily an implementation and design paper rather than a controlled impact evaluation. It reports conceptual comparisons to other AI tutoring systems and argues that contextualized prompts and conversational feedback can improve engagement, critical thinking, and personalized learning, but it does not provide rigorous outcome data from a trial. The main conclusion is that LLM-enabled formative assessment can be integrated with learning analytics infrastructure to support scalable instructional feedback in data-science courses, with future work needed for formal multi-course evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that VITA/BotCaptain can improve teaching efficiency by automating formative assessment, generating contextual feedback, and surfacing underperforming students through dashboards for just-in-time intervention. However, no quantitative impact estimate is reported; the evidence is design- and implementation-based rather than experimental.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, automated formative assessment, learning analytics dashboard utility

finding.finding_summary: The system is intended to support engagement, self-paced learning, and reflective interaction through always-available chatbot support and adaptive feedback. The paper claims these features can promote engagement and reflective reasoning, but it does not report measured gains on engagement or self-regulation outcomes.
finding.measure: Engagement, reflective reasoning, self-paced learning support

finding.finding_summary: A major pedagogical goal is to foster critical thinking and metacognition via Socratic dialogue, contextual prompts, and reflection exercises. The paper presents examples of these interaction patterns and reports that embedded prompts produce more pedagogically aligned and reflective dialogue, but it does not provide a controlled measure of critical-thinking gains.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, metacognitive reflection, dialogue quality

finding.finding_summary: The paper is situated in data-science education and uses formative assessments, quiz tracking, and Socratic prompts to support understanding of statistical and ethical reasoning in course content. The evidence is descriptive, showing that contextualized prompts and adaptive dialogue better align with course objectives, but no statistical learning gains are reported.
finding.measure: Understanding of data-science course concepts, quiz performance, reasoning in ethics/statistics tasks

paper_profiles.title: Optimizing Peer Grading: A Systematic Literature Review of Reviewer Assignment Strategies and Quantity of Reviewers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how peer-grading systems can be optimized by changing two design features: how reviewers are assigned to submissions and how many reviews each submission receives. The authors conducted a systematic literature review of 87 studies published from 2010 to 2024, spanning traditional classrooms and MOOCs, to synthesize evidence on reviewer assignment strategies and review-count effects.

The review identifies four main assignment strategies: random, competency-based, social-network-based, and bidding-based. Random assignment is the most common but can create fairness and accuracy problems when low-quality or inconsistent reviewers are unevenly distributed. Competency-based assignment is presented as a more robust alternative because it can improve grading accuracy and fairness, while social-network and bidding approaches remain under-studied and need more empirical testing.

For review quantity, the literature suggests that three to five reviews per submission is often the best balance between grading reliability, student workload, and learning benefits. The review reports that accuracy generally improves as the number of reviewers increases, but gains diminish after about five to six reviewers. The paper concludes that peer-grading systems can be made more effective through better reviewer allocation and a moderate number of reviews, but stronger causal evidence is still needed for comparing assignment strategies and for isolating effects on learning outcomes beyond accuracy.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, reviewer-assignment strategy and review count strongly affect grading efficiency, reliability, and workload. The review concludes that 3–5 reviews per submission generally balances grading accuracy with student workload, while benefits from additional reviewers diminish beyond about 5–6 reviews.
finding.measure: Number of reviews per submission; grading reliability/accuracy; reviewer workload

finding.finding_summary: The review reports that peer-grading design can influence student engagement and participation, but effects depend on workload and assignment structure. More than five reviews per student may lead to disengagement or rushed grading, whereas three to five reviews is described as supporting engagement without excessive burden.
finding.measure: Student engagement, participation, perceived workload

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that peer assessment can support learning outcomes such as perspective-taking and receiving complementary feedback from different reviewers, which are durability-related skills. However, the evidence is synthesized qualitatively from prior studies rather than estimated as a single pooled effect, so no overall effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Learning outcomes from peer feedback diversity; complementary perspectives

paper_profiles.title: Tuned Models of Peer Assessment in MOOCs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to make peer assessment in massive open online courses more accurate, fair, and efficient. The authors argue that peer grading is essential for scaling open-ended assignments, but that simple aggregation methods such as taking the median of peer scores can produce substantial error and uneven grading quality.

They propose probabilistic peer-grading models that estimate each submission’s true score while also inferring individual grader bias and reliability. Three variants are evaluated: a basic bias/reliability model, a temporal model that carries grader bias across assignments, and a coupled model that lets grading reliability depend on a student’s own assignment score. The paper uses two Coursera HCI course offerings (n=7,240 students total; 63,199 peer grades) and evaluates the models on held-out ground-truth submissions. The best model reduces RMSE relative to the baseline median rule and also produces calibrated uncertainty estimates that could support reallocating graders to submissions that need more feedback.

Beyond grade prediction, the paper uses the inferred grading parameters to study grading behavior. It reports correlational findings about which students grade more reliably, how time spent grading relates to grading consistency, how comment length and sentiment relate to residuals, and whether grading ability helps predict future course participation. The authors conclude that peer-grading metadata can provide both better scoring and educationally useful signals about engagement.

finding.finding_summary: Probabilistic peer-grading models substantially improved grading accuracy over the baseline median rule, reducing RMSE from 7.95 to 5.30 on HCI1 and from 6.43 to 4.73 on HCI2. The paper also shows that calibrated uncertainty can identify submissions that need more graders, suggesting a more efficient allocation of grading effort.
finding.measure: Peer grading accuracy (RMSE on ground-truth submissions) and confidence-based allocation efficiency
finding.study_size: n=7,240 students; 63,199 peer grades; ground-truth simulations with 3,000 runs per submission
finding.effect_size: RMSE reduced by 33% (7.95 to 5.30) on HCI1 and 31% (6.43 to 4.73) on HCI2
finding.std_deviation: Average error SD reported as 7.23 baseline vs 4.77 PG3 on HCI1; 6.19 baseline vs 4.52 PG3 on HCI2

finding.finding_summary: Grading-related variables predicted future course participation better than assignment grade alone. Adding grader bias and reliability to a linear classifier improved AUC from 0.93 to 0.98 for predicting whether a student would participate in the next assignment, suggesting that peer-grading behavior captures engagement beyond achievement.
finding.measure: Future course participation / dropout prediction (AUC)

finding.finding_summary: The study found that students who graded more carefully tended to be more reliable graders, and that better assignment performers were generally stronger graders. It also reports that time spent grading had a non-linear relationship with grading consistency, with a 'sweet spot' around 20 minutes and significantly lower residual standard deviation than longer grading times (p<0.001, diff=0.3 SD).
finding.measure: Grading residuals / consistency, time spent grading, and assignment score as predictors of grading quality
finding.effect_size: diff = 0.3 standard deviations for residual SD at the sweet spot; AUC=0.97605 for comment/feature model shown in related analysis, but not central to this finding

finding.finding_summary: Comments linked to larger negative grading residuals were typically longer, suggesting students wrote more when critiquing weaker submissions. The paper also finds that comment sentiment was generally neutral to positive, indicating an effort to provide balanced peer feedback rather than uniformly negative responses.
finding.measure: Free-response comment length and sentiment polarity versus grading residual

paper_profiles.title: Scaffolding Collaborative Learning in STEM: A Two-Year Evaluation of a Tool-Integrated Project-Based Methodology
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates a redesigned project-based learning approach in a master’s-level Biomedical Image Processing course within a Machine Learning for Health program. The authors ask whether integrating collaborative digital tools (Google Colab and Weights & Biases), structured rubrics, and peer assessment can improve student engagement, transparency, fairness of grading, and the quality of collaborative work beyond a traditional evaluation model.

The intervention was implemented over two academic years with 49 total students (25 in 2023/2024 and 24 in 2024/2025), after a pre-intervention baseline cohort from 2022/2023. Students worked in teams on a deformable image registration project, with coursework organized around shared coding, experiment tracking, rubric-guided reporting, oral presentations, and anonymous peer evaluation. The study uses survey responses, grade distributions, and Shannon entropy of grades to compare the redesigned framework with the earlier cohort.

Findings suggest that the tool-integrated, rubric-based model was associated with greater grade dispersion and higher entropy than the pre-intervention cohort, indicating more differentiated and potentially fairer assessment. Student surveys were broadly positive across both implementation years, with high reported engagement, perceived usefulness of collaboration, and support for transparency in evaluation, although perceptions of tool usefulness and peer-assessment fairness were mixed in the second year. The authors conclude that the approach is scalable within this STEM master’s context and may support collaborative and transferable skills, while noting the need for better onboarding and continued refinement of peer evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: Student survey results indicated high engagement, satisfaction, and perceived usefulness of the project-based, tool-supported learning model. In 2023/2024, most students reported strong satisfaction and valued the project’s contribution to their learning process; in 2024/2025, 66.7% reported high satisfaction and 95.8% rated collaborative learning as very helpful, though views on tool usefulness were more mixed.
finding.measure: End-of-course Likert survey of satisfaction, engagement/participation, tool usefulness, and collaborative learning perceptions

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with students reporting gains in collaboration, communication, problem-solving, and reflective practice. Survey responses in both cohorts emphasized collaborative learning, and the paper argues that structured peer assessment and shared coding/reporting environments supported critical engagement, individual responsibility, and transferable skills for future academic or professional contexts.
finding.measure: Self-report survey items on collaborative learning, perceived skill development, and future usefulness; course-grade structure emphasizing peer evaluation and presentations

finding.finding_summary: Students reported strong conceptual understanding of deformable image registration and the course design was intended to support scientific documentation, experimental analysis, and reproducible research practices. Across the implementation years, most students rated their understanding highly, suggesting the project-based workflow supported technical learning in biomedical image processing.
finding.measure: Survey ratings of conceptual understanding; project report rubric and registration performance metrics (R score)

finding.finding_summary: The redesigned evaluation framework was associated with more differentiated grade distributions and higher Shannon entropy compared with the pre-intervention baseline, which the authors interpret as improved fairness and reduced grade compression. Reported entropy increased from 0.87 in 2022/2023 to 1.55 in 2023/2024 and 1.81 in 2024/2025; the pre-intervention cohort also had a compressed grade range with mean=9.27 and SD=0.33, while later cohorts showed broader dispersion (SD=0.70 and 0.90).
finding.measure: Grade distributions and Shannon entropy of course project grades

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that Google Colab and Weights & Biases improved experiment tracking, reporting, and instructor monitoring, making collaboration and formative supervision more transparent and manageable. However, the evidence is primarily descriptive and based on student perceptions rather than direct workload or time-efficiency metrics.
finding.measure: Survey perceptions of tool effectiveness; descriptive account of experiment tracking/report generation and instructor dashboards

paper_profiles.title: Socratic Mind: Impact of a Novel GenAI-Powered Assessment Tool on Student Learning and Higher-Order Thinking
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study evaluates whether a Generative AI-powered formative assessment tool, Socratic Mind, can improve student learning beyond immediate engagement in a large online introductory computing course. The paper asks whether AI-mediated Socratic questioning influences engagement patterns, perceived learning, actual academic performance, and higher-order thinking skills such as problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection.

Socratic Mind was embedded as an optional extra-credit assignment in a 16-week asynchronous undergraduate CS1301 course at a U.S. research university. Students interacted with the tool through adaptive, multi-turn dialogue, either by typing or speaking responses, and received personalized follow-up questions and feedback. The study used a quasi-experimental, mixed-methods design combining system logs, surveys, course performance data, regression analyses, difference-in-differences models, and thematic analysis of open-ended responses.

Findings indicate high behavioral, affective, and cognitive engagement, with positive user experience strongly associated with perceived learning. In terms of actual performance, students who used the tool showed a smaller decline in quiz scores over time than comparison peers, with the buffering effect estimated at about 3.3 points and especially pronounced for lower-performing students. However, perceived learning did not consistently align with quiz or test performance. Qualitative results suggest many students believed the tool improved their problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection, while effects on verbal communication were weaker because many participants used text rather than audio input. Overall, the paper concludes that dialogic GenAI-based formative assessment can support engagement, perceived learning, and some actual performance gains in higher education, especially for struggling learners.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high engagement and positive UX with the GenAI tool. Across n=171 respondents, behavioral engagement (M=4.07, SD=0.61), affective engagement (M=3.96, SD=0.76), and cognitive engagement (M=3.96, SD=0.68) were all high, and UX subscales correlated positively with engagement (rs=.33 to .54).
finding.measure: Self-reported affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement; UX survey; interaction logs

finding.finding_summary: The tool was perceived to improve higher-order thinking skills, especially problem-solving, critical thinking, and self-reflection. In open-ended responses (n=141), 69% reported positive changes in problem-solving, 62% in critical thinking, and 60% in self-reflection; effects on verbal communication were smaller, with 38% positive and 56% no change.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of open-ended survey responses about problem-solving, critical thinking, self-reflection, and verbal communication

finding.finding_summary: The quasi-experimental analysis found that students who engaged with Socratic Mind experienced a smaller decline in quiz performance over time. In the DiD quiz model (n=171 analyzed survey sample; academic data drawn from the larger course cohort), the treatment-by-post interaction was positive and significant (β=.107, p<.05), corresponding to an estimated 3.30-point buffering effect against the average post-intervention quiz decline.
finding.measure: Unit-level quiz scores and test scores; difference-in-differences regression

paper_profiles.title: aiPlato: A Novel AI Tutoring and Stepwise Feedback System for Physics Homework
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory paper evaluates aiPlato, an AI-enabled homework platform for open-ended physics problems, in a large introductory mechanics course. The system provides stepwise feedback through tools such as Evaluate My Work, AI Tutor Chat, hints, and partial-credit grading, with the goal of supporting productive struggle and formative assessment during homework completion.

The study was conducted in a Spring 2025 undergraduate physics course at the University of Texas at Arlington. Four optional extra-credit assignments on aiPlato were offered to students, and the authors analyzed usage logs, final exam performance, course grades, and end-of-semester survey responses from consenting students (n=87). Students who used aiPlato more intensively tended to have higher final exam scores and better course grade outcomes; the adjusted difference between high- and low-engagement groups was about 13.86 percentage points on the final exam, corresponding to Cohen’s d≈0.81. However, the authors explicitly note that participation was not randomized and that the results are associational, not causal.

Qualitative survey findings showed that students generally valued the stepwise feedback and perceived the platform as more approachable than traditional homework systems, though they reported issues with handwriting recognition, interface lag, and occasional unhelpful AI responses. Overall, the paper argues that aiPlato is feasible and promising for supporting open-ended homework in physics, but that stronger controlled studies are needed to establish causal learning effects and to test longer-term impacts.

finding.finding_summary: Students who engaged more with aiPlato tended to perform better on the cumulative final exam in an introductory physics course. In the adjusted analysis, the high-engagement group scored 13.86 percentage points higher than the low-engagement group, with the authors reporting Cohen’s d≈0.81 (n=87; 39 low, 32 medium, 16 high engagement).
finding.measure: Cumulative final exam score

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports strong evidence of student engagement, persistence, and productive struggle with the homework platform. All 61 students who reached the first problem used Evaluate My Work, and students frequently revised work multiple times; survey responses also indicated that aiPlato made problems more approachable and engaging.
finding.measure: Platform usage logs; end-of-semester Likert survey responses about engagement/approachability
finding.study_size: n=87 survey respondents; usage logs from 87 consenting students

finding.finding_summary: The platform was intended to support stepwise reasoning, and students’ use patterns suggest improved reflective problem solving and self-correction. The study describes frequent iterative use of Evaluate My Work, with students revising derivations multiple times, and reports that students found the feedback helpful for understanding where their reasoning went wrong.
finding.measure: Interaction logs (revision frequency, tool use) and qualitative survey feedback on reasoning support

finding.finding_summary: The authors report that aiPlato reduced routine homework-related email questions to the instructor and centralized feedback within the platform. They present this as a practical benefit for managing large-enrollment physics homework, though the reduction is descriptive rather than experimentally measured.
finding.measure: Instructor-reported reduction in homework clarification emails; usage of built-in support tools

paper_profiles.title: The impact of gamification on learning outcomes: experiences from a Biomedical Engineering course
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether adding gamified activities to an undergraduate biomedical engineering course improves student learning outcomes, engagement, and related soft skills. The authors frame the work around the Theory of Gamified Learning, arguing that gamification may affect outcomes both directly and indirectly through continuous assessment performance.

The intervention was implemented in the “Biomedical Applications of Nanotechnology” course at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid across the 2020–2023 academic years. It included two main gamified components: “Nanogames,” an interactive midterm activity with team-based quizzes and leaderboard competition, and “NanoTechStart,” an entrepreneurial pitch activity in which small teams developed and presented a nanotechnology startup proposal. Data came from grades, continuous evaluation scores, and student/faculty surveys, with comparison against a 2017–2018 control cohort that had no gamification elements.

Results suggest that the gamified version of the course was associated with higher pass rates, higher final grades, and very positive student perceptions of knowledge gain, soft-skill development, and satisfaction. In the moderated-mediation analysis, gamification significantly predicted continuous evaluation performance and final course score, and continuous evaluation significantly predicted final score; however, the moderation path was not significant. The study therefore supports a positive direct effect of gamification and a significant indirect pathway through continuous assessment, but it is limited by its quasi-experimental, single-course design and reliance on survey and grade outcomes in a higher-education context.

finding.finding_summary: The gamified course was associated with improved academic performance on course assessments that included understanding and application of biomedical nanotechnology concepts. In the 2020–2023 gamified cohorts (n=45 total across years; regression model n=41), the course total score improved relative to the non-gamified control year (2017–2018, n=17), with pass rates rising from 70.6% to 100% and final grades shifting upward (p=0.00003 for pass-rate/achievement differences; p<0.0001 for final-score distribution).
finding.measure: Course grades, pass rates, continuous evaluation, and midterm/final assessment performance in Biomedical Applications of Nanotechnology
finding.study_size: n=45 gamified participants across 2020–2023; control n=17 (15 took exam)

finding.finding_summary: Students reported high satisfaction and perceived gains in engagement, motivation, and soft skills after the gamified activities. For Nanogames, 93.7% of participants reported overall satisfaction and 100% reported improved soft skills; for NanoTechStart, 76.2% reported overall satisfaction and 81.0% reported improved soft skills, with activity ratings generally above 4.0 on a 5-point scale.
finding.measure: Student satisfaction and perception surveys (Likert-scale ratings; overall satisfaction; perceived soft-skill improvement; engagement/motivation-related items)
finding.study_size: Nanogames n=16; NanoTechStart n=21 (survey respondents in 2022–2023)
finding.std_deviation: Nanogames overall satisfaction SD=0.6; NanoTechStart overall satisfaction SD=1.0

finding.finding_summary: The gamified activities were associated with perceived improvements in teamwork, collaboration, communication, leadership, critical thinking, and problem-solving. The paper reports that all Nanogames participants (100%) and 81.0% of NanoTechStart participants perceived improved soft skills, and the activities were explicitly designed to foster team-based problem-solving and entrepreneurial presentation skills.
finding.measure: Student self-reports of soft skills, teamwork, communication, leadership, and problem-solving; activity-based collaborative performance
finding.std_deviation: Nanogames soft-skill rating SD=0.6; NanoTechStart soft-skill rating SD=0.9

finding.finding_summary: Faculty reported that the digital and gamified structure made monitoring progress and feedback more efficient. The paper states that the integration of digital platforms supported more efficient monitoring of student progress and improved feedback practices, although no formal efficiency metric or workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Faculty perceptions of monitoring/feedback efficiency and course coordination

paper_profiles.title: Knowing About Knowing: An Illusion of Human Competence Can Hinder Appropriate Reliance on AI Systems
paper_profiles.venue: CHI ’23 (Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a metacognitive bias—the Dunning-Kruger Effect (DKE)—can reduce people’s appropriate reliance on AI systems in human-AI decision making. The authors ask whether users who overestimate their own performance are less likely to follow AI advice when it is appropriate, and whether a tutorial intervention plus explanations can improve calibration and reliance.

The study uses a 2×2 factorial experiment with 249 adult crowdworkers from Prolific completing a difficult logical reasoning / reading-comprehension task based on the ReClor dataset. Participants made an initial answer, then saw AI advice; some conditions also included logic-units-based explanations, and some included a tutorial phase with performance feedback and contrastive explanations designed to reveal mistakes and calibrate self-assessment. The task was not an educational classroom intervention per se, but a human-AI interaction experiment in a decision-making setting.

Results showed that participants who overestimated their performance relied significantly less on the AI system than participants with accurate self-assessment or underestimation, leading to lower accuracy and poorer appropriate reliance. The tutorial intervention significantly improved self-assessment calibration, especially for overestimators, but its effects on reliance and performance were limited overall; for underestimators, it sometimes worsened appropriate reliance and performance. Logic-units-based explanations did not meaningfully improve calibration, reliance, or performance. Overall, the paper concludes that miscalibrated self-assessment can hinder appropriate reliance on AI, and that simple tutorials may help some users but can also have unintended consequences.

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally studies metacognition and calibration of self-assessment as predictors of reliance on AI advice. In a sample of n=249 adults, participants who overestimated their performance showed significantly lower appropriate reliance and lower accuracy than participants with accurate self-assessment or underestimation (e.g., RAIR and RSR were both significantly worse for overestimators, p<.001). The tutorial improved self-assessment calibration, but the downstream reliance effects were mixed and depended on whether participants initially over- or underestimated themselves.
finding.measure: Self-assessment calibration; appropriate reliance on AI (RAIR, RSR, agreement fraction, switch fraction); task accuracy

finding.finding_summary: The study also examines whether AI advice, explanations, and tutorial calibration improve final task performance on a logical reasoning task. Participants who overestimated themselves achieved significantly lower final accuracy than other groups, and the tutorial did not produce a broadly positive performance effect; for underestimators, accuracy decreased after tutorial (0.73 to 0.55), while for overestimators the accuracy change was not statistically significant. Overall performance remained below the AI’s 66.7% accuracy, indicating limited efficiency gains from the intervention.
finding.measure: Task accuracy on logical reasoning decisions; accuracy with initial disagreement
finding.std_deviation: 0.16 (overall accuracy SD); 0.17 agreement fraction SD; 0.27 switch fraction SD

finding.finding_summary: Although not an affective intervention study, the paper substantively measures trust and reliance-related self-regulation constructs, including propensity to trust, trust in automation, and perceived helpfulness of explanations. The tutorial improved self-assessment calibration but did not clearly reshape subjective trust; participants generally rated logic-units explanations as only slightly helpful or very slightly helpful (57.2%), suggesting limited engagement with the explanation format.
finding.measure: Trust in Automation (TiA-Trust), propensity to trust (TiA-PtT), perceived helpfulness of explanations

finding.finding_summary: The paper has a broader institutional implication for the design of human-AI systems and training interventions, showing that user tutorials can improve calibration and sometimes appropriate reliance, but may also have unintended negative effects for some users. The authors argue that system designers should consider user metacognition and confidence calibration when deploying AI decision aids.
finding.measure: Design implications for human-AI decision support and reliance calibration

paper_profiles.title: A New Item Response Theory Model for Open-Ended Online Homework with Multiple Allowed Attempts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a measurement problem in formative assessment: standard item response theory (IRT) models do not fit open-ended online homework well when students can make multiple attempts. The authors ask whether adding learner-level traits for random guessing and copying can better recover students’ underlying ability from homework data, and whether those traits align with self-reported homework behaviors.

The study introduces a new three-trait IRT variant (ability, guessing, copying) and fits it to first-attempt homework data from a large undergraduate introductory physics course (256 students, 401 homework problems), using exam performance as the reference for "true" ability. The model suggests that copying is the larger source of distortion on first attempts, with about 12% average copying across students and little dependence on ability, while guessing matters more for lower-ability students. A reduced model with copying only performed better than the full model in predicting exam-derived ability, and the new traits also improved estimation stability for item difficulty and discrimination. The modeled guessing/copying tendencies were broadly consistent with self-reported gender differences in homework behavior.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is primarily a psychometric/methodological study about improving measurement of student ability from open-ended online homework, not an intervention on achievement. Using 256 undergraduate physics students and 401 homework problems, the authors show that a model with learner-level copying and guessing traits fits homework data better and recovers exam-referenced ability more accurately than a standard 2PL model, with the copying-only model outperforming the full model for predicting exam ability.
finding.measure: Correlation and regression relationship between homework-derived ability estimates and exam-derived ability estimates; model fit and parameter convergence

paper_profiles.title: An epistemology and expectations survey about experimental physics: Development and initial results
paper_profiles.venue: Physical Review Special Topics - Physics Education Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the need for a valid assessment tool to evaluate undergraduate physics laboratory courses beyond content knowledge, focusing on students’ epistemological beliefs about experimental physics and what they think is expected for earning a good grade. The authors develop the Colorado Learning Attitudes about Science Survey for Experimental Physics (E-CLASS), designed to compare students’ personal views about doing experiments in class with their perceptions of what experimental physicists think about research, and to add a third set of items about course expectations.

The study combines iterative survey design with validation interviews, expert faculty review, and large-scale administration. The survey went through multiple rounds of student interviews to refine wording, clarify context, and distinguish classroom from research settings; 42 student interviews and 23 faculty responses were used for validity evidence. Initial results from 45 classes at 20 institutions show that students often hold more expert-like views about research than about classroom experiments, with notable gaps around asking questions, understanding uncertainty, and the purpose of lab reports. The paper concludes that E-CLASS can serve as a useful formative assessment tool for undergraduate lab instruction, though participation rates and cross-level comparisons remain challenges.

finding.finding_summary: The E-CLASS was designed primarily to measure students’ epistemological beliefs about experimental physics, including scientific reasoning in lab contexts. In validation results, upper-division students showed more expert-like responses than introductory students on classroom and research epistemology scores (classroom mean expert-like fraction 0.66 vs 0.61, d=0.38; research 0.82 vs 0.78, d=0.28), and several items highlighted reasoning-related gaps such as interpreting uncertainty, making predictions, and using data to draw conclusions.
finding.measure: E-CLASS epistemology survey responses about experimentation, uncertainty, predictions, and scientific reasoning
finding.study_size: multiple classes; validation interviews n=42; expert faculty n=23; survey administration across 45 classes

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes items on enjoyment, confidence, interest, and perceptions of capability, indicating an affective/self-perception component of laboratory learning. The report notes that students’ interest in physics during the semester is tracked, and that upper-division students had somewhat more expert-like responses; however, the paper does not provide a causal estimate of change in engagement or motivation from a specific intervention.
finding.measure: Survey items on enjoyment, confidence, interest, and perceived ability to do research/experiments
finding.study_size: multiple classes; exact counts for affective outcomes not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Several survey statements directly target durable skills such as metacognition, collaboration, and problem-solving in laboratory settings. Expert validation and class results showed substantial splits between students’ views of classroom work and professional research on items like thinking up one’s own questions, working in groups, and choosing analysis methods without explicit directions, suggesting these skills are not yet strongly developed in many lab courses.
finding.measure: E-CLASS items on collaboration, problem-solving, and metacognitive/strategic thinking in experiments
finding.study_size: multiple classes; validation interviews n=42; expert faculty n=23

finding.finding_summary: A central contribution of the paper is institutional: the authors develop and deploy a formative assessment system intended to help instructors improve laboratory curricula and compare courses. The tool was used in 45 classes at 20 institutions, and instructors received reports summarizing student participation, pre/post shifts, and comparison-group benchmarks; the paper reports that several schools were already using the reports to evaluate curricular changes.
finding.measure: Adoption and use of the E-CLASS assessment/reporting system across institutions and courses

paper_profiles.title: Humans can learn to detect AI-generated texts, or at least learn when they can’t
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether people can learn to distinguish human-written from AI-generated text when they receive immediate feedback, and whether feedback helps them better calibrate their confidence. It also examines whether judgments depend on text readability, stylistic/register features, AI-use frequency, and attitudes toward AI.

The authors created 672 paired Czech text continuations using human-written excerpts from the Koditex corpus and GPT-4o-generated continuations, then ran an online experiment with 254 Czech native speakers. Participants were randomly assigned to either immediate feedback after each trial or delayed feedback only at the end. Across 20 trials (17 experimental items and 3 attention checks), participants identified which text was human-written, rated readability, and reported confidence. Mixed-effects logistic regressions showed that immediate feedback improved accuracy over trial order and improved confidence calibration: the feedback group reached 65.1% accuracy versus 55.4% in the no-feedback group, and confidence was more predictive of correctness in the feedback condition. Participants without feedback relied more on stereotyped assumptions about AI writing (more static, prepared, cohesive, and polythematic) and on the belief that human texts are more readable.

The study concludes that the skill of detecting AI-generated text can be improved through explicit feedback, but everyday exposure to AI alone does not appear to help. It also finds that feedback reduces overconfidence and weakens reliance on misleading stylistic cues. The findings are framed as especially relevant for educational contexts, where false confidence about identifying AI-generated content could lead to mistaken judgments about student work.

finding.finding_summary: Immediate feedback improved participants’ ability to distinguish AI-generated from human-written text in a reading/authorship-identification task. Accuracy was 65.1% in the feedback group versus 55.4% in the no-feedback group (n=254 total; 17 scored trials per participant), with trial order significantly improving correctness only in the feedback condition (estimate=0.053, p<0.001).
finding.measure: Accuracy in identifying which of two text excerpts was AI-generated vs human-written

finding.finding_summary: Feedback improved confidence calibration, meaning participants were more likely to be confident when they were actually correct. Overall confidence levels were similar across conditions (feedback 4.2 vs no-feedback 4.3 on a 7-point scale), but in the no-feedback group higher confidence predicted lower correctness (estimate=-0.14, p=0.005), indicating overconfidence without corrective input.
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence in authorship judgments and its relation to correctness
finding.confidence_interval: Feedback mean confidence 4.0–4.4; no-feedback 4.2–4.5; no-feedback confidence effect CI -0.23 to -0.042

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies metacognitive calibration and the use of feedback to improve judgment accuracy. Immediate feedback helped participants update misconceptions about AI text and better align confidence with actual performance, especially at high confidence levels where the no-feedback group made the most errors.
finding.measure: Confidence calibration; correctness as a function of confidence and feedback

paper_profiles.title: Level Up Peer Review in Education: Investigating genAI-driven Gamification system and its influence on Peer Feedback Effectiveness
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether a gamified peer-assessment platform with generative AI support can improve peer feedback in a software engineering classroom. The authors identify a common problem in peer review activities: students often provide too little feedback, and the feedback they do provide is frequently low in quality, especially in terms of specificity and relevance. They propose Socratique, a web-based platform that combines points, badges, leaderboards, rewards, and a GenAI tutor to scaffold feedback writing in real time.

The intervention was evaluated in a randomized controlled experiment in a 12-unit master’s course on functional programming at Carnegie Mellon University Silicon Valley during Spring 2024. Thirty-four master’s students were randomly assigned to either a gamified treatment or a non-gamified control; both groups used the same peer-review platform and both had access to the GenAI tutor, but only the treatment group saw and received the full gamification incentives. Feedback quantity was measured by the number of voluntary peer reviews submitted, and quality was scored with an instructor rubric covering clarity, relevance, and specificity.

Results show that the treatment group submitted more voluntary feedback overall and received higher overall feedback-quality scores than the control group. The strongest quality gains were in relevance and specificity, while clarity was high in both groups and did not differ meaningfully. Survey data also indicated that students in the gamified condition consulted the AI assistant more often. Overall, the study suggests that combining gamification with AI scaffolding can increase engagement in peer review and improve certain aspects of feedback quality, though the sample is small and the setting is limited to graduate software engineering students.

finding.finding_summary: The treatment group showed higher peer-feedback engagement, submitting more voluntary reviews than the control group. Across both sessions, the treatment mean was 23.0 reviews versus 16.9 in the control group, with a significant condition effect (F(1,23)=4.11, p=.05, ηp²=.15; t(23)=-2.03, p=.05).
finding.measure: Number of voluntary peer reviews submitted

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved the quality of peer feedback, especially in relevance and specificity, which are core review and critique skills. Overall quality was higher in the treatment group (M=5.6 out of 9) than the control group (M=4.1), with a significant condition effect (F(1,21)=5.82, p=.03, ηp²=.22); relevance and specificity also showed significant treatment effects.
finding.measure: Instructor-rated peer feedback rubric scores for clarity, relevance, and specificity

finding.finding_summary: The platform’s GenAI assistance was used more frequently in the gamified condition, suggesting improved in-process support for composing feedback. In the end-of-semester survey, treatment students reported greater use of the AI assistant (M=5.6) than control students (M=3.4), t(23)=-3.34, p=.003, indicating the system increased the use of automated scaffolding during review tasks.
finding.measure: Self-reported frequency of consulting the AI feedback assistant
finding.study_size: n=25 survey respondents (n=14 control, n=11 treatment)

paper_profiles.title: Mentoring Software in Education and Its Impact on Teacher Development: An Integrative Literature Review
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal on Integrating Technology in Education (IJITE)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how mentoring software may support teacher development, with particular attention to retention, satisfaction, professional growth, and the practical barriers schools face when adopting such tools. The author frames mentoring software as a digital extension of traditional mentoring that can add structured goal setting, progress monitoring, analytics, communication tools, and scalable matching between mentors and mentees.

The study uses an integrative literature review approach, searching Google Scholar for peer-reviewed articles and conference proceedings from 2020–2024. After screening 961 records, the author reports 17 included studies, synthesizing evidence from education as well as healthcare and corporate sectors to identify design features and implementation lessons relevant to school-based mentoring. The review concludes that mentoring software can strengthen teacher support, collaboration, satisfaction, and retention, but adoption is constrained by cost, institutional resistance, and data privacy concerns.

Because this is a narrative/integrative review, the paper does not report a single original empirical study or pooled quantitative effect size. Its contribution is primarily conceptual and synthesizing: it argues that digital mentoring platforms are most effective when they complement human relationships and are aligned with institutional goals, and it recommends future longitudinal research to assess long-term effects on teacher retention, job satisfaction, and student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that mentoring software improves administrative and mentoring workflow efficiency through mentor-mentee matching, progress tracking, automated reminders, scheduling tools, and analytics dashboards. However, no original effect size, confidence interval, or study-level quantitative estimate is reported in this paper.
finding.measure: Administrative workload, progress tracking, communication efficiency, and mentoring program management

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central focus is on how mentoring software affects teacher retention, professional growth, and institutional mentoring systems. Across the reviewed literature, the author concludes that digital mentoring platforms can strengthen organizational support structures, improve retention, and foster a more data-driven culture, but implementation is limited by cost, institutional resistance, and privacy concerns.
finding.measure: Teacher retention, professional growth, institutional adoption barriers, and program sustainability

paper_profiles.title: The use of feedback and feed-forward action plans on the development of clinical skills in undergraduate medical students
paper_profiles.venue: University of KwaZulu-Natal PhD thesis; includes published article in BMC Medical Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This doctoral thesis examines how feedback and feed-forward action plans affect the development of clinical skills in undergraduate medical students, with a focus on making formative assessment more usable for learners. The study is motivated by a perceived gap between the provision of feedback by tutors and the extent to which students actually understand, accept, and use it to improve performance.

The work combines qualitative and quantitative approaches in the context of a clinical skills laboratory at the University of KwaZulu-Natal. Five semi-structured focus groups with 25 third-year medical students were used to explore psychological barriers and facilitators to feedback receptivity, and the thesis also analyzes 1,025 tutor and peer feedback responses in 2nd- and 3rd-year clinical skills logbooks using a deliberate practice-based scoring system.

Findings suggest that feedback use is shaped by awareness, understanding, agency, and volition. Students were more likely to engage with feedback when it aligned with their goals, came from trusted teachers, and was embedded in constructive relationships; lower-performing students often felt less able to use self- and peer-feedback. The quantitative analysis found that tutor and peer comments did include task, gap, and action-plan elements, but the overall quality was only moderate and often nonspecific. The thesis concludes that adding structured feed-forward prompts to logbooks and promoting learner responsibility can strengthen self-regulation, feedback literacy, and a more sustainable feedback culture in clinical skills training.

finding.finding_summary: The qualitative component found that medical students' receptivity to feedback was shaped by awareness, cognizance, agency, and volition. Feedback that aligned with personal goals and came from trusted teachers supported engagement, while time constraints, uncertainty, and low confidence hindered uptake; the thesis reports these as facilitators and barriers rather than a single uniform effect.
finding.measure: Focus group interviews on feedback receptivity, interpretation, and uptake

finding.finding_summary: Students' ability to use feedback was tied to self-regulation, reflection, self-assessment, and goal setting. The thesis argues that feed-forward action plans encourage learners to identify gaps, set performance improvement goals, and convert feedback into action, thereby strengthening metacognitive and self-directed learning processes.
finding.measure: Thematic analysis of feedback receptivity and use; student reflections on self and peer feedback

finding.finding_summary: In the logbook analysis, tutor and peer feedback comments contained all three deliberate-practice components: task, performance gap, and action plan. However, the overall quality of feedback was only moderate and less specific, with average scores at or below 2, indicating partial but meaningful alignment with clinical skills learning objectives.
finding.measure: Deliberate-practice-based feedback scoring of tutor and peer written comments in clinical skills logbooks

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how formative assessment can be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard, in a university setting. The authors argue that frequent, low-stakes assessment with immediate feedback can improve learning by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses early and by keeping them engaged throughout the semester.

The implementation described is a proposed series of weekly or fortnightly online tests using Blackboard’s test tool, with detailed automated feedback and options for additional discussion support. The paper also reports results from a student questionnaire about continuous assessment and the Blackboard test option. Students generally supported the approach because it broke content into manageable topic-sized assessments, provided immediate teacher feedback, and allowed them to track progress.

The context is an undergraduate population at Swinburne University of Technology’s Sarawak Campus, with students from Business, Engineering, and IT streams. The study is primarily descriptive and perception-based rather than experimental; it combines a demonstration of the online assessment approach with survey data on student attitudes. The main conclusion is that technology-mediated formative assessment is viewed favorably and is presented as potentially beneficial for both learning processes and summative exam preparation, though students also expressed concern that frequent testing could create stress and overemphasize grades.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that splitting course work into small-topic assessments was useful and supported learning in steps rather than only for final exams. The paper describes a Blackboard-based formative assessment model (weekly/fortnightly tests with detailed immediate feedback) that students perceived as helpful for subject understanding and preparation for summative semester exams, but no achievement outcome data were reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment and Blackboard online test implementation

finding.finding_summary: Students generally favored frequent internal assessments because they felt these provided constant feedback and helped them monitor their progress, which can support motivation and self-regulation. However, some students also reported that too many tests created stress and pressure to perform, indicating both beneficial and adverse affective responses.
finding.measure: Survey responses on views of frequent assessments, feedback, and stress/pressure

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes metacognition and reflection as central to formative assessment, and students said the feedback helped them identify strengths, weaknesses, and whether they were on track. The Blackboard implementation was intended to support progressive topic learning and self-monitoring, but the study measured perceptions rather than direct changes in durable skills.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of feedback utility for self-checking strengths/weaknesses and staying on track

finding.finding_summary: The Blackboard option was viewed as more convenient and flexible than classroom testing, largely because it provided immediate feedback and could be administered as repeated online assessments. The paper suggests this may streamline assessment and feedback delivery, but it does not report workload or time-savings data for teachers or students.
finding.measure: Student preferences comparing Blackboard tests versus classroom tests

paper_profiles.title: Changing Roles and Identities in a Teacher-Driven Professional Development Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development community changed over time and whether it began to resemble a community of practice. The authors are interested in whether giving teachers substantial agency to design their own professional learning, conduct classroom research, and lead professional activities can shift participation, leadership, and professional identity.

The intervention studied is Streamline to Mastery, a five-year professional development program for physical science/physics teachers in high-needs urban schools. Four teachers from two urban high schools participated in regular evening meetings with researchers, planned and carried out action research in their classrooms, exchanged emails, prepared conference presentations, and gradually took on more responsibility for setting agendas and initiating discussion. Data sources included 42 hours of video, email threads, and focus-group interviews.

Findings suggest that teacher participation increased over time in multiple ways: teachers sent a larger share of emails, increasingly initiated new email threads, and took over agenda-setting in meetings. The paper also reports a rise in challenging discourse, interpreted as evidence that the group moved from a researcher-led hierarchy toward a more egalitarian community of expert learners. The authors conclude that empowering teachers within a collaborative community may support professional growth, leadership, and the formation of a community of practice.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers showed increasing participation, agency, and leadership over the year in the Streamline community. Email activity, thread initiation, and agenda-setting shifted from being researcher-dominated to teacher-led, and teachers reported awareness of their growing responsibility and confidence in the group.
finding.measure: Email participation/origination, agenda-setting in meeting videos, focus-group interview reports of role change
