finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies collaborative and critical-thinking-related behaviors within a professional learning community. Over time, teachers increasingly challenged one another's ideas, debated instructional responsibilities, and engaged in shared problem solving, which the authors interpret as evidence of a developing community of practice.
finding.measure: Frequency and nature of 'challenging' discourse in meeting transcripts; collaborative agenda-setting and discussion patterns

finding.finding_summary: The program is designed to build teacher leadership and potentially influence broader educational discourse, and the paper reports early evidence of that shift. Teachers began planning workshops, presenting at a regional conference, and participating more actively in the national education conversation, suggesting growing institutional influence beyond their classrooms.
finding.measure: Conference presentation preparation, workshop planning, participation in broader professional discourse, leadership roles in the PD community

paper_profiles.title: Changing Identities and Evolving Conceptions of Inquiry through Teacher-Driven Professional Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development program, Streamline to Mastery, influenced participating science teachers’ conceptions of inquiry and their roles within a professional learning community. The central problem is that many physics teachers teach outside their content area and may have unclear or incomplete conceptions of scientific inquiry; the study asks whether sustained collaborative, teacher-led PD can help teachers develop a shared and more expert-like understanding of inquiry.

The intervention is a five-year professional development model in which secondary physical science teachers partnered with university researchers to design their own learning experiences, share lessons, reflect on practice, and discuss inquiry-oriented teaching. Four teachers from two urban high schools in the Rocky Mountain West participated in the first cohort, with data drawn from lesson reflections, survey responses, meeting videos, emails, and interviews. The study focuses on changes in teachers’ discourse about inquiry and shifts in participation, agenda-setting, and challenging discourse over time.

Findings suggest that teachers’ talk about inquiry became more aligned with the National Research Council’s five essential features of inquiry, and that they collectively developed a shared definition of inquiry. The paper also reports increasing teacher agency: more teacher-originated emails, more teacher-led discussion threads, greater agenda-setting responsibility, and more willingness to challenge one another’s ideas. The authors conclude that sustained, reflective, teacher-driven community work can support growth in professional understanding and leadership, though they note that consistent implementation of inquiry in classroom practice remains unverified.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ conceptions of classroom inquiry became more expert-like over time, with lesson reflections and survey responses showing increased references to the National Research Council’s five essential features of inquiry. Across five lesson-sharing reflections and two survey administrations (10th and 17th month), references to explain and communicate increased, and the group eventually co-constructed a shared definition of inquiry: “Socially constructing evidence-based meaning of phenomena through intentionally sequenced events.”
finding.measure: Teacher responses to inquiry survey items; lesson-sharing reflections coded for five essential features of inquiry

finding.finding_summary: The study found growing collaboration, critical discussion, and shared leadership among teachers in the professional community. Over time, teachers sent a larger share of emails, initiated more new discussion threads, set more meeting agendas, and increasingly challenged one another’s ideas; however, no formal effect sizes were reported.
finding.measure: Email participation and thread origination; meeting agenda-setting from video coding; challenging discourse in meeting transcripts; focus group interview

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a teacher-driven professional development model can shift a professional community away from a hierarchical structure toward a more egalitarian community of expert learners. The evidence is qualitative and descriptive, based on changes in leadership roles and participation patterns within the Streamline to Mastery program rather than institutional outcomes at the school or district level.
finding.measure: Participation patterns in the professional development community (emails, agenda-setting, discourse roles)

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how science and mathematics teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy that uses classroom response systems (“clickers”) to drive question-based, dialogic, formative classroom discussion. The authors frame the work as a teacher-change study: they want to understand how teachers adapt to TEFA, what tensions they encounter, and how professional development can better support implementation over time.

The intervention combines the technology, the TEFA pedagogy, and an intensive professional development program. The PD starts with a four-day summer workshop and continues with weekly after-school meetings in the first year, then less frequent support in later years. The paper describes a longitudinal, staggered-site design across several Massachusetts school systems, with approximately 39 middle- and high-school math and science teachers participating. Data sources include implementation logs, surveys, interviews, journals, classroom video, and PD transcripts.

The paper’s main contribution is descriptive and developmental rather than causal in the experimental sense. Through four teacher case narratives and cross-case observations, the authors argue that teachers typically progress from mastering the technology to grappling with question design, classroom discourse, student responsiveness, and fit with curriculum and school constraints. The paper concludes that TEFA is hard to learn but feasible, that intensive and responsive PD matters, and that teachers often make substantial changes in pedagogy and classroom interaction over one to two years, including greater student-student discussion, more formative use of student responses, and increased comfort with the approach.

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes high school and middle school mathematics teachers and shows that TEFA became useful for math instruction, especially for reviewing content and gauging understanding. However, the authors do not report student achievement scores or experimental effects; instead, the evidence is teacher-reported and case-based, suggesting that TEFA could support math learning opportunities while also creating substantial class-time and prep-time demands.
finding.measure: Teacher reports, classroom observations, and implementation logs related to mathematics instruction and review questions

finding.finding_summary: Science teachers used TEFA to promote question-driven instruction, dialogic discourse, and formative assessment in science classrooms. Across the cases and videotaped lessons, teachers increased discussion time, student-student interaction, and the use of student thinking to adjust instruction, indicating improved opportunities for scientific reasoning and conceptual discussion, though no standardized achievement effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Classroom video, teacher interviews, and observations of science question cycles and discussion
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers across multiple sites; four focal teacher cases

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported changes in student participation, engagement, confidence, and willingness to discuss ideas, and some teachers used TEFA to improve classroom management and motivation. The evidence is qualitative and teacher-reported rather than student-test based, but the paper suggests that TEFA increased students’ engagement in discussion and their responsiveness to classroom norms.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, student survey perceptions, and classroom participation patterns
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; student surveys administered in participating classes

finding.finding_summary: This is a central focus of the paper: TEFA is presented as a way to develop students’ discussion skills, metacognition, and ability to reason about ideas in a collaborative setting, while teachers themselves develop instructional agility and responsiveness. The authors report increased student-student interaction, more varied discussion formats, and teachers’ greater use of formative information to adjust instruction, all of which indicate gains in collaboration, metacognitive attention, and adaptive thinking opportunities, though no numeric effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Classroom video coding, teacher reflections, interview data, and implementation logs
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers across four sites; four focal teacher narratives

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is the implementation burden of TEFA: teachers repeatedly experienced pressure on prep time, class time, and technological reliability. At the same time, some teachers became more efficient at question design and classroom orchestration, and the authors argue that formative assessment information improved instructional decision-making; overall, the evidence points to a tradeoff between pedagogical value and workload.
finding.measure: Teacher journals, implementation logs, monthly surveys, and case narratives about prep time, class time, and technology glitches
finding.study_size: approximately n=39 teachers; implementation logs collected daily

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the professional development model and implementation design have implications for scalability, school-based peer learning, and future controlled implementation studies. It does not report institutional outcome effects, but it does show that on-site, critical-mass PD supported teacher collaboration and that district/school context affected feasibility and technology adoption.
finding.measure: Project design observations and teacher participation across school sites
finding.study_size: four school sites in three school systems; approximately n=39 teachers

paper_profiles.title: A novel density-based approach for estimating unknown means, distribution visualisations and meta-analyses of quantiles
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in meta-analysis: many studies with continuous outcomes report only quantiles such as medians, quartiles, and ranges rather than means and standard deviations. The authors propose a novel density-based approach that uses flexible quantile-based distributions and percentile matching to reconstruct unknown distributional parameters from summary statistics, without assuming a parametric form upfront.

The paper develops two main tools. First, it estimates means and standard deviations from 3-point and 5-point summaries using the generalized lambda distribution and the skew logistic distribution, and compares these estimates against common methods in simulation. Second, it proposes quantile-based meta-analysis methods for directly pooling medians, quartiles, and ratios of interquartile ranges when quantiles are the substantive target. The methods are demonstrated through simulations and an applied example using COVID-19 age data from a systematic review, where the authors meta-analyze differences in quartiles and dispersion between survivors and non-survivors.

Overall, the paper finds that the proposed density-based estimators work as well as or better than widely used approaches for estimating means from quantile summaries, especially under skewed data. The quantile-meta-analysis methods also produce sensible pooled estimates and confidence intervals, showing that directly meta-analyzing quantiles can be more appropriate than converting everything to means in some settings. The work is methodological rather than educational intervention research, and it does not study formative assessment, teacher professional development, implementation fidelity, curriculum pressure, or technology-mediated delivery.

finding.finding_summary: In simulation studies, the proposed generalized lambda and skew logistic approaches estimated unknown means from quantile summaries as well as or better than existing methods across the scenarios considered. The paper reports average relative error (ARE) across 1,000 simulated samples for multiple distributions and sample sizes, finding the proposed methods competitive with or superior to Luo et al. (2018) and other standard estimators.
finding.measure: Accuracy of estimated sample means from quantile summaries (average relative error, ARE)
finding.study_size: 1,000 simulated datasets per scenario; sample sizes n=25 to 1000

finding.finding_summary: The proposed quantile-based meta-analysis methods yielded accurate pooled estimates and confidence intervals for quartile differences and ratios of interquartile ranges in a real COVID-19 example. In the age meta-analysis of 29 studies, pooled differences were statistically significant and coherent with the visual distribution analyses; for example, the pooled median difference was 12.819 years with 95% CI (10.203, 15.435), and the ratio of squared IQRs was 0.482 with 95% CI (0.374, 0.620).
finding.measure: Meta-analytic pooled differences in quartiles and ratio of squared IQR widths
finding.effect_size: 0.482 for ratio of squared IQRs; 12.819 for median difference
finding.confidence_interval: (0.374, 0.620) for IQR ratio; (10.203, 15.435) for median difference

paper_profiles.title: ACDC: Adaptive Curriculum Planning with Dynamic Contrastive Control for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning in Robotic Manipulation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of sparse-reward goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) in robotic manipulation, where agents struggle to learn efficiently across tasks with different difficulty levels and goal geometries. The authors argue that existing experience replay and prioritization methods improve sample efficiency but do not sufficiently control which experiences are emphasized as training progresses.

To address this, the paper proposes ACDC, a two-level framework that combines Adaptive Curriculum (AC) Planning with Dynamic Contrastive (DC) Control. AC scores trajectories using a blend of diversity and quality, with the weighting adaptively adjusted according to the agent’s success rate and training progress; DC then uses those scores to form contrastive positive/negative pairs and learn trajectory representations that guide experience selection. The approach is evaluated on six OpenAI Gym robotic manipulation benchmarks across Fetch and Shadow Dexterous Hand settings, with additional ablations and sensitivity analyses showing that the adaptive curriculum and contrastive control each contribute to performance gains.

The study is entirely in robotic reinforcement learning rather than education. Its main empirical conclusion is that ACDC improves final success rates, convergence speed, and cumulative regret relative to HER, CHER, DTGSH, and other baselines, especially on harder high-dimensional manipulation tasks. The paper also reports that the method transfers to SAC-based agents and is robust across multiple hyperparameter settings, but it does not examine any educational outcomes or human learners.

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; primarily educators and researchers, with illustrative examples spanning high school and undergraduate contexts
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative/practical guide on how generative AI, especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, can support formative assessment and feedback. The authors frame formative assessment through the familiar questions of where learners are going, where they currently are, and how to move them forward, then map LLM use cases onto those functions. The paper argues that LLMs can help with student-friendly learning objectives, co-constructing success criteria, generating exemplars, creating questions, and producing feedback, but that these uses must remain grounded in pedagogical expertise.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the article reviews existing literature and provides worked examples and prompt templates for educators. It emphasizes that LLMs can save teacher time and make formative assessment more scalable, especially in large classes or resource-constrained settings, but warns about limitations such as variable output quality, over-reliance by students, and the fact that many current evaluation metrics miss formative dimensions like task-, process-, and self-regulation-level feedback. The authors repeatedly stress that teachers must review, adapt, and contextualize AI outputs.

The paper also discusses how LLMs may help overcome systemic barriers to formative assessment and suggests future research directions, including better evaluation metrics, prompt repositories, and AI-aware assessment design. Because the paper is a conceptual review/guide rather than an empirical evaluation, it does not provide effect sizes or direct causal evidence. Its main contribution is a pedagogically organized framework for thinking about LLM-enabled formative assessment in classrooms.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload and save time by automating or accelerating tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating sample work, and creating assessment questions or feedback. However, this is presented as a conceptual/practical claim rather than an empirically tested effect, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / time-saving potential for creating formative assessment materials

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests LLM-supported formative assessment can foster metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking by helping students interpret learning goals, reflect on exemplar quality, and revise work based on feedback. The paper also cautions that over-reliance on LLMs may undermine these skills if not designed carefully.
finding.measure: Metacognition, self-regulation, critical thinking, and reflection in formative assessment tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper gives multiple examples of LLM use in writing-related formative assessment, including simplifying learning objectives, generating sample methods sections, and supporting feedback on student writing. These applications are discussed as pedagogical possibilities rather than as outcomes from an evaluation study, so no quantitative effect is reported.
finding.measure: Writing quality / writing-related formative tasks such as methods sections and essay exemplars

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly uses science examples, especially biology and fMRI methods writing, to illustrate how LLMs can support formative assessment in scientific contexts. The emphasis is on helping students understand scientific procedures and communicate methods more clearly, but the paper does not report empirical effects on scientific reasoning outcomes.
finding.measure: Scientific learning goals and methods-section writing in biology/neuroimaging examples

paper_profiles.title: Meta-analysis of Bayesian analyses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a new Bayesian meta-analytic framework for combining the posterior distributions produced by multiple related studies, rather than the usual point estimates or summary statistics. The central question is how to perform meta-analysis when each study already yields a posterior over its local effect of interest, and how to use those posteriors both to estimate a shared overall effect and to refine the study-specific posteriors post hoc.

The proposed method, called meta-analysis of Bayesian analyses (MBA), replaces conventional likelihood terms with expected likelihood factors computed from each study’s posterior distribution. This produces a "superposterior" for the global effect and a joint model that can also update local posteriors by borrowing strength across studies. The paper proves theoretical properties of the update rule, including order-invariance and posterior concentration, and shows that standard random-effects and fixed-effects meta-analysis arise as special cases under appropriate assumptions.

The framework is illustrated with numerical examples using likelihood-free Bayesian analyses, including an MA(2) time-series example and a tuberculosis outbreak dynamics example. In both cases, MBA aggregates independently computed posteriors and improves identifiability or stability relative to naive combination strategies, while retaining uncertainty information better than methods that collapse each posterior to a single point estimate.

paper_profiles.title: A Bias Correction Method in Meta-analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials with no Adjustments for Zero-inflated Outcomes
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a statistical problem in meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials: when outcomes are count data with many zeros, studies that analyze them with a standard Poisson model can produce biased intervention effects. The authors argue that this bias can carry into aggregate-data meta-analysis and propose a bias-correction procedure called Zero-inflation Bias Correction (ZIBC) that adjusts conventional Poisson estimates to approximate what a zero-inflated Poisson model would have produced.

The method requires only summary-level information from each trial, including the conventional regression estimate, arm-level outcome averages, and zero proportions. It is designed for two-arm randomized trials and is applied study-by-study before pooling effects in a standard random-effects meta-analysis. The paper evaluates the method in simulations and two real examples: a meta-analysis of alcohol intervention trials from Project INTEGRATE and a dental caries prevention trial in five-year-old children.

Across simulations, the ZIBC method generally recovered the true intervention effect well over a range of zero-inflation levels, with performance close to the zero-inflated Poisson 'true' model and better than the conventional Poisson model. In the alcohol meta-analysis, the correction changed some study-level and pooled log incidence rate ratios, while in the dental caries example it substantially altered the estimated effect for boys and girls. The authors conclude that ZIBC is a practical alternative when individual participant data are unavailable, but it should be used cautiously when zero rates are extremely high or when the intervention and control groups have similar zero rates.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate educational achievement outcomes directly, but it does apply and evaluate a meta-analytic correction method across intervention trials, including a real-world alcohol intervention meta-analysis and a dental caries prevention trial. Across simulations and examples, the corrected estimates were closer to the zero-inflated Poisson benchmark than the conventional Poisson estimates, with the pooled estimate in Project INTEGRATE shifting from ˆβ1,CV = -0.07 to ˆβ1,ZIBC = -0.09, matching the 'true' estimate of -0.09.
finding.measure: Meta-analytic log incidence density ratio for intervention effects across trials
finding.study_size: n=10 trials in the main simulation examples; n=10 studies in the Project INTEGRATE application; 2 strata in the dental caries example

paper_profiles.title: Food Delivery Time Prediction in Indian Cities Using Machine Learning Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of predicting food delivery times more accurately in densely populated Indian cities. The authors argue that prior approaches rely too heavily on static historical data and miss dynamic contextual factors such as traffic density, weather, local events, and geographic distance between restaurant and customer.

To address this, they build and compare several machine learning regression models on a Kaggle dataset of 45,000 delivery records spanning multiple Indian cities. After preprocessing the data and engineering features such as haversine distance and time-based variables, they evaluate Linear Regression, Decision Tree, Bagging, Random Forest, Elastic Net, SVM, XGBoost, and LightGBM using MSE and R² with 5-fold cross-validation and a held-out test set.

The study finds that LightGBM performs best, achieving R² = 0.76 and MSE = 20.59, outperforming baseline linear and tree-based models. Ablation results and feature importance analysis indicate that traffic density, weather conditions, and geospatial proximity are key predictors. The paper concludes that integrating real-time contextual and spatial data can substantially improve predictive accuracy and support better logistics decisions, though it remains a predictive modeling study rather than a causal intervention study.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that machine learning models, especially LightGBM, improved predictive performance for delivery-time estimation, which the authors link to better logistics planning and resource allocation. LightGBM achieved R² = 0.76 and MSE = 20.59 on a dataset of 41,368 cleaned records, outperforming Linear Regression (R² = 0.44, MSE = 49.08), Random Forest (R² = 0.66, MSE = 30.03), and XGBoost (R² = 0.71, MSE = 25.37).
finding.measure: Prediction error in food delivery time forecasting (MSE, R²)

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI and Creativity: A Systematic Literature Review and Meta-Analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether generative AI improves creativity, whether human-AI collaboration outperforms unaided humans, and whether GenAI changes the diversity of ideas produced in creative tasks. The authors conduct a systematic literature review and random-effects meta-analysis of 28 studies (8214 participants) identified from Web of Science, SSRN, arXiv, and manual search, extracting 127 effect-size estimates.

The included studies span text-to-text GenAI models, especially GPT-4 and GPT-3.5, and a range of creativity tasks such as creative writing, alternate uses, consequences, divergent association, ideation, and creative problem solving. The meta-analysis finds no meaningful average difference between GenAI and humans in direct creative performance (g=-0.048), but a small positive effect when humans collaborate with GenAI versus work alone (g=0.273). In contrast, collaboration with GenAI significantly reduces idea diversity (g=-0.863), suggesting a homogenization trade-off.

The paper also explores heterogeneity by model, task type, and participant background. It finds that GPT-4 tends to perform best in direct comparison with humans, but GPT-3.5 appears more beneficial in collaborative settings; laypeople benefit more from GenAI assistance than domain experts; and simpler tasks like alternate uses and consequences tasks are more favorable to GenAI than creative writing. Overall, the paper concludes that GenAI is best understood as an augmentative tool for creativity, with benefits that depend strongly on task and model choices and with a notable risk of reduced idea diversity.

finding.finding_summary: The meta-analysis directly evaluates creativity as a durable skill across 28 studies (m=8214; 127 effect-size estimates). GenAI alone shows no significant overall advantage over humans (g=-0.048, 95% CI [-0.257, 0.161]), but humans supported by GenAI perform better than humans alone (g=0.273, 95% CI [0.018, 0.528]), indicating a small collaborative benefit.
finding.measure: Creativity performance in creative tasks (e.g., creativity scales, originality, novelty, semantic distance, cosine similarity)

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies use creative writing tasks, and the meta-analysis reports that GenAI versus human-only performance on creative writing favors humans (g=-0.717, 95% CI [-1.010, -0.424]), while human-GenAI collaboration in creative writing is near null (g=0.048, 95% CI [-0.412, 0.508]). This indicates that GenAI is not uniformly beneficial for writing-related creative output.
finding.measure: Creative writing performance

finding.finding_summary: The discussion interprets the collaboration gains as consistent with a facilitation mechanism such as faster drafting and broader ideation, suggesting productivity benefits in creative workflows. However, the paper does not directly measure task time or workload, so this is a secondary but substantive implication rather than a primary outcome.
finding.measure: Creative workflow performance / collaborative output quality

paper_profiles.title: Formative Assessment and its E-learning Implementation
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the International Conference for Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conference paper examines how formative assessment might be implemented through an e-learning platform, specifically Blackboard Learning System, in a university setting. The authors motivate the study by arguing that formative assessment should support learning through frequent testing, timely feedback, and opportunities for students to reflect and improve before summative exams.

The paper describes a proposed implementation in which weekly or fortnightly online tests are delivered through Blackboard, with immediate score reporting and detailed feedback. It also discusses design features such as open-book testing, question randomization, and use of discussion forums or virtual classroom tools to strengthen feedback interactions. The empirical component is a student survey at Swinburne University of Technology (Sarawak Campus) using a 16-item questionnaire, including closed and open-ended items about continuous assessment and Blackboard test delivery.

Findings from the survey indicate generally favorable student perceptions of frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based testing, mainly because of immediate feedback, convenience, and the ability to study smaller topic units incrementally. Students also believed the approach could help them keep up with the subject throughout the semester and improve summative exam preparation. However, some students expressed concerns that too many tests could create stress or pressure and that frequent assessment might overemphasize learning at the expense of grades.

finding.finding_summary: Students responded favorably to frequent internal assessments and Blackboard-based formative tests, largely because they perceived them as motivating, flexible, and helpful for tracking their progress. The survey found support for immediate feedback and smaller topic assessments, although some students also reported stress/pressure from too many tests and concern that learning could be overemphasized relative to grades.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of continuous assessment, need for teacher feedback, and attitudes toward Blackboard online testing from a questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that formative assessment supports metacognitive processes by helping students identify strengths and weaknesses, reflect on feedback, and monitor whether they are on track. In the survey, students reported that immediate, detailed feedback helped them correct mistakes without delay and learn individual topics progressively.
finding.measure: Student perceptions related to learning in steps, checking learning, immediate feedback, and reflection on strengths/weaknesses

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents formative assessment as a way to improve subject learning and preparation for summative semester examinations in a university course context. Students believed frequent Blackboard assessments helped them stay in touch with the subject throughout the semester and would support performance on end-of-semester exams, but no direct achievement outcomes were reported.
finding.measure: Student perceptions of subject learning and preparation for summative semester examination

paper_profiles.title: Changing Roles and Identities in a Teacher-Driven Professional Development Community
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development program, Streamline to Mastery, supports physics and physical science teachers in developing agency, leadership, and a shared community of practice. The authors ask how teachers’ participation and leadership roles change over time and whether the group exhibits features of a community of practice.

The intervention is a five-year professional development model in which teachers design much of the PD for themselves and for one another, conduct classroom action research, present at conferences, and participate in regular meetings with a small research team. Four teachers from two urban high schools in high-needs districts participated in this first cohort. Data came from 42 hours of video, email threads, and a focus-group interview.

Findings suggest that over the course of the year teachers increasingly took ownership of the community: they sent more emails, initiated more discussion threads, and began setting meeting agendas. The authors also observed a rise in challenging discourse, indicating that teachers moved from a more hierarchical structure toward a more egalitarian, collaborative community of expert learners. The paper concludes that professional growth may be supported by creating communities in which teachers’ own expertise and everyday experiences are treated as resources for change.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers showed increased collaboration, leadership, and critical engagement over time in the Streamline community. Across the year, they increasingly initiated email threads, set meeting agendas, and challenged one another’s ideas; the authors describe a more than four-fold increase in challenging statements during the middle period compared with the early meetings.
finding.measure: Email participation/origination, meeting agenda-setting, and coded instances of challenging discourse in meeting videos

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that a teacher-driven professional development model can shift the structure of a PD community from hierarchical to more egalitarian, with teachers taking on leadership roles in program planning and dissemination. Evidence includes teachers increasingly setting agendas, initiating communication, and helping plan workshops and future cohorts, suggesting growth in teacher leadership and community governance.
finding.measure: Observed role changes in PD meetings, email threads, and focus-group interview responses

paper_profiles.title: Changing Identities and Evolving Conceptions of Inquiry through Teacher-Driven Professional Development
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a teacher-driven professional development program, Streamline to Mastery, shaped participating science teachers’ conceptions of inquiry and their roles within a professional community. The central problem is that inquiry-oriented science teaching is often defined inconsistently and teachers may hold vague or mixed conceptions of what inquiry means in practice. The authors ask how teachers’ talk about inquiry changed over time and how their participation and leadership roles evolved in the program.

The program involved four physical science teachers from two urban high schools in the Rocky Mountain West, all working in high-needs schools. Teachers and university researchers met every other week over the first 18 months of a five-year PD initiative to share lessons, reflect on inquiry-oriented instruction, discuss classroom experiences, and co-develop the direction of the PD. Data included lesson-sharing reflections, survey responses, 42 hours of video, email threads, interviews, and member checking. The analysis was qualitative and interpretive, using the five essential features of inquiry from the NRC framework as well as emergent coding of discourse and participation.

The authors conclude that teachers’ conceptions of inquiry became more explicit and more aligned with the NRC framework over time, moving from ambiguous use of terms like hands-on and constructivism toward a shared definition centered on socially constructing evidence-based meaning of phenomena through intentionally sequenced events. They also report increases in teacher agency: teachers sent more emails, initiated more discussion threads, set more meeting agendas, and increasingly challenged one another’s ideas. The paper argues that sustained teacher-driven collaboration grounded in classroom experience can support both conceptual growth and the development of a more egalitarian community of practice, though the authors note that consistent implementation in classroom practice was not empirically verified in this study.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ conceptions of scientific inquiry became more expert-like over the course of the professional development program. In lesson reflections and survey responses, references aligned with the NRC inquiry framework increased over time; for example, the frequency of Communicate and Explain references increased approximately five-fold across the two survey administrations (month 10 to month 17), while lesson reflections by the fifth lesson referenced four of the five essential inquiry features. The study is based on n=4 teachers and reports discourse and survey coding rather than student outcome data.
finding.measure: Teacher conceptions of classroom scientific inquiry measured through lesson-sharing reflections, open-ended inquiry survey responses, and coded video discourse

finding.finding_summary: Teachers showed growth in collaboration, critical discourse, and leadership within the professional community. Over time, teachers increased their share of emails, began more new discussion threads, set more meeting agendas, and more frequently challenged one another’s ideas; the authors describe a shift toward more egalitarian participation. Because the evidence is qualitative and descriptive, no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Participation and leadership in the professional learning community, including email activity, agenda setting, and coded 'challenging' discourse

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports increased teacher agency, confidence, and willingness to engage in skeptical discourse as the PD progressed. Teachers became more comfortable questioning one another, taking responsibility for agenda setting, and contributing as expert learners, suggesting gains in self-efficacy and engagement within the community. The findings are based on qualitative analysis of meetings, emails, and interviews with n=4 teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher agency, participation, and willingness to challenge peers in a PD community

paper_profiles.title: Teacher Learning of Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how teachers learn to implement Technology-Enhanced Formative Assessment (TEFA), a pedagogy built around classroom response system technology (“clickers”) and designed to promote question-driven instruction, dialogic whole-class discussion, formative assessment, and meta-level communication. The central research question is not student achievement, but teacher change: how teachers’ beliefs, practices, and classroom routines evolve as they participate in an intensive professional development program.

The study followed approximately 39 science and mathematics teachers across multiple western Massachusetts school sites in a longitudinal delayed-intervention design. Data sources included professional development meeting transcripts, teacher journals, implementation logs, monthly surveys, classroom video, student surveys, and interviews. The paper presents detailed case narratives for four teachers (two high school, two middle school) to illustrate distinct learning trajectories and the tensions they encountered, including curriculum coverage pressure, preparation time, student participation, classroom control, and fit between TEFA and local student needs.

The main conclusion is that teachers can learn TEFA, but the process is difficult, nonlinear, and highly individualized. Teachers generally moved from mastering the technology to adapting question design, then classroom discourse, then using formative assessment information to adjust instruction. The authors argue that intensive, responsive professional development can support substantial teacher change, but implementation fidelity and long-term sustainability depend on how teachers reconcile TEFA with curriculum demands, classroom management, and their own pedagogical beliefs. The paper also suggests that formative assessment can become integrated into teaching even when teachers adapt or partially redefine TEFA to fit their contexts.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on implementation burden and teacher workload. Teachers repeatedly reported that TEFA increased preparation time for crafting effective questions and consumed class time needed for content coverage, even as it became easier with practice for some teachers (for example, Tracy and Kim). No effect size is reported; the evidence is qualitative and based on teacher logs, journals, interviews, and observations (n≈39 teachers, with four detailed cases).
finding.measure: Teacher preparation time, class time spent on TEFA, implementation logs, journals, interviews, classroom video

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports changes in teacher and student engagement, confidence, and persistence around TEFA. Teachers often began uncertain or anxious, but many grew more comfortable and motivated as they experienced successful implementation; students’ participation sometimes increased when teachers adjusted TEFA routines. No standardized effect size is reported; evidence comes from logs, journals, interviews, and videotaped lessons.
finding.measure: Teacher confidence/comfort, student participation, classroom engagement, self-reported attitudes

finding.finding_summary: A major theme is growth in teachers’ pedagogical reasoning, metacognition, and adaptive expertise. Across cases, teachers became better at interpreting student thinking, adjusting instruction in real time, and using formative information to refine questioning and discussion; the authors also note increased student-to-student discourse and more varied discussion formats. No quantitative effect size is reported; findings are drawn from mixed qualitative/observational evidence across the project.
finding.measure: Teacher reflections, classroom discourse patterns, instructional adjustment in response to student thinking

finding.finding_summary: Although the study is not an achievement trial, it includes mathematics teachers and describes how TEFA was used to support math learning, especially for review and exam preparation in Gina’s case and for discussion-driven instruction in Kim’s case. The paper claims teachers used formative assessment to better understand student thinking in math, but it does not report test-score outcomes or effect sizes. Evidence is qualitative and case-based.
finding.measure: Mathematics classroom discussion, formative assessment use, exam review activities

finding.finding_summary: The TEFA pedagogy is explicitly designed to develop scientific reasoning through question-driven instruction, dialogical discourse, and formative assessment, and the paper reports that teachers increasingly elicited student reasoning and student-to-student argumentation. In science classrooms, teachers used TEFA to draw out multiple ideas and adjust instruction based on student thinking, but no student achievement measures or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Classroom discourse about scientific ideas, student reasoning, teacher adjustments based on formative assessment

paper_profiles.title: A Practical Guide for Supporting Formative Assessment and Feedback Using Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative, practice-oriented review that asks how generative AI—especially large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT—can be used to support formative assessment and feedback. The authors organize the discussion around a formative assessment framework: clarifying where the learner is going, understanding where the learner is, and helping learners move forward. They argue that current LLM use in education has expanded rapidly, but much of it is not well aligned to core formative assessment principles.

The paper does not report a new empirical study. Instead, it synthesizes literature and provides concrete classroom examples and prompt templates showing how educators might use LLMs to rewrite learning objectives in student-friendly language, co-construct success criteria, generate exemplar student work, create diagnostic questions, and produce feedback at different levels (task, process, self-regulation). The context is mainly K-12 and undergraduate teaching, with examples from secondary biology and undergraduate fMRI courses.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can augment, but should not replace, expert pedagogy. The authors emphasize that effective use depends on teacher judgment, careful prompting, contextual adaptation, and attention to limitations such as output variability, superficial benchmarks, overreliance by students, and the need for better formative-assessment-specific evaluation metrics. The paper is primarily a conceptual/practical guide rather than causal evidence on student outcomes or implementation moderators.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI/LLMs can save educators time by automating or accelerating formative-assessment tasks such as rewriting learning objectives, generating questions, creating sample work, and drafting feedback. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a narrative/practice review rather than a primary study.
finding.measure: teacher time, task efficiency, workload reduction (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames LLM-supported formative assessment as a way to promote higher-order and durable skills, especially metacognition, self-regulation, and critical thinking. It argues that activities like co-constructing success criteria and evaluating LLM-generated exemplars can help students reflect on and improve their own learning, but no direct empirical effect is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, metacognition, self-regulation (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that formative assessment supported by LLMs may improve student engagement and support learners in taking a more active role in their learning. These claims are discussed conceptually in relation to motivation, engagement, and student agency, but they are not backed by new empirical data in the paper.
finding.measure: student engagement, agency, motivation (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses LLM use for writing-related formative tasks such as improving learning objectives, generating sample work, and supporting method-section writing in an fMRI course. These examples are intended to improve writing clarity and alignment with instructional goals, but the article does not present direct outcome data.
finding.measure: writing quality / clarity of learning objectives and sample work (conceptual examples)

finding.finding_summary: Using an undergraduate fMRI example, the paper shows how LLMs could support students in writing method sections and understanding experimental design elements. This is presented as a pedagogical application for scientific writing and reasoning, but no empirical evaluation is reported.
finding.measure: scientific writing / method-section construction in fMRI coursework (conceptual examples)

paper_profiles.title: Interdisciplinary Teams for Teacher Professional Development
paper_profiles.population: Secondary school teachers (preservice and inservice STEM teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper describes the design and iterative refinement of the San Antonio Teacher Training Astronomy Academy (SATTAA), a 2-week teacher professional development program aimed at improving astronomy content knowledge and pedagogical capacity for secondary school teachers. The authors frame the work around a theory of change in which increased teacher confidence and expertise in astronomy, combined with stronger pedagogical and technology integration, should support better student engagement and retention in STEM fields.

Rather than testing a single intervention arm, the paper reports three annual iterations of the program (2018-2020) and the interdisciplinary process used to redesign it based on participant and facilitator feedback. The program combined astronomy content led by subject-matter experts with STEM pedagogy, hands-on inquiry activities, informal education partnerships, and in 2020 a fully online format due to COVID-19. The participant pool included preservice teachers only in 2018, mixed preservice/inservice teachers in 2019, and a larger mostly inservice cohort in 2020.

The paper’s main conclusions are that interdisciplinary design, iterative refinement, and flexible delivery formats can support teacher learning and participation. Across years, participants reported higher astronomy understanding, greater interest, and appreciation for the program; the authors also report a significant pre-post gain in astronomy content knowledge for a subsample (n=18, t=5.24, effect size=1.24). The online format reduced logistical burden and expanded access, while mixed teams and alumni networking were seen as beneficial for sustaining collaboration and lesson development.

finding.finding_summary: The program produced measurable gains in astronomy content knowledge among participants. For the 18 teachers with pre/post data, correct responses to 15 astronomy questions increased from M=6.83 (SD=3.167) at pretest to M=8.72 (SD=2.845) at posttest, with a statistically significant paired-samples t-test (t=5.24, n=18, p=0.000) and a large effect size of 1.24.
finding.measure: Pre/post astronomy content knowledge quiz (15 moderately difficult questions)

finding.finding_summary: Participants consistently reported increases in interest in astronomy and understanding of the content across all three iterations. On 5-point Likert scales, interest and understanding improved for preservice and inservice teachers alike, with the largest reported gain in understanding among 2020 preservice teachers (+2.0).
finding.measure: Pre/post self-reported interest and understanding ratings (5-point Likert scales)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants benefited from collaborative lesson planning, mixed preservice/inservice team structures, and networking through the emerging community of practice. Teachers said the program deepened pedagogical connections and supported co-planning, with inservice participants specifically noting benefits from exchanging classroom tips and refining lessons with partners.
finding.measure: Participant feedback from reflections, focus groups, and qualitative comments about collaboration and lesson planning

finding.finding_summary: The program expanded access and participation through a fully online delivery in 2020 and by creating an alumni network to sustain engagement beyond the 2-week institute. The authors report that online delivery enabled participation for teachers who otherwise could not have joined and reduced logistical demands, while also supporting broader geographic reach and a continuing community of practice.
finding.measure: Program implementation and participant feedback regarding online access, networking, and alumni engagement
finding.study_size: n=19 in 2020; alumni group across cohorts

paper_profiles.title: Teacher-Driven Professional Development and the Pursuit of a Sophisticated Understanding of Inquiry
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a small group of practicing physical science teachers developed a more sophisticated understanding of scientific inquiry while participating in Streamline to Mastery, a teacher-driven professional development program. The authors focus on whether and how teachers’ conceptions of inquiry changed over time as they engaged in collaborative lesson-sharing, reflective writing, semi-weekly meetings, and teacher-led discourse about inquiry-oriented instruction.

The program was designed so that teachers chose their own growth goals and worked with researchers as collaborators rather than recipients of expert-led training. Four middle and high school teachers from urban, high-needs schools participated; most had three or fewer years of teaching experience, and all had master’s degrees. Data came from lesson-sharing reflections, repeated open-ended inquiry survey prompts, and video of professional development meetings, analyzed through the five essential features of inquiry from the NRC framework.

The main finding is that teachers’ language and conceptions of inquiry became more aligned with the NRC inquiry framework over the course of the first year. Early on, their definitions were vague and mixed with terms such as hands-on, constructivism, and real-world relevance; later, they referenced more of the five essential features, especially evidence and explanation, and eventually developed a shared, teacher-generated definition of inquiry. The paper argues that teacher-driven, collaborative professional learning grounded in teachers’ own practice may be more effective for developing deep pedagogical understanding than traditional expert-delivered professional development.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ conceptions of inquiry became more expert-like over the first year of the professional development program. In lesson reflections, references aligned with the NRC’s five essential features of inquiry increased across five lessons, and in the inquiry survey the frequency of Communicate and Explain references increased approximately five-fold from the first to second administration, while Evidence stayed roughly the same.
finding.measure: Open-ended lesson-sharing reflections and repeated inquiry survey prompts coded against the five essential features of scientific inquiry from the NRC framework

paper_profiles.title: A LLM-Driven Multi-Agent System for Professional Development of Mathematics Teachers
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents I-VIP (Intelligent Virtual Interactive Program), an LLM-driven multi-agent tutoring platform designed to support mathematics teacher professional development (PD). The authors frame the problem as a lack of equitable, timely, and scalable PD opportunities for teachers, especially when PD requires domain-specific knowledge and tailored feedback that general-purpose chatbots do not provide.

The system combines a conversational interface with domain-authored learning materials, interactive tools (e.g., notebooks and draw boards), retrieval-augmented generation, and multi-agent LLM modules for intention detection, answer judging, and feedback generation. The platform is organized around mathematics PD content on proportion, ratio, and multiplication, and it logs user interactions and supports diagnosis activities to track progress.

Evaluation consists of a small online user study with five PhD and postdoctoral education students who completed all 51 activities and rated system responses, plus an offline prompt-optimization experiment on previously observed failure cases. The paper reports very high response satisfaction (97.49% positive feedback across 14,491 responses) and improved accuracy after prompt optimization / few-shot methods, but it does not report learner outcome gains for teachers’ knowledge or classroom practice. Overall, the contribution is primarily a system/design paper with preliminary usability and component-performance evidence rather than a causal evaluation of PD impact.

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to improve the scalability and timeliness of teacher professional development through an LLM-based conversational platform with interactive tools and automated feedback. In a small online evaluation, five PhD/postdoctoral participants completed 51 activities and provided 14,491 feedback clicks, with 97.49% positive feedback for system responses, suggesting high usability and responsiveness rather than a measured productivity effect.
finding.measure: User satisfaction / feedback clicks on system responses

paper_profiles.title: Estimating Causal Moderation Effects with Randomized Treatments and Non-Randomized Moderators
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A (Forthcoming)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a general statistical framework for estimating causal moderation effects when the treatment is randomized but the moderator is not. The central question is not whether treatment effects vary across subgroups, but whether changing a third variable would actually change the size of the treatment effect. The paper argues that common subgroup analysis and standard interaction regressions generally do not identify this causal moderation estimand when the moderator is observational.

The proposed solution is a "parallel estimation framework": split the sample by treatment status, estimate the effect of the moderator on the outcome within each treatment arm using covariate adjustment or other suitable identification strategies, and then take the difference between those two within-arm effects. The paper derives identification assumptions under selection on observables, shows how matching and regression can be implemented, and explains why conventional approaches can be biased when moderators are non-randomized. It also discusses sensitivity analysis and alternative identification strategies such as instrumental variables or regression discontinuity within treatment arms.

To illustrate the framework, the paper reanalyzes two political science applications: a General Social Survey framing experiment on whether the term "welfare" changes support for public assistance, moderated by party identification; and a conjoint experiment on asylum seeker preferences, moderated by nationalism. In both cases, conventional subgroup and interaction-regression estimates suggest stronger moderation than the causal-moderation estimates obtained from the parallel framework. The main conclusion is methodological: researchers should not interpret ordinary subgroup differences or simple interaction terms as causal moderation unless the moderator itself is identified causally.

finding.finding_summary: The paper makes a methodological contribution to causal inference by showing that common approaches to moderation analysis can be biased when the moderator is non-randomized. It provides a generalized framework for identifying and estimating causal moderation effects with randomized treatments and observational moderators, and demonstrates via two applications that conventional estimates can substantially overstate moderation relative to the proposed approach.
finding.measure: Validity of causal moderation estimation methods; comparison of conventional subgroup/interaction estimators with parallel estimation framework

paper_profiles.title: Sustainable, Local Socio-Economic Development Through Astronomy: A Preprint
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This preprint asks how astronomy can be leveraged as a driver of sustainable local socio-economic development, especially in communities near observatories and astronomy-related facilities. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes case studies from South Africa, Indonesia, Chile, South West Asia, and India to identify how astronomy initiatives have affected local economies, employment, tourism, and STEM participation.

The paper describes community-oriented astronomy projects such as the SALT collateral benefits programme, observatory-linked community development efforts, astrotourism initiatives, and astronomy-based livelihood creation. Across these examples, the authors emphasize consultation with local stakeholders, teacher training, visitor centres, homestays, and partnerships as mechanisms for translating astronomy infrastructure into local benefits.

The main conclusion is that astronomy can produce meaningful community and economic benefits when projects are participatory, context-sensitive, and sustained by local ownership and monitoring. The paper also notes recurring challenges, including unequal benefit distribution, limited local control, and sustainability gaps after external funding ends. It ultimately proposes practical guidelines for planning and evaluating astronomy-for-development initiatives rather than presenting causal evidence on educational outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that astronomy-related education and outreach initiatives were used to promote STEM participation and interest, but it does not present direct causal evidence on scientific reasoning outcomes. In the Chile ALMA case, science and English programmes in a local school reportedly improved students' performance in national tests, but no exact effect size or study design is provided.
finding.measure: Student performance in national tests; STEM participation and engagement

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that astronomy initiatives can inspire curiosity, engagement, and sustained interest in STEM among learners and teachers. Examples include teacher training, school visits, learner workshops, and public outreach, but the paper does not report causal estimates or standardized social-emotional measures.
finding.measure: Teacher participation, learner workshop reach, and reported STEM interest/engagement

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studies how astronomy projects affect local socio-economic systems, including employment, tourism, community development, and institutional partnerships. Case examples report that SALT attracted more than 50,300 visitors over 2015-2018, about 6% of Sutherland’s population was directly employed by the observatory, and 20% reported indirect benefits; however, these are descriptive claims rather than controlled causal estimates.
finding.measure: Visitor counts, local employment, indirect benefits, community development indicators, and project sustainability

paper_profiles.title: Robust Estimation of Moderated Causal Excursion Odds Ratio in Micro-Randomized Trials
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops statistical methods for estimating moderated causal excursion effects on the odds-ratio scale in micro-randomized trials (MRTs). The motivation is that many MRTs with binary proximal outcomes are analyzed using relative risk or risk difference, but odds ratios can be more stable and interpretable in some settings, especially when researchers want valid predicted probabilities and to examine effect moderation.

The authors propose two estimators: a doubly robust estimator for settings where the MRT randomization depends only on the chosen moderator set (Simple Randomization), and an alternative estimator for more general randomization schemes that incorporate an association model. They also extend the framework to other link functions and prove consistency/asymptotic normality under stated conditions. Performance is evaluated via simulations, and the methods are applied to the Drink Less MRT, a 30-day smartphone push-notification study in 349 adults aimed at improving near-term app engagement and reducing alcohol consumption.

In the Drink Less application, daily push notifications significantly increased near-term app engagement, with an estimated marginal log odds ratio of 1.36 (95% CI [1.18, 1.54]), and there was no evidence of significant moderation by decision point, prior app use, or prior-day notification. The paper’s contribution is methodological rather than educational, and it does not study formative assessment or school-based learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: In the Drink Less MRT application (n=349 adults; 30 days; daily randomization), push notifications significantly increased near-term app engagement, measured as whether the participant opened the app in the hour after the notification. The estimated marginal effect was a log odds ratio of 1.36 (95% CI [1.18, 1.54]), corresponding to an odds ratio of 3.89.
finding.measure: Near-term app engagement (indicator of opening the app in the hour following the notification)

paper_profiles.title: Transitioning STEM-focused Teacher Professional Development from f2f to Online
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a STEM-focused teacher professional development program in astronomy (SATTAA) changed when it shifted from a fully face-to-face format in 2019 to a fully online format in 2020 during COVID-19. The guiding question is whether in-service teachers’ perceptions of the logistics and key benefits differed across the two iterations, with special attention to what was preserved, what had to be adapted, and what participants valued most.

The authors describe the program’s redesign through a sociocultural constructivist and TPACK lens, emphasizing content learning, pedagogy, technology, field trips, and collaborative lesson design. The study is based on teacher feedback, schedule/time-allocation comparisons, and qualitative coding of oral and written participant responses. The 2020 online version used Zoom, digital resource sharing, recordings, and virtual field trips, while also adding technology practice/support for facilitators.

Participants were in-service teachers from schools serving higher proportions of economically disadvantaged and underrepresented-minority students than the city average, making the context especially relevant to equity and access. Across both years, teachers rated the PD as highly useful and effective for future astronomy teaching, valued the content, resources, and collaboration, and reported that the online version was at least as effective as the face-to-face version for many purposes. The main differences were that face-to-face field trips were preferred over virtual ones, and technology became a notable benefit in the online iteration, especially as a communication and learning tool. The authors conclude that a virtual format can maintain quality while expanding reach and reducing logistical burdens, though experiential field trips remain stronger in person.

finding.finding_summary: The online redesign substantially reduced logistics time from 21% of contact hours in 2019 to 4% in 2020, while increasing time devoted to pedagogy-focused engagement from 16% to 24% and content learning from 63% to 72%. Teachers also reported that the fully online format made participation possible for some who otherwise could not have attended, indicating improved access and reduced travel burden.
finding.measure: Program time allocation, participant perceptions of logistics and access
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers total across both iterations (2019 n=5, 2020 n=15; one teacher appears to have participated in both years not clearly stated)

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently described the PD as valuable, effective, and highly relevant to their future teaching, and many expressed enthusiasm, excitement, and a desire for more SATTAA opportunities. The online group also reported that the program fostered collaboration and community, and all participants in 2020 said the experience should be retained for future iterations.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions, relevance ratings, and qualitative feedback on enthusiasm/community
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers total across both iterations

finding.finding_summary: The program was reported to strengthen collaborative work, peer networking, and technology-related problem solving, all of which were central to teachers’ perceived benefits. In particular, the online iteration highlighted technology as a tool for communication, content learning, and supporting students, suggesting gains in adaptive and collaborative professional skills rather than only content knowledge.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding of teacher statements about collaboration, networking, and technology use
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers total across both iterations

finding.finding_summary: Although the study does not measure student outcomes directly, the PD was designed to improve teachers’ astronomy content knowledge and pedagogical/technological capacity for teaching astronomy, and teachers reported feeling better prepared to teach the content. The authors conclude that both iterations were highly useful for future astronomy teaching, with the online version at least as effective as the face-to-face version for supporting teacher learning.
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of future astronomy teaching preparedness and content usefulness
finding.study_size: n=21 teachers total across both iterations

paper_profiles.title: Training the trainer: Professional Development for High School Physics Teachers with Low Physics Background
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the shortage of well-prepared high school physics teachers in Texas and asks whether an intensive professional development program can improve teachers’ physics content knowledge and confidence. The program, Mitchell Institute Physics Enhancement Program (MIPEP), is a two-week summer PD experience designed for in-service high school physics teachers with limited prior physics coursework. It combines university physics instruction, hands-on demonstrations, lab activities, and pedagogy sessions led by master teachers, while aligning content to Texas state standards.

The study reports on cohorts from 2014-2018 and a remote version delivered in 2020 due to the pandemic. Teachers completed a 62-item pre/post diagnostic assessment of physics knowledge and confidence, and a smaller follow-up assessment was administered to some prior participants in fall 2018 to examine persistence of gains. Across cohorts, most participants showed positive gains in physics knowledge and confidence immediately after the program, and some gains persisted on the delayed assessment, though the follow-up sample was small.

The 2020 online delivery, conducted synchronously via Zoom with mailed experiment kits and virtual demonstrations, produced modest gains that were broadly comparable to earlier in-person cohorts. The paper concludes that MIPEP can improve teachers’ content knowledge and confidence, and that a university-based, content-focused PD model with pedagogical support and a community-of-practice component may be a useful model for similar programs. The evidence is based on within-group pre/post change rather than a comparison group, so it is descriptive rather than causal.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers’ physics content knowledge improved after the two-week PD across cohorts, with mean normalized gain Kavg=0.19 (SD=0.20) from pre- to post-assessment for all years combined (N=97 matched knowledge responses). The 2020 remote cohort also showed improvement, with Kavg=0.15 (SD=0.27; n=33 paired responses).
finding.measure: 62-item physics content knowledge diagnostic assessment (pre/post and delayed follow-up)
finding.study_size: N=97 matched knowledge responses across 2014-2018; n=33 paired responses in 2020

finding.finding_summary: Participants’ confidence in their physics knowledge increased substantially after MIPEP. The all-years combined mean normalized confidence gain was Cavg=0.40 (SD=0.33) from pre- to post-assessment (N=94 matched confidence responses), and the 2020 cohort showed Cavg=0.43 (SD=0.20; n=33 paired responses).
finding.measure: Self-reported confidence ratings on a 5-point Likert scale for each assessment item
finding.study_size: N=94 matched confidence responses across 2014-2018; n=33 paired responses in 2020

finding.finding_summary: A delayed follow-up in fall 2018 suggested some persistence of confidence gains among prior participants, with an average normalized confidence gain of Cavg=0.30 (SD=0.37) between pre-program and subsequent assessment (N=19 matched responses). The delayed gains were smaller than immediate post-program gains but still positive.
finding.measure: Delayed follow-up confidence assessment using the same 62-item instrument
finding.study_size: N=19 matched responses on the subsequent assessment

paper_profiles.title: Responsive Professional Development: A Facilitation Approach for Teachers’ Development in a Physics Teaching Community of Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a responsive professional development (PD) model was designed and enacted within the Illinois Physics and Secondary Schools (IPaSS) partnership program. The central question is whether a facilitation approach grounded in communities of practice (CoP) and continuous responsiveness to teacher needs can support teacher learning, participation, and movement from peripheral to more central roles in a professional community.

The IPaSS program links the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign with high school physics teachers and provides university-level physics curricular resources, equipment (iOLab), a flipped-learning platform (SmartIllinois), and year-round PD support. The PD model included intensive summer workshops, online meetings across the year, daily/pre-meeting surveys, and facilitator adaptations based on teacher feedback. Teachers were also invited to share expertise, co-design activities, and take on mentoring or leadership roles. The program was intentionally flexible, allowing gradual implementation of materials and tailoring support to teachers’ varied backgrounds, school contexts, and course assignments.

Using interviews with 13 teachers, survey data, and observation notes, the authors found that teachers perceived the program very positively. Teachers reported pedagogical and instructional support, professional growth opportunities, and social/personal benefits such as confidence, belonging, and relationship building. They also valued access to practical materials, sustained university support, and flexible implementation. The paper concludes that responsiveness—being attentive and adaptive to teachers’ needs—can strengthen teacher participation in a CoP and support professional growth, especially when PD is prolonged, collaborative, and context-sensitive.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the IPaSS PD strengthened physics instruction through access to university-level labs, problem-solving pedagogy, and activities emphasizing experimental design and data analysis. The paper does not report student achievement effects, but it provides qualitative evidence that the program supported teachers’ uptake of scientific-practice-oriented materials and their understanding of physics content and lab work.
finding.measure: Teacher interviews and survey responses about perceived instructional support, physics content knowledge, and use of iOLab / lab activities

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described improved confidence, sense of belonging, and willingness to participate in the community as a result of the responsive PD. These effects were based on qualitative interview evidence, including reports of reduced feelings of isolation, increased comfort sharing vulnerabilities, and stronger identification with the teacher community.
finding.measure: Interview-coded themes on confidence, belonging, and community involvement

finding.finding_summary: The study provides strong qualitative evidence that the PD fostered collaboration, mentorship, reflection, and leadership development among teachers. Teachers reported learning from peers, exchanging instructional practices, co-facilitating workshops, and moving into leadership roles within the community, indicating growth in collaboration and professional agency.
finding.measure: Interview-coded themes on collaboration, mentoring, leadership, and reflective practice

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly reported that the program’s ready-made, practical materials and continued support reduced the time and effort required to search for resources and adapt instruction. Flexibility in uptake and sustained follow-up were described as helping teachers implement materials at their own pace and with less burden.
finding.measure: Interview and survey reports of practical materials, access to resources, and implementation flexibility
finding.study_size: n=13 teachers interviewed; survey data from 14 teachers referenced

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the IPaSS partnership created a durable university–school bridge and a growing physics-teacher community of practice, with increased participation over four years (from 4 to 40 teachers). Although this is not an outcome evaluated with formal causal inference, the evidence suggests institutional strengthening through sustained partnership, teacher leadership, and cross-pollination of resources across cohorts.
finding.measure: Program growth, teacher participation, and qualitative evidence of partnership/community development
finding.study_size: Program grew from 4 to 40 teachers over four years; 13 teachers interviewed

paper_profiles.title: Crowd Coach: Peer Coaching for Crowd Workers’ Skill Growth
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction (PACM HCI), CSCW
paper_profiles.population: Adult crowd workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk (novice AMT workers in the field experiment; broader AMT workers in the deployment)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses whether peer coaching can support skill development for crowd workers without relying on requesters or domain experts. The authors argue that crowd markets generally do not provide structured opportunities for workers to improve their speed or quality, even though skill growth could help workers earn more and access better opportunities.

To address this, they introduce Crowd Coach, a Chrome extension for Amazon Mechanical Turk that lets workers submit short coaching snippets for specific task types and receive selected snippets from peers while working. The system includes micro-coaching, task-based categorization, a reputation/voting mechanism for selecting useful advice, and a display that surfaces highly rated coaching snippets in-context.

The paper evaluates the system in two ways: a controlled field experiment with 90 novice AMT workers completing audio transcription tasks, and a real-world deployment with 179 workers using the tool across multiple task types. In the experiment, workers receiving selected peer coaching completed transcription tasks significantly faster than those in the control or random-coaching conditions, without a statistically significant loss in accuracy.
