In deployment, workers actively used the system, generally rated it useful, and preferred coaching that was either clearly specific to a task or clearly generalizable across tasks, highlighting design tensions around coaching granularity and task relevance.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled field experiment with 90 novice AMT workers, selected peer coaching (Crowd Coach) significantly reduced audio transcription completion time compared with both the control and random-coaching conditions, while transcription accuracy did not significantly differ across groups. The main dependent measures were transcription completion time and word error rate (WER) across three transcription tasks; the reported completion time means were 184.1 seconds for Crowd Coach versus 262.79 seconds in control and 284.21 seconds in random coaching.
finding.measure: Audio transcription completion time; transcription accuracy measured by word error rate (WER)
finding.study_size: n=90 (26 control, 26 random coaching, 25 Crowd Coach completed all three tasks; 13 dropped out)
finding.std_deviation: SD=12.36 (Crowd Coach completion time); SD=37.38 (control); SD=46.44 (random coaching)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s central outcome is task efficiency in crowd work, operationalized as completion time. Selected peer coaching improved workers’ speed substantially in the controlled field experiment: the one-way MANOVA found significant differences across conditions (F(2,74)=17.53, p<0.0001), and the univariate ANOVA for completion time was also significant (F(2,74)=54.18, p<0.0001). Post hoc tests showed Crowd Coach reduced completion time relative to control and random coaching, without a significant accuracy penalty.
finding.measure: Task completion time for audio transcription tasks

Subject-area moderation is still missing: there is no evidence yet on whether formative assessment effects differ by discipline (e.g., math, science, literacy, ELA, STEM, language learning).

The sweep has not clearly captured primary causal studies that isolate formative assessment interventions (RCTs, quasi-experiments, cluster trials) as distinct from broader assessment/feedback or teacher-effectiveness papers.
Several retrieved items appear off-target (e.g., Teach for America, classroom environments, student attitudes) and do not meaningfully advance the research question.
A K–12 umbrella review was found, but an umbrella review is not enough on its own unless it reports moderator analyses by grade level and subject area; that is not yet established from the snippet.
The sweep does not yet identify direct comparative evidence between K–12 and postsecondary settings; it mainly summarizes K–12 findings and offers only indirect higher-education remarks.
The postsecondary side lacks meta-analyses or rigorous systematic reviews focused specifically on formative assessment outcomes in college/university classrooms.
Evidence by grade band within K–12 (elementary vs middle vs high school) is not sufficiently separated, so the requested variation by grade level is still unresolved.
Evidence by subject area in postsecondary education is missing; the sweep needs discipline-specific studies (e.g., STEM, writing, language, health professions) rather than general claims.

The current sources include at least one potentially off-target item (e.g., service learning / flipped classroom) and do not yet surface core formative-assessment intervention studies in higher education.
The comparative claim that formative assessment may work differently by educational level is currently inferential rather than supported by direct head-to-head or stratified meta-analytic evidence.

The sweep has only surfaced one broad meta-analysis on formative assessment in reading, and its moderators are largely study-level design features (grade, intervention type, duration, differentiation, sample size, publication type, cultural setting) rather than the target subgroup moderators.
No direct evidence was found on prior achievement as a moderator of formative assessment effects.
No evidence was found on English learner / ELL / bilingual / multilingual status as a moderator.
No evidence was found on disability / special education status as a moderator.
No intersectional or combined-moderator evidence was found (e.g., prior achievement x EL status, disability x prior achievement, EL x disability).

The sweep appears to miss potentially relevant causal studies or meta-regressions that explicitly analyze subgroup effects for formative assessment/assessment for learning/feedback interventions in literacy, math, or general K-12 outcomes.
The sweep does not surface direct evidence on formative assessment effects by prior achievement, English learner status, disability status, or their intersections.
Most retrieved items are off-topic methodological or unrelated tech/AI papers, with no clear causal studies or meta-analyses of subgroup moderators in education.

Missing key study types: randomized/quasi-experimental formative assessment interventions with moderator analyses, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses testing heterogeneity by student characteristics.
Missing population-specific evidence likely relevant to English learners and students with disabilities, including interaction effects combining these characteristics with baseline achievement.

The sweep has not yet surfaced direct comparative studies of formative assessment versus retrieval practice / low-stakes quizzing / practice testing conditions; the only retrieved item is a generic formative practices paper and not a head-to-head comparison.
No evidence yet of randomized, quasi-experimental, or controlled comparative designs that pit formative assessment against summative-only assessment or feedback-only conditions.
The current results are missing well-known educational psychology / assessment studies on test-enhanced learning in classroom or lab settings that would help answer the comparative question.
There is no clear coverage of structured feedback-only interventions or analyses separating feedback from assessment frequency, which is central to the thread.

The sweep has some relevant comparative evidence, but it is not yet sufficient to answer the thread. The current findings are mostly general or indirect and do not clearly establish direct head-to-head comparisons between formative assessment and retrieval practice, low-stakes quizzing, summative-only conditions, or feedback-only conditions.

The evidence appears skewed toward single studies in specific contexts (e.g., medical education, EFL, flipped classrooms) rather than a balanced set of direct comparative studies across educational levels and subjects.

The sweep does not yet surface classic or foundational experimental work on test-enhanced learning and feedback timing that would help compare formative assessment against retrieval-practice or feedback-only control conditions.
There is no clear coverage of meta-analyses or systematic reviews that synthesize direct comparisons among formative assessment, practice testing, and summative-only assessment.
The search failures indicate the current retrieval strategy is missing many relevant studies rather than exhaustively covering the domain.

The sweep has not yet surfaced direct causal evidence (RCTs, quasi-experiments, or classroom interventions) linking formative assessment to retention, transfer, or self-regulation outcomes; the one retrieved study is mainly about motivation/engagement and appears to be a review of association evidence rather than a causal test.
Postsecondary evidence is not yet adequately covered; the current hit is K–12-focused and does not resolve whether formative assessment affects outcomes in college/university classrooms.

Meta-analytic and systematic-review evidence specific to non-achievement outcomes is still missing or too thin; the sweep so far does not identify a clear synthesis on retention, transfer, self-regulation, or engagement.

The search appears to over-index on broad motivational terms and may miss studies using adjacent constructs/labels such as feedback interventions, assessment for learning, retrieval practice with formative quizzes, classroom response systems, progress monitoring, or self-regulated learning interventions.
No clear studies on retention/transfer outcomes are visible, and the evidence for self-regulation is limited to perceptions/associations rather than demonstrated behavioral or learning effects.

The sweep is heavy on recent primary studies about engagement, motivation, and feedback, but it does not yet clearly capture the central evidence base on whether formative assessment improves outcomes beyond immediate achievement, especially retention, transfer, and self-regulation.

A key missing piece is the foundational meta-analytic/systematic review literature on formative assessment/assessment for learning in K–12 and higher education, including classic syntheses that directly evaluate long-term or non-test outcomes.

There is little explicit evidence on retention and transfer outcomes; most retrieved items appear to focus on engagement, motivation, self-efficacy, or general achievement rather than delayed posttests or far transfer.
Postsecondary coverage is uneven: many items are classroom interventions, but the sweep lacks broader higher-ed RCTs or meta-analyses specifically on self-regulation, metacognition, and retention.

The results are skewed toward digital/gamified/feedback-adjacent interventions that may not be cleanly formative assessment, so the evidence base for formative assessment proper remains under-specified.

Coverage is dominated by one meta-analysis on formative assessment and a couple of failed broad searches; it does not yet establish direct causal evidence (randomized trials, quasi-experiments) on implementation moderators.

The thread specifically asks about teacher professional development, implementation fidelity, curriculum pressure, and technology-mediated delivery; these moderators are not yet systematically covered, and curriculum pressure/technology delivery are effectively absent.
The current evidence is mostly about general meta-analytic subgroup effects in reading, not formative assessment broadly across subjects or implementation conditions.

No clear retrieval of studies examining moderation of effect sizes by training dosage, coaching, fidelity of enactment, school accountability/curriculum constraints, or digital/computer-assisted formative assessment delivery.
Need at least a targeted set of primary studies plus meta-analyses that explicitly test moderator effects rather than general effectiveness papers.

The sweep is heavily skewed toward arXiv/preprints and education-conference style papers, with no clear direct causal evidence or meta-analyses on implementation moderators for formative assessment from the broader peer-reviewed literature.

Teacher professional development is represented, but mostly by descriptive teacher-change/identity papers rather than studies testing whether PD modifies formative assessment effects, implementation fidelity, or student outcomes.
Implementation fidelity as a moderator is not yet directly covered; there is no strong evidence on dosage, coaching, fidelity, or implementation quality shaping effectiveness.
Curriculum pressure/testing accountability as a moderator is not clearly covered; this is a core contextual factor in formative assessment implementation but not yet surfaced.

Technology-mediated delivery is present, but mostly as single intervention descriptions or conceptual guides; missing are comparative studies or syntheses on whether tech delivery changes implementation success or outcomes.
No obvious meta-analyses or systematic reviews on formative assessment interventions with moderator analyses were found in the current set.
